    Appendix A Random access in detail

    One setting for every example.

    The repository sets the window size and the symmetry variants per example. We read every example periodically, at window size N=3 and with no symmetry variants, one setting for all, so that no example gets a setting chosen for it. The images are the repository’s samples; its README credits the people and games they come from.

    Periods.

    Let T be the longest finite side of the blocks of the pairs in A. A shift by a vector of Tℤ² maps every block of every pair onto a block of the same pair, so it permutes the coins without changing their law, and the output commutes with it. Since block boundaries are fixed in absolute coordinates, a generator on the scale pairs alone is translation-equivariant under these shifts and in general under no other; one in the general form commutes with the shifts by common multiples of T and p that map every further lattice onto itself. In practice the coins are hashes of the seed, the coarsened cell and a channel index, computed where they are needed. A rule that applies a radius-one update for R rounds to coins alone is a random-access generator of radius R; ours reads 24 scale pairs besides the cell’s own coins, with period T=16 (Section 4). The row-type sampler draws the row types of a band of L rows from that band’s coins at a cost proportional to L, and the phase channels are functions of the coordinates, so both fit the general form of Definition 1.

    The three properties.

    Any region S is computed from the coins read on S and on a margin of width r, with a fixed number of hashes per cell wherever S lies, a coin of whole rows being one hash however long the rows. Independent computations of overlapping regions hash the same coins at the same cells, so they agree cell for cell: seams are exact, and many machines generate one world with nothing shared but the seed. An edit that overrides the coins read in S, giving the cells of S new values of every coin they read while every other cell keeps its coins, changes the output only within distance r of S, so edits are contained; redrawing a coin that a whole block shares can instead change the output anywhere within distance r of the block.

    The mended output.

    A random-access generator must satisfy K from what it sees within distance r of each cell, and the last step of our pipeline reaches farther. The mender (Section 5) re-solves the defects that the rule leaves, block by block on a lattice fixed in absolute coordinates and with randomness hashed from the seed and the block coordinates, so its output depends on a cell’s position modulo twice the block size as well as on the coins, and a change it makes can travel beyond the rule’s radius. The mended output has a reach, a distance beyond which no coin can change a cell’s mended color, and we call such a construction random access in the extended sense: it is a generator in the general form of Definition 1 with its reach in place of the radius r, so the three properties hold with the reach as the margin, and Proposition 1 covers it. Appendix S1.3 bounds the reach of our pipeline, and Section 6.4 measures the smaller margin at which every canvas we tested agrees.

    Appendix B Proofs

    Throughout, K⊆[C]^N×N is the set of allowed windows, a coloring is x:ℤ²→[C], Q^Pᵥ(x) is the P×P patch of x whose corner is v, and Wᵥ(x)=Q^Nᵥ(x) is the window at v. A generator on independent coins of radius r is a translation-equivariant map from i.i.d. coins (ωᵥ) to X with Xᵥ a fixed function of the coins within ℓ_∞ distance r of v (Definition 2). The law of X is then translation-invariant.

    B.1 The full labeling

    For a weakly connected component c of G_P,e, give each edge (a,b) the weight +1 and let d_c be the greatest common divisor of the signed lengths of the closed walks of c that may traverse edges in either direction (d_c=0 when every such walk has signed length zero, so that c has no directed cycle). Fixing a root, every patch of c gets a level modulo d_c, and φ(a)=(c,level) with σ(c,i)=(c,i+1\bmodd_c) is a transported quantity on all of V_P, with no exception for edges that enter or leave a strongly connected component. Invariants are the case of several components; phases the case d_c≥2. Table 4 reports constants for this labeling.

    B.2 Theorem 1

    Let k=2r+P and uⱼ=je for j=0,…,k. Write A for the event that the patches Q^P_uⱼ(X) are locally valid for every j. On A, each pair of consecutive patches agrees on its overlap, so it is an edge of G_P,e and φ(Q^P_uⱼ₊₁)=σ(φ(Q^P_uⱼ)); hence φ(Q^P_uₖ)=σᵏ(φ(Q^P_u₀)). The patch at u₀ is a function of the coins in the box [-r,P-1+r] along e, and the patch at uₖ of the coins in [k-r,k+P-1+r]; since k≥2r+P the two boxes are disjoint, and the two patches are independent. Writing p⁽ᵛ⁾ for the law of φ at v on the event that the patch is locally valid, translation invariance gives p^(u₀)=p^(uₖ)=p, so

    \Pr[A] ≤ ∑ₛpₛ p_σᵏ(s) ≤ \maxₜpₜ∑ₛpₛ ≤ \maxₜpₜ.

    If A fails, some patch on the segment contains a forbidden window. A patch contains (P-N+1)² windows, so \Pr[Q^Pᵥ∉V_P]≤(P-N+1)²ε, and a union bound over the k+1 patches gives 1-\maxₜpₜ≤\Pr[Aᶜ]≤(k+1)(P-N+1)²ε, which is the claim. ∎

    For a one-way quantity, write s\leadstot when component t is reachable from component s in G_P,e, with s\leadstos. The same steps give, on A, that φ(Q^P_uₖ) is reachable from φ(Q^P_u₀), so \Pr[A]≤∑_s\leadstotpₛ pₜ by independence, and the union bound gives

    ε ≥ (1-∑_s\leadstotpₛ pₜ)/((2r+P+1)(P-N+1)²).

    For an invariant or a phase the only pairs allowed are t=σᵏ(s), the sum is at most \maxₛpₛ, and this is the bound of Theorem 1. Appendix B.5 bounds the numerator for a one-way quantity from below by the constant κ(δ).

    B.3 Inequality (1)

    For P=N the patch is the window, so pₛ=h({w∈K:φ(w)=s}), where h is the law of W₀(X) on all of [C]^N×N. Since f puts no mass outside K, h(B)≤f(B)+δ for every set B of windows, with δ the total variation between h and f; pooling the forbidden windows into one outcome, as Section 2 does, leaves this total variation unchanged, for the same reason. Hence \maxₛpₛ≤\maxₛf(φ=s)+δ, and Theorem 1 with P=N gives ε(2r+N+1)≥κ_f-δ. ∎

    B.4 Corollary 1

    The proof of Theorem 1 uses only the overlap graph of the locally valid patches, so it holds with K₀=K∖J in place of K, a window being forbidden for K₀ when it lies outside K₀. Let h be the law of the window of X at a cell, and write D=2r+N+1 and Bₛ={w∈K₀:φ(w)=s}. The windows outside K₀ have density ε+h(J), and at P=N the theorem gives (ε+h(J))D≥1-h(Bₛ) for the value s with the largest h(Bₛ). As in the proof of inequality (1), h(B)≤f(B)+δ for every set B of windows in K. Applied to J∪Bₛ, this gives h(Bₛ)≤θ+(1-κ_J)+δ-h(J), so εD≥κ_J-θ-δ-(D-1)h(J); applied to J, it gives h(J)≤θ+δ. Hence εD≥κ_J-(θ+δ)D, which is the claim. When J is empty, h(J)=0 and the first step with h(Bₛ)≤1-κ_f+δ gives inequality (1). ∎

    B.5 The linear program

    Let P≥N. A distribution q on V_P is stationary if every (P-1)×P pattern has the same mass as the first P-1 rows of a patch and as its last P-1 rows, and every P×(P-1) pattern the same mass as the first P-1 columns and as the last P-1 columns. The N×N window then has the same law at every position in the patch, and we call it the N×N marginal of q. For a translation-invariant random coloring X without defects, the law of Q^P₀(X) is a stationary distribution on V_P, since the patches at 0 and at a unit vector have the same law and share all but one row or column, and its N×N marginal is the window law of X. The constant κ(δ) of Section 3 is one minus the largest occupancy q(φ=s) over the values s and the stationary q whose N×N marginal lies within δ of f in total variation, a linear program for each value. Such an X whose window statistics lie within δ of f therefore has \maxₛpₛ≤1-κ(δ).

    A one-way quantity. When φ is the strongly connected component, let fₛ be the example’s share of patches in component s. The example’s constant is κ_f=1-∑_s\leadstotfₛfₜ, and for such a quantity κ(δ) names a lower bound on 1-∑_s\leadstotpₛpₜ that the program gives: the sum, over ordered pairs of components visited by the example with t not reachable from s, of the products of the smallest occupancies the program allows to s and to t. It is a lower bound because ∑ₛpₛ≤1 gives 1-∑_s\leadstotpₛpₜ≥∑_s\not\leadstotpₛpₜ, with equality when no patch has a defect, and because for a coloring without defects whose window statistics lie within δ of f each pₛ is at least the smallest occupancy the program allows to s.

    With defects. For P≥N, let q be the law of Q^P₀(X) on all P×P colorings and q_V its restriction to V_P, of mass 1-β with β≤(P-N+1)²ε. Translation invariance makes q exactly stationary, so for each (P-1)×P or P×(P-1) sub-pattern the masses that q_V gives it from the two sides differ in total by at most 2β; and the N×N marginal of q_V is within δ+β of f in total variation. Let κ(δ,η) be one minus the largest occupancy of any single value of φ over nonnegative q on V_P with total mass in [1-η,1], stationarity violated by at most 2η in total, and N×N marginal within δ+η of f. It is a linear program, decreasing in η, and κ(δ,0)=κ(δ) is the constant above. Then \maxₛpₛ≤1-κ(δ,β), and Theorem 1 gives, for any η₀≥0,

    ε≥\min{η₀/(P-N+1)²,(κ(δ,η₀))/((2r+P+1)(P-N+1)²)}.

    The program over exactly stationary measures, η=0, is what Table 4 reports. The table has 14 rows with an invariant or a phase: the 12 certified examples with one, and Chess and Stripes, two controls whose only K-valid colorings are the two phases of a period-two pattern (Appendix S2.4). With defects allowed at η₀=0.01 and δ=0.05, the program stays positive on 14 of these rows, with a smallest value of 0.030 on Skyline2, so a generator whose statistics lie within that slack has a defect density of order 1/r with that constant. For P=N the program is stricter than inequality (1), which gives κ_f-δ: on Skyline2, κ(0.05) is 0.047 against κ_f-0.05=0.015. ∎

    B.6 Theorem 2

    Let τ be the translation by e and τ^′ the unit translation orthogonal to it. A factor of i.i.d. coins is mixing under the action of ℤ², since the coins are, and mixing passes to factors. As the ℤ² action is mixing, every sub-action generated by a single nonzero translation is mixing as well, and hence ergodic; in particular τ^D is ergodic for every D≥1. On the event, of probability one, that X is K-valid, every patch is locally valid and consecutive patches along e form edges of G_P,e.

    Invariants and phases. Under the full labeling φ=(c,z) with σ(c,z)=(c,z+1\bmodd_c). Let ψ(v)=σ⁻ʲ(φ(Q^Pᵥ(X))) for v=je+v^′ with v^′ on the line through the origin orthogonal to e; along every line parallel to e, ψ is constant. Let λ be its value on the line through the origin. A component with d_c=0 has no directed cycle and so carries no bi-infinite walk. The patches along a line parallel to e in a K-valid coloring form such a walk, so they lie in one component, with d_c≥1, whose levels modulo d_c are finitely many, and λ takes finitely many values; let D be a common multiple of the d_c≥1, so that σ^D is the identity. Then λ(τ^DX)=λ(X), so each event {λ=s} is τ^D-invariant and has probability zero or one: λ is almost surely a constant s₀. Since τX has the law of X and λ(τX)=σ(λ(X)), also σ(s₀)=s₀, which forces d_c₀=1 for the component c₀ of s₀. The line through τ^′ m of the origin has the law of the line through the origin, so its value is s₀ almost surely too, for every m, and φ=s₀ at every cell almost surely.

    One-way quantities. Let φ be the strongly connected component, and m the number of components. Along a line it never returns to a component it has left, so it changes at most m-1 times on the whole line. If q is the probability that it changes between v and v+e, the expected number of changes on a segment of n steps is nq by stationarity, and it is at most m-1 for every n; so q=0, and φ is constant along lines almost surely. It is then an invariant, and the argument above makes it a single value at every cell.

    Statistics. With φ concentrated on one value, \maxₛpₛ=1, while every stationary distribution without defects whose window marginal is within δ of f has \maxₛpₛ≤1-κ(δ) (for a one-way quantity, 1-∑_s\leadstotpₛpₜ≥κ(δ), and concentration makes the left side zero). The law of X is such a distribution when its window statistics are within δ of f, so κ(δ)>0 rules this out. For P=N, pₛ≤f(φ=s)+δ as in the proof of inequality (1), so 1≤1-κ_f+δ, that is, δ≥κ_f. ∎

    B.7 Proposition 1

    In full, part (c) reads as follows. Suppose every block has length at most T along e and the lattice has period T along e, where a coin shared along a whole line orthogonal to e, or along a group of consecutive such lines, counts as a block, and let Xᵥ also read coins shared along whole lines parallel to e, or along groups of consecutive such lines, and over the whole plane. Take φ under the full labeling, let D≥1 be a common multiple of the positive values of d_c, let μ be the probability, averaged over the cells of one period of the lattice, that a cell’s patch is locally valid and lies in a component c whose d_c does not divide T, d_c=0 included. Then

    ε ≥ (μ)/(2 (2r+(D+1)T+P) (P-N+1)²).

    Part (a) gives no floor when the quantity is fixed by position, and blocks fixed in absolute coordinates tell a rule its position, since it sees the coins change at a block boundary. A rule that leaves no forbidden window must fix the quantity by position. Two cells far apart along e read disjoint sets of coins, apart from coins shared along whole lines or over the plane, so given those shared coins their values of the quantity are independent; validity along the line between them makes each value determine the other; and two independent values that determine each other are constant. Each value is therefore fixed by the cell’s position within the lattice’s period and by the shared coins, so the law of the layout repeats with period T along e, which a phase of period d allows without defects only when d divides T. When it does not, (c) gives a floor of the same order as (a), in proportion to the mass μ of the components whose period does not divide T; when P=N and the window statistics lie within δ of the example’s, μ is at least the example’s mass less δ. A coin shared along a whole line, ℓ=∞, escapes (a): two cells of the line read the same coin however far apart they are, so they can agree on an invariant along that line with no defect between them, while different lines carry different values. The construction in (b) copies the example on every block, so it says nothing about variation.

    (a) Follow the proof of Theorem 1 with k=ℓ+2r+P. The patch at u₀ reads the independent coins in the box [-r,P-1+r] along e and the coins of the blocks that meet it; the patch at uₖ those of [k-r,k+P-1+r]. A block meeting both boxes would cover the k-2r-P+2=ℓ+2 cells from P-1+r to k-r, which no block of length at most ℓ does, so the two patches are again independent. The law of X is now invariant only under the lattice’s periods, so the laws p^(u₀) and p^(uₖ) may differ; with p^* the largest p⁽ᵛ⁾ₛ over cells and values, \Pr[A]≤∑ₛp^(u₀)ₛ p^(uₖ)_σᵏ(s)≤p^*. Average the union bound over the starting cell u in one period of the lattice: the average of \Pr[Q^Pᵥ∉V_P] over a period is at most (P-N+1)²ε, with ε the density of forbidden windows, so 1-p^*≤(k+1)(P-N+1)²ε. The one-way version and inequality (1) follow as before, with δ the largest distance from f of the window statistics at a single cell.

    (b) Since K and f are read from the example with wrap-around, tiling the plane with the example leaves no forbidden window and gives the example’s window frequencies. A window inside one block is a window of the tiling at a uniformly random translation, whose law is f, and it is allowed. A window meets two blocks only if its corner lies within N-1 cells of a block’s boundary along one of the two axes, which holds for a share at most 2(N-1)/ℓ of cells. Hence ε≤2(N-1)/ℓ, and the window law averaged over cells is within 2(N-1)/ℓ of f in total variation.

    (c) Let G be the coins shared along whole lines parallel to e or along groups of consecutive such lines, and over the plane. All coins are independent, so given G the other coins are still independent with their own laws. The translation by Te fixes every coin of G and permutes the other coins, cell coins to cell coins and the coin of every block, a group of lines orthogonal to e included, to the coin of its translate, a block of the same kind, since the lattice has period T along e; it therefore preserves their joint law, given G as well. As X commutes with that translation, the conditional probabilities qₛ(v)=\Pr[Q^Pᵥ∈V_P, φ(Q^Pᵥ)=s|G] satisfy qₛ(v+Te)=qₛ(v). Let k be the smallest integer with k≡1\pmodD and kT≥2r+T+P; then kT+1≤2r+(D+1)T+P, since k lies within D-1 of ⌈(2r+T+P)/T⌉. Let uₖ=u₀+kTe. As in (a), the patches at u₀ and uₖ read disjoint sets of coins outside G, so they are independent given G. On the event A that every patch on the segment between them is locally valid, φ(Q^P_uₖ)=σᵏᵀ(φ(Q^P_u₀)). Hence, with q=q(u₀),

    \Pr[A|G] ≤ ∑ₛqₛ q_σᵏᵀ(s).

    On a component with d_c≥1, σᵏᵀ=σᵀ, since kT≡T modulo d_c. If d_c divides T, σᵏᵀ fixes every value, and the terms add to at most the component’s mass Q_c=∑_s∈cqₛ. If it does not, σᵏᵀ=σᵀ shifts the level by T\bmodd_c≠0; if d_c=0, the level is an integer and σᵏᵀ shifts it by kT≥1. In both cases σᵏᵀ maps the component’s values one to one and moves every value, and for any such map π, (∑ₛqₛ)²≥∑ₛqₛ²+∑ₛqₛ q_π(s)≥2∑ₛqₛ q_π(s): the pairs (s,π(s)) are distinct and off the diagonal, and qₛ q_π(s)≤(qₛ²+q_π(s)²)/2. Those terms add to at most Q_c²/2≤Q_c/2. So \Pr[A|G]≤1-μ_G/2, with μ_G the conditional mass at u₀ of the components whose d_c does not divide T, and taking expectations, \Pr[Aᶜ] is at least half the probability that the patch at u₀ is locally valid with φ in such a component. Averaging the union bound over u₀ in one period of the lattice, as in (a), gives μ/2≤(kT+1)(P-N+1)²ε, a floor slightly sharper than the statement’s, which Appendix B.9 evaluates. ∎

    B.8 Proposition 2

    Let ωᵥ=(Uᵥ,tᵥ), with Uᵥ uniform on [0,1] and tᵥ uniform over one period of the tiling Y, all independent. Let Bᵣ(v)={v+u:∥u∥_∞≤r}, let mᵥ be the cell of smallest priority in Bᵣ(v) (ties have probability zero), and let Xᵥ=Y(v-mᵥ+t_mᵥ). Then Xᵥ is a fixed function of the coins in Bᵣ(v), and shifting all coins by a vector shifts X by the same vector, so the min-coin copy is a generator on independent coins of radius r.

    Fix a window, the N×N square W of cells with corner w. The boxes Bᵣ(v), v∈W, have as their union a square U of side 2r+N and as their intersection a square I of side 2r+2-N, which is not empty since r≥N. Let z be the cell of smallest priority in U. If z∈I, then z lies in every box and has the smallest priority in each, so mᵥ=z for every v∈W. Conversely, if mᵥ=z^′ for every v∈W, then z^′∈I and z^′ has the smallest priority in every box, hence in U, so z^′=z. The priorities are independent and continuous, so z is uniform on U, and the cells of W copy from one cell with probability |I|/|U|=1-qᵣ. On that event the window of X at w is the window of Y at w-z+t_z. Given the priorities, which fix z, the translation t_z is uniform over the period and independent of them, so the window is a window of the tiling at a uniform translation: it is allowed and its law is f. Hence ε≤qᵣ, and the law h of the window is (1-qᵣ)f+qᵣg for some law g, so ∥h-f∥_TV=qᵣ∥g-f∥_TV≤qᵣ. With a=(2r+2-N)/(2r+N), which lies in (0,1) since 2≤N≤r, qᵣ=(1-a)(1+a)<2(1-a)=4(N-1)/(2r+N).

    For the comparison in Section 3, let P=N. Every generator on independent coins of radius r whose window statistics lie within qᵣ of f has ε≥(κ_f-qᵣ)/(2r+N+1) by inequality (1). The map q↦q(2r+N+1)/(κ_f-q) increases on [0,κ_f), so whenever κ_f(2r+N)>4(N-1) the ratio of the min-coin copy’s ε to that floor is less than

    (4(N-1) (2r+N+1))/(κ_f (2r+N)-4(N-1)),

    which tends to 4(N-1)/κ_f as r grows. ∎

    B.9 What the bounds bind in our pipeline

    Theorems 1 and 2 bind generators on independent coins, among them the independent-coin rule of Section 3, with or without its repair rounds. They do not bind the method. Its row types and the octaves’ coins of whole rows are shared along whole lines, which escape both theorems and Proposition 1(a), and its phase channels are functions of the coordinates, which no result of Section 3 restricts. The octaves, the coins on the scale pairs that our rule reads (Section 4), fall under Proposition 1(c) as a whole: their coins of finite scale lie on blocks nested in one lattice of period T=16, and their other coins are shared along whole rows, whole columns or the plane. Among the certified examples the resulting floor binds only Fabric, whose phase has period 5, which does not divide T. There it lies above the threshold of validity before mending, and below it after. Once mended, no output has a floor from Section 3 above that threshold on any certified example, so no result there requires the mended independent-coin rule to be invalid; where we searched for witnesses, they show why it is (Section 6.1).

    These conclusions rest on the following values. The rule runs 32 rounds of a radius-one update, so its radius is 32, and each of its four repair rounds adds N cells, for a radius of 44. Mending at the main radius works on blocks of side ℓ=48, and its eight class steps carry a change at most 760 cells (Appendix S1.3), so the reach of the whole pipeline is r=804 cells. The threshold of validity is one forbidden window in a thousand (Section 2).

    Fabric under the octaves. Fabric’s phase has period 5 and is read off single windows, so P=N. The octaves fall under Proposition 1(c) with T=16 and D=5, and the components whose period does not divide T hold 0.60 of the example’s windows, which is μ for a rule whose window statistics match the example’s. At radius 32, k=6 and 2(kT+1)(P-N+1)²=194, so such a rule leaves at least 3.0·10⁻³ of its windows forbidden, and with its repair rounds, at radius 44, at least 1.6·10⁻³; both lie above the threshold. The mended output commutes only with shifts by common multiples of T and of twice the mender’s block, so with that period, 96 cells, in place of T and with the pipeline’s reach as the radius the floor falls to 1.5·10⁻⁴, below the threshold.

    The mended independent-coin rule. The mender’s randomness is hashed from the seed and the coordinates of its blocks, of side ℓ in both passes, so the mended output of the independent-coin rule falls under Proposition 1(a) with the pipeline’s reach as the radius. Its denominator is (2r+ℓ+P+1)(P-N+1)², which is 1660 when P=N, and its numerator is at most one, so at this reach the bound of (a) cannot reach the threshold whatever the output’s statistics. For an output that spreads the quantity at every cell as the example does and has its statistics, the numerator is the example’s own spread, which on every row of Table 4 with an invariant or a phase is the column κ(0), equal to κ_f when P=N. The floor computed from that column is not itself a column of the table, whose floor at radius 32 is that of Theorem 1 for the raw rule. Its largest value over those rows, Chess and Stripes included, is 4.6·10⁻⁴, on RedMaze.

    B.10 Two classes of constraints

    Section 3 cites the following two bounds. Let ε(r) be the smallest density of forbidden windows over generators on independent coins of radius r.

    Proposition 3(two classes).

    (a) If the locally checkable labeling of K is solvable in O(\log^*n) rounds on n×n toroidal grids, then ε(r)≤Ce⁻ᶜʳ for constants C,c>0 that depend on K. (b) If K is an agreement constraint, that is, for some P≥N every locally valid P×P patch is the restriction of one of m≥2 translates of a periodic pattern and distinct translates differ on every block of P×(P-1) or (P-1)×P cells, then ε(r)≥1/(2(2r+P+1)(P-N+1)²).

    Proof of (a).[Brandt et al. (2017)] show that such a K admits an algorithm in the normal form A^′∘Sₖ: a maximal independent set (MIS) of the k-th power of the grid, followed by a finite function of the MIS within a constant radius ρ₀. Run the MIS with fresh priorities in every round: in each round every undecided vertex draws a uniform priority from its coins; a vertex whose priority is below those of all its undecided neighbors (in the power graph, of degree Δ=(2k+1)²-1) joins the set, and its neighbors are removed. Whatever the history, the vertex’s own priority is one of at most Δ+1 fresh independent draws in its undecided closed neighborhood, so it is such a local minimum with probability at least 1/(Δ+1); hence it is still undecided after t rounds with probability at most (1-1/(Δ+1))ᵗ. After t rounds the decided vertices form an independent set that is maximal except in the neighborhoods of the vertices still undecided; decide those arbitrarily and apply A^′. A cell is defective only if some vertex within distance ρ₀+k of it is undecided, since A^′ reads the set within radius ρ₀ and the set can fail to be maximal only within distance k of an undecided vertex, so the defect density is at most C(1-1/(Δ+1))ᵗ with C=(2ρ₀+2k+1)², and the construction reads coins within radius O(kt)=r. [Brandt et al. (2017)] prove the normal form correct on all sufficiently large tori; since A^′ is a finite-radius function of an MIS of the power grid, and any finite MIS configuration of the plane extends to an MIS of a large torus (copy it with a margin of width k onto a torus large enough that the copy does not wrap onto itself, then add vertices outside the region greedily until the set is maximal), the rule is correct on the plane as well. The known rate is faster: a finitary-factor solution whose coding radius exceeds r with probability at most 1/tower(cr) exists [(Grebík & Rozhoň, 2023, Cor. 3.3)], and cutting it off at radius r gives ε(r)≤C/tower(cr).

    Proof of (b). The phase of a locally valid patch, the index of the translate it comes from, is a transported quantity along every lattice direction, with σ the permutation of translates induced by the unit shift. Since m≥2, some unit vector e is not a period of the pattern, so σ along e has no fixed point. Translation invariance gives \Pr[phase(v)=i]=\Pr[phase(v+e)=i], and the two events exclude each other, because on both of them the phase at v+e would be σ(i)≠i. Each therefore has probability at most \tfrac12, and \maxᵢpᵢ≤\tfrac12. Theorem 1 along e gives the claim. ∎

    The same argument shows that a forced edit on an agreement constraint can need an unbounded repair: pin a cell to a phase its neighborhood does not have, and any valid completion within radius ρ would have to change phase across the boundary of the ball, which the transport rules out. This is the witness of Appendix B.11 in its simplest form.

    B.11 Witnesses

    A transported quantity can also prove that a particular mending instance has no completion. A mending instance frees the cells of a region F and fixes all others, and a completion is valid if every window that touches F is allowed. Let a and b be locally valid patches at u and u+ke, entirely outside F, such that every window of the patches Q^Pᵤ₊ⱼₑ, 0≤j≤k, either touches F or lies in fixed cells and is allowed. In any valid completion every one of these patches is then locally valid, so by the argument of Theorem 1φ(b)=σᵏ(φ(a)). If φ(b)≠σᵏ(φ(a)), no valid completion exists, and we call the pair a witness: it proves without any search that the instance has no completion (Figure 2(d); Appendix S4.1 counts the witnesses on the failed instances). ∎

    B.12 A sequence of row types at finite radius

    Coins shared along whole rows can carry an invariant along rows at finite radius, once the rule turns them into an allowed sequence of row types, one in which every two consecutive types can be consecutive in a coloring free of forbidden windows. Suppose some type τ can follow itself, as the sky above a skyline can. Fix finitely many stretches, sequences of types x₁,…,xₘ such that τ,x₁,…,xₘ,τ is allowed, such as a course of bricks, and let M be the length of the longest. Give each row y a uniform coin U_y shared along the row, and call y a start if U_y

    B.13 The certificate search

    On every public example where the search of Section 4 reports a phase, and on Chess and Stripes, d_c equals the period of the strongly connected component that holds the example’s patches in c, the greatest common divisor of its cycle lengths, which d_c in general only divides, since every directed cycle is a closed walk. We also searched the two diagonals. Two patches one step apart along a diagonal leave two corner cells of their union outside both, so an edge there asks the whole box of side P+1 to be locally valid. On the public examples the diagonals certify none that the axis directions leave uncertified; among the examples from other implementations they certify GbDiamond (Appendix E). Appendix D gives the order in which the search tries patch sizes and directions.

    Appendix C Proofs of the characterization

    Theorems 1 and 2 bound generators whose distant cells share no randomness. Run given the coins that a generator shares along the quantity’s direction, their two arguments prove Theorem 3, and where the example’s rows glue, a generator that reads the row types band by band, and its position, needs nothing more (Theorem 4).

    C.1 The setting

    We read Definition 1 as follows. The input of a generator in the general form consists of finitely many families of coins. A family is a lattice of blocks fixed in absolute coordinates, every block a rectangle, possibly unbounded in one direction or in both; each block carries a vector of coins, and these vectors are i.i.d. within a family and independent across families. The cells’ own coins form one family, whose blocks are single cells, and so does every scale pair of Section 2 and every further lattice of Definition 1. Cell v reads v\bmodp and the coins of the blocks that meet the box v+[-r,r]².

    Fix an axis direction e. The extent of a family along e is the length of its blocks along e: one for the cells, 2ⁱ along rows and 2ʲ along columns for the scale pair (i,j), one or w for whole lines orthogonal to e or groups of w consecutive such lines, and infinite for whole lines parallel to e, groups of such lines and the plane. The coins shared along e, Gₑ, are the coins of the families of infinite extent along e, and we use the same symbol for the σ-field they generate. All other coins belong to families of finite extent, and ℓ in Theorem 3(b) is the largest of these extents. Throughout, a function of some coins means a measurable function of them, and equalities between random variables hold almost surely.

    For a translation t of ℤ² write τₜ for the translation of colorings, (τₜx)ᵥ=xᵥ₊ₜ, and θₜ for the translation of coins, which gives every block B the coins of B+t. As in Section 3, Λ is the lattice of translations t∈pℤ² that map the blocks of every family to blocks of the same family; it has full rank, and T is the least positive integer with Te∈Λ. For t∈Λ, cell v of X(θₜω) reads the coins that cell v+t of X(ω) reads, and v\bmodp=(v+t)\bmodp, so

    X(θₜω) = τₜ X(ω) (t∈Λ).

    		(2)

    This is what it means for X to commute with the translations in Λ. Besides the radius and the blocks read, which the counting bounds use, it is all that the proofs below use of X, so the arguments from ergodicity hold for every measurable function of the coins and of the position modulo p with this property. Since θₜ permutes the blocks of each family, it preserves the law of the coins, so the law of X is invariant under τₜ for t∈Λ, and in general under no other translation. A function a on the cells that is periodic under Λ, such as the probability that the window at v is forbidden, has an average avgᵥa(v) over the cells of one period of Λ that does not depend on the period chosen, and avgᵥa(v+u)=avgᵥa(v) for every u∈ℤ². The density of forbidden windows is ε=avgᵥ\Pr[Wᵥ(X)∉K]. For a random quantity a(v) attached to each cell, such as 1-\maxₛqₛ(v) in Theorem 3(b), we write ā=avgᵥ𝔼[a(v)]; its expectation is periodic under Λ as well, since θₜ maps the coins of Gₑ to coins of Gₑ.

    C.2 Theorem 3(b): the floor given the shared coins

    In full, part (b) reads as follows. If φ is transported, X has radius r and every block it reads whose coins are not in Gₑ has length at most ℓ along e, a cell’s own coins counting as a block of length one, then

    ε ≥ (1-\maxₛqₛ̄)/((2r+P+ℓ)(P-N+1)²),

    where qₛ(v) is the probability given Gₑ that the P×P patch of X at v is locally valid and has φ=s, and the bar takes the expectation, averaged over the cells of one period of Λ.

    The counting argument of Theorem 1 needs two patches far apart along e to be independent. Given Gₑ they are, once their distance exceeds the extent of every other block.

    Lemma 1.

    Let X have radius r, let every family outside Gₑ have extent at most ℓ along e, and let k≥2r+P+ℓ-1. For every cell v, the patches Q^Pᵥ(X) and Q^Pᵥ₊ₖₑ(X) are independent given Gₑ.

    Proof. The patch at v is a function of v\bmodp, of the coins of Gₑ and of the other coins of the blocks that meet the box v+[-r,P-1+r]², and the patch at v+ke is a function of the same kind for the box shifted by ke. Counted from v along e, the two boxes cover the positions -r to P-1+r and k-r to k+P-1+r. A block that meets both is a rectangle with a cell in each, so along e it covers every position from P-1+r to k-r, which are k-2r-P+2≥ℓ+1 positions, more than any block outside Gₑ covers. The two patches therefore read disjoint sets of coins outside Gₑ, and these coins are independent of one another and of Gₑ. ∎

    As in Theorem 3, qₛ(v) is the probability given Gₑ that Q^Pᵥ(X) is locally valid and has φ=s.

    Proposition 4(the floor given the shared coins, sharp form).

    Under the assumptions of Lemma 1, for a transported quantity φ along e with bijection σ,

    ε (k+1)(P-N+1)²(3)
    ≥ avgᵥ 𝔼[1-∑ₛqₛ(v) q_σᵏ(s)(v+ke)],

    and for a one-way quantity the same holds with ∑_s\leadstotqₛ(v) qₜ(v+ke) in place of the sum.

    Proof. Let A be the event that the k+1 patches Q^Pᵥ₊ⱼₑ(X), 0≤j≤k, are all locally valid. On A consecutive patches agree on their overlap, so they are edges of G_P,e, and φ(Q^Pᵥ₊ₖₑ(X))=σᵏ(φ(Q^Pᵥ(X))). By Lemma 1,

    \Pr[A|Gₑ]≤∑ₛ\Pr[φ(Q^Pᵥ)=s,
    φ(Q^Pᵥ₊ₖₑ)=σᵏ(s)\bigm|Gₑ]
    =∑ₛqₛ(v) q_σᵏ(s)(v+ke),

    where each event includes that both patches are locally valid. If A fails, one of the k+1 patches holds a forbidden window, and a patch holds (P-N+1)² windows, so \Pr[Aᶜ]≤∑ⱼ₌₀ᵏ∑ᵤ\Pr[Wᵥ₊ⱼₑ₊ᵤ(X)∉K], with u running over the corners of the windows of a patch. Averaged over v in one period of Λ, each of the (k+1)(P-N+1)² terms becomes ε. Hence avgᵥ𝔼[1-∑ₛqₛ(v) q_σᵏ(s)(v+ke)]≤avgᵥ\Pr[Aᶜ]≤(k+1)(P-N+1)²ε. For a one-way quantity, on A the component at v+ke is reachable from the one at v, which gives the second form in the same way. ∎

    Proof of Theorem 3(b). Since σᵏ is a bijection, ∑ₛqₛ(v) q_σᵏ(s)(v+ke)≤\maxₛqₛ(v)∑ₜqₜ(v+ke)≤\maxₛqₛ(v). With k=2r+P+ℓ-1, inequality (3) becomes the bound of Theorem 3(b). ∎

    For a one-way quantity the sum over the pairs s\leadstot can exceed \maxₛqₛ(v), so its floor is the second form of Proposition 4, as in Appendix B.2.

    Defects, fidelity and what is shared.

    Let pₛ(v)=𝔼[qₛ(v)] be the probability that the patch at v is locally valid with φ=s. The gain at v,

    I(v) = 𝔼[\maxₛqₛ(v)]-\maxₛpₛ(v) ≥ 0,

    is how much knowing Gₑ raises the chance of guessing the value of φ at v. Since 𝔼[1-\maxₛqₛ(v)]=1-\maxₛpₛ(v)-I(v), Theorem 3(b) reads ε(2r+P+ℓ)(P-N+1)²+avgᵥI(v)≥avgᵥ(1-\maxₛpₛ(v)). When P=N, let δᵥ be the total variation between the law of the window Wᵥ(X) and f, with all forbidden windows pooled into one outcome. As in the proof of inequality (1), pₛ(v)≤f(φ=s)+δᵥ, so 1-\maxₛpₛ(v)≥κ_f-δᵥ, and with δ̄=avgᵥδᵥ and Ī=avgᵥI(v),

    ε (2r+N+ℓ) + δ̄ + Ī ≥ κ_f.

    		(4)

    A generator can thus meet the example’s spread κ_f with forbidden windows, with window laws that differ from f at each position, or with coins shared along e that reveal the quantity. For a generator that commutes with every translation and shares nothing, Ī=0, ℓ=1 and δ̄ is the distance δ of its statistics from f, so (4) is inequality (1). In general δ̄ averages the distance at each position and can exceed the distance of the averaged statistics: the example tiled from absolute coordinates has the example’s statistics, yet at each cell a window fixed in advance, and it meets (4) through δ̄ alone.

    The earlier floors as cases.

    When nothing is shared, Gₑ is trivial and ℓ=1, and a generator on independent coins has qₛ(v)=pₛ at every cell, so Theorem 3(b) is Theorem 1. When no block is unbounded along e and blocks have extent at most ℓ, as in Proposition 1(a), Gₑ is again trivial and qₛ(v)=pₛ(v)≤p^*, the largest of these probabilities over cells and values, so part (b) gives the floor of that proposition with 2r+P+ℓ in place of 2r+ℓ+P+1: its proof (Appendix B.7) separates the two patches by one step more than they need.

    Proposition 1(c) works by a different mechanism. There a rule may fix the quantity by its position given the shared coins, so that \maxₛqₛ(v)=1 wherever the patch is locally valid and the numerator of part (b) vanishes. Defects are forced instead because the layout repeats with period T while σᵀ moves every value of a phase whose period does not divide T. The sharp form (3) sees this. Translation by Te fixes every coin of Gₑ and permutes the others without changing their law, so by (2) qₛ(v+Te)=qₛ(v). Take the separation kT of Appendix B.7, with k≡1 modulo a common multiple D of the positive d_c and kT≥2r+T+P; this exceeds 2r+P+ℓ-1, since there every block outside Gₑ has length at most T along e. Then (3) reads ε(kT+1)(P-N+1)²≥avgᵥ𝔼[1-∑ₛqₛ(v) q_σᵏᵀ(s)(v)], and the argument of Appendix B.7 bounds the sum by 1-μ_G/2, with μ_G the conditional mass defined there, which gives Proposition 1(c) in the sharper form proved there, with T the period of Λ along e. The max form alone gives nothing in this case.

    C.3 Theorem 3(a): the quantity is a function of the shared coins

    Theorem 2 uses ergodicity in place of a radius, and given Gₑ the remaining coins are still ergodic under translation along e.

    The coins given Gₑ. Write the coins as ω=(γ,ω^′), with γ the coins of Gₑ and ω^′ the others; the two are independent. The coins of ω^′ are indexed by the cells, the bounded blocks, and the lines orthogonal to e and groups of them. The translation θ_Te maps each of these indices to another of the same family and fixes none, while it maps every block of infinite extent along e to itself and so fixes every coin of γ. Choose one index in every orbit of θ_Te and let ξₙ collect the coins of the n-th translates of the chosen indices. The ξₙ, n∈ℤ, are i.i.d., and θ_Te shifts the sequence (ξₙ) by one place, so under θ_Te the coins ω^′ form a Bernoulli shift. A Bernoulli shift is mixing, so θ_DTe is ergodic on ω^′ for every D≥1. By (2), X(γ,θ_Teω^′)=τ_TeX(γ,ω^′) for every γ, and the law of ω^′ does not depend on γ. Let E be the event that X is K-valid. It has probability one, so for almost every γ it has probability one in ω^′, and it is invariant under θ_Te, since a translate of a K-valid coloring is K-valid.

    Proof of part (a) for a transported quantity. Fix a cell v^′ on the line through the origin orthogonal to e, and let λ(X)=φ(Q^P_v^′(X)). On E the patches along the line through v^′ parallel to e are locally valid and consecutive ones are edges of G_P,e, so

    φ(Q^P_v^′+je(X)) = σʲ(λ(X)) (j∈ℤ).

    		(5)

    These patches form a bi-infinite walk in the finite graph G_P,e, so some patch a occurs twice, m≥1 steps apart, and φ(a)=σᵐ(φ(a)): the values along the line lie in a finite orbit of σ. Since φ takes finitely many values on V_P, finitely many finite orbits meet them; let D≥1 be a common multiple of their lengths, so that σ^D fixes every value that λ takes on E. Under the full labeling these orbits are the levels of the components with d_c≥1, as in the proof of Theorem 2, and if σ has finite order, D can be that order. By (5) with j=T, λ(τ_TeX)=σᵀ(λ(X)) on E, so λ(τ_DTeX)=λ(X) on E. Fix γ outside a null set. The function ω^′↦λ(X(γ,ω^′)) is invariant under θ_DTe on the invariant event E of probability one, so by ergodicity it is almost surely a constant h(v^′,γ), a measurable function of γ, since it is the value s with \Pr[λ(X)=s|Gₑ]=1. As ω^′ and θ_Teω^′ have the same law, λ(X(γ,θ_Teω^′))=σᵀ(λ(X(γ,ω^′))) has the law of λ(X(γ,ω^′)); both are constants, so σᵀ(h(v^′,γ))=h(v^′,γ). Put hᵥ=σʲ∘h(v^′,·) for v=v^′+je. By (5), φ(Q^Pᵥ(X))=hᵥ(Gₑ) almost surely, at all cells at once since they are countably many, with hᵥ₊ₑ=σ∘hᵥ and h_v+Te=σᵀ∘hᵥ=hᵥ. ∎

    Proof of part (a) for a one-way quantity. Let φ be the strongly connected component and m the number of components. Along a line free of forbidden windows φ never returns to a component it has left, so it changes at most m-1 times on the whole line. Let cⱼ=1 if X∈E and the components at v^′+je and v^′+(j+1)e differ, and cⱼ=0 otherwise. Given γ the law of X is invariant under τ_Te, so 𝔼[c_j+T|γ]=𝔼[cⱼ|γ], and n∑ⱼ₌₀ᵀ⁻¹𝔼[cⱼ|γ]=𝔼[∑ⱼ₌₀ⁿᵀ⁻¹cⱼ\bigm|γ]≤m-1 for every n. Hence every cⱼ vanishes almost surely: φ is constant along each line parallel to e, and λ(τ_TeX)=λ(X) almost surely. Ergodicity of θ_Te given γ, applied to the events {λ(X)=s}, which are invariant up to null sets, makes λ(X) a function h(v^′,Gₑ), and hᵥ=h(v^′,·) at every cell v of the line. ∎

    Order parameters.

    The same argument needs no patch. Let Ω^′ be a measurable set of K-valid colorings with τₑΩ^′=Ω^′, V a finite set and σ a bijection of V. A measurable map Φ:Ω^′→V is an order parameter along e if Φ(τₑx)=σ(Φ(x)) for every x∈Ω^′. The value λ above is one, with Ω^′ the K-valid colorings and V the union of the finite orbits of σ that meet the values of φ, but an order parameter need not be a function of any finite patch.

    Proposition 5(order parameters).

    Let X be as in Theorem 3 with X∈Ω^′ almost surely, and let Φ be an order parameter along e on Ω^′. Then Φ(X)=h(Gₑ) almost surely for a measurable h with σᵀ∘h=h.

    Proof. Let D be the order of σ. The event {X∈Ω^′} is invariant under θ_Te, and on it Φ(τ_DTeX)=σ^DT(Φ(X))=Φ(X). As in the proof of part (a), ergodicity of θ_DTe given γ makes Φ(X) almost surely a constant h(γ), and the invariance of the law of ω^′ under θ_Te gives σᵀ(h(γ))=h(γ). ∎

    SmileCity’s lattice of faces.

    SmileCity’s example has eight rows and eight columns. Its first and last rows and columns are black, and the six by six cells inside them hold a face in which no cell is black. In a coloring, call a face run a run of non-black cells in a row with a black cell at each end; in the tiled example every face run is six cells wide and starts at a column of one residue class modulo eight. Let Ω₁ be the set of K-valid colorings that have a face run and in which all face runs, in all rows, start at columns of one residue class modulo eight, and let Φ(x)∈ℤ/8 be that class, the offset of the faces of x along rows. Write e₁ and e₂ for the unit steps along rows and along columns. Translating a coloring along the rows moves its face runs and translating it along the columns does not, so Ω₁ is invariant under both translations and

    Φ(τ_e₁x)=Φ(x)-1, Φ(τ_e₂x)=Φ(x) (x∈Ω₁).

    So Φ is an order parameter along rows, with σ the step s↦s-1 of order eight, and along columns, with σ the identity. Over all K-valid colorings no finite patch fixes this lattice (Appendix S3), which is why the certificate search cannot find it.

    What both the coins shared along rows and those shared along columns determine is determined by the coins they have in common.

    Lemma 2.

    Let U, U^′ and Π be independent random elements of standard Borel spaces, and Z a random variable with finitely many values. If Z=a(U,Π) and Z=b(U^′,Π) almost surely for measurable a and b, then Z=c(Π) almost surely for a measurable c.

    Proof. The law of (U,U^′,Π) is the product of the three laws, so by Fubini’s theorem, for almost every value π of Π, a(U,π)=b(U^′,π) almost surely. Fix such a π and a value s. The events {a(U,π)=s} and {b(U^′,π)=s} are independent, as U and U^′ are, and differ by a null set, so their common probability equals its own square and is zero or one. Hence a(U,π) is almost surely a constant c(π), the value s with \Pr[a(U,π)=s]=1, which is measurable in π by Fubini’s theorem, and Z=c(Π) almost surely. ∎

    In the language of σ-fields, the σ-fields of (U,Π) and of (U^′,Π) meet, up to null sets, in the σ-field of Π.

    Corollary 3(SmileCity’s lattice).

    On SmileCity, let X be as in Theorem 3, K-valid almost surely, and suppose that its faces lie on one lattice along rows, that is, X∈Ω₁ almost surely. Then the offset Φ(X) is almost surely a function of the coins shared over the whole plane, and the period of Λ along rows is a multiple of eight. Equivalently, the residue modulo eight of the columns where face runs start, counted from a cell v, is a function of those coins and of v. A generator that reads no coin shared over the whole plane puts its faces at the same offset in every world.

    Proof. By Proposition 5 along rows, Φ(X)=h₁(G_e₁) with σ^T₁∘h₁=h₁, that is, h₁-T₁≡h₁ modulo eight, where T₁ is the period of Λ along rows, so eight divides T₁. By Proposition 5 along columns, Φ(X)=h₂(G_e₂). Every family of coins has infinite extent along rows only, along columns only, along both, which makes its blocks the whole plane, or along neither. Let U, U^′ and Π collect the coins of the families of the first three kinds. They are independent, G_e₁ is generated by (U,Π) and G_e₂ by (U^′,Π), so Lemma 2 with Z=Φ(X) gives Φ(X)=c(Π). The offset counted from v is Φ(X) minus the column of v, modulo eight. Without coins shared over the plane, Π is trivial and Φ(X) is a constant. ∎

    The hypothesis that the faces lie on one lattice cannot be dropped, since validity alone does not put them there. The example’s black first and last rows span the whole width, so a window that meets the two black rows between consecutive rows of faces sees at most one row of faces, and is a window of the tiled example at that row’s shift. Shifting each band of eight rows of the tiled example, the rows 8b to 8b+7, by its own amount along the rows therefore leaves every window allowed. Drawing the shift of each band from a coin of the band gives a generator in the general form whose output is K-valid for every value of its coins and has the example’s statistics exactly, and whose offset varies from band to band with coins shared along rows. Appendix S3 finds with a complete solver the same freedom between strips of faces separated by two black rows across the width, and another along a row, through a column of faces three cells wide that never closes. On the colorings in which the face runs of row y share one class modulo eight, that class is an order parameter along rows, so for a generator whose worlds are almost surely such colorings it is a function of G_e₁ and of y by Proposition 5, but it need not be the same on every row.

    Rigid layouts.

    Part (a) and Proposition 5 constrain a generator that shares nothing along e, and they constrain phases whatever is shared.

    Corollary 4(rigid layouts).

    Let X be as in Theorem 3, K-valid almost surely. (a) If X reads no coin shared along e, then at every cell every transported or one-way quantity along e almost surely takes a value fixed in advance, the same in every world, and this layout is periodic under Λ; every order parameter along e is almost surely a constant. (b) Under the full labeling, almost surely every patch of X lies in a component whose d_c divides T. When P=N, the total variation between the window statistics of X and f is therefore at least the example’s share of windows in the other components.

    Proof. (a) With Gₑ trivial the functions hᵥ of part (a) and h of Proposition 5 are constants. For t∈Λ, φ(Q^Pᵥ₊ₜ(X))=φ(Q^Pᵥ(τₜX)), and τₜX=X(θₜω) has the law of X, so hᵥ₊ₜ=hᵥ. (b) By part (a) of Theorem 3, at every cell the value (c,z) of the full labeling is almost surely fixed by σᵀ, which adds T to the level modulo d_c, and d_c≥1 on a line free of forbidden windows; so d_c divides T. When P=N the window law of X at every cell puts no mass on the windows of the other components, while f puts the example’s share on them. ∎

    Part (a) is why a generator given the phase channels and no coin shared along the phase’s direction lays the phase out the same way for every seed. Part (b) is Proposition 1(c) without a radius. On Fabric, whose phase period 5 does not divide the octaves’ period T=16, the components whose period does not divide T hold 0.60 of the example’s windows (Appendix B.9), so a generator whose lattice Λ has that period along the phase’s direction and whose output is free of forbidden windows, at any depth, has window statistics at least that far from the example’s.

    C.4 Theorem 4: when the row types are enough

    Theorem 4 gives a generator free of forbidden windows that reads only the coin from which its band’s row types are drawn and its position.

    Rows and strips. Let the example have H rows and W columns, read with wrap-around, and let Y_c, c∈ℤ/H, be its rows, each a sequence of period W. The alphabet ℝ consists of the rows τˢY_c of the example at every horizontal shift s∈ℤ/W, at most HW rows. A sequence of rows of ℝ is valid if every N consecutive rows form a strip all of whose windows lie in K, a finite condition since the rows share the period W. In a valid sequence the strip of P rows that starts at a given row is locally valid at every column, and its P×P patches are consecutive patches along rows, so they lie in one weak component of G_P,e, the strip’s type. As in Section 4, the type of row y of a coloring is the type of the strip of P rows from y-j₀, where j₀=⌊P/2⌋.

    The sampler’s sequences. Band b holds the rows bL to bL+L-1. The sampler draws for it the types t₀,…,t_L+1 of the rows bL to bL+L+1, with (t₀,t₁) and (t_L,t_L+1) both the anchor α, every three consecutive types shown by the example and every free run within the run limits (Appendix D). Consecutive bands agree on the two rows they share, which both give the anchor. Let W be the finite set of type sequences that the sampler can draw for a band.

    Realizations. A realization of w=(t₀,…,t_L+1)∈W is a valid sequence R₀,…,R_L+P-2 of rows of ℝ in which, for j=0,…,L-1, the strip of P rows that starts at Rⱼ has type t_j+j₀. Placed at the rows bL to bL+L+P-2, the strip that starts at row bL+j is the strip from y-j₀ for y=bL+j+j₀, so the realization gives every row y from bL+j₀ to bL+L-1+j₀ the type t_y-bL that w assigns it. The rows bL to bL+j₀-1 take their types from the realization of band b-1, whose sequence gives them the anchor’s types, as w does. This indexing needs t_L-1+j₀ to lie in the sequence, that is j₀≤2, which holds for P≤5 and so on every example of the corpus, read at P=3 or P=4; a larger P would need an anchor that fixes j₀ consecutive types.

    The example’s rows glue if there is a strip Z=(Z₀,…,Z_P-2) of rows of ℝ such that every w∈W has a realization with R₀,…,R_P-2 equal to Z and R_L,…,R_L+P-2 equal to Z. The rows of Z carry their shifts, so Z is the same at both ends at the same shift. Shifting a realization along the rows gives a realization of the same sequence, since neither K nor the types change, so pinning Z at one end costs nothing; pinning it at both ends is the condition.

    Proof of Theorem 4. Let the rows glue with the strip Z, and let L≥P-1, as on every example of the corpus (Table 2). The bands are the blocks of a lattice fixed in absolute coordinates, groups of L consecutive rows, so their coins form a family of infinite extent along rows. From the coin ω_b of band b the sampler draws w⁽ᵇ⁾∈W, and a fixed rule, deterministic or using further coins of the same band, chooses a realization ρ⁽ᵇ⁾=(R⁽ᵇ⁾₀,…,R⁽ᵇ⁾_L+P-2) of w⁽ᵇ⁾ that begins and ends with Z, which exists because the rows glue. The output is X_(x,y)=R⁽ᵇ⁾_y-bL(x) for bL≤y

    The rows (b+1)L to (b+1)L+P-2 lie in band b+1, since L≥P-1, and there the output is R⁽ᵇ⁺¹⁾₀,…,R⁽ᵇ⁺¹⁾_P-2, which is Z, which is R⁽ᵇ⁾_L,…,R⁽ᵇ⁾_L+P-2. So the output agrees with ρ⁽ᵇ⁾ on all the rows bL to bL+L+P-2. A window whose top row y lies in band b occupies the rows y to y+N-1≤bL+L+N-2≤bL+L+P-2, so it is a window of the valid sequence ρ⁽ᵇ⁾ and lies in K, for every value of the coins. The same comparison applies to the strips of P rows that start in band b, so every row y from bL+j₀ to bL+L-1+j₀ has the type that w⁽ᵇ⁾ gives it, and the row types of the output are the sampled ones. ∎

    The statistics of a generator that glues rows.

    Suppose the rule records, with every row it outputs, the row c of the example and the shift s it copies, so that the row is τˢY_c. A stretch is a maximal run of output rows that copy consecutive rows c,c+1,… of the example at one shift, and a cut is the boundary between two consecutive stretches. A cut is free if every strip of N rows across it is nonetheless a strip of the tiled example up to a horizontal shift; a cut with N-1 copies of one row on each side is free when the example repeats that row N times in a row, as the skylines repeat a row of sky. Let ρ_cut be the expected share of rows y whose strip of N rows from y crosses a cut that is not free. Every other row y starts a strip of N rows that is a strip of the tiled example up to shift; let ν(c) be the expected share of rows whose strip is the example’s strip from row c, taking the least such c when several qualify, and ν̄=ν/(1-ρ_cut) the row usage. Shares are taken over the rows of a band, and U_H is the uniform law on the H rows of the example.

    Proposition 6(statistics).

    The window statistics h_X of such a generator satisfy ∥h_X-f∥_TV≤∥ν̄-U_H∥_TV+ρ_cut. When P=N, every generator whose output is K-valid with the sampled row types satisfies ∥h_X-f∥_TV≥∥π_S-π_f∥_TV, where π_S gives the expected share of each type among the rows of a sampled band and π_f its share among the rows of the example.

    Proof. The law of X is invariant under translation by L rows and by p columns, so its window statistics are the window law averaged over the rows of one band and the columns of one period, a multiple of W. For c∈ℤ/H let f_c be the uniform law on the W windows of the example’s strip from row c, so that f=1/H∑_cf_c. A row y whose strip is the example’s strip from row c at some shift contributes, over the columns of a period, the windows of that strip, each equally often, that is, the law f_c. Hence h_X=∑_cν(c)f_c+ρ_cut g for some law g, and

    ∥h_X-f∥_TV
