一句话：WFC 式按需生成的数学前提：局部约束可能要求任意远的两个窗口一致，什么时候才可行？

要点：

  • 问题设定很具体：种子噪声让游戏按需生成无界世界的任意区域；这里问的是「每个小窗口都必须来自同一个示例」时，生成器需要什么——正是 Wave Function Collapse 的隐含约束
  • 难点在于局部约束可能需要任意远的一致性：砖墙里每一行都要在灰缝之间保持位置，远处的一致性无法靠局部窗口自己保证
  • 论文研究「局部生成器」（每个格子是它附近随机性的固定函数），并给出当约束携带一个跨示例变化的量时，这类生成何时可行、必须共享什么

为什么值得看：程序化生成长期靠经验调参，这条把「按需无界生成」的前提写成可判定的条件：哪些信息必须被所有局部生成器共享。做开放世界、无限地形的团队可以据此判断自己的生成器是不是从一开始就注定接缝。

中文摘要：程序化游戏会用种子噪声按需生成无界世界的任意区域，Wave Function Collapse 是典型做法，它隐含一个很强的约束：每一个小窗口都必须来自同一个示例。这篇论文研究这个设定下「局部生成器」需要什么——所谓局部生成器，指每个格子是它附近随机性的固定函数。难点在于局部约束有时会要求任意远的一致性：砖墙的每一行都要在灰缝之间保持位置，这种全局一致无法由局部窗口自己保证。作者进一步分析当约束携带一个跨示例变化的量时，这类按需生成在什么条件下可行，以及所有局部生成器必须共享哪些信息，从而把「无限世界能不能由局部规则拼出来」变成可以判断的问题。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·核心检索（English）

原文发布：2026-11-03

本期推送：2026-11-04

Infinite Worlds from One Example: What Local Generators Must Share

Abstract

Seeded noise lets games generate any region of an unbounded world on demand. We ask what such a generator needs when every small window must come from one example, the constraint behind Wave Function Collapse. The difficulty is that local constraints can require agreement over arbitrary distances: in a brick wall, each row keeps its place between the mortar lines. We study local generators, each cell a fixed function of the randomness near it. When the constraints carry a quantity that varies across the example, no generator that applies one rule, ignoring position, to independent randomness at every cell can be both exactly valid and faithful to the example’s statistics, however far each cell reads. At radius r, staying faithful forces forbidden windows at a density of at least order 1/r, and a construction attains this order. To vary the quantity between exactly valid worlds, a generator needs randomness shared along its direction. We give a finitely checkable condition under which row types drawn from the seed and the position modulo a fixed period suffice for exact validity without learning. A search over the example’s patches certifies these quantities and names the input each needs. Across 52 public examples of Wave Function Collapse and 27 from other implementations, it certifies only examples where a learned generator on independent randomness stays far from valid after repair. Given that input, a neural cellular automaton and a diffusion model become valid on 10 and 8 of the 12 certified examples that receive one, and on none from independent randomness. Valid means at most one forbidden window in a thousand after repair. With octaves of seeded noise elsewhere, the automaton is valid on 45 of the 52 public examples and 21 of the 27 from other implementations, and repair keeps random access.

Keywords:

procedural content generation, wave function collapse, neural cellular automata, local algorithms, factors of i.i.d.

1 Introduction

Games generate unbounded worlds from seeded noise. A terrain height is a hash of its coordinates and a seed, so any region can be computed on its own and in any order, and machines that share the seed make the same world. When every small window of a map must come from a designer’s example, worlds are made by search instead. Wave Function Collapse [(Gumin, 2016)] fills a canvas in a data-dependent order and restarts when the constraints run into a contradiction. Model synthesis [(Merrell, 2009)] modifies a valid model one overlapping block at a time, so that a contradiction costs one block, and block solvers built on it [(Boris the Brave, 2021; Kleineberg, 2023)] give random access by re-solving blocks over a fixed periodic background, which they keep where a block cannot be solved. Where validity fixes a row’s place, as in a brick wall, their worlds keep the background’s rows. Learned generators with random access, such as InfiniteDiffusion for terrain [(Goslin, 2026)], carry no hard constraint.

We study random access through locality: each cell is a fixed function of the randomness near it, which may include coins shared along whole rows or on blocks that meet its neighborhood (Section 2). A cellular automaton run for a fixed number of rounds is local in this sense, and so is a diffusion sampler whose convolutional denoiser draws fresh noise at every step. A generator may also read its position modulo a fixed period; one that reads its position with no period, or randomness at unboundedly many scales, can also give random access but lies outside this model. We ask what a local generator must be given, whatever its architecture, to make worlds whose every window comes from one example (Figure 1).

A brick wall shows what independent coins, which give each cell randomness of its own, cannot do (Figure 2). No window of the example lets a mortar row step up or end, so a row’s place among the mortar lines is a quantity that validity carries along the whole row. A local generator on independent coins decides it at distant cells of a row independently, and wherever they disagree a forbidden window lies between them. [Bergmann et al. (2017)] observed the same of textures: a generator on independent noise with a limited receptive field cannot align distant regions. For any quantity that validity carries along an axis and the statistics make vary, a generator of radius r on independent coins leaves forbidden windows at a density of order at least 1/r unless its statistics stray from the example’s. At any depth, that is, however far each cell reads, no such generator is both free of forbidden windows and faithful to the statistics (Section 3). This holds even where one repeated color satisfies every constraint, so that the constraints alone are solvable in constant time [(Brandt et al., 2017)]. The order cannot be improved: the min-coin copy, which copies the example over regions drawn from the coins, stays within a constant factor of the bound, and a rule learned on independent coins leaves forbidden windows at about the copy’s rate (Figure 3).

The example alone shows whether the theorems apply. A search over the overlap graphs of the example’s locally valid patches finds quantities that validity carries, and we call an example with one certified (Section 4). We call a generator valid on an example when, after mending, a local re-solve around each forbidden window, at most one window in a thousand stays forbidden on each canvas. On 21 public examples, which we call resistant, a rule learned on independent coins stays far from valid. The search certifies 13 of them and none of the others. Where mending fails on a certified example, at the radii we examined, the re-solve mostly holds a witness, two frozen patches whose values of the quantity no valid filling can join (Figure 2(d)), and the min-coin copy, mended the same way, is valid on no certified example at radii up to 128 (Section 6.1).

A shared input escapes the bound, and random access allows one. An invariant along rows is supplied as row types drawn band by band from the seed with the example’s own transitions, and a phase as the coordinates modulo its period, both at bounded work per cell (Section 4). Coins shared on blocks of bounded length help only as a larger radius would, unless the generator ties the quantity to their grid (Proposition 1). The position alone also escapes the bound but gives one world, the example tiled from absolute coordinates. A generator free of forbidden windows, at any depth, can vary the quantity between worlds only through randomness shared along whole lines (Theorem 3). Where the example’s rows glue, a condition decided by a finite computation on the example, that is also enough: a generator that reads only its band’s coin and its position leaves no forbidden window for any value of the coins (Theorem 4).

The rows glue on seven of the eight examples with a row invariant, all but 3Bricks. These are the examples where the copier, which fills the sampled rows with stretches of the example’s rows, exists and leaves no forbidden window (Section 4). With the copier, or a lookup of the example at the coordinates modulo the period, the input carries validity by itself, without learning or mending, on ten of the twelve certified examples that receive one.

A learned local generator can use the input as well. A small neural cellular automaton [(Mordvintsev et al., 2020)], learned from the single example and given this input, is valid after mending on the same ten certified examples, all but 3Bricks and SmileCity. On the octaves of seeded noise alone, which share coins along whole rows as well as on blocks, it is valid on five of the twelve, and on independent coins on none. On the nine certified examples where it is valid on all eight canvases, no canvas keeps a forbidden window, while no generator on independent coins with the same statistics could be free of them, at any depth on most of these examples and at the radius of the whole pipeline on the rest (Section 6.2). A convolutional diffusion model given the input is valid on eight of the twelve, five of them without copying the example (Section 6.5).

Outside the corpus on which we built the procedure, the automaton is valid on all five examples we held out, two of them only with the input. On 27 examples taken from other implementations of Wave Function Collapse and related generators, the search again certifies only examples that resist independent coins, and the automaton, given the input where a certificate exists and the octaves elsewhere, is valid on 21 of them, against 18 on the octaves alone (Section 6.2).

Where a copier exists, learning is not what makes the worlds valid or new. The automaton composes its rows instead of copying them, and on Wall its canvases lie where Theorem 2 excludes the law of every generator on independent coins (Figure 5), but a block solver that re-solves the copier’s canvases does the same without learning (Section 6.3). Learning adds something of its own where nothing is certified, as the prior from which a mender starts. From a rule learned on the octaves, one mender makes 34 of the 39 uncertified examples valid, more than from any prior without learning that we gave it, though a block solver started from the tiled example needs no prior and is valid there by construction.

With the octaves where nothing is certified and the input elsewhere, the automaton, which we call the method, is valid on 45 of the 52 public examples. Most of that validity comes with the mender, which rewrites a median of 18% of the cells where the method ends valid. Regions mended separately agree once each carries a margin as wide as a mending change can travel, so the method keeps random access (Section 6.4).

Our contributions are the lower bound, its counterpart at any depth and a construction that attains its order (Section 3); a necessary condition on what a local generator free of forbidden windows must share to vary the quantity between worlds, and a sufficient one decided on the example; the certificate and the input built from it, which keeps random access (Section 4); and a measured account of what a learned rule adds to that input (Section 6). Appendix S8 gives, for most experiments, the outcome we expected before the run beside the outcome observed.

2 Setting

A world is a coloring x:ℤ²→[C] in C colors, and one example decides which N×N windows it may contain and how often. The coloring x is K-valid if every window lies in the set K⊆[C]^N×N of allowed windows, and a window outside K is forbidden. As in Wave Function Collapse’s overlapping model [(Gumin, 2016)], K holds the windows of the example, read with wrap-around and without rotations or reflections, and their frequencies f are its window statistics, so the plane tiled with the example is K-valid with statistics exactly f. A coloring is measured by its density of forbidden windows and the total variation of its window frequencies from f, forbidden windows pooled as one outcome. The examples are the 52 public bitmap examples of the WaveFunctionCollapse repository, none chosen for this study, read at N=3. A generator is valid on an example when, after mending, at most one window in a thousand is forbidden on each canvas of the protocol (Section 5), a weaker demand than K-validity, which the theorems concern.

Coins are uniform numbers hashed from the seed and the coordinates, shared over blocks as in seeded noise. A scale paira=(i,j), with i,j∈{0,1,2,…}∪{∞}, puts the cell v=(x,y) in the block of vᵃ=(⌊x/2ⁱ⌋,⌊y/2ʲ⌋), of 2ⁱ×2ʲ cells fixed in absolute coordinates (rows, columns or the plane when a scale is ∞); for a finite set A of pairs, each block w of each a∈A carries independent coins ω_a,w, and cell v reads ω(v)=(ω_a,vᵃ)_a∈A.

Definition 1(random-access generator).

A random-access generator of radius r on the scale pairs A is a map from the coins to a coloring X of the form Xᵥ=g((ω(v+u))_∥u∥_∞≤r) for one fixed function g. In the general form, g also reads v\bmodp, the position of v modulo a fixed period p in each coordinate, and ω(v) also lists the coins of the block that holds v in each of finitely many further lattices of blocks fixed in absolute coordinates, every block with coins of its own.

Definition 2(generator on independent coins).

When A={(0,0)}, every cell has coins of its own, the vectors (ωᵥ)_v∈ℤ² are i.i.d., and Xᵥ=g((ωᵥ₊ᵤ)_∥u∥_∞≤r). Such a generator commutes with every translation, and Xᵥ is a fixed function of the coins within ℓ_∞ distance r of v. In the language of ergodic theory it is a block factor of an i.i.d. process, that is, a finitary factor whose coding radius is bounded [(Holroyd et al., 2017; Grebík & Rozhoň, 2023; Berlow et al., 2025)].

A random-access generator is local: any region follows from the coins within distance r of it at a fixed cost per cell, so regions computed apart agree cell for cell, and editing a region’s coins changes the output only within that distance. The inputs of Section 4, row types drawn band by band from the seed and the coordinates modulo a period, fit the general form, and so does the mended output, with a reach, beyond which no coin changes a cell’s color, in place of the radius (Appendix A).

3 Limits of local generators

When validity carries a quantity along an axis and the example’s statistics make it vary, no local generator on independent coins is both free of forbidden windows and faithful to the statistics, at any depth; at radius r a faithful one’s density of forbidden windows falls as 1/r at best, an order that is attained. A generator free of forbidden windows that escapes these bounds carries the quantity as a function of its position and of randomness shared along the axis.

Quantities carried by validity.

A P×P patch, P≥N, is locally valid if all its N×N windows lie in K, and V_P is the set of such patches. For an axis direction e, the overlap graphG_P,e on V_P has an edge from a to b when b can follow a one step along e, agreeing with it on their overlap. A transported quantity is a map φ on V_P with a bijection σ of its values such that φ(b)=σ(φ(a)) on every edge. For an invariant, φ is the weakly connected component and σ the identity, so it cannot change along a line parallel to e without a forbidden window; along rows it is the row type (Figure 2). For a phase, σ adds one modulo d, where d≥2 divides the signed length of every closed walk in a weak component; in a checkerboard it is the column’s parity. The full labeling gives each locally valid patch its weak component c and its level modulo d_c, the greatest common divisor of these lengths in c (Appendix B.1). A one-way quantity, the strongly connected component of G_P,e, can move along an edge to a component it reaches but never return.

Theorem 1(a floor from a transported quantity).

Let g be a generator on independent coins of radius r (Definition 2) with output X, and let φ be a transported quantity along e at patch size P. Let pₛ be the probability that the P×P patch of X at a cell is locally valid and has φ=s. Then the density ε of forbidden windows of X satisfies

ε ≥ (1-\maxₛpₛ)/((2r+P+1)(P-N+1)²).

The theorem binds every such generator, whatever its architecture or training, among them the learned rule of Section 5 on each cell’s own coins alone, the independent-coin rule. Patches 2r+P apart along e read disjoint coins, so their values of φ agree after that many steps of σ with probability at most \maxₛpₛ, as validity between them would require (Appendix B.2).

Defects against fidelity.

The bound vanishes only if φ is concentrated on one value, which the example’s statistics forbid. When P=N, a generator within total variation δ of f has pₛ≤f(φ=s)+δ, and Theorem 1 becomes an inequality between validity, fidelity and radius:

ε (2r+N+1) + δ ≥ κ_f, κ_f=1-\maxₛf(φ=s).

(1)

For any P, a linear program gives κ(δ), one minus the largest share of one value of φ under a stationary distribution on V_P whose N×N marginal lies within δ of f, with κ(0)=κ_f and κ(δ)≥κ_f-δ when P=N (Appendix B.5).

Rare changes.

A quantity that the example lets change, but rarely, still sets a floor at finite radius. Let J⊂K be a set of windows with total frequency θ=f(J) in the example, and let φ be a transported quantity along e at P=N with K∖J in place of K, so that along a line it departs from σ only at a window of J. On a wall, a window that let a mortar row step up would be such a change.

Corollary 1(rare changes).

Let g be a generator on independent coins of radius r whose output has a density ε of forbidden windows and window statistics within total variation δ of f. With κ_J=1-\maxₛf({w∈K∖J:φ(w)=s}),

(ε+δ+θ) (2r+N+1) ≥ κ_J.

The proof runs Theorem 1 on K∖J in place of K, with the windows of J counted as forbidden (Appendix B.4); when J is empty, the same proof gives inequality (1). A generator with ε=δ=0 needs 2r+N+1≥κ_J/θ, so a quantity that may change at a share θ of windows requires coordination over distances of at least order 1/θ.

Unbounded radius.

A factor of i.i.d. coins is X=F(ω) for a measurable map F that commutes with every translation of ℤ², such as a generator on independent coins or a rule run for any number of rounds.

Theorem 2(no generator driven by independent coins).

Let X be a factor of i.i.d. coins that is K-valid almost surely, and let φ be a transported or one-way quantity along an axis direction e, under the full labeling of Appendix B or, for a one-way quantity, under the labeling by strongly connected components. Then almost surely φ takes one and the same value at every cell, and that value lies in a component without a phase. Hence if κ(δ)>0, the window statistics of X lie farther than δ from f; for P=N their total variation from f is at least κ_f.

Its proof uses ergodicity in place of a radius, which makes the value that a line free of forbidden windows carries almost surely one constant (Appendix B).

Corollary 2(convolutional diffusion samplers).

Let X be the output of a diffusion sampler run on the whole plane without padding, whose denoiser is convolutional with a finite receptive field at each step and whose noise is drawn independently at every cell and step, however many steps it takes. If X is K-valid almost surely and κ(δ)>0 for a transported quantity of the example, the window statistics of X lie farther than δ from f; for P=N their total variation from f is at least κ_f.

Run without padding, the sampler commutes with every translation, so its output is a factor of i.i.d. coins and Theorem 2 applies; zero padding would let it read its position [(Xu et al., 2021)].

Local algorithms.

A K-valid coloring is a locally checkable labeling of the grid [(Brandt et al., 2017)]. Some such labelings admit generators on independent coins whose defects fall exponentially in the radius, while on agreement constraints such as checkerboards none does better than order 1/r (Proposition 3 in Appendix B, after [Brandt et al. (2017)] and [Grebík & Rozhoň (2023)]). Both theorems rest on classical arguments for factors of i.i.d. processes and add a trade between defects, fidelity and radius that binds even constraints a constant coloring satisfies.

Coins shared on blocks.

The octaves of seeded noise share coins over blocks, which both theorems exclude.

Proposition 1(coins shared on blocks).

Let X commute with the periods of a lattice of blocks fixed in absolute coordinates, and let Xᵥ be a function of the independent coins within distance r of v and of coins attached to the blocks that meet that box. (a) If every block has length at most ℓ along e, Theorem 1 holds with 2r+ℓ in place of 2r, where ε is the density of forbidden windows and pₛ is taken at the cell where it is largest. (b) With K and f read from the example with wrap-around, copying the tiled example on every block of an ℓ×ℓ lattice, under a uniform translation drawn from the block’s coin, reads one coin per cell and gives ε≤2(N-1)/ℓ, with window statistics within 2(N-1)/ℓ of f. (c) If the lattice has period T along e and Xᵥ may also read coins shared along whole lines and over the plane, a floor of the same order holds on the components of the full labeling whose period d_c does not divide T, with a multiple of T in place of ℓ (stated in full in Appendix B.7).

A coin shared over a length ℓ along e thus adds about ℓ/2 to the radius while the quantity stays spread at every cell, and one shared along a whole line escapes (a). Part (c) binds a rule that fixes the quantity by the position that blocks fixed in absolute coordinates reveal.

The floor’s order is attained.

The min-coin copy copies the example as (b) does, over regions drawn from independent coins: every cell v draws a priority, uniform on [0,1], and a translation tᵥ of the tiled example Y, uniform over one period, and copies the translate drawn by the cell mᵥ of lowest priority within distance r of v: Xᵥ=Y(v-mᵥ+t_mᵥ). Forbidden windows occur only where the regions of cells that share mᵥ, each a copy of the tiled example, meet.

Proposition 2(the floor’s order is attained).

Let N≥2, and read K and f from the example with wrap-around, as in Section 2. For every radius r≥N, the min-coin copy is a generator on independent coins of radius r, and its density of forbidden windows ε and the total variation δ of its window statistics from f satisfy

ε ≤ qᵣ, δ ≤ qᵣ, where
qᵣ = 1-(2r+2-N/2r+N)² < 4(N-1)/2r+N.

Here qᵣ is the probability that the cells of a window do not all copy from one cell; when they do, the window is one of the tiling at a uniform translation (Appendix B.8). Inequality (1) sets the copy, whose statistics lie within qᵣ of f, a floor of (κ_f-qᵣ)/(2r+N+1), and once 4(N-1)<κ_f(2r+N) the copy stays within a multiple of that floor that falls toward 4(N-1)/κ_f, 12 on Wall. The order 1/r of Theorem 1 therefore cannot be improved, only its constant. In Figure 3 the copy sits at up to about 170 times the floor on the certified examples with a transported quantity (Appendix S4.2), and the independent-coin rule lies within a factor of two of the copy at its own radius on all twelve of them. The diffusion model from noise lies far above the copy at its own radius, so its radius alone does not explain its rate (Appendix S5).

What a generator must share.

For a generator in the general form of Definition 1 and an axis direction e, the coins shared along e, Gₑ, are those of its blocks that are unbounded along e: whole lines parallel to e, groups of such lines, and the plane. Let Λ be the lattice of translations in multiples of the period p that map every lattice of blocks to itself, and T its period along e.

Theorem 3(what a generator free of forbidden windows must share).

Let X be a random-access generator in the general form, or any measurable function of its coins and of the position modulo p that commutes with the translations in Λ, and let φ be a transported or one-way quantity along an axis direction e. (a) If X is K-valid almost surely, then at every cell the value of φ is almost surely a function of Gₑ and of the cell, and along e this function repeats with period T. (b) If φ is transported and X has radius r, the floor of Theorem 1 holds given Gₑ, with the largest length along e of the other blocks it reads added to 2r (stated in full in Appendix C.2).

Part (a) is Theorem 2 run given Gₑ: translation by Te fixes those coins and moves the others, which stay independent, and no assumption on the statistics enters. On finite grids the same dichotomy separates shared from private randomness [(Balliu et al., 2025)]. Part (b) is Theorem 1 run given Gₑ and contains it and Proposition 1(a), so a shared input lowers the floor only through what it reveals about the quantity (Appendix C).

Without coins shared along e, a generator free of forbidden windows thus lays the quantity out the same way in almost every world, even if it reads its position. Since the layout repeats with period T, a phase whose period does not divide T cannot be carried without defects at any depth (Corollary 4 in Appendix C). Functions of the coordinates, such as the example tiled from absolute coordinates, satisfy (a) but repeat one world. For the layout of the quantity to differ between worlds, a generator free of forbidden windows therefore needs an input shared along the quantity’s direction that, with the position, fixes the quantity at every cell: for an invariant, values shared along whole lines; for a phase, a period T that is a multiple of its own and a shared coin that shifts it. Section 4 draws an allowed sequence of row types band by band from the seed, which a rule on coins shared along whole rows would have to do itself (Appendix B.12).

The same transport limits editing a valid world. If two K-valid colorings agree outside a finite region, a transported quantity takes the same value on both at every cell, since along each line parallel to e it is carried in from outside. A local edit therefore keeps every row’s type, and changing a row’s type means editing every patch along that row, in both directions without end. This is why block solvers over a fixed background keep its rows.

4 Finding the quantity and supplying it

The example alone shows what a local generator must be given: a search of its locally valid patches finds the quantity that validity carries, before anything is trained, and its kind names an input that supplies it and keeps random access.

The search.

For each axis direction e, and for the two diagonals, the search builds G_P,e for P from N upward until the number of locally valid patches passes 200 000 (Appendix B.13). It reports an invariant when two weak components hold patches of the example, a phase when a weak component c that holds some of them has d_c≥2, and a one-way quantity when two strongly connected components hold them. A quantity found this way, together with κ(0)>0, is a certificate: it proves a floor for every generator on independent coins whose statistics lie within δ of the example’s whenever κ(δ)>0 (Section 3), and an example with one is certified. The search is one-sided: an uncertified example may have a floor that a larger patch or another kind of quantity would reveal, and a certified one a second quantity, as SmileCity does (Appendix S3).

The input.

The kind of the example’s first certificate, under a fixed tie-break (Appendix D), decides what the rule reads besides the octaves:

  • •

    an invariant: the type of each line along its axis, from the row-type sampler;

  • •

    a phase of period d: the phase channels of period d;

  • •

    a one-way quantity or an invariant along a diagonal, which have no input of their own, or no certificate at all: the octaves alone.

    • The row-type sampler.

    Along rows, where every certified invariant of the corpus runs, the type of row y is the certificate’s label of the strip of P rows from y-⌊P/2⌋. The sampler’s states are the pairs of consecutive types and its steps the triples that the example shows. It cuts the rows into bands of L rows starting at the multiples of L, fixes the state at the first row of each band to an anchor, and draws the other states from the example’s transition frequencies, conditioned on returning to the anchor at the band’s end, so the anchor falls on the same rows in every world, a constraint that an offset hashed from the seed would lift (Section 8). The draw reads only the seed and the band’s index, so the state of any row costs work bounded by L, and the rule receives it as one-hot channels (Appendix D).

    When the row types are enough.

    On most examples with a row invariant, the row types and the position are enough to vary the quantity between worlds with no forbidden window. Call a sequence of L+P-1 rows of the example, each at some horizontal shift, a realization of the types drawn for a band if all its windows lie in K and its strips of P rows give the band’s rows those types (Appendix C.4). The example’s rows glue if there is a strip Z of P-1 such rows for which every type sequence that the sampler can draw for a band has a realization that begins and ends with Z.

    Theorem 4(when the row types are enough).

    Let the example carry an invariant along rows, with the row-type sampler drawing bands of L≥P-1 rows and P≤5, as on every example here, and let its rows glue with the strip Z. Let a generator fill the rows of each band with the first L rows of a realization of the band’s types that begins and ends with Z, chosen by a fixed rule from the coin from which the sampler draws the band’s types. It is a random-access generator in the general form that reads only that coin and its position modulo a period, and its output is K-valid for every value of the coins.

    Two consecutive bands both carry Z on the rows where they meet, so every window of the output lies within one realization (Appendix C). The copier, which also fills each band with stretches of the example’s rows, chains its offsets toward the next band’s in place of a fixed strip, so it is valid by construction, not by the theorem (Section 6.2). Gluing is decided by a finite computation on the example (Appendix C.5). The rows glue on every example with a row invariant but 3Bricks, and these are the examples where the copier exists; on them the computation came after the copier’s results and explains them. On the three held-out walls it came first, and there too the rows glue and the copier leaves no forbidden window.

    The phase channels.

    For a phase of period d the rule receives one-hot channels of x\bmodd and of y\bmodd in absolute coordinates. As functions of the coordinates, they keep random access and exact seams.

    The octaves.

    Besides its own coins, every cell reads coins of every scale pair (i,j) with i,j∈{0,2,3,4,∞} other than (0,0). Their blocks run from squares of side 4, 8 and 16 to whole rows, columns and the plane, the finite ones nested in one lattice of period T=16, and where nothing is certified they give coarse structure, as octave noise does for terrain.

    The failures of five certified examples, 3Bricks, Fabric, Skyline, Skyline2 and Wall, shaped parts of this procedure (Appendix D); the other certified examples test it within the corpus, the held-out ones as it stood when they ran, and those from other implementations as it stands (Section 6.2).

    5 Generators and protocol

    The tiled example is valid and has the example’s window statistics exactly, so validity and fidelity alone cannot show that a generator does anything. We compare the learned generators with generators that show what copying and mending achieve without learning (Table 1), and measure copying and variation by normalized agreement with the tiled example, repetition of its patches and aligned variation between seeds, except where every valid world is a translate of the tiling (Appendix S2.3).

    The learned automaton.

    The method’s rule is a neural cellular automaton [(Mordvintsev et al., 2020)] learned from the single example (Figure S1): a radius-one update run without padding for 32 rounds, so a local generator of radius 32 on the input of Section 4. Training asks every round for allowed windows with the example’s frequencies, and a variation term penalizes agreement between two runs that differ only in their fine coins, against the shortcut of Proposition 1(b); rules trained without it do not copy either (Appendix S6.6). Then four repair rounds recolor cells under forbidden windows with coins hashed from the seed and the position (Appendix S1). The octave rule is the same construction on the octaves alone; the independent-coin rule, which reads no shared coins and so cannot take that shortcut, was trained before we added the variation term and has none.

    The diffusion model.

    A convolutional diffusion model is trained on each example by Gaussian diffusion on the one-hot colors [(Ho et al., 2020)], with the standard loss and no term for forbidden windows. It samples with one step of its unpadded denoiser at each of 50 noise levels, under noise hashed from the seed, step and coordinates, so a cell depends on independent noise within 300 cells. It is trained from two training seeds, from noise alone on the certified examples and on controls, and with the input of Section 4, without the octaves, wherever a certificate names one (Appendix S5).

    Mending.

    Mending re-solves what repair leaves in two passes over a lattice of 48×48 blocks fixed in absolute coordinates. It frees the cells around each defect, out to the mending radius 24, and re-solves them with Wave Function Collapse’s propagation, cluster by cluster where a block’s defects cannot be completed together (Appendix S1.3). It thus rewrites part of the output of its prior, the generator it starts from (Section 6.3). No coin farther than 804 cells from a cell can change its mended color, the reach of the whole pipeline: the rule’s radius with its repair rounds, plus the 760 cells that a mending change can travel.

    Protocol.

    Validity is judged on three 256×256 canvases per example, drawn on coin seeds that every generator shares, the development seeds. A robustness test adds five canvases on the robustness seeds, and a last test three on fresh seeds that no decision used; the rules counted are trained from training seed 0 (Table S1). The examples fall into three classes by what mending within radius 8, without cluster completion, makes of the independent-coin rule on one canvas: it leaves at most one window in a thousand forbidden on the mendable examples, at most one in a hundred on the partial ones, and more on the resistant ones, which resist independent coins. Every certified example lies far from these boundaries, with at least 0.024 of its windows forbidden.

    6 Results

    6.1 Independent coins fail where the certificate finds a quantity

    The certificate picks out the examples on which independent coins fail. It certifies 13 of the 21 examples that resist independent coins (Section 5, Table 4) and none of the 31 others (Figure 4). Against the 21 examples that independent coins mend, leaving out the partial ones, a one-sided Fisher exact test gives p=8·10⁻⁶ if the examples are counted as independent, which variants of one picture are not (Appendix E). On examples from other implementations, which played no part in designing the search, it again certifies only examples that resist (Section 6.2).

    Once mended, the rule on independent coins is valid on most uncertified examples, and on no certified one at any mending radius we tried (Appendix S4.3). The theorems explain this failure without forcing it at our threshold: mending gives a generator on independent coins the pipeline’s reach as its radius (Proposition 1(a)), and at that reach the floor for a generator with the example’s statistics lies below the threshold on every certified example (Appendix B.9).

    The failure is not peculiar to learning. The min-coin copy, which attains the floor’s order, is valid after mending on none of the certified examples at radii up to 128, while at radius 64 it is already valid on 19 examples that do not resist (Appendix S4.2). On Wall it is still invalid at radius 512, and if its rate kept falling as 1/r it would reach the threshold only near radius 2 700.

    Sampled from noise alone, the diffusion model fails on every certified example but also on most of the uncertified controls that the independent-coin rule makes valid, so at its training budget it cannot test the certificate’s selectivity (Table S8).

    Mending stalls on the certified examples for the reason the theorems give. At the radii we examined, most instances it cannot complete hold a witness, two frozen patches on one line whose values of the quantity no valid filling can join (Figure 2(d), Table S2).

    The eight resistant examples without a certificate show no quantity carried along a line. They stay uncertified when the search widens to larger patches, knight-move directions and tall strips (Appendix F). In the worlds of Wave Function Collapse, a global solver, the dependence between 3×3 windows persists to 64 cells along the quantity’s direction on every certified example but Skyline2, and along no direction on the eight without one (Appendix F.1). Whatever constrains them is not a quantity carried along a line, at least not one visible at the patch sizes and distances we measured.

    6.2 Local generators given the certificate’s input

    The input often carries validity by itself, on ten of the twelve certified examples that receive one. The copier, which exists where the rows glue (Section 4), leaves no forbidden window on any of its seven examples even before mending (Table S13). Where the example is one period of its phase, as on Fabric, RedMaze and SimpleMaze, reading it at the coordinates the phase channels give yields the tiled example; on SmileCity, whose example spans several periods, it does not (Appendix S3).

    Given the input, the method is valid on 11 of the 13 certified examples, all of which defeat the rule on independent coins (Figure 4). The octaves, which include coins shared along whole rows, already give six of them; the input adds six, Wall among them, and loses 3Bricks. On Fabric, by Proposition 1(c), every rule on the octaves that matches the example’s statistics has a floor above the threshold before mending, though not after (Appendix B.9), while given the phase channels the rule leaves nothing to mend. With the octaves where nothing is certified, the method is valid on 45 of the 52 public examples, against 28 for the rule on independent coins.

    On most of the certified examples the theorems set the method’s worlds beyond the reach of independent coins. On nine certified examples no canvas of the method keeps a forbidden window (Table 5, Figure 5). On Wall and five others the program of Section 3 stays positive at the canvases’ largest distance from the example’s statistics, so no generator on independent coins free of forbidden windows comes as close at any depth (Theorem 2); on Fabric, RedMaze and SimpleMaze the method’s world is the tiled example, which no such generator reaches in any case. On the other three the statistics lie too far for Theorem 2. There Theorem 1 still requires a generator on independent coins whose most common row type is no more common than in the method’s worlds to leave at least four forbidden windows per canvas in expectation, but at the pipeline’s reach it forces each one only somewhere along a stretch longer than a canvas is wide, so a clean canvas is weak evidence there.

    The method holds up on examples that shaped nothing in the procedure. It is valid on every certified example whose failures played no part in designing it (Section 4) but SmileCity, and on all five examples we drew or transposed for the test: three walls, two of them transposed so that their invariant runs along columns, and two mazes, one certified. On transposed Wall and on the certified maze the octaves alone fail (Appendix E). It leaves 3Bricks and SmileCity invalid: on SmileCity the rule mixes two lattices of faces along the rows, which no finite patch certifies (Appendix S3), and on 3Bricks one of its three canvases stays just above the threshold (Appendix S6.9).

    Examples that we neither drew nor tuned against test the procedure from further outside. We ran it unchanged on 27 example images from eight other open-source implementations of Wave Function Collapse and related generators (Appendix E), and the method is valid on 21 of them, more than the octave rule or independent coins (Table S11). The certified examples carry the difference: the method is valid on all four that receive an input and the octave rule on one, though on three of them, each one period of a pattern, the method’s world is the tiled example. Where nothing is certified the method is the octave rule, which does about as well there as tiles of the example shifted block by block under the same mender.

    6.3 What a learned rule adds

    What does a learned rule add to an input that already carries validity? Where a copier exists, the input alone makes the worlds valid, and a block solver without learning, run on the copier’s canvases, makes them new as well. The copier is valid on all seven examples where it exists (Section 6.2) but copies: every row of its canvases is a row of the example up to a horizontal shift (Table S13). The rule composes its rows instead: on Wall none of the rows inside its courses is a row of the example (Table S14), and on every example with a row invariant none of its 16×16 patches that hold no forbidden window before mending occurs in the tiled example (Table S15). The composition is therefore the rule’s own, and on Flowers, MoreFlowers and Skyline, where mending touches almost every patch, the mender’s as well.

    A block solver without learning composes as well once it starts from the copier’s canvases. The re-solved copier re-solves every block of such a canvas in two passes on the random-access block solver’s lattice. It starts from a canvas without forbidden windows, and each re-solve keeps every window it touches allowed and always has a completion, the block’s current content, so it leaves no forbidden window on any seed. As in the rule’s worlds, none of its rows with more than one color is a row of the example, and its statistics lie closer to the example’s than the rule’s on all but Platformer (Table S13).

    The layout of rows is the sampler’s, which draws a new sequence of row types from each seed. Every filler that reads it follows it, while the block solvers run from the tiled example keep the tiling’s sequence on every seed, since a block re-solved under frozen surroundings cannot change a row’s type (Appendix S6.5). On Wall none of the method’s canvases has the tiling’s sequence and no two agree up to a shift; only the rows around the band anchors share their type on every canvas (Figure S4). The method’s normalized agreement with the tiling is 0.09, where an i.i.d. draw scores zero and the tiling one, against 0.67 for the random-access block solver (Table S16).

    On Wall the rule’s statistics lie farther from the example’s than either copier’s, mostly because its bricks run longer (Table S14). A sampler written by hand composes less well: the Metropolis filler, which composes on the row types and reads far beyond the rule’s radius, is valid on four of the examples with a row invariant, and the rule on seven (Appendix S6.4).

    Learning adds something of its own where nothing is certified, as the prior from which one mender starts. From the octave rule the mender makes 34 of the 39 uncertified examples valid, and from any prior without learning that we gave it no more than 23, the count of block-shifted tiles (Appendices S6.3 and S4.2). On the examples from other implementations the octave rule leads block-shifted tiles where nothing is certified only by a single example (Section 6.2). The block solvers need no prior and are valid on the uncertified examples by construction, and where the octave rule is valid at mending radius 8, mostly on uncertified examples, the random-access block solver varies about as much as the rule and keeps a little more of the tiling’s layout (Appendix S6.5).

    Most of the rule’s validity comes with the mender. Before mending the method is valid on 4 of the 52 examples, City, Fabric, RedMaze and SimpleMaze. On the examples it makes valid, mending rewrites a median of 18% of the cells (Figure 4), and almost every rewritten cell would make a window forbidden if its old color returned (Appendix S6.1).

    6.4 Random access after mending

    Mending keeps random access once each chunk carries a margin as wide as a mending change can travel, at most 760 cells. Every input channel is a function of the seed and the coordinates, so chunks agree before mending, and the mender seeds every solve by the seed, its block’s absolute coordinates and the cluster’s index (Appendix S1.3). A narrower margin sufficed on every canvas we tested: at 256 cells each agrees cell for cell with its separately mended chunks (Appendix S6.7). On twelve canvases 2048 cells wide, whose edge lies beyond a mending change’s reach of the chunk, so that the chunk sees the values of the unbounded world, the agreement holds at each margin we tried, from 256 to 760 cells. At 256 cells a chunk of 256² cells generates and mends 9 times its own area, and 48 times at the margin the construction guarantees; the ratio falls as chunks grow.

    A mender of longer reach makes more examples valid, at a wider margin. Mending within radius 48 instead of 24 widens the guaranteed margin from 760 to 1528 cells and adds Skew1 and ScaledMaze, valid on all eight canvases and without copying, for 47 of the 52 public examples. A mender close to a global solver also makes Mountains and SmileCity valid, with window statistics about 2.1 times as far from the example’s, and still leaves Lake and Link2 invalid (Appendix S6.8).

    6.5 A diffusion model given the input

    Does the input help a learned generator of another kind? It does for the convolutional diffusion model of Section 5. From noise alone, where Theorem 1 binds it at its radius and Corollary 2 at any number of steps, the model is valid on none of the twelve certified examples that receive an input (Section 6.1). Given the input, it is valid after mending on eight of them at both training seeds. It follows the input: on all twelve the quantity switches value along its direction at least ten times less often than from noise alone, and on Wall its share of forbidden windows before mending falls from 0.22 to 0.012, near the method’s.

    Where the model is valid and its worlds can differ from the tiling, it does not copy. On Fabric, RedMaze and SimpleMaze, whose valid worlds are essentially translates of the tiling (Appendix S2.3), its world is the tiled example, as the method’s is. On the other five it makes valid, few of its 16×16 patches occur in the tiled example and none of its rows with more than one color is a row of the example, while every row of the copier’s canvases is (Table S8). It falls short of the method only on Skyline and Skyline2, where it leaves about five times as many forbidden windows before mending as the method and stays invalid after mending (Appendix S5).

    7 Related work

    Constrained content.

    Wave Function Collapse [(Gumin, 2016)] and model synthesis [(Merrell, 2009; Merrell & Manocha, 2011)] are read as constraint solving [(Karth & Smith, 2017)] and extended with a hierarchy [(Nie et al., 2024)] or with learned constraints or orders of collapse [(Bhaumik et al., 2026; Yiu et al., 2025)], and neural cellular automata enforce the constraints with a mixed-integer program [(Zhang et al., 2023)], all by global search; our generators are local.

    Random access.

    Non-parametric texture synthesis [(Efros & Leung, 1999)] is sequential. Wang tiles [(Cohen et al., 2003; Wei, 2004; Lagae & Dutré, 2006)], by-example noise [(Heitz & Neyret, 2018)] and parallel synthesis [(Lefebvre & Hoppe, 2005)] compute any part of an unbounded texture on its own, and InfinityGAN [(Lin et al., 2022)] and InfiniteDiffusion [(Goslin, 2026)] learn random access without hard constraints. Constrained worlds are grown in the order of exploration [(Kleineberg, 2019)] or re-solved block by block [(Boris the Brave, 2021; Kleineberg, 2023)], after model synthesis [(Merrell, 2009)], over a known-good background that [Boris the Brave (2021)] makes optional at the cost of its fallback for failed blocks. Here an input named by the example lets local generators meet the constraint.

    Local computation.

    The K-valid colorings form a subshift of finite type [(Lind & Marcus, 1995)]. Classifications of locally checkable labelings on grids [(Brandt et al., 2017; Grebík & Rozhoň, 2023; Berlow et al., 2025)] and local mending [(Balliu et al., 2022)] describe what rules of bounded radius with coins can satisfy [(Luby, 1986; Jeavons et al., 2016, after)]. [Balliu et al. (2025)] separate shared from private randomness with grids on which every row must output one bit: with private coins and too few rounds to see a whole row, its nodes can agree only by fixing the bit by their vertical position, while with shared randomness each node reads the shared bit at its row. Theorem 3 finds this dichotomy for every quantity that validity carries along an axis, at any depth, with the example’s statistics in place of their adversarial input. Finitary codings [(Holroyd et al., 2017; Spinka, 2020)] let the radius be random but almost surely finite, and finitely dependent colorings [(Holroyd & Liggett, 2016)] ask only for independence at a distance. Local computation algorithms [(Rubinfeld et al., 2011)], local access to huge random objects [(Goldreich et al., 2010; Biswas et al., 2020)] and perfect sampling of infinite Gibbs measures [(Anand & Jerrum, 2022)] answer local queries about one consistent sample. Height functions and tiling groups [(Conway & Lagarias, 1990; Thurston, 1990)] carry quantities like ours along paths and give criteria for whether a region can be tiled; we find ours by searching the example. These concern satisfiability or a given measure, not an example’s statistics.

    Local samplers.

    Short-range denoisers can miss long-range structure [(Montanari, 2023, Section 6)]: a local denoiser succeeds once its radius exceeds the data’s Markov length by a logarithmic factor, and fails where that length diverges [(Hu et al., 2025)]. Trained denoisers are local in practice [(Niedoba et al., 2025; Lukoianov et al., 2025)], and by locality and equivariance convolutional diffusion models sample locally consistent mosaics of training patches [(Kamb & Ganguli, 2025)]. By Corollary 2, such a sampler, run on the whole plane from independent noise, cannot be both free of forbidden windows and faithful where validity carries a quantity that the statistics make vary. Sampling can need far more rounds than constructing: a uniform independent set needs rounds of the order of the diameter on some graphs, though the empty set is one [(Feng et al., 2017)]. Gibbs measures have related limits [(van den Berg & Steif, 1999)], and for diffusion models, generating scale by scale eases the sampling of long-range structure [(Guth et al., 2022)].

    Shared inputs.

    Seeded noise sums octaves of interpolated gradients hashed on integer lattices [(Perlin, 1985; Perlin, 2002; Lagae et al., 2010)], and our octaves are such noise without interpolation. Learned generators of unbounded images draw multiscale randomness too [(Skorokhodov et al., 2021; Henzler et al., 2020)]. [Bergmann et al. (2017)] observed that a texture generator on independent noise with a limited receptive field [(Jetchev et al., 2016)] is a mixing process that cannot align distant regions, and gave theirs a global channel and periodic channels with a random phase, which for a phase is the input Theorem 3 asks for. Under a hard constraint we bound the defects that independent noise costs, find in the example which shared input a generator needs, and show that a generator free of forbidden windows can vary the quantity between worlds only through randomness shared along the axis. The row-type sampler combines the recursive method of random generation [(Nijenhuis & Wilf, 1978; Flajolet et al., 1994)] with counter-based random numbers [(Salmon et al., 2011)], and the certificate sets the period of our phase channels and the sampler’s automaton.

    Learning from one image.

    Neural cellular automata learn update rules from one target [(Mordvintsev et al., 2020; Niklasson et al., 2021)] or generate levels under quality-diversity search [(Earle et al., 2022)], SinGAN [(Shaham et al., 2019)] and TOAD-GAN [(Awiszus et al., 2020)] learn from one image or level, and a diffusion sampler with a closed-form patch denoiser needs no training [(Qiu et al., 2026)]. Run for a fixed number of steps on coins indexed by position, a texture automaton is a local generator with random access, as ours is, but none of these works holds its output to a hard constraint.

    8 Limitations

    We built the certificate search, the inputs and the training recipe on the public examples, and widened the search after its first count (Section 6.1), so the counts on them show agreement on the corpus the procedure was built on rather than a test on new examples. Even the certified examples whose failures shaped none of it test it only within that corpus, and on most of them the octave rule alone is valid as well. The tests from outside it are the five examples we drew or transposed, where the input decides the outcome on two, and the 27 examples from other implementations, where it decides the outcome only on GbLattice, GbTriangles and GbZigzag, each one period of a pattern and all from one repository (Section 6.2).

    The certificate is one-sided: an uncertified example may carry a quantity that the search does not cover, and a certified example may carry a second quantity that no input of the procedure fixes, as SmileCity does (Section 4). The worlds of a global solver show no persistent dependence on the resistant examples without a certificate, but that test can miss a quantity, as it misses the certified Skyline2’s (Appendix F.1). Theorem 4 needs the example’s rows to glue, which they do not on 3Bricks; whether other rows realize its row types there, and which condition is necessary as well as sufficient, is open (Appendix C). The procedure has no input for a one-way quantity or for an invariant along a diagonal, so on Town and on GbDiamond the method is the octave rule, and every certified invariant in the corpus runs along rows, so only the transposed walls test the procedure along columns (Section 6.2).

    The phase channels fix the layout to the coordinates, so on Fabric and the mazes every coin seed we drew gives the same canvas, though worlds with their statistics leave a seed little to choose beyond the translate (Appendix S2.3). An offset hashed from the seed, a coin shared over the plane and so allowed by Theorem 3, would let the seed place the phase or the anchor rows of the row-type sampler and keep random access; we did not train with one. Mending rewrites cells with Wave Function Collapse’s completions, and we have not divided the credit for validity between the rule and the mender on each example (Section 6.3). A mender of longer reach adds valid examples only at a wider margin, and on Lake and Link2 none that we ran gives valid worlds (Section 6.4). Validity allows up to one forbidden window in a thousand on each canvas, a threshold we chose; Figure 4 shows the examples on which no canvas keeps one.

    Each count rests on one training run per example and on three canvases. Trained from two more seeds, the method stays valid at both on ten of the eleven certified examples it makes valid at the first, and at each new seed the octave rule is valid on slightly fewer examples than at the first (Table S10). Judged on eight canvases instead of three, the method is no longer valid on Skyline2 and Town (Appendix S6.1). At the reach of the whole pipeline, clean canvases set the method apart from generators on independent coins only weakly (Section 6.2). The diffusion model ran at one training budget (Appendix S5). We ran one window size, N=3, without symmetry variants, and only in two dimensions but for one maze of voxels (Appendix S2.4).

    9 Conclusion

    A local generator needs more than independent coins to make the worlds that some examples allow. When validity carries a quantity along an axis and the example’s statistics make it vary, no generator on independent coins is both free of forbidden windows and faithful to the statistics, however far each cell reads, and at a finite radius its defects fall only as the inverse of the radius, an order that is attained. A certificate computed from the example finds such a quantity on most of the public examples that resist independent coins and on none of the others, and on examples from other implementations it again certifies only examples that resist. An input that distant cells share escapes the bound without giving up random access, and at any depth a generator free of forbidden windows needs one to vary the quantity between worlds; where the example’s rows glue, as on every example with a row invariant but 3Bricks, the row types drawn from the seed and the position are enough. Copying the example along this input already gives valid worlds on all but two of the certified examples that receive it, and a learned cellular automaton or a convolutional diffusion model given it becomes valid on most of them, where on independent coins it is valid on none. Learning adds something of its own where nothing is certified, as the prior from which a mender starts, though a block solver started from the tiled example is valid there by construction. The learned rule needs a mender that rewrites part of each world, and regions mended separately are guaranteed to agree once each carries a margin as wide as a mending change can travel. What stays open is structure that the certificate does not name, such as the lattice of SmileCity’s faces, an input for a quantity that can change only one way or that runs along a diagonal, and a condition for worlds free of forbidden windows where the rows do not glue, as on 3Bricks.

    Appendix A Random access in detail

    One setting for every example.

    The repository sets the window size and the symmetry variants per example. We read every example periodically, at window size N=3 and with no symmetry variants, one setting for all, so that no example gets a setting chosen for it. The images are the repository’s samples; its README credits the people and games they come from.

    Periods.

    Let T be the longest finite side of the blocks of the pairs in A. A shift by a vector of Tℤ² maps every block of every pair onto a block of the same pair, so it permutes the coins without changing their law, and the output commutes with it. Since block boundaries are fixed in absolute coordinates, a generator on the scale pairs alone is translation-equivariant under these shifts and in general under no other; one in the general form commutes with the shifts by common multiples of T and p that map every further lattice onto itself. In practice the coins are hashes of the seed, the coarsened cell and a channel index, computed where they are needed. A rule that applies a radius-one update for R rounds to coins alone is a random-access generator of radius R; ours reads 24 scale pairs besides the cell’s own coins, with period T=16 (Section 4). The row-type sampler draws the row types of a band of L rows from that band’s coins at a cost proportional to L, and the phase channels are functions of the coordinates, so both fit the general form of Definition 1.

    The three properties.

    Any region S is computed from the coins read on S and on a margin of width r, with a fixed number of hashes per cell wherever S lies, a coin of whole rows being one hash however long the rows. Independent computations of overlapping regions hash the same coins at the same cells, so they agree cell for cell: seams are exact, and many machines generate one world with nothing shared but the seed. An edit that overrides the coins read in S, giving the cells of S new values of every coin they read while every other cell keeps its coins, changes the output only within distance r of S, so edits are contained; redrawing a coin that a whole block shares can instead change the output anywhere within distance r of the block.

    The mended output.

    A random-access generator must satisfy K from what it sees within distance r of each cell, and the last step of our pipeline reaches farther. The mender (Section 5) re-solves the defects that the rule leaves, block by block on a lattice fixed in absolute coordinates and with randomness hashed from the seed and the block coordinates, so its output depends on a cell’s position modulo twice the block size as well as on the coins, and a change it makes can travel beyond the rule’s radius. The mended output has a reach, a distance beyond which no coin can change a cell’s mended color, and we call such a construction random access in the extended sense: it is a generator in the general form of Definition 1 with its reach in place of the radius r, so the three properties hold with the reach as the margin, and Proposition 1 covers it. Appendix S1.3 bounds the reach of our pipeline, and Section 6.4 measures the smaller margin at which every canvas we tested agrees.

    Appendix B Proofs

    Throughout, K⊆[C]^N×N is the set of allowed windows, a coloring is x:ℤ²→[C], Q^Pᵥ(x) is the P×P patch of x whose corner is v, and Wᵥ(x)=Q^Nᵥ(x) is the window at v. A generator on independent coins of radius r is a translation-equivariant map from i.i.d. coins (ωᵥ) to X with Xᵥ a fixed function of the coins within ℓ_∞ distance r of v (Definition 2). The law of X is then translation-invariant.

    B.1 The full labeling

    For a weakly connected component c of G_P,e, give each edge (a,b) the weight +1 and let d_c be the greatest common divisor of the signed lengths of the closed walks of c that may traverse edges in either direction (d_c=0 when every such walk has signed length zero, so that c has no directed cycle). Fixing a root, every patch of c gets a level modulo d_c, and φ(a)=(c,level) with σ(c,i)=(c,i+1\bmodd_c) is a transported quantity on all of V_P, with no exception for edges that enter or leave a strongly connected component. Invariants are the case of several components; phases the case d_c≥2. Table 4 reports constants for this labeling.

    B.2 Theorem 1

    Let k=2r+P and uⱼ=je for j=0,…,k. Write A for the event that the patches Q^P_uⱼ(X) are locally valid for every j. On A, each pair of consecutive patches agrees on its overlap, so it is an edge of G_P,e and φ(Q^P_uⱼ₊₁)=σ(φ(Q^P_uⱼ)); hence φ(Q^P_uₖ)=σᵏ(φ(Q^P_u₀)). The patch at u₀ is a function of the coins in the box [-r,P-1+r] along e, and the patch at uₖ of the coins in [k-r,k+P-1+r]; since k≥2r+P the two boxes are disjoint, and the two patches are independent. Writing p⁽ᵛ⁾ for the law of φ at v on the event that the patch is locally valid, translation invariance gives p^(u₀)=p^(uₖ)=p, so

    \Pr[A] ≤ ∑ₛpₛ p_σᵏ(s) ≤ \maxₜpₜ∑ₛpₛ ≤ \maxₜpₜ.

    If A fails, some patch on the segment contains a forbidden window. A patch contains (P-N+1)² windows, so \Pr[Q^Pᵥ∉V_P]≤(P-N+1)²ε, and a union bound over the k+1 patches gives 1-\maxₜpₜ≤\Pr[Aᶜ]≤(k+1)(P-N+1)²ε, which is the claim. ∎

    For a one-way quantity, write s\leadstot when component t is reachable from component s in G_P,e, with s\leadstos. The same steps give, on A, that φ(Q^P_uₖ) is reachable from φ(Q^P_u₀), so \Pr[A]≤∑_s\leadstotpₛ pₜ by independence, and the union bound gives

    ε ≥ (1-∑_s\leadstotpₛ pₜ)/((2r+P+1)(P-N+1)²).

    For an invariant or a phase the only pairs allowed are t=σᵏ(s), the sum is at most \maxₛpₛ, and this is the bound of Theorem 1. Appendix B.5 bounds the numerator for a one-way quantity from below by the constant κ(δ).

    B.3 Inequality (1)

    For P=N the patch is the window, so pₛ=h({w∈K:φ(w)=s}), where h is the law of W₀(X) on all of [C]^N×N. Since f puts no mass outside K, h(B)≤f(B)+δ for every set B of windows, with δ the total variation between h and f; pooling the forbidden windows into one outcome, as Section 2 does, leaves this total variation unchanged, for the same reason. Hence \maxₛpₛ≤\maxₛf(φ=s)+δ, and Theorem 1 with P=N gives ε(2r+N+1)≥κ_f-δ. ∎

    B.4 Corollary 1

    The proof of Theorem 1 uses only the overlap graph of the locally valid patches, so it holds with K₀=K∖J in place of K, a window being forbidden for K₀ when it lies outside K₀. Let h be the law of the window of X at a cell, and write D=2r+N+1 and Bₛ={w∈K₀:φ(w)=s}. The windows outside K₀ have density ε+h(J), and at P=N the theorem gives (ε+h(J))D≥1-h(Bₛ) for the value s with the largest h(Bₛ). As in the proof of inequality (1), h(B)≤f(B)+δ for every set B of windows in K. Applied to J∪Bₛ, this gives h(Bₛ)≤θ+(1-κ_J)+δ-h(J), so εD≥κ_J-θ-δ-(D-1)h(J); applied to J, it gives h(J)≤θ+δ. Hence εD≥κ_J-(θ+δ)D, which is the claim. When J is empty, h(J)=0 and the first step with h(Bₛ)≤1-κ_f+δ gives inequality (1). ∎

    B.5 The linear program

    Let P≥N. A distribution q on V_P is stationary if every (P-1)×P pattern has the same mass as the first P-1 rows of a patch and as its last P-1 rows, and every P×(P-1) pattern the same mass as the first P-1 columns and as the last P-1 columns. The N×N window then has the same law at every position in the patch, and we call it the N×N marginal of q. For a translation-invariant random coloring X without defects, the law of Q^P₀(X) is a stationary distribution on V_P, since the patches at 0 and at a unit vector have the same law and share all but one row or column, and its N×N marginal is the window law of X. The constant κ(δ) of Section 3 is one minus the largest occupancy q(φ=s) over the values s and the stationary q whose N×N marginal lies within δ of f in total variation, a linear program for each value. Such an X whose window statistics lie within δ of f therefore has \maxₛpₛ≤1-κ(δ).

    A one-way quantity. When φ is the strongly connected component, let fₛ be the example’s share of patches in component s. The example’s constant is κ_f=1-∑_s\leadstotfₛfₜ, and for such a quantity κ(δ) names a lower bound on 1-∑_s\leadstotpₛpₜ that the program gives: the sum, over ordered pairs of components visited by the example with t not reachable from s, of the products of the smallest occupancies the program allows to s and to t. It is a lower bound because ∑ₛpₛ≤1 gives 1-∑_s\leadstotpₛpₜ≥∑_s\not\leadstotpₛpₜ, with equality when no patch has a defect, and because for a coloring without defects whose window statistics lie within δ of f each pₛ is at least the smallest occupancy the program allows to s.

    With defects. For P≥N, let q be the law of Q^P₀(X) on all P×P colorings and q_V its restriction to V_P, of mass 1-β with β≤(P-N+1)²ε. Translation invariance makes q exactly stationary, so for each (P-1)×P or P×(P-1) sub-pattern the masses that q_V gives it from the two sides differ in total by at most 2β; and the N×N marginal of q_V is within δ+β of f in total variation. Let κ(δ,η) be one minus the largest occupancy of any single value of φ over nonnegative q on V_P with total mass in [1-η,1], stationarity violated by at most 2η in total, and N×N marginal within δ+η of f. It is a linear program, decreasing in η, and κ(δ,0)=κ(δ) is the constant above. Then \maxₛpₛ≤1-κ(δ,β), and Theorem 1 gives, for any η₀≥0,

    ε≥\min{η₀/(P-N+1)²,(κ(δ,η₀))/((2r+P+1)(P-N+1)²)}.

    The program over exactly stationary measures, η=0, is what Table 4 reports. The table has 14 rows with an invariant or a phase: the 12 certified examples with one, and Chess and Stripes, two controls whose only K-valid colorings are the two phases of a period-two pattern (Appendix S2.4). With defects allowed at η₀=0.01 and δ=0.05, the program stays positive on 14 of these rows, with a smallest value of 0.030 on Skyline2, so a generator whose statistics lie within that slack has a defect density of order 1/r with that constant. For P=N the program is stricter than inequality (1), which gives κ_f-δ: on Skyline2, κ(0.05) is 0.047 against κ_f-0.05=0.015. ∎

    B.6 Theorem 2

    Let τ be the translation by e and τ^′ the unit translation orthogonal to it. A factor of i.i.d. coins is mixing under the action of ℤ², since the coins are, and mixing passes to factors. As the ℤ² action is mixing, every sub-action generated by a single nonzero translation is mixing as well, and hence ergodic; in particular τ^D is ergodic for every D≥1. On the event, of probability one, that X is K-valid, every patch is locally valid and consecutive patches along e form edges of G_P,e.

    Invariants and phases. Under the full labeling φ=(c,z) with σ(c,z)=(c,z+1\bmodd_c). Let ψ(v)=σ⁻ʲ(φ(Q^Pᵥ(X))) for v=je+v^′ with v^′ on the line through the origin orthogonal to e; along every line parallel to e, ψ is constant. Let λ be its value on the line through the origin. A component with d_c=0 has no directed cycle and so carries no bi-infinite walk. The patches along a line parallel to e in a K-valid coloring form such a walk, so they lie in one component, with d_c≥1, whose levels modulo d_c are finitely many, and λ takes finitely many values; let D be a common multiple of the d_c≥1, so that σ^D is the identity. Then λ(τ^DX)=λ(X), so each event {λ=s} is τ^D-invariant and has probability zero or one: λ is almost surely a constant s₀. Since τX has the law of X and λ(τX)=σ(λ(X)), also σ(s₀)=s₀, which forces d_c₀=1 for the component c₀ of s₀. The line through τ^′ m of the origin has the law of the line through the origin, so its value is s₀ almost surely too, for every m, and φ=s₀ at every cell almost surely.

    One-way quantities. Let φ be the strongly connected component, and m the number of components. Along a line it never returns to a component it has left, so it changes at most m-1 times on the whole line. If q is the probability that it changes between v and v+e, the expected number of changes on a segment of n steps is nq by stationarity, and it is at most m-1 for every n; so q=0, and φ is constant along lines almost surely. It is then an invariant, and the argument above makes it a single value at every cell.

    Statistics. With φ concentrated on one value, \maxₛpₛ=1, while every stationary distribution without defects whose window marginal is within δ of f has \maxₛpₛ≤1-κ(δ) (for a one-way quantity, 1-∑_s\leadstotpₛpₜ≥κ(δ), and concentration makes the left side zero). The law of X is such a distribution when its window statistics are within δ of f, so κ(δ)>0 rules this out. For P=N, pₛ≤f(φ=s)+δ as in the proof of inequality (1), so 1≤1-κ_f+δ, that is, δ≥κ_f. ∎

    B.7 Proposition 1

    In full, part (c) reads as follows. Suppose every block has length at most T along e and the lattice has period T along e, where a coin shared along a whole line orthogonal to e, or along a group of consecutive such lines, counts as a block, and let Xᵥ also read coins shared along whole lines parallel to e, or along groups of consecutive such lines, and over the whole plane. Take φ under the full labeling, let D≥1 be a common multiple of the positive values of d_c, let μ be the probability, averaged over the cells of one period of the lattice, that a cell’s patch is locally valid and lies in a component c whose d_c does not divide T, d_c=0 included. Then

    ε ≥ (μ)/(2 (2r+(D+1)T+P) (P-N+1)²).

    Part (a) gives no floor when the quantity is fixed by position, and blocks fixed in absolute coordinates tell a rule its position, since it sees the coins change at a block boundary. A rule that leaves no forbidden window must fix the quantity by position. Two cells far apart along e read disjoint sets of coins, apart from coins shared along whole lines or over the plane, so given those shared coins their values of the quantity are independent; validity along the line between them makes each value determine the other; and two independent values that determine each other are constant. Each value is therefore fixed by the cell’s position within the lattice’s period and by the shared coins, so the law of the layout repeats with period T along e, which a phase of period d allows without defects only when d divides T. When it does not, (c) gives a floor of the same order as (a), in proportion to the mass μ of the components whose period does not divide T; when P=N and the window statistics lie within δ of the example’s, μ is at least the example’s mass less δ. A coin shared along a whole line, ℓ=∞, escapes (a): two cells of the line read the same coin however far apart they are, so they can agree on an invariant along that line with no defect between them, while different lines carry different values. The construction in (b) copies the example on every block, so it says nothing about variation.

    (a) Follow the proof of Theorem 1 with k=ℓ+2r+P. The patch at u₀ reads the independent coins in the box [-r,P-1+r] along e and the coins of the blocks that meet it; the patch at uₖ those of [k-r,k+P-1+r]. A block meeting both boxes would cover the k-2r-P+2=ℓ+2 cells from P-1+r to k-r, which no block of length at most ℓ does, so the two patches are again independent. The law of X is now invariant only under the lattice’s periods, so the laws p^(u₀) and p^(uₖ) may differ; with p^* the largest p⁽ᵛ⁾ₛ over cells and values, \Pr[A]≤∑ₛp^(u₀)ₛ p^(uₖ)_σᵏ(s)≤p^*. Average the union bound over the starting cell u in one period of the lattice: the average of \Pr[Q^Pᵥ∉V_P] over a period is at most (P-N+1)²ε, with ε the density of forbidden windows, so 1-p^*≤(k+1)(P-N+1)²ε. The one-way version and inequality (1) follow as before, with δ the largest distance from f of the window statistics at a single cell.

    (b) Since K and f are read from the example with wrap-around, tiling the plane with the example leaves no forbidden window and gives the example’s window frequencies. A window inside one block is a window of the tiling at a uniformly random translation, whose law is f, and it is allowed. A window meets two blocks only if its corner lies within N-1 cells of a block’s boundary along one of the two axes, which holds for a share at most 2(N-1)/ℓ of cells. Hence ε≤2(N-1)/ℓ, and the window law averaged over cells is within 2(N-1)/ℓ of f in total variation.

    (c) Let G be the coins shared along whole lines parallel to e or along groups of consecutive such lines, and over the plane. All coins are independent, so given G the other coins are still independent with their own laws. The translation by Te fixes every coin of G and permutes the other coins, cell coins to cell coins and the coin of every block, a group of lines orthogonal to e included, to the coin of its translate, a block of the same kind, since the lattice has period T along e; it therefore preserves their joint law, given G as well. As X commutes with that translation, the conditional probabilities qₛ(v)=\Pr[Q^Pᵥ∈V_P, φ(Q^Pᵥ)=s|G] satisfy qₛ(v+Te)=qₛ(v). Let k be the smallest integer with k≡1\pmodD and kT≥2r+T+P; then kT+1≤2r+(D+1)T+P, since k lies within D-1 of ⌈(2r+T+P)/T⌉. Let uₖ=u₀+kTe. As in (a), the patches at u₀ and uₖ read disjoint sets of coins outside G, so they are independent given G. On the event A that every patch on the segment between them is locally valid, φ(Q^P_uₖ)=σᵏᵀ(φ(Q^P_u₀)). Hence, with q=q(u₀),

    \Pr[A|G] ≤ ∑ₛqₛ q_σᵏᵀ(s).

    On a component with d_c≥1, σᵏᵀ=σᵀ, since kT≡T modulo d_c. If d_c divides T, σᵏᵀ fixes every value, and the terms add to at most the component’s mass Q_c=∑_s∈cqₛ. If it does not, σᵏᵀ=σᵀ shifts the level by T\bmodd_c≠0; if d_c=0, the level is an integer and σᵏᵀ shifts it by kT≥1. In both cases σᵏᵀ maps the component’s values one to one and moves every value, and for any such map π, (∑ₛqₛ)²≥∑ₛqₛ²+∑ₛqₛ q_π(s)≥2∑ₛqₛ q_π(s): the pairs (s,π(s)) are distinct and off the diagonal, and qₛ q_π(s)≤(qₛ²+q_π(s)²)/2. Those terms add to at most Q_c²/2≤Q_c/2. So \Pr[A|G]≤1-μ_G/2, with μ_G the conditional mass at u₀ of the components whose d_c does not divide T, and taking expectations, \Pr[Aᶜ] is at least half the probability that the patch at u₀ is locally valid with φ in such a component. Averaging the union bound over u₀ in one period of the lattice, as in (a), gives μ/2≤(kT+1)(P-N+1)²ε, a floor slightly sharper than the statement’s, which Appendix B.9 evaluates. ∎

    B.8 Proposition 2

    Let ωᵥ=(Uᵥ,tᵥ), with Uᵥ uniform on [0,1] and tᵥ uniform over one period of the tiling Y, all independent. Let Bᵣ(v)={v+u:∥u∥_∞≤r}, let mᵥ be the cell of smallest priority in Bᵣ(v) (ties have probability zero), and let Xᵥ=Y(v-mᵥ+t_mᵥ). Then Xᵥ is a fixed function of the coins in Bᵣ(v), and shifting all coins by a vector shifts X by the same vector, so the min-coin copy is a generator on independent coins of radius r.

    Fix a window, the N×N square W of cells with corner w. The boxes Bᵣ(v), v∈W, have as their union a square U of side 2r+N and as their intersection a square I of side 2r+2-N, which is not empty since r≥N. Let z be the cell of smallest priority in U. If z∈I, then z lies in every box and has the smallest priority in each, so mᵥ=z for every v∈W. Conversely, if mᵥ=z^′ for every v∈W, then z^′∈I and z^′ has the smallest priority in every box, hence in U, so z^′=z. The priorities are independent and continuous, so z is uniform on U, and the cells of W copy from one cell with probability |I|/|U|=1-qᵣ. On that event the window of X at w is the window of Y at w-z+t_z. Given the priorities, which fix z, the translation t_z is uniform over the period and independent of them, so the window is a window of the tiling at a uniform translation: it is allowed and its law is f. Hence ε≤qᵣ, and the law h of the window is (1-qᵣ)f+qᵣg for some law g, so ∥h-f∥_TV=qᵣ∥g-f∥_TV≤qᵣ. With a=(2r+2-N)/(2r+N), which lies in (0,1) since 2≤N≤r, qᵣ=(1-a)(1+a)<2(1-a)=4(N-1)/(2r+N).

    For the comparison in Section 3, let P=N. Every generator on independent coins of radius r whose window statistics lie within qᵣ of f has ε≥(κ_f-qᵣ)/(2r+N+1) by inequality (1). The map q↦q(2r+N+1)/(κ_f-q) increases on [0,κ_f), so whenever κ_f(2r+N)>4(N-1) the ratio of the min-coin copy’s ε to that floor is less than

    (4(N-1) (2r+N+1))/(κ_f (2r+N)-4(N-1)),

    which tends to 4(N-1)/κ_f as r grows. ∎

    B.9 What the bounds bind in our pipeline

    Theorems 1 and 2 bind generators on independent coins, among them the independent-coin rule of Section 3, with or without its repair rounds. They do not bind the method. Its row types and the octaves’ coins of whole rows are shared along whole lines, which escape both theorems and Proposition 1(a), and its phase channels are functions of the coordinates, which no result of Section 3 restricts. The octaves, the coins on the scale pairs that our rule reads (Section 4), fall under Proposition 1(c) as a whole: their coins of finite scale lie on blocks nested in one lattice of period T=16, and their other coins are shared along whole rows, whole columns or the plane. Among the certified examples the resulting floor binds only Fabric, whose phase has period 5, which does not divide T. There it lies above the threshold of validity before mending, and below it after. Once mended, no output has a floor from Section 3 above that threshold on any certified example, so no result there requires the mended independent-coin rule to be invalid; where we searched for witnesses, they show why it is (Section 6.1).

    These conclusions rest on the following values. The rule runs 32 rounds of a radius-one update, so its radius is 32, and each of its four repair rounds adds N cells, for a radius of 44.
