Mending at the main radius works on blocks of side ℓ=48, and its eight class steps carry a change at most 760 cells (Appendix S1.3), so the reach of the whole pipeline is r=804 cells. The threshold of validity is one forbidden window in a thousand (Section 2).

    Fabric under the octaves. Fabric’s phase has period 5 and is read off single windows, so P=N. The octaves fall under Proposition 1(c) with T=16 and D=5, and the components whose period does not divide T hold 0.60 of the example’s windows, which is μ for a rule whose window statistics match the example’s. At radius 32, k=6 and 2(kT+1)(P-N+1)²=194, so such a rule leaves at least 3.0·10⁻³ of its windows forbidden, and with its repair rounds, at radius 44, at least 1.6·10⁻³; both lie above the threshold. The mended output commutes only with shifts by common multiples of T and of twice the mender’s block, so with that period, 96 cells, in place of T and with the pipeline’s reach as the radius the floor falls to 1.5·10⁻⁴, below the threshold.

    The mended independent-coin rule. The mender’s randomness is hashed from the seed and the coordinates of its blocks, of side ℓ in both passes, so the mended output of the independent-coin rule falls under Proposition 1(a) with the pipeline’s reach as the radius. Its denominator is (2r+ℓ+P+1)(P-N+1)², which is 1660 when P=N, and its numerator is at most one, so at this reach the bound of (a) cannot reach the threshold whatever the output’s statistics. For an output that spreads the quantity at every cell as the example does and has its statistics, the numerator is the example’s own spread, which on every row of Table 4 with an invariant or a phase is the column κ(0), equal to κ_f when P=N. The floor computed from that column is not itself a column of the table, whose floor at radius 32 is that of Theorem 1 for the raw rule. Its largest value over those rows, Chess and Stripes included, is 4.6·10⁻⁴, on RedMaze.

    B.10 Two classes of constraints

    Section 3 cites the following two bounds. Let ε(r) be the smallest density of forbidden windows over generators on independent coins of radius r.

    Proposition 3(two classes).

    (a) If the locally checkable labeling of K is solvable in O(\log^*n) rounds on n×n toroidal grids, then ε(r)≤Ce⁻ᶜʳ for constants C,c>0 that depend on K. (b) If K is an agreement constraint, that is, for some P≥N every locally valid P×P patch is the restriction of one of m≥2 translates of a periodic pattern and distinct translates differ on every block of P×(P-1) or (P-1)×P cells, then ε(r)≥1/(2(2r+P+1)(P-N+1)²).

    Proof of (a).[Brandt et al. (2017)] show that such a K admits an algorithm in the normal form A^′∘Sₖ: a maximal independent set (MIS) of the k-th power of the grid, followed by a finite function of the MIS within a constant radius ρ₀. Run the MIS with fresh priorities in every round: in each round every undecided vertex draws a uniform priority from its coins; a vertex whose priority is below those of all its undecided neighbors (in the power graph, of degree Δ=(2k+1)²-1) joins the set, and its neighbors are removed. Whatever the history, the vertex’s own priority is one of at most Δ+1 fresh independent draws in its undecided closed neighborhood, so it is such a local minimum with probability at least 1/(Δ+1); hence it is still undecided after t rounds with probability at most (1-1/(Δ+1))ᵗ. After t rounds the decided vertices form an independent set that is maximal except in the neighborhoods of the vertices still undecided; decide those arbitrarily and apply A^′. A cell is defective only if some vertex within distance ρ₀+k of it is undecided, since A^′ reads the set within radius ρ₀ and the set can fail to be maximal only within distance k of an undecided vertex, so the defect density is at most C(1-1/(Δ+1))ᵗ with C=(2ρ₀+2k+1)², and the construction reads coins within radius O(kt)=r. [Brandt et al. (2017)] prove the normal form correct on all sufficiently large tori; since A^′ is a finite-radius function of an MIS of the power grid, and any finite MIS configuration of the plane extends to an MIS of a large torus (copy it with a margin of width k onto a torus large enough that the copy does not wrap onto itself, then add vertices outside the region greedily until the set is maximal), the rule is correct on the plane as well. The known rate is faster: a finitary-factor solution whose coding radius exceeds r with probability at most 1/tower(cr) exists [(Grebík & Rozhoň, 2023, Cor. 3.3)], and cutting it off at radius r gives ε(r)≤C/tower(cr).

    Proof of (b). The phase of a locally valid patch, the index of the translate it comes from, is a transported quantity along every lattice direction, with σ the permutation of translates induced by the unit shift. Since m≥2, some unit vector e is not a period of the pattern, so σ along e has no fixed point. Translation invariance gives \Pr[phase(v)=i]=\Pr[phase(v+e)=i], and the two events exclude each other, because on both of them the phase at v+e would be σ(i)≠i. Each therefore has probability at most \tfrac12, and \maxᵢpᵢ≤\tfrac12. Theorem 1 along e gives the claim. ∎

    The same argument shows that a forced edit on an agreement constraint can need an unbounded repair: pin a cell to a phase its neighborhood does not have, and any valid completion within radius ρ would have to change phase across the boundary of the ball, which the transport rules out. This is the witness of Appendix B.11 in its simplest form.

    B.11 Witnesses

    A transported quantity can also prove that a particular mending instance has no completion. A mending instance frees the cells of a region F and fixes all others, and a completion is valid if every window that touches F is allowed. Let a and b be locally valid patches at u and u+ke, entirely outside F, such that every window of the patches Q^Pᵤ₊ⱼₑ, 0≤j≤k, either touches F or lies in fixed cells and is allowed. In any valid completion every one of these patches is then locally valid, so by the argument of Theorem 1φ(b)=σᵏ(φ(a)). If φ(b)≠σᵏ(φ(a)), no valid completion exists, and we call the pair a witness: it proves without any search that the instance has no completion (Figure 2(d); Appendix S4.1 counts the witnesses on the failed instances). ∎

    B.12 A sequence of row types at finite radius

    Coins shared along whole rows can carry an invariant along rows at finite radius, once the rule turns them into an allowed sequence of row types, one in which every two consecutive types can be consecutive in a coloring free of forbidden windows. Suppose some type τ can follow itself, as the sky above a skyline can. Fix finitely many stretches, sequences of types x₁,…,xₘ such that τ,x₁,…,xₘ,τ is allowed, such as a course of bricks, and let M be the length of the longest. Give each row y a uniform coin U_y shared along the row, and call y a start if U_y

    B.13 The certificate search

    On every public example where the search of Section 4 reports a phase, and on Chess and Stripes, d_c equals the period of the strongly connected component that holds the example’s patches in c, the greatest common divisor of its cycle lengths, which d_c in general only divides, since every directed cycle is a closed walk. We also searched the two diagonals. Two patches one step apart along a diagonal leave two corner cells of their union outside both, so an edge there asks the whole box of side P+1 to be locally valid. On the public examples the diagonals certify none that the axis directions leave uncertified; among the examples from other implementations they certify GbDiamond (Appendix E). Appendix D gives the order in which the search tries patch sizes and directions.

    Appendix C Proofs of the characterization

    Theorems 1 and 2 bound generators whose distant cells share no randomness. Run given the coins that a generator shares along the quantity’s direction, their two arguments prove Theorem 3, and where the example’s rows glue, a generator that reads the row types band by band, and its position, needs nothing more (Theorem 4).

    C.1 The setting

    We read Definition 1 as follows. The input of a generator in the general form consists of finitely many families of coins. A family is a lattice of blocks fixed in absolute coordinates, every block a rectangle, possibly unbounded in one direction or in both; each block carries a vector of coins, and these vectors are i.i.d. within a family and independent across families. The cells’ own coins form one family, whose blocks are single cells, and so does every scale pair of Section 2 and every further lattice of Definition 1. Cell v reads v\bmodp and the coins of the blocks that meet the box v+[-r,r]².

    Fix an axis direction e. The extent of a family along e is the length of its blocks along e: one for the cells, 2ⁱ along rows and 2ʲ along columns for the scale pair (i,j), one or w for whole lines orthogonal to e or groups of w consecutive such lines, and infinite for whole lines parallel to e, groups of such lines and the plane. The coins shared along e, Gₑ, are the coins of the families of infinite extent along e, and we use the same symbol for the σ-field they generate. All other coins belong to families of finite extent, and ℓ in Theorem 3(b) is the largest of these extents. Throughout, a function of some coins means a measurable function of them, and equalities between random variables hold almost surely.

    For a translation t of ℤ² write τₜ for the translation of colorings, (τₜx)ᵥ=xᵥ₊ₜ, and θₜ for the translation of coins, which gives every block B the coins of B+t. As in Section 3, Λ is the lattice of translations t∈pℤ² that map the blocks of every family to blocks of the same family; it has full rank, and T is the least positive integer with Te∈Λ. For t∈Λ, cell v of X(θₜω) reads the coins that cell v+t of X(ω) reads, and v\bmodp=(v+t)\bmodp, so

    X(θₜω) = τₜ X(ω) (t∈Λ).

    		(2)

    This is what it means for X to commute with the translations in Λ. Besides the radius and the blocks read, which the counting bounds use, it is all that the proofs below use of X, so the arguments from ergodicity hold for every measurable function of the coins and of the position modulo p with this property. Since θₜ permutes the blocks of each family, it preserves the law of the coins, so the law of X is invariant under τₜ for t∈Λ, and in general under no other translation. A function a on the cells that is periodic under Λ, such as the probability that the window at v is forbidden, has an average avgᵥa(v) over the cells of one period of Λ that does not depend on the period chosen, and avgᵥa(v+u)=avgᵥa(v) for every u∈ℤ². The density of forbidden windows is ε=avgᵥ\Pr[Wᵥ(X)∉K]. For a random quantity a(v) attached to each cell, such as 1-\maxₛqₛ(v) in Theorem 3(b), we write ā=avgᵥ𝔼[a(v)]; its expectation is periodic under Λ as well, since θₜ maps the coins of Gₑ to coins of Gₑ.

    C.2 Theorem 3(b): the floor given the shared coins

    In full, part (b) reads as follows. If φ is transported, X has radius r and every block it reads whose coins are not in Gₑ has length at most ℓ along e, a cell’s own coins counting as a block of length one, then

    ε ≥ (1-\maxₛqₛ̄)/((2r+P+ℓ)(P-N+1)²),

    where qₛ(v) is the probability given Gₑ that the P×P patch of X at v is locally valid and has φ=s, and the bar takes the expectation, averaged over the cells of one period of Λ.

    The counting argument of Theorem 1 needs two patches far apart along e to be independent. Given Gₑ they are, once their distance exceeds the extent of every other block.

    Lemma 1.

    Let X have radius r, let every family outside Gₑ have extent at most ℓ along e, and let k≥2r+P+ℓ-1. For every cell v, the patches Q^Pᵥ(X) and Q^Pᵥ₊ₖₑ(X) are independent given Gₑ.

    Proof. The patch at v is a function of v\bmodp, of the coins of Gₑ and of the other coins of the blocks that meet the box v+[-r,P-1+r]², and the patch at v+ke is a function of the same kind for the box shifted by ke. Counted from v along e, the two boxes cover the positions -r to P-1+r and k-r to k+P-1+r. A block that meets both is a rectangle with a cell in each, so along e it covers every position from P-1+r to k-r, which are k-2r-P+2≥ℓ+1 positions, more than any block outside Gₑ covers. The two patches therefore read disjoint sets of coins outside Gₑ, and these coins are independent of one another and of Gₑ. ∎

    As in Theorem 3, qₛ(v) is the probability given Gₑ that Q^Pᵥ(X) is locally valid and has φ=s.

    Proposition 4(the floor given the shared coins, sharp form).

    Under the assumptions of Lemma 1, for a transported quantity φ along e with bijection σ,

    ε (k+1)(P-N+1)²(3)
    ≥ avgᵥ 𝔼[1-∑ₛqₛ(v) q_σᵏ(s)(v+ke)],

    and for a one-way quantity the same holds with ∑_s\leadstotqₛ(v) qₜ(v+ke) in place of the sum.

    Proof. Let A be the event that the k+1 patches Q^Pᵥ₊ⱼₑ(X), 0≤j≤k, are all locally valid. On A consecutive patches agree on their overlap, so they are edges of G_P,e, and φ(Q^Pᵥ₊ₖₑ(X))=σᵏ(φ(Q^Pᵥ(X))). By Lemma 1,

    \Pr[A|Gₑ]≤∑ₛ\Pr[φ(Q^Pᵥ)=s,
    φ(Q^Pᵥ₊ₖₑ)=σᵏ(s)\bigm|Gₑ]
    =∑ₛqₛ(v) q_σᵏ(s)(v+ke),

    where each event includes that both patches are locally valid. If A fails, one of the k+1 patches holds a forbidden window, and a patch holds (P-N+1)² windows, so \Pr[Aᶜ]≤∑ⱼ₌₀ᵏ∑ᵤ\Pr[Wᵥ₊ⱼₑ₊ᵤ(X)∉K], with u running over the corners of the windows of a patch. Averaged over v in one period of Λ, each of the (k+1)(P-N+1)² terms becomes ε. Hence avgᵥ𝔼[1-∑ₛqₛ(v) q_σᵏ(s)(v+ke)]≤avgᵥ\Pr[Aᶜ]≤(k+1)(P-N+1)²ε. For a one-way quantity, on A the component at v+ke is reachable from the one at v, which gives the second form in the same way. ∎

    Proof of Theorem 3(b). Since σᵏ is a bijection, ∑ₛqₛ(v) q_σᵏ(s)(v+ke)≤\maxₛqₛ(v)∑ₜqₜ(v+ke)≤\maxₛqₛ(v). With k=2r+P+ℓ-1, inequality (3) becomes the bound of Theorem 3(b). ∎

    For a one-way quantity the sum over the pairs s\leadstot can exceed \maxₛqₛ(v), so its floor is the second form of Proposition 4, as in Appendix B.2.

    Defects, fidelity and what is shared.

    Let pₛ(v)=𝔼[qₛ(v)] be the probability that the patch at v is locally valid with φ=s. The gain at v,

    I(v) = 𝔼[\maxₛqₛ(v)]-\maxₛpₛ(v) ≥ 0,

    is how much knowing Gₑ raises the chance of guessing the value of φ at v. Since 𝔼[1-\maxₛqₛ(v)]=1-\maxₛpₛ(v)-I(v), Theorem 3(b) reads ε(2r+P+ℓ)(P-N+1)²+avgᵥI(v)≥avgᵥ(1-\maxₛpₛ(v)). When P=N, let δᵥ be the total variation between the law of the window Wᵥ(X) and f, with all forbidden windows pooled into one outcome. As in the proof of inequality (1), pₛ(v)≤f(φ=s)+δᵥ, so 1-\maxₛpₛ(v)≥κ_f-δᵥ, and with δ̄=avgᵥδᵥ and Ī=avgᵥI(v),

    ε (2r+N+ℓ) + δ̄ + Ī ≥ κ_f.

    		(4)

    A generator can thus meet the example’s spread κ_f with forbidden windows, with window laws that differ from f at each position, or with coins shared along e that reveal the quantity. For a generator that commutes with every translation and shares nothing, Ī=0, ℓ=1 and δ̄ is the distance δ of its statistics from f, so (4) is inequality (1). In general δ̄ averages the distance at each position and can exceed the distance of the averaged statistics: the example tiled from absolute coordinates has the example’s statistics, yet at each cell a window fixed in advance, and it meets (4) through δ̄ alone.

    The earlier floors as cases.

    When nothing is shared, Gₑ is trivial and ℓ=1, and a generator on independent coins has qₛ(v)=pₛ at every cell, so Theorem 3(b) is Theorem 1. When no block is unbounded along e and blocks have extent at most ℓ, as in Proposition 1(a), Gₑ is again trivial and qₛ(v)=pₛ(v)≤p^*, the largest of these probabilities over cells and values, so part (b) gives the floor of that proposition with 2r+P+ℓ in place of 2r+ℓ+P+1: its proof (Appendix B.7) separates the two patches by one step more than they need.

    Proposition 1(c) works by a different mechanism. There a rule may fix the quantity by its position given the shared coins, so that \maxₛqₛ(v)=1 wherever the patch is locally valid and the numerator of part (b) vanishes. Defects are forced instead because the layout repeats with period T while σᵀ moves every value of a phase whose period does not divide T. The sharp form (3) sees this. Translation by Te fixes every coin of Gₑ and permutes the others without changing their law, so by (2) qₛ(v+Te)=qₛ(v). Take the separation kT of Appendix B.7, with k≡1 modulo a common multiple D of the positive d_c and kT≥2r+T+P; this exceeds 2r+P+ℓ-1, since there every block outside Gₑ has length at most T along e. Then (3) reads ε(kT+1)(P-N+1)²≥avgᵥ𝔼[1-∑ₛqₛ(v) q_σᵏᵀ(s)(v)], and the argument of Appendix B.7 bounds the sum by 1-μ_G/2, with μ_G the conditional mass defined there, which gives Proposition 1(c) in the sharper form proved there, with T the period of Λ along e. The max form alone gives nothing in this case.

    C.3 Theorem 3(a): the quantity is a function of the shared coins

    Theorem 2 uses ergodicity in place of a radius, and given Gₑ the remaining coins are still ergodic under translation along e.

    The coins given Gₑ. Write the coins as ω=(γ,ω^′), with γ the coins of Gₑ and ω^′ the others; the two are independent. The coins of ω^′ are indexed by the cells, the bounded blocks, and the lines orthogonal to e and groups of them. The translation θ_Te maps each of these indices to another of the same family and fixes none, while it maps every block of infinite extent along e to itself and so fixes every coin of γ. Choose one index in every orbit of θ_Te and let ξₙ collect the coins of the n-th translates of the chosen indices. The ξₙ, n∈ℤ, are i.i.d., and θ_Te shifts the sequence (ξₙ) by one place, so under θ_Te the coins ω^′ form a Bernoulli shift. A Bernoulli shift is mixing, so θ_DTe is ergodic on ω^′ for every D≥1. By (2), X(γ,θ_Teω^′)=τ_TeX(γ,ω^′) for every γ, and the law of ω^′ does not depend on γ. Let E be the event that X is K-valid. It has probability one, so for almost every γ it has probability one in ω^′, and it is invariant under θ_Te, since a translate of a K-valid coloring is K-valid.

    Proof of part (a) for a transported quantity. Fix a cell v^′ on the line through the origin orthogonal to e, and let λ(X)=φ(Q^P_v^′(X)). On E the patches along the line through v^′ parallel to e are locally valid and consecutive ones are edges of G_P,e, so

    φ(Q^P_v^′+je(X)) = σʲ(λ(X)) (j∈ℤ).

    		(5)

    These patches form a bi-infinite walk in the finite graph G_P,e, so some patch a occurs twice, m≥1 steps apart, and φ(a)=σᵐ(φ(a)): the values along the line lie in a finite orbit of σ. Since φ takes finitely many values on V_P, finitely many finite orbits meet them; let D≥1 be a common multiple of their lengths, so that σ^D fixes every value that λ takes on E. Under the full labeling these orbits are the levels of the components with d_c≥1, as in the proof of Theorem 2, and if σ has finite order, D can be that order. By (5) with j=T, λ(τ_TeX)=σᵀ(λ(X)) on E, so λ(τ_DTeX)=λ(X) on E. Fix γ outside a null set. The function ω^′↦λ(X(γ,ω^′)) is invariant under θ_DTe on the invariant event E of probability one, so by ergodicity it is almost surely a constant h(v^′,γ), a measurable function of γ, since it is the value s with \Pr[λ(X)=s|Gₑ]=1. As ω^′ and θ_Teω^′ have the same law, λ(X(γ,θ_Teω^′))=σᵀ(λ(X(γ,ω^′))) has the law of λ(X(γ,ω^′)); both are constants, so σᵀ(h(v^′,γ))=h(v^′,γ). Put hᵥ=σʲ∘h(v^′,·) for v=v^′+je. By (5), φ(Q^Pᵥ(X))=hᵥ(Gₑ) almost surely, at all cells at once since they are countably many, with hᵥ₊ₑ=σ∘hᵥ and h_v+Te=σᵀ∘hᵥ=hᵥ. ∎

    Proof of part (a) for a one-way quantity. Let φ be the strongly connected component and m the number of components. Along a line free of forbidden windows φ never returns to a component it has left, so it changes at most m-1 times on the whole line. Let cⱼ=1 if X∈E and the components at v^′+je and v^′+(j+1)e differ, and cⱼ=0 otherwise. Given γ the law of X is invariant under τ_Te, so 𝔼[c_j+T|γ]=𝔼[cⱼ|γ], and n∑ⱼ₌₀ᵀ⁻¹𝔼[cⱼ|γ]=𝔼[∑ⱼ₌₀ⁿᵀ⁻¹cⱼ\bigm|γ]≤m-1 for every n. Hence every cⱼ vanishes almost surely: φ is constant along each line parallel to e, and λ(τ_TeX)=λ(X) almost surely. Ergodicity of θ_Te given γ, applied to the events {λ(X)=s}, which are invariant up to null sets, makes λ(X) a function h(v^′,Gₑ), and hᵥ=h(v^′,·) at every cell v of the line. ∎

    Order parameters.

    The same argument needs no patch. Let Ω^′ be a measurable set of K-valid colorings with τₑΩ^′=Ω^′, V a finite set and σ a bijection of V. A measurable map Φ:Ω^′→V is an order parameter along e if Φ(τₑx)=σ(Φ(x)) for every x∈Ω^′. The value λ above is one, with Ω^′ the K-valid colorings and V the union of the finite orbits of σ that meet the values of φ, but an order parameter need not be a function of any finite patch.

    Proposition 5(order parameters).

    Let X be as in Theorem 3 with X∈Ω^′ almost surely, and let Φ be an order parameter along e on Ω^′. Then Φ(X)=h(Gₑ) almost surely for a measurable h with σᵀ∘h=h.

    Proof. Let D be the order of σ. The event {X∈Ω^′} is invariant under θ_Te, and on it Φ(τ_DTeX)=σ^DT(Φ(X))=Φ(X). As in the proof of part (a), ergodicity of θ_DTe given γ makes Φ(X) almost surely a constant h(γ), and the invariance of the law of ω^′ under θ_Te gives σᵀ(h(γ))=h(γ). ∎

    SmileCity’s lattice of faces.

    SmileCity’s example has eight rows and eight columns. Its first and last rows and columns are black, and the six by six cells inside them hold a face in which no cell is black. In a coloring, call a face run a run of non-black cells in a row with a black cell at each end; in the tiled example every face run is six cells wide and starts at a column of one residue class modulo eight. Let Ω₁ be the set of K-valid colorings that have a face run and in which all face runs, in all rows, start at columns of one residue class modulo eight, and let Φ(x)∈ℤ/8 be that class, the offset of the faces of x along rows. Write e₁ and e₂ for the unit steps along rows and along columns. Translating a coloring along the rows moves its face runs and translating it along the columns does not, so Ω₁ is invariant under both translations and

    Φ(τ_e₁x)=Φ(x)-1, Φ(τ_e₂x)=Φ(x) (x∈Ω₁).

    So Φ is an order parameter along rows, with σ the step s↦s-1 of order eight, and along columns, with σ the identity. Over all K-valid colorings no finite patch fixes this lattice (Appendix S3), which is why the certificate search cannot find it.

    What both the coins shared along rows and those shared along columns determine is determined by the coins they have in common.

    Lemma 2.

    Let U, U^′ and Π be independent random elements of standard Borel spaces, and Z a random variable with finitely many values. If Z=a(U,Π) and Z=b(U^′,Π) almost surely for measurable a and b, then Z=c(Π) almost surely for a measurable c.

    Proof. The law of (U,U^′,Π) is the product of the three laws, so by Fubini’s theorem, for almost every value π of Π, a(U,π)=b(U^′,π) almost surely. Fix such a π and a value s. The events {a(U,π)=s} and {b(U^′,π)=s} are independent, as U and U^′ are, and differ by a null set, so their common probability equals its own square and is zero or one. Hence a(U,π) is almost surely a constant c(π), the value s with \Pr[a(U,π)=s]=1, which is measurable in π by Fubini’s theorem, and Z=c(Π) almost surely. ∎

    In the language of σ-fields, the σ-fields of (U,Π) and of (U^′,Π) meet, up to null sets, in the σ-field of Π.

    Corollary 3(SmileCity’s lattice).

    On SmileCity, let X be as in Theorem 3, K-valid almost surely, and suppose that its faces lie on one lattice along rows, that is, X∈Ω₁ almost surely. Then the offset Φ(X) is almost surely a function of the coins shared over the whole plane, and the period of Λ along rows is a multiple of eight. Equivalently, the residue modulo eight of the columns where face runs start, counted from a cell v, is a function of those coins and of v. A generator that reads no coin shared over the whole plane puts its faces at the same offset in every world.

    Proof. By Proposition 5 along rows, Φ(X)=h₁(G_e₁) with σ^T₁∘h₁=h₁, that is, h₁-T₁≡h₁ modulo eight, where T₁ is the period of Λ along rows, so eight divides T₁. By Proposition 5 along columns, Φ(X)=h₂(G_e₂). Every family of coins has infinite extent along rows only, along columns only, along both, which makes its blocks the whole plane, or along neither. Let U, U^′ and Π collect the coins of the families of the first three kinds. They are independent, G_e₁ is generated by (U,Π) and G_e₂ by (U^′,Π), so Lemma 2 with Z=Φ(X) gives Φ(X)=c(Π). The offset counted from v is Φ(X) minus the column of v, modulo eight. Without coins shared over the plane, Π is trivial and Φ(X) is a constant. ∎

    The hypothesis that the faces lie on one lattice cannot be dropped, since validity alone does not put them there. The example’s black first and last rows span the whole width, so a window that meets the two black rows between consecutive rows of faces sees at most one row of faces, and is a window of the tiled example at that row’s shift. Shifting each band of eight rows of the tiled example, the rows 8b to 8b+7, by its own amount along the rows therefore leaves every window allowed. Drawing the shift of each band from a coin of the band gives a generator in the general form whose output is K-valid for every value of its coins and has the example’s statistics exactly, and whose offset varies from band to band with coins shared along rows. Appendix S3 finds with a complete solver the same freedom between strips of faces separated by two black rows across the width, and another along a row, through a column of faces three cells wide that never closes. On the colorings in which the face runs of row y share one class modulo eight, that class is an order parameter along rows, so for a generator whose worlds are almost surely such colorings it is a function of G_e₁ and of y by Proposition 5, but it need not be the same on every row.

    Rigid layouts.

    Part (a) and Proposition 5 constrain a generator that shares nothing along e, and they constrain phases whatever is shared.

    Corollary 4(rigid layouts).

    Let X be as in Theorem 3, K-valid almost surely. (a) If X reads no coin shared along e, then at every cell every transported or one-way quantity along e almost surely takes a value fixed in advance, the same in every world, and this layout is periodic under Λ; every order parameter along e is almost surely a constant. (b) Under the full labeling, almost surely every patch of X lies in a component whose d_c divides T. When P=N, the total variation between the window statistics of X and f is therefore at least the example’s share of windows in the other components.

    Proof. (a) With Gₑ trivial the functions hᵥ of part (a) and h of Proposition 5 are constants. For t∈Λ, φ(Q^Pᵥ₊ₜ(X))=φ(Q^Pᵥ(τₜX)), and τₜX=X(θₜω) has the law of X, so hᵥ₊ₜ=hᵥ. (b) By part (a) of Theorem 3, at every cell the value (c,z) of the full labeling is almost surely fixed by σᵀ, which adds T to the level modulo d_c, and d_c≥1 on a line free of forbidden windows; so d_c divides T. When P=N the window law of X at every cell puts no mass on the windows of the other components, while f puts the example’s share on them. ∎

    Part (a) is why a generator given the phase channels and no coin shared along the phase’s direction lays the phase out the same way for every seed. Part (b) is Proposition 1(c) without a radius. On Fabric, whose phase period 5 does not divide the octaves’ period T=16, the components whose period does not divide T hold 0.60 of the example’s windows (Appendix B.9), so a generator whose lattice Λ has that period along the phase’s direction and whose output is free of forbidden windows, at any depth, has window statistics at least that far from the example’s.

    C.4 Theorem 4: when the row types are enough

    Theorem 4 gives a generator free of forbidden windows that reads only the coin from which its band’s row types are drawn and its position.

    Rows and strips. Let the example have H rows and W columns, read with wrap-around, and let Y_c, c∈ℤ/H, be its rows, each a sequence of period W. The alphabet ℝ consists of the rows τˢY_c of the example at every horizontal shift s∈ℤ/W, at most HW rows. A sequence of rows of ℝ is valid if every N consecutive rows form a strip all of whose windows lie in K, a finite condition since the rows share the period W. In a valid sequence the strip of P rows that starts at a given row is locally valid at every column, and its P×P patches are consecutive patches along rows, so they lie in one weak component of G_P,e, the strip’s type. As in Section 4, the type of row y of a coloring is the type of the strip of P rows from y-j₀, where j₀=⌊P/2⌋.

    The sampler’s sequences. Band b holds the rows bL to bL+L-1. The sampler draws for it the types t₀,…,t_L+1 of the rows bL to bL+L+1, with (t₀,t₁) and (t_L,t_L+1) both the anchor α, every three consecutive types shown by the example and every free run within the run limits (Appendix D). Consecutive bands agree on the two rows they share, which both give the anchor. Let W be the finite set of type sequences that the sampler can draw for a band.

    Realizations. A realization of w=(t₀,…,t_L+1)∈W is a valid sequence R₀,…,R_L+P-2 of rows of ℝ in which, for j=0,…,L-1, the strip of P rows that starts at Rⱼ has type t_j+j₀. Placed at the rows bL to bL+L+P-2, the strip that starts at row bL+j is the strip from y-j₀ for y=bL+j+j₀, so the realization gives every row y from bL+j₀ to bL+L-1+j₀ the type t_y-bL that w assigns it. The rows bL to bL+j₀-1 take their types from the realization of band b-1, whose sequence gives them the anchor’s types, as w does. This indexing needs t_L-1+j₀ to lie in the sequence, that is j₀≤2, which holds for P≤5 and so on every example of the corpus, read at P=3 or P=4; a larger P would need an anchor that fixes j₀ consecutive types.

    The example’s rows glue if there is a strip Z=(Z₀,…,Z_P-2) of rows of ℝ such that every w∈W has a realization with R₀,…,R_P-2 equal to Z and R_L,…,R_L+P-2 equal to Z. The rows of Z carry their shifts, so Z is the same at both ends at the same shift. Shifting a realization along the rows gives a realization of the same sequence, since neither K nor the types change, so pinning Z at one end costs nothing; pinning it at both ends is the condition.

    Proof of Theorem 4. Let the rows glue with the strip Z, and let L≥P-1, as on every example of the corpus (Table 2). The bands are the blocks of a lattice fixed in absolute coordinates, groups of L consecutive rows, so their coins form a family of infinite extent along rows. From the coin ω_b of band b the sampler draws w⁽ᵇ⁾∈W, and a fixed rule, deterministic or using further coins of the same band, chooses a realization ρ⁽ᵇ⁾=(R⁽ᵇ⁾₀,…,R⁽ᵇ⁾_L+P-2) of w⁽ᵇ⁾ that begins and ends with Z, which exists because the rows glue. The output is X_(x,y)=R⁽ᵇ⁾_y-bL(x) for bL≤y

    The rows (b+1)L to (b+1)L+P-2 lie in band b+1, since L≥P-1, and there the output is R⁽ᵇ⁺¹⁾₀,…,R⁽ᵇ⁺¹⁾_P-2, which is Z, which is R⁽ᵇ⁾_L,…,R⁽ᵇ⁾_L+P-2. So the output agrees with ρ⁽ᵇ⁾ on all the rows bL to bL+L+P-2. A window whose top row y lies in band b occupies the rows y to y+N-1≤bL+L+N-2≤bL+L+P-2, so it is a window of the valid sequence ρ⁽ᵇ⁾ and lies in K, for every value of the coins. The same comparison applies to the strips of P rows that start in band b, so every row y from bL+j₀ to bL+L-1+j₀ has the type that w⁽ᵇ⁾ gives it, and the row types of the output are the sampled ones. ∎

    The statistics of a generator that glues rows.

    Suppose the rule records, with every row it outputs, the row c of the example and the shift s it copies, so that the row is τˢY_c. A stretch is a maximal run of output rows that copy consecutive rows c,c+1,… of the example at one shift, and a cut is the boundary between two consecutive stretches. A cut is free if every strip of N rows across it is nonetheless a strip of the tiled example up to a horizontal shift; a cut with N-1 copies of one row on each side is free when the example repeats that row N times in a row, as the skylines repeat a row of sky. Let ρ_cut be the expected share of rows y whose strip of N rows from y crosses a cut that is not free. Every other row y starts a strip of N rows that is a strip of the tiled example up to shift; let ν(c) be the expected share of rows whose strip is the example’s strip from row c, taking the least such c when several qualify, and ν̄=ν/(1-ρ_cut) the row usage. Shares are taken over the rows of a band, and U_H is the uniform law on the H rows of the example.

    Proposition 6(statistics).

    The window statistics h_X of such a generator satisfy ∥h_X-f∥_TV≤∥ν̄-U_H∥_TV+ρ_cut. When P=N, every generator whose output is K-valid with the sampled row types satisfies ∥h_X-f∥_TV≥∥π_S-π_f∥_TV, where π_S gives the expected share of each type among the rows of a sampled band and π_f its share among the rows of the example.

    Proof. The law of X is invariant under translation by L rows and by p columns, so its window statistics are the window law averaged over the rows of one band and the columns of one period, a multiple of W. For c∈ℤ/H let f_c be the uniform law on the W windows of the example’s strip from row c, so that f=1/H∑_cf_c. A row y whose strip is the example’s strip from row c at some shift contributes, over the columns of a period, the windows of that strip, each equally often, that is, the law f_c. Hence h_X=∑_cν(c)f_c+ρ_cut g for some law g, and

    ∥h_X-f∥_TV

item.title: 分别生成零件就等于能装起来吗？Composable CAD 让 VLM 先产出一整个可互换的设计空间 ｜ Composable CAD: Sketch-to-CAD Program Synthesis in Parts
item.description:
一句话：零件级独立生成会丢比例与对齐、接缝处还接不上；解法是先造「可互换部件的设计空间」。

要点：

  • 现实工作流：设计师本来就是一件一件建 CAD 模型、并反复迭代单个部件；而现有 VLM 虽然能从草图合成 CAD 程序，但**独立生成零件并不保证它们可组合**
  • 具体失效：部件之间会丢掉原本的比例与对齐关系，在相接处还可能接不上
  • Composable CAD 用现成 VLM 合成一个「设计空间」——独立采样、可互换的部件集合，从而在生成阶段就把可组合性纳入约束

为什么值得看：AI 造资产最常见的天花板是「单件很漂亮，装不到一起」。这条把可组合性提到生成目标层面，对做模块化关卡、装备系统与程序化建筑管线的团队有直接参考价值。

中文摘要：设计师通常是一件一件地建 CAD 模型，并在设计过程中反复迭代单个部件。近期的视觉语言模型已经能从草图合成 CAD 程序，但独立生成零件并不能保证它们可组合：部件可能丢掉原本的比例与对齐关系，或者在相接的地方根本接不上。Composable CAD 因此提出一个以「可组合」为目标的框架：用现成的 VLM 合成一个设计空间，其中的部件可以独立采样、互相替换，从生成阶段就把可组合性纳入约束，而不是事后修补。对模块化资产（关卡、建筑、装备）的 AI 生成来说，这正对着「单件好看但装不起来」这个最常见的天花板。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·核心检索（English）

原文发布：2026-11-03

本期推送：2026-11-04

Composable CAD: Sketch-to-CAD Program Synthesis in Parts

Abstract

Designers often build CAD models part by part, and may iterate on individual components throughout the design process. Recent vision-language models (VLMs) can synthesize CAD programs from sketches, but generating parts independently does not ensure that they are composable: components may lose the intended proportions and alignments or fail to join correctly where they meet. We present Composable CAD, a framework that uses off-the-shelf VLMs to synthesize a design space of independently sampled, interchangeable component programs, where any selection composes into a coherent CAD model. We recover design constraints from the sketch and use them to construct a coarse proxy that establishes how the components are sized, aligned, and attached. We then generate each component independently from its proxy and apply a deterministic rewrite to ensure that neighboring components meet at their prescribed interfaces. We evaluate Composable CAD across a range of objects and sketch styles and conduct two user studies. Compared to VLM-only baselines, our method produces more detailed, composable designs.

1 Introduction

In industrial design workflows, designers typically begin with a sketch [EMA24, BH20]. The sketch records the initial concept: which parts make up the design, how those parts are laid out in space, and what details set the design apart. Sketching serves as the front end of ideation, letting designers visualize and test ideas rapidly [ES07, Bux07]. Once designers settle on a concept, they rebuild it in a CAD tool at higher fidelity and explore more precise variations of it [SXZ∗17, LYZ∗24].

Recent vision-language models (VLMs) attempt to automate CAD generation from sketches [Ant26, Gem25]. A designer can provide a foundation model an input text prompt “generate CAD for a chair” and sketch and receive a CAD program as output  [Ant26, Gem25]. A growing body of work in this space instantiates agentic coding loops where the model executes its CAD programs, inspects renders for visual feedback, and revises the CAD geometry over several rounds [ATZ∗25, MKC∗25, OMSR25, FNY∗26, BLBF26, AAMJ26].

However, independently generated parts which may be valid in isolation, are not necessarily composable: the parts may not fit together, fail to join without gaps or overlaps, and have hallucinated away from the original proportions, alignments, and design intents defined in the original sketch (Figure 1). Guaranteeing composability in CAD generation raises a few challenges. First, the agent must preserve the designer-set constraints – the part decomposition, proportions, and alignments laid out in the sketch. Second, the agent must preserve the structural constraints and relationships between parts, so they can join without gaps or volumetric overlap. This is difficult for VLMs because the surfaces where parts meet are often implicit in CAD programs and emerge only when the operations execute. An extrusion, for example, creates surfaces with no explicit handle in the code. Additionally, structured exploration can give users choices for how to refine the generated CAD assembly.

We present Composable CAD, a framework that turns a concept sketch into a design space of independently sampled, composable part programs (Figure ). Designers explore alternatives for each part and compose a design from their selections. Sketch-derived relations guide part proportions, alignments, and attachments, while a deterministic rewriting algorithm enforces structural compatibility across the sampled variants.

Our system follows a two-stage, coarse-to-fine pipeline. In the planning stage, we recover attachment, alignment, and proportion relations from the sketch and use them to construct a coarse proxy that fixes the layout of the parts. In the detail generation stage, we elaborate each part independently from its proxy. Finally, we use a deterministic rewrite algorithm to reconcile independently generated parts at their connecting surfaces, making them interchangeable across samples.

We demonstrate Composable CAD across a variety of objects and sketch styles, producing composable, part-based design spaces. Compared with VLM baselines that generate objects as a whole or create parts separately, our method produces detailed parts while maintaining composability across variants. We conducted two user studies: one comparing the perceptual quality of our outputs to a single-pass VLM baseline, and another comparing our part-based exploration workflow to a VLM-only baseline. Our results show that participants preferred our generated shapes and favored our part-based workflow of selecting and combining individual parts.

In summary, our contributions are:

  • •

    A formulation of sketch-to-CAD synthesis as a design space of independently sampled, interchangeable part programs, and its application to exploratory design.

  • •

    A coarse-to-fine generation pipeline that recovers geometric relations from the sketch, plans the object as a shared proxy, and generates each part independently.

  • •

    A deterministic rewrite algorithm that localizes connecting surfaces and edits independently generated part programs to meet congruently.

    • 2 Related Works

    Our work builds on three areas of research: sketch-based modeling, CAD program synthesis, and part-based shape generation. We refer to recent surveys for broader discussions of these domains [LB25, RGJ∗23].

    Sketch-based modeling.

    Generating 3D geometry from 2D sketches has a long history. Early methods reconstruct 3D shapes from line drawings using geometric regularities such as parallelism, orthogonality, planarity, and symmetry [LS96, LCLT08, YLT13, CSMS13, PCV16]. Later methods handle curved geometry, over-sketching, and construction lines [XCS∗14, SKSK09, BBS08, SS14, GHL∗20, HGSB22, YDSG21]. We similarly exploit geometric cues in sketch strokes, but use them to constrain VLM-generated CAD rather than reconstruct geometry directly.

    We contribute to the family of works that infer parametric shapes or CAD operations from sketches [HKYM17, NGDGA∗16, LPBM20, LPBM22, PMKB23, SLX∗25, LMK∗26]. Closest to ours, Free2CAD [LPBM22] and CADrawer [LMK∗26] parse strokes into sequences of CAD operations. While these methods reconstruct a single shape from a drawing, we generate multiple programs per part that can be independently sampled and recombined.

    CAD Program Generation.

    Prior work generates CAD programs from diverse inputs, including voxel grids [SGL∗18, TLS∗19, LWJ∗22], point clouds [WXW18, DIP∗18, WXZ21, LOWS24, GLP∗22, SLK∗20, RDM∗25], and boundary representations [XPC∗21], among others [CF25, WZW∗24]. More recent work uses language and vision-language models for CAD program synthesis. Early approaches train or fine-tune models on CAD sequences [XWZ∗24, RDM∗25, KSS∗24, LML∗25, KDA∗24, WYSB25, DAHA25, YSH24, ZSW∗25], but are limited by the scale and operation coverage of available CAD datasets. Recent methods instead place off-the-shelf models in agentic loops, where they generate CAD code, inspect execution results and rendered views, and revise their output over multiple rounds [ATZ∗25, MKC∗25, OMSR25, FNY∗26, BLBF26, AAMJ26]. We build on this training-free paradigm, but generate independently sampled programs for each part rather than a single CAD program. We reconcile their connecting geometry with a deterministic rewrite, making parts interchangeable across samples.

    Part-based generation and composition.

    Representing shapes as structured arrangements of parts is common in shape programs and procedural modeling, where programs encode both the parts and their relationships [MWH∗06, JBX∗20, JCG∗21, JGMR23, LMAR24]. Parametric design systems similarly expose part-based design spaces for interactive exploration [SXZ∗17, KGC∗17, MGB∗18, WZN∗19]. We build on this idea, using CAD programs to represent and vary independently generated parts.

    Recent systems also generate or compose shapes part by part. Compos3D [FLFM26] synthesizes a coherent mesh from a user-arranged composition of parts. Recent vehicle-design systems combine parts across multiple views or sketch and generate parts individually [LYL∗25, YLMB26]. ArtiCAD [SGZ∗26] generates articulated CAD assemblies from text or images, but does not address interchangeability across independently sampled variants. We target this problem directly, using sketch-derived relations to guide part generation and a deterministic rewrite to make variants interchangeable.

    3 Overview

    Given a concept sketch, Composable CAD generates several CAD program variants for each component (Figure 2). We give a high-level overview of the pipeline here; Appendices B–F provide full details.

    We first plan the object as a coarse proxy, using geometric relations recovered from the sketch to establish how its components are sized, aligned, and attached. The proxy then provides the context for generating each component independently and defines the interfaces where neighboring components should meet. Finally, a deterministic rewrite seats each generated component against these interfaces. The rewritten components can be freely recombined: they do not overlap, meet exactly at shared interfaces, and form a single connected solid. A material budget limits how much the rewrite may alter the sampled geometry (Section 4).

    To ground this workflow in practice, we conducted a formative study with industrial designers prior to development (Appendix A). Designers described an early phase of loose sketching followed by a 3D realization phase, where they work part by part and may divide components across collaborators. They also described producing useful design variants as time-consuming, particularly when variants require adding or reworking detail. Our system targets this later phase, supporting part-based exploration while keeping independently generated components mutually compatible [Bux07].

    We formulate composability through two types of constraints: design constraints, set by the designer’s sketch, and structural constraints, which guarantee valid composition. Design constraints capture the sketch’s intent: which components attach, how they align, and their relative proportions. Because these relations are recovered from an imprecise 2D drawing, we treat them as guidance rather than enforce them exactly. Structural constraints specify the exact geometry required for components to compose without gaps or volumetric overlap. We use the design constraints to construct the shared proxy, then derive the structural constraints from it.

    Our pipeline has two stages (Figure 2). The planning stage uses design constraints from the sketch to construct a shared proxy and derive its structural constraints. The detail generation stage then elaborates each component independently from the proxy, followed by a deterministic rewrite that enforces the structural constraints. Figure 3 shows these programs and constraints.

    3.1 Planning

    The planning stage reasons over the whole object once, establishing how its components belong together before any of them is elaborated. We first segment the sketch into semantic components (Appendix B) and recover four types of design constraints: attachment, alignment, proportion, and mirroring. We extract these relations geometrically (Appendix C) rather than asking the VLM to infer them, since VLMs remain unreliable at quantitative spatial reasoning [LMFA24, CXK∗24]. We detect stroke junctions, which identify attachments; junction-incident strokes then vote for the object’s coordinate axes, and projecting component regions onto these axes gives alignment and proportion. Mirroring comes from the segmentation.

    The design constraints guide the VLM in constructing a coarse proxy of the object, with one simple volume per component (Appendices D-E). We compile each relation into a function that checks whether it holds on the generated proxy. Figure 3 shows this process for the chair: the backrest, for example, has constraints on its proportion, attachment to the seat pan, and alignment with neighboring components. We execute these checks and return any violations to the VLM for one round of refinement (Figure 3c). We treat these relations as guidance rather than requirements: both their recovery and the underlying freehand sketch are approximate, so the VLM may overrule a relation that conflicts with the shape it is building. Mirroring is exact because we generate one member of a mirrored pair and reflect it for the other.

    Once the proxy is fixed, we use it to determine exactly where neighboring components should meet. We represent each component by its axis-aligned proxy box and trim overlapping boxes so their interiors are disjoint. Where two attached boxes meet, their shared planar boundary defines a connecting surface (Figure 3e). The resulting proxy boxes and connecting surfaces form the structural constraints: each component must remain within its proxy and meet its neighbors at the prescribed surfaces.

    3.2 Independent Detail Generation

    Once planning is complete, we elaborate each component independently and in parallel; see Appendix F for full details. In the detail generation stage, we provide the VLM with only the component’s proxy program and corresponding sketch region. Rather than generating a new program from scratch, the VLM edits the proxy program, which represents the component as a simple volume, and elaborates it into detailed geometry. The proxy carries the global information needed to place the component, while the sketch region provides the visual information needed to elaborate it. We draw several variants for each component from independent VLM calls.

    We can generate components independently and in parallel because each component does not need to see the whole object, only enough context to know where it belongs. Giving the VLM the whole object instead introduces irrelevant context that can degrade generation [SCM∗23, LKW∗25]; in our evaluation, focused per-component generation produces more detailed programs (Section 6.4).

    While the proxy guides placement, it does not guarantee that the detailed geometry still reaches its connecting surfaces. We therefore apply a deterministic rewrite (Section 4) to seat each sampled component against these surfaces before adding it to the design space.

    4 Deterministic Rewrite

    We now describe our deterministic rewrite algorithm for seating independently generated components against the structural constraints defined during planning.

    4.1 Seating a Component

    Our deterministic rewrite enforces the structural constraints while preserving the generated geometry wherever possible. It seats each component inside its proxy and against its connecting surfaces using three increasingly geometry-changing operations (Figure 4). We say a component is seated when it remains within its proxy and covers each connecting surface without extending beyond its interface plane. We first translate the component to the center of its proxy, then scale it to reach its connecting surfaces while remaining within the proxy. Finally, we form a flat face at each interface: if the generated surface falls short of the connecting surface, we union material to fill the gap; if it protrudes beyond it, we cut the excess. Figure 4 shows both cases. These operations modify only the residual geometry needed to establish the interface; we bound the total modification with the material budget described in Section 6.3.

    We perform this step geometrically rather than ask the VLM to repair its program because connecting surfaces are often implicit in CAD code. An extrusion, for example, creates faces with no explicit handle in the program; their positions are known only after execution. Placing such a face at a prescribed interface therefore requires reasoning about geometry that the program does not explicitly represent. Predicting program outputs remains unreliable even for short functions [GRL∗24], and quantitative spatial reasoning is itself difficult for VLMs [LMFA24, CXK∗24]. We instead operate on the executed geometry and append deterministic CadQuery operations to the sampled program.

    4.2 Rewrite Algorithm

    Let P_c be the sampled program for component c, V_c its executed solid, B_c its proxy, and S_c={s₁,…,sₙ} its connecting surfaces. Algorithm 1 rewrites P_c by appending translation, scaling, union, and cutting operations. We append rather than modify the sampled construction to preserve as much of the VLM-generated geometry as possible.

    The operations are applied from least to most geometry-changing. First, we translate the component to the center of its proxy, preserving its geometry exactly. Second, we scale each axis until the component reaches its connecting surfaces while remaining within its proxy; scaling changes dimensions but preserves its features and their arrangement. Third, we classify the generated surface at each interface as concave or convex. A concave surface falls short of the interface, so we union an extrusion of the connecting surface inward until it reaches the component. A convex surface protrudes beyond it, so we cut away the excess. Appendix G explains why this choice preserves more of the sampled geometry.

    4.3 Composability Guarantee

    Because every variant is rewritten against the same proxy and connecting surfaces, the rewrite can operate on each component independently while ensuring that the resulting variants remain interchangeable.

    Proposition 1.

    . Let the component proxies have pairwise disjoint interiors, with each attached pair sharing one planar connecting surface. Under the sample conditions of Appendix H, if Algorithm 1 completes within the material budget for every component, then any selection of one rewritten sample per component has pairwise disjoint interiors, every attached pair meets exactly along its shared connecting surface, and their union is one connected solid.

    The sample conditions require nonempty, connected material within each proxy and that the generated geometry can be seated at each interface by the corresponding cut or union; Appendix H states them formally. Intuitively, keeping every component inside its proxy prevents volumetric overlap, while neighboring components cover the same connecting surface without extending beyond it. Since the attachment graph is connected, these shared interfaces make the assembled object connected.

    The guarantee does not bound how much the rewrite must change a sampled component. A highly distorted interface may require a large cut or union, which would defeat the purpose of preserving the sampled geometry. We therefore cap the volume changed by scaling, cutting, and union at 10% of the shape’s total volume, and report failure when a component cannot be seated within this budget. Section 6.3 evaluates this tradeoff.

    5 Applications

    Composable CAD supports three applications: exploring the part-based design space, editing individual components, and fabricating interchangeable parts.

    5.1 Design-Space Exploration

    Our system exposes a part-based design space for exploring variations of the input sketch. The designer browses alternatives for each component and composes a design by selecting one of each; because the components are interchangeable, any selection can be freely recombined. We generate five variants per component independently and in parallel from the same proxy, varying the sampling temperature from 0.1 to 0.5 to produce a range of designs (Appendix F).

    We show results on sketches from OpenSketch [GSH∗19], DifferSketching [XSL∗22], SlowSketch [BDM∗20], and AmateurSketch [QGS∗21], spanning a range of drawing styles and levels of detail. For each, we show the input sketch, generated design space, and several recombined outputs (Figures 5, 6, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17). Insets highlight components that differ across outputs and remain compatible when recombined.

    5.2 Editing

    Our structural constraints make component-level editing natural: removing a component leaves its proxy and connecting surfaces fixed, so any replacement inherits exactly the constraints of the original. The deterministic rewrite (Section 4) seats the replacement against these interfaces, while every other component remains unchanged.

    We demonstrate three ways to provide a replacement: redrawing the component as a sketch (Figure 7), borrowing a finished component from another design (Figure 18), or describing its replacement in text (Figure 19). In each case, only the selected component changes. The replacement remains compatible with the full design space, so it can be recombined with variants of every other component and exploration can continue from the edited design.

    5.3 Fabrication

    Composable CAD also supports physical assembly: the flat, congruent connecting surfaces produced by our system provide natural interfaces for joining components. We demonstrate this by 3D printing an entire design space—every sample of every component—and assembling designs from components across different samples (Figure 8). Because the components meet at the same connecting surfaces, the recombination available in the digital design space carries over to the physical parts.

    The joints are independent as well. For each connecting surface, we place a peg on one component and a socket on the other, with no coordination between their generation. Since both are derived from the same connecting surface, they are congruent by construction (Appendix I). See the supplemental video for additional examples.

    6 Evaluation

    We evaluate Composable CAD on the properties our method is designed to provide: preserving the sketch’s design constraints, maintaining structural validity under part recombination, and producing detailed CAD programs, together with the cost of generation. We compare against VLM-only baselines across a corpus of objects and sketch styles, and complement them with qualitative results and two user studies.

    6.1 Baselines

    We compare against two VLM-only baselines and one ablation of our method. The first tests direct sketch-to-CAD generation with an agentic VLM; the second gives the VLM the same coarse-to-fine generation strategy as our method, but without our geometric constraints or deterministic rewrite. Finally, we compare our pipeline with and without the deterministic rewrite to isolate its effect on composability. Prompts for the VLM baselines are given in Appendix J.

    S1: VLM one pass. We use this baseline to represent a practical single-pass setting. Given the sketch, the VLM segments the object and generates one CadQuery program with one function per component. We use high thinking with a five-minute budget.

    S2: VLM two passes. This baseline tests whether coarse-to-fine generation alone is sufficient. The VLM first generates a whole-object proxy, then elaborates each component with the full proxy program as context. It performs its own segmentation and uses no geometric constraints or deterministic rewrite. We use high thinking with no time limit, allowing the VLM to complete the more time-consuming two-stage generation.

    S3: Ours without rewrite. We run our full pipeline but disable the deterministic rewrite (Section 4). Sketch-derived relations still guide proxy generation, and components are independently elaborated from their proxies, but they are not reconciled at their connecting surfaces.

    Ours. Our complete pipeline, using the same VLM with medium thinking.

    6.2 Evaluation Protocol

    We evaluate on 33 objects randomly selected from the sketch datasets used in Section 5.1, spanning different object types, drawing styles, and levels of detail. Each method generates five program variants per object. We evaluate these programs both as generated and after recombination. As generated evaluates each program directly, with all components coming from the same variant, giving 33×5=165 shapes per method. Recombined forms 25 additional shapes per object by randomly selecting one component from across the five variants, giving 33×25=825 shapes per method. This tests whether components generated in different samples remain interchangeable. Shapes are normalized to a 10×10×10 cm bounding box before geometric measurement. Non-executable outputs are rare, since each setup executes its generated programs and uses the VLM to repair compilation errors.

    6.3 Quantitative Results

    We quantify how well each method preserves the sketch constraints, maintains composability, and generates detailed CAD programs.

    Design Constraints. To measure satisfaction of design constraints, we evaluate how well the generated shapes preserve the alignment, proportion, and mirroring relations recovered from the sketch. We reuse the executable relation functions of Appendix D: proportion compares a component’s x:y:z extents with the ratio recovered from the sketch, alignment checks the specified component anchors along each axis, and mirroring checks that mirrored components match in extent. We omit attachment because physical contact is enforced by the structural constraints and evaluated separately below.

    We report the fraction of extracted relations that pass in Table 1. Because S₁ and S₂ determine their own segmentation, we extract relations using each setup’s own part list. Results show that our planning stage substantially preserves these relations. S₃ scores highest on proportion and alignment, while our complete method is slightly lower because the rewrite modifies geometry after the relations have been checked. Neither is expected to reach 100%: design constraints are soft guidance, and the VLM may overrule a recovered relation when constructing the proxy. Both S₃ and ours satisfy mirroring by construction because mirrored components are generated once and reflected.

    Structural Validity. We next evaluate whether independently generated components compose correctly, particularly after recombination. We measure three conditions. No overlap requires that no two components intersect. Attached requires every pair marked as attached by the sketch to have surfaces within 0.1 cm. Valid interface requires each attached pair to meet over a flat contact region whose side exceeds \max(0.3cm,t), where t is the component’s cross-sectional thickness at the interface. Figure 10 illustrates these failure modes. For our method, the interface is the computed connecting surface; because the VLM baselines have no explicit interface, we take it as the region of one component’s boundary within 0.1 cm of the other.

    Table 2 reports these conditions both as generated and after recombination. Our method maintains similar structural validity in both settings: 93.3% of generated shapes and 91.5% of recombined shapes satisfy all three conditions. In contrast, the single-pass baseline drops from 73.9% to 9.9% after recombination, since components generated together may not remain compatible when mixed across samples. S₂ and S₃ likewise remain substantially below our method, showing the role of the deterministic rewrite in making independently sampled components interchangeable.

    Material Budget. The material budget limits how much the rewrite may alter a component after detail generation. We measure rewrite cost as the volume changed by scaling, cutting, and union, and cap it at 10% of the shape’s total volume; translation does not contribute because it preserves geometry exactly. If any component cannot be seated within this budget, the composed shape is scored as failing all three structural conditions.

    Table 3 varies the budget from 1% to 20%. A tight budget preserves more of the sampled geometry but leaves the rewrite too little room to establish some interfaces, while a larger budget improves structural validity at the cost of modifying more geometry. We use 10% throughout the paper, at which 91.5% of recombined shapes satisfy all three structural conditions.

    Program Detail. Component-wise generation produces substantially richer CAD programs. Table 4 reports number of CAD operations and lines of code across the four setups. The one-pass baseline averages 53.2 CAD operations, compared with 85.6 for the two-pass VLM baseline and 127.5 for our complete method. S3 and ours have the same line count because the rewrite appends operations to the returned component rather than adding source lines, increasing the operation count without changing program length. Figure 9 shows the corresponding qualitative differences in generated geometry.

    VLM-Based Repair Our deterministic rewrite raises a natural alternative: can the VLM itself repair independently generated components? We test this on the same 825 recombined S3 shapes used above. Gemini 3.1 Pro receives the complete CadQuery program and may repeatedly execute and revise it for up to three minutes to remove gaps and overlaps, produce flat interfaces, and preserve component detail. Appendix K includes the full prompt.

    Table 5 shows that VLM repair improves overlap and attachment, but not valid interfaces: the fraction satisfying all structural conditions changes from 55.2% before repair to 54.1% afterward. Our deterministic rewrite reaches 91.5% with negligible additional runtime. This advantage likely comes from operating explicitly in 3D: the VLM must reason about interfaces indirectly through CAD code, whereas our rewrite measures and modifies the executed geometry directly, making it better suited to enforcing the precise interfaces required for composability.

    Generation Cost Finally, Table 6 reports generation time and token usage. The one-pass baseline is fastest and uses the fewest tokens, but produces substantially less detailed programs. Generating components independently in parallel makes S₃ and ours faster than sequential two-pass generation. Our pipeline uses more tokens than the VLM-only baselines because it also reasons over design-constraint feedback. The deterministic rewrite itself adds negligible runtime and consumes no VLM tokens.

    6.4 Qualitative Results

    We show qualitative results of our method compared with baselines and with prior systems. Figure 9 illustrates the benefit of component-wise generation. A single VLM pass captures the coarse shape but often omits component detail, such as wheel structure, grilles, bumpers, and body features. Giving components their own generation produces substantially richer geometry, and our per-component generation adds further detail.

    This added detail comes with a challenge: independently generated components may not fit together. Figure 10 shows the three failure modes we observe: components may overlap, fail to touch, or touch over an invalid interface. Our deterministic rewrite resolves these failures by seating components against their shared connecting surfaces, producing flat, congruent contact while retaining their detail.

    Beyond these differences in detail and composability, our system also targets a broader setting than prior sketch-to-CAD systems (Figure 11). CADrawer [LMK∗26] and Free2CAD [LPBM22] reconstruct a single part from a clean line drawing, whereas our inputs span a broader range of drawing styles and complexity and our outputs are multi-part design spaces rather than single reconstructions. CADrawer reports quality degrading markedly beyond roughly 15 CAD operations; our programs can be substantially longer, with around 100 operations for the car in Figure 11.

    6.5 Perceptual Preference Study

    We next evaluate the perceptual quality of our generated outputs relative to direct VLM generation. We compare our method with the single-pass VLM baseline in a preference study with 12 participants, each evaluating 15 randomly selected sketches. For each sketch, participants saw the two outputs side by side in randomized, unlabeled order and indicated their preference on detail, proportion, fidelity to the input sketch, and overall quality. Appendix L gives the full protocol.

    Participants preferred our outputs on all four criteria (Table 7): 77.8% for detail, 66.7% for proportion, 70.0% for fidelity, and 75.6% overall. All preferences were significantly above chance under an exact two-sided binomial test.

    6.6 Exploration Study

    We also conducted a study with six participants to investigate how the design space is used. Appendix M gives the full study protocol and findings; we provide a summary here.

    Each participant drew two sketches of their own choosing and explored one with our system and one with a VLM-only baseline, in counterbalanced order (Figure 20). In both conditions, the design space was generated from the participant’s sketch. In the baseline, the sketch produced 16 whole-shape generations; participants chose five favorites, edited each with a text instruction, and then explored a design space formed by recombining their segmented components. Because these shapes are generated and segmented independently, their components are not guaranteed to fit together when recombined. Our system instead generates a per-component design space directly from the sketch for selection and composition.

    We then conducted a semi-structured interview to understand participants’ workflow preferences, how component compatibility affected exploration, and how exploration developed their initial sketches. All participants preferred selecting components to selecting whole shapes: they often liked components from several designs rather than any single generated shape. They also found selection easier than describing desired components in text, since they did not always have the words for the component they wanted. Component compatibility also mattered: floating and overlapping components in the baseline drew immediate negative reactions, and participants said these failures could make it impossible to explore a combination further.

    Participants reported that exploring our design spaces often developed their rough sketches and suggested new ideas, although whole-shape variants could sometimes suggest more divergent alternatives by changing the entire design at once. Finally, participants wanted more control over segmentation granularity. Some wanted finer components while others found excessive segmentation distracting, but all requested hierarchical segmentation that would let them open a component and explore it at finer granularity. Figure 21 shows designs participants produced with our system.

    7 Discussion and Limitations

    We discuss three aspects of our current formulation that shape its scope: component decomposition, geometry representation, and the relations between components.

    Part decomposition.

    We currently segment each object into a single flat set of components. This fixes the granularity of exploration: a designer can vary a component, but cannot open it and explore its subcomponents independently. Participants in our exploratory study explicitly asked for this capability. Future work could support hierarchical decomposition, allowing designers to move between object-, component-, and subcomponent-level exploration.

    Geometry representation.

    Our components are represented as CadQuery programs, which favor prismatic operations such as profiles, extrusions, fillets, and booleans. This representation works less well for objects whose identity lies in freeform surfaces, such as car bodies; for these shapes, our variants primarily change the massing rather than the surface design. Future work could extend our representation with NURBS or other freeform operations while retaining part-level interchangeability.

    Constraints and interfaces.

    Our formulation supports four design relations—attachment, alignment, proportion, and mirroring—and structural constraints that keep components disjoint and make attached pairs meet over a single flat interface. This excludes curved or disconnected interfaces, as well as design requirements such as clearance, function, manufacturability, and more general symmetry. Future work could expand both the relation vocabulary and the interface representation to support a broader range of assemblies and design requirements.

    8 Conclusion

    We presented Composable CAD, a system for generating a part-based design space from a concept sketch. Generating components independently gives each component its own detail and variants, but those variants are only useful as a design space if they can be freely recombined. We make this possible by recovering the sketch’s attachment, alignment, and proportion relations to guide component generation, and by deterministically rewriting the resulting programs so their components meet at shared interfaces. The resulting components are interchangeable across samples, allowing designers to explore, edit, and physically assemble different combinations without regenerating the rest of the design. We hope composable part generation opens new ways to use generative CAD for design exploration.

    （参考文献见原文。）

    Appendix A Formative Study

    To ground our system design in real practice, we conducted semi-structured interviews with three industrial designers spanning a range of career stages and specializations (Table 8). We report two findings.

    Design has two phases.

    Participants described their work as two phases: an early phase of brainstorming and loose sketching, where they explore many ideas quickly, and a later phase of building and adjustment, where they realize the shape in 3D and vary its parameters to produce different designs. Our system targets the second phase, where designers want to build the shape from the input sketch quickly while also exploring variants of it.

    Exploration is the bottleneck.

    Participants told us that producing variants is time-consuming. Adjusting parameters alone is straightforward, but the variants worth exploring usually require changing the program itself, adding or reworking detail, which is far more effort. This is the work our system aims to take on for them.

    Feature Requests

    We list the core capabilities participants asked for, which motivated our system design and are what our system is built to provide.

  • 1.

    Quick building from a sketch. Given the input sketch, the designer can obtain the 3D shape quickly.

  • 2.

    Imagine and fill in. Where the sketch is loose or silent, the system plausibly completes what it leaves unspecified.

  • 3.

    Part-based exploration in 3D. Designers explore in 3D without committing to a single idea, so the system offers alternatives per part that recombine freely rather than one whole-shape variant.

  • 4.

    Multi-part compatibility. Independently explored parts stay mutually compatible, so a designer, or a collaborator owning one part, can revise a part and still assemble a valid whole.

    • Appendix B Sketch Segmentation

    Sketch segmentation has been widely studied [YZF∗21, QGXS22, TVY∗25]. We segment the input sketch in two API calls: one to identify semantic parts and one to generate a color-coded segmentation mask. We first give the sketch to Gemini 3.1 Pro [Goo26b] and prompt it to list the object’s semantic parts; for the chair, these are the base, column, seat pan, backrest, and the two armrests. The part-list prompt is:

    You are given a single freehand concept sketch of one object. List the object’s semantic parts: the parts a designer would model and vary separately. Output one part per line, as a short lowercase noun label, and nothing else. Merge duplicate instances only if they are identical; otherwise label them separately (e.g. “left armrest”, “right armrest”).

    We then provide the sketch, part list, and color legend to Gemini 3 Pro Image Preview (gemini-3-pro-image-preview) [Goo26a], requesting a color-coded mask with the same dimensions as the input. We use the image returned by the API as the segmentation mask and recover each part’s region by extracting the pixels of its assigned color. The mask prompt is:

    You are given the same sketch and a list of its parts: {part_list}. Return a single image with the exact same width and height as the input. Paint the region of each part in a solid, flat, distinct color, using this assignment: {color_legend}. Fill each part’s full area, keep boundaries tight to the drawn strokes, and paint the background pure black (0,0,0). Do not draw outlines, labels, gradients, shading, or anti-aliased edges: use only the exact assigned colors and black.

    Appendix C Geometric Prior

    We recover the design constraints from the vectorized strokes and the part masks in four deterministic passes. Junctions tell us where strokes cross and which parts touch; from the junctions we recover the object’s coordinate axes; and against those axes we compute the alignment and proportion relations, since both are defined per axis. We first crop the sketch to its drawn content and resize it into a 256×256 box, with a margin of 20 pixels on each side, so every sketch is processed at the same resolution and all thresholds below are stated in pixels of that box.

    Junctions.

    A junction is where one stroke meets another, and it is the primary 2D cue for which parts contact (Figure 22a). For an endpoint of stroke A meeting stroke B, we register a T-junction when the strokes differ in direction by at least 25^∘ (so a collinear break is not counted), the endpoint projects to the interior of B at parameter t∈[0.15,0.85] (a mid-stroke hit, not B’s endpoint), and the perpendicular distance from the endpoint to B is at most 8px. Near-duplicate junctions are merged within small pixel clusters. We then attribute each junction to parts with a KD-tree over the masks, assigning it to its two nearest parts when both lie within 13px. Votes accumulate over unordered part pairs, and every voted pair emits an attachment relation, promoted to a resting relation when the vertical offset dominates (dy>0.6dx).

    Axes.

    The relations we extract are all stated per world axis, so we next recover the object’s coordinate frame (Figure 22b). The vertical axis is fixed by convention: designers draw the up-direction vertical on the page, so we take world z to project onto the image’s vertical direction. The two horizontal axes are recovered by voting with the junctions, since at each junction the two crossing strokes are corner edges rather than arbitrary marks and so are strong evidence for the axis directions. We collect the direction of every junction-incident stroke, drop those within 15^∘ of vertical, and cluster the rest by angle, each junction contributing a vote to its cluster. The two highest-voted clusters give the horizontal axis directions, which we orthogonalize against z to form the frame. A part’s extent along an axis is then read by projecting its mask onto that axis direction, which is what the following two passes use.

    Alignment.

    With the axes fixed, we find which parts line up along each (Figure 22c). Alignment is stated between anchors: on a given axis, a part contributes three of them, its minimum, its center, and its maximum, so that a designer’s flush edge, shared centerline, or edge-to-center placement are all expressed in the same way. We project every part’s mask onto the axis, collect the anchors of all parts, and cluster their values by complete linkage: a new cluster starts whenever a value exceeds the current cluster’s minimum by more than 7px, so each cluster spans at most 7px and no chaining occurs. A cluster holding anchors from at least two distinct parts is kept, and each pair of parts within it emits an alignment relation on that axis, recording which anchor each side contributed and the residual offset between them.

    Proportion.

    For each part we compute an x:y:z shape hint from its extent along the three axes (Figure 22d), read in the recovered frame rather than from the silhouette, since a single isometric view cannot separate the three axes. We divide the three extents by the longest, so the longest axis is 1.0, and snap each ratio to a 0.1 grid floored at 0.1.

    Appendix D Design Constraints as Functions

    Each design constraint from the sketch is compiled into a small function over the generated program, so that checking a relation is just executing the programs. Figure 23 shows the three stroke-derived design constraints: proportion, attachment, and alignment; mirroring comes from the segmentation and is checked the same way. To evaluate a program, we execute it to obtain the parts, then call each relation’s relation function on them. The result is a per-relation pass or fail with its residual, which is the report returned to the VLM (Section 3) as natural language feedback.

    Appendix E Proxy Generation

    We generate the initial proxy with Gemini 3.1 Pro (gemini-3.1-pro) [Goo26b], giving it the input sketch and the prompt:

    You are given a concept sketch of a single object and the list of its parts: {part_list}. Write a CadQuery program that reconstructs the object as a proxy. Represent each part as one simple primitive volume, and define exactly one function per part, each named after its part and returning that part’s solid (for example, def backrest() -> cq.Workplane).
