This appendix provides (i) implementation details and the full hyperparameter list (AppendixA), (ii) the held-out re-rendering evaluation protocol (AppendixB), (iii) ablations of the seam correction (one gain per camera, luminance vs. RGB) on Panoptic, on a synthetic capture with ground truth, and on our in-house five-camera capture (AppendixC), (iv) a comparison against applying an offline texturing method to our own geometry (AppendixD), (v) the quality/runtime/memory tradeoff of finer voxel sizes (AppendixE), (vi) an ablation of the depth tolerance in occlusion-aware view selection (AppendixF), (vii) an SfM+MVS application example (AppendixG), and (viii) a statement on the use of large language models (AppendixH). An accompanying video (project page: https://unclearness.github.io/grtmesh/) shows (1) the seam correction on the 100 held-out frames of the evaluation in Sec.4.2 (office2, frames 400–697 at stride 3, camera 7), playing the re-rendering without (left) and with (right) correction; (2) the texture atlas and the solved gain fields over time; (3) free-view comparisons of our output with nvblox and the offline baseline on office2 and band2 over 800 continuous frames; and (4) the noise-removal, inpainting, and seam-correction ablations on the in-house capture (AppendixC) with its luminance and RGB gain fields. The video shows the temporal behavior of the correction; the fixed 10cm evaluation is reported in Sec.4.2 and the ablations below.

Appendix A Implementation Details and Hyperparameters

All runtime and quality numbers were obtained on a workstation with an AMD Ryzen Threadripper 9970X, 256GB of RAM, and an NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Max-Q. Tab.4 lists the Panoptic defaults of Sec.4; ablations and the auxiliary capture specify their overrides. We stabilize the seam correction gain field across frames with an exponential moving average, gₜ←α gₜ+(1-α) gₜ₋₁, with α=0.15 and the zero-mean gauge re-applied after the blend. Fig.9 illustrates how the seam residuals are sampled, including the direction and magnitude of the sub-pixel inset.

Runtime protocol.

Runtimes are measured on frames 400–2399 (band2: 1397–3396) and reported as the mean over the fastest 95% of the timed frames, which removes start-up and scheduling outliers. Frames are decoded into host memory before timing; our times start with the batched upload of the raw color and depth images and include their undistortion and depth-to-color registration on the GPU (2.2ms together at 0.02m). The baselines perform these two steps on the CPU, outside their timed region. Over all 2000 frames without the trimming, the full method takes 13.2ms on average at 0.02m (95th percentile 15.2ms), against 13.1ms in Tab.1.

At 0.01m and 0.005m the baselines are timed on every fourth and every tenth frame of the same range (500 and 200 frames; nvblox at 0.005m: the first 60 of these). nvblox (nvblox_torch 0.0.9) does not release GPU memory when its mapper is cleared, so memory grows until the device is full and the following frames stall. We therefore recreate the mapper outside the timed region whenever device memory use exceeds 50% (90% at 0.005m). The first frames after each recreation re-grow the memory pool and stall. At 0.02m and coarser, these stalls fall in the trimmed 5%. At 0.01m we use frames 18–57 after each recreation (291 of 500, fastest-95% mean). At 0.005m, memory fills within five timed frames, so we use the single regrowth-free frame of each segment (12 of 60 timed frames, plain mean). Excluding the stalls favors nvblox. On exactly the same frames, our method is 23.7× and 29.4× faster than nvblox at 0.01m and 0.005m, as with the reported means.

Open3D (CUDA) is the tensor VoxelBlockGrid of Open3D 0.19 on the GPU (block resolution 16, truncation of four voxels, mesh weight threshold 0.5; the default of 3 removes most of the surface). Its time covers the image upload, block allocation and integration per camera, Marching Cubes, and the mesh download. Its 0.02m0.16m runs were repeated back to back because the first sweep drifted between jobs; the two sweeps differ by up to 1.9ms per setting.

Kernel launches per frame.

The launch counts in the pipeline figure (Fig.2) were measured with Nsight Systems on office2 (ten frames, five Kinects, 0.02m): TSDF fusion 1; Marching Cubes 12; noise removal Nₙᵣ=100 label-propagation launches (the iteration cap, which the room-scale meshes reach in every frame; a convergence flag is read back every ten iterations) plus about 28 launches for edge sorting, adjacency construction, and compaction, and 3 for normal computation and smoothing; texture mapping 2 (view selection and UV generation) plus 13 launches that rebuild the fixed-size-array adjacency of the compacted mesh (edge sort); inpainting Nᵢₚ=5 (the cap, reached in every frame); and seam correction N_sc=55: 12 Jacobi iterations of four kernels (clear, splat seams, update, gauge) plus proxy construction, seam detection, residual sampling, the temporal EMA blend and its gauge re-application, residual statistics, and the bake (53 on the first frame, which has no EMA history). In total, about 219 kernel launches per frame. The GPU input preprocessing adds 25 more (five per camera: color and depth undistortion, z-buffer clear, depth reprojection into the color view, and upsampling), 244 in all.

Noise-removal iteration cap.

The cap of 100 label-propagation iterations bounds the latency of noise removal, but on our room-scale meshes propagation has not yet converged when it stops. We reran 30 frames (400–690, stride 10) with a cap of 5000 and the same convergence check: propagation converges after 111–241 iterations at 0.02m and 241–591 at 0.01m (office2 and band2), and after 791 to more than 5000 at 0.005m (office2). With the cap, a large component can still carry several labels, and a part with fewer than 500 faces is removed with the noise. Compared with the long runs, the cap removes on average 0.02–0.05% and at most 0.12% of the output faces per frame. The component analysis is therefore an approximation with a bounded number of iterations; all reported results use the cap.

Texture atlas.

The atlas is the vertical stack of the input color images, one 1920×1080 band per Kinect in input order, i.e. 1920×5400 pixels for five Kinects (Fig.8). A face textured from camera k receives as UVs the pixel coordinates of its projection into band k; an inpainted face receives the UV of one vertex of a neighboring face and is therefore filled with a uniform color; and the seam correction multiplies band k by \exp(ĝₖ) in place, so the mesh UVs never change. Image regions that no face samples simply stay in the atlas: the layout needs no chart packing, and the corrected atlas of the frame shown is a 1.9MB JPEG. The layout also suits real-time delivery: it is fixed and each band is the camera image itself, so consecutive atlases keep a constant resolution and are temporally coherent, and the atlas sequence can be streamed with a standard video encoder (compression is not evaluated here).

A.1 Seam Correction Sampling and Solver

Section3.6 gives the seam-to-field formulation. Here we detail its implementation. We read seams directly from the fixed-size-array face adjacency, processing each face pair once. A candidate is discarded if the face-normal dot product is below 0.5, or if either projected triangle has twice-area below one full-resolution pixel squared (including collapsed inpainted faces). For each retained seam we sample eight edge parameters tᵢ=(i+\tfrac12)/8. In each camera, the projected point is moved by 0.5 proxy pixels toward that face’s projected opposite vertex, as illustrated in Fig.9. These positions lie near corresponding shared-edge locations; after the independent insets they need not be projections of the same 3D point. Samples outside the proxy or with linear luminance below 0.01 in either view are rejected. The median log-luminance difference supplies dₛ, and the valid-sample fraction supplies wₛ. There is no additional robust penalty on the resulting least-squares residual.

Proxy and discrete constraints.

We build the linear-RGB proxy by 1/8 box reduction of each input camera band. This reduces the influence of texture detail and small misalignments on the residual. One constraint per seam is assigned to the nearest grid cell at the inset midpoint in each camera. Bilinear assignment would couple multiple same-camera unknowns in each data term; the nearest-cell construction instead retains a graph of pairwise differences. Bilinear interpolation is used only when applying the solved field to the atlas.

Matrix-free update.

We use the notation gₖ[p], a(s), b(s), pₐˢ, p_bˢ of Sec.3.6. For cell p of camera k, let ℕ(p) be its four-neighbors in the same grid and S(p) the seams assigned to it, i.e. with (a(s),pₐˢ)=(k,p) or (b(s),p_bˢ)=(k,p). For such a seam let (k^′ₛ,qₛ) be the other camera and its cell, and let σ_p,s be +1 if k=a(s) and -1 if k=b(s). The update is

\beginsplitnumₚ&=λₛₘ∑_q∈ℕ(p)gₖ[q]+∑_s∈S(p)wₛ(g_k^′ₛ[qₛ]+σ_p,sdₛ), denₚ&=λₐ+λₛₘ|ℕ(p)|+∑_s∈S(p)wₛ, gₖ⁺[p]&=(1-ω) gₖ[p]+ω numₚ/denₚ.\endsplit

(2)

Here numₚ and denₚ are the numerator and denominator of the weighted average numₚ/denₚ; the anchor adds λₐ to denₚ and nothing to numₚ because its target is g=0. Every frame starts from g=0, and all cells are updated from the previous iterate (Jacobi). We use λₛₘ=30, λₐ=0.02, ω=0.7, and twelve iterations. The anchor makes the unprojected linear system strictly diagonally dominant. After every update, the implementation first clamps each value to [-0.15,0.15] and then subtracts the mean over all camera cells. Consequently the clamp is a bound before gauge removal, not a strict bound on the final re-centered field. An optional reference-camera mode sets that camera’s grid to zero instead of removing the mean. Luminance uses one scalar field; RGB mode solves three independent channels.

Temporal filtering and bake.

Continuous capture uses the EMA specified above, with the gauge re-applied after blending. On office2 frames 400–699, it reduces the mean frame-to-frame change of the (clamped) log-gain grid from 0.0079 to 0.0010, and the 99th percentile over cells and frames from 0.057 to 0.0072; without it, single cells jump by several percent between frames. Filtering is in camera-grid coordinates and does not require mesh correspondences across frames. For each atlas pixel, the band layout identifies its camera and image coordinates. We interpolate that camera’s field bilinearly, clamp the interpolated log-gain again to [-0.15,0.15], and multiply the original linear RGB by \exp(ĝ), where ĝ denotes this clamped value. The applied gain therefore remains in approximately [0.86,1.16], even if the gauge-shifted grid exceeds the update clamp. We then convert back to sRGB. This leaves image detail in the original texture while modulating it with a coarse spatial correction; it does not repair geometric misalignment or sharp local seams.

Constraint and output seam residuals.

Table3 reports two seam residuals. The constraint residual (Constr.) is computed inside the solver: the mean |dₛ| over the sampled seams before, and |dₛ-(gₐ₍ₛ₎[pₐˢ]-g_b(s)[p_bˢ])| after, using the EMA-blended grid at the nearest cell, without interpolation or the bake clamp. The output residual (Output) is measured after the bake: it applies the same seam detection and sampling (Fig.9) to the atlas the system writes (8-bit JPEG), so it includes the bilinear field interpolation, the clamp, and quantization. “Before” reads the correction-off run and “after” the full run, each with its own mesh. Both residuals are measured between the input cameras on the evaluated frames.

GPU reuse.

Faces, normals, camera labels, and projected coordinates remain on the device from reconstruction and texturing. The correction also reuses the existing fixed-size-array adjacency, avoiding another edge-key sort (about 1.7ms per frame). It needs no new camera projection and no geometry re-upload. Proxy construction, residual sampling, field updates, and atlas bake execute on the GPU. Persistent buffers avoid per-frame allocations, and the iterations require no CPU synchronization.

Appendix B Held-out Re-rendering Protocol

We reconstruct the textured mesh from one set of Kinects and render it from a disjoint set, so the evaluation views are never used as input. Concretely, we reconstruct from the even Kinects {2,4,6,8,10} and evaluate on the odd Kinects {1,3,5,7,9}, at a voxel size of 0.02m (cmu-room). For each held-out camera we render the reconstructed mesh with its calibrated intrinsics/extrinsics (Blender/EEVEE, emission shading) and compare to that camera’s real, undistorted RGB image.

Shared valid-pixel mask.

Each method leaves different uncovered (black) pixels where faces are unseen or removed. Scoring each method only on its own covered pixels would compare different pixel sets and make the numbers incomparable. We therefore evaluate every method on the intersection of all methods’ covered pixels: a pixel is valid only if every method renders non-black there (a light morphological opening removes speckle). PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS are computed on this single shared mask and averaged with a 5% trimmed mean. PSNR uses only the masked pixels. SSIM and LPIPS (AlexNet) are computed on the full frame after every pixel outside the mask is set to the same constant in both images (black for SSIM and mid-gray for LPIPS, whose input range is [-1,1]). All metrics use sRGB values in [0,1].

Subsets.

The quality numbers of Sec.4.2 and the luminance-vs-RGB ablation use frames 400–697 at stride 3 (100 evaluated frames) per sequence and the same common mask over all eight evaluated variants. The offline-texturing comparison (AppendixD) uses frames 400–429; the voxel-size and occlusion ablations use the 50-frame subsets specified in their captions. Within each comparison, all methods are evaluated on the same frames and mask. For the quality and seam numbers of Sec.4 and the luminance-vs-RGB ablation, our method reconstructs every frame from 400 to 699 in order, and only every third frame is rendered and evaluated. The correction-on variants use the gain-field EMA (α=0.15) throughout, as do the runtimes in Tab.1; its history starts at frame 400 (the first field is used as is) without a separate warm-up.

Rounding.

Differences, ratios, and percentages in the text and in the Δ columns of this appendix are computed from unrounded metrics, so they can differ in the last digit from values recomputed from the rounded table entries.

Appendix C Seam Correction Variants

Our seam correction estimates a single luminance gain field by default, which preserves chroma and solves a third as many parameters as a per-channel (RGB) field; the RGB field uses the same solver with three independent channels and is meant for cameras whose white balance differs. We compare the two variants on Panoptic, whose Kinects share their white balance, on a synthetic capture with known per-camera differences, and on our in-house capture, whose cameras run their own white balance.

Panoptic.

Tab.5 compares the two fields on the same 100-frame held-out set and common mask as Tab.2. Correcting chroma in addition to luminance changes the re-rendering metrics negligibly (PSNR within 0.002, SSIM within 0.0002, LPIPS within 0.0005 on both sequences in Tab.5): the inter-camera differences are dominated by exposure, and the luminance field is sufficient.

Spatial field vs. one gain per camera.

To test whether the spatial field is needed, we also solve a single luminance gain per camera (a 1×1 field) with the same solver, gain bound, and temporal filter (“constant” in Tab.5). It reaches only 72% / 35% of the PSNR gain, 54% / 30% of the SSIM gain, and 50% / 50% of the LPIPS gain of the 24×16 field over no correction (office2 / band2). Per image pair, the field scores higher than the constant gain in SSIM and LPIPS on 499–500 of the 500 pairs of each sequence and in PSNR on 418 and 370. The seam constraint residual falls by 13.8% / 7.8% with the constant gain against 36.5% / 31.8% with the field (Tab.3). The variation of the gain within each camera therefore matters beyond a per-camera exposure offset.

Synthetic capture with ground truth.

Our in-house capture cannot be released, and neither it nor Panoptic has images free of inter-camera color differences. We therefore render a synthetic stand-in in Blender, whose generation scripts are released with the code: a person animated with CMU motion capture [6] dances for 150 frames on a 3×3 m floor, seen by ten 1280×720 RGB-D cameras on a circle, with an empty background. All materials are Lambertian and the lighting is fixed, so a surface point has the same color in every camera. We then multiply each camera’s linear color by a fixed smooth gain: an exposure offset (log) of +0.10, -0.10, +0.10, -0.10, and 0 in order around the circle, assigned separately to the five reconstruction and the five held-out cameras, so most neighboring cameras of a group differ by about 22%, plus a small linear gradient and a small white-balance shift; every gain stays within ±0.14 per channel and is zero-mean over the reconstruction cameras. This is the ideal case for our model: the differences are multiplicative, low-frequency, and within the default bound. We reconstruct the foreground at 0.01m from the five even cameras and evaluate on the five odd ones against the unperturbed renders on all 150 frames and the shared mask. As for the in-house capture, the correction uses |g|≤0.4 and λₛₘ=5, and the seams are sampled on a 1/2 instead of a 1/8 proxy. This is a limitation of the default: the 1/8 proxy suits scenes that fill the image, as in Panoptic, but here the person covers only a small part of each image, the proxy boxes at its seams mix in background and other body parts, and the gains solved on the body do not follow the applied ones. A small subject needs a finer proxy.

Tab.6 shows that the correction recovers most of the loss caused by the gains: 94% (luminance) and 97% (RGB) of the SSIM gap and 87% / 95% of the LPIPS gap to the reconstruction from unperturbed input, and 57% / 59% of the 0.34dB PSNR gap. The seam constraint residual (Tab.3) drops from 0.091 to 0.049, close to the mismatch on the unperturbed input (0.048), which reflects geometric and sampling error alone. Fig.10(a) shows seams on the floor and on the shirt: without correction the surface breaks into brighter and darker patches where the texture switches between cameras; with either field the patches disappear.

We compare the applied log-gain h with the recovered gain -g, the negated correction field. The correction is relative, so -g is not expected to equal h. A seam constrains only the difference between the two cameras that meet there: across the seams, the recovered difference matches the applied one (r=0.97, slope 0.94), which is what removes the seams. Each camera’s own level is not observed; it is set by the zero-mean gauge and, away from the seams, by the smoothness term and the anchor toward unit gain. The per-camera gain at the same seams therefore follows the applied one with less than half its amplitude (r=0.83, slope 0.41; Fig.10(b)), and a gain common to all cameras would not be recovered at all.

In-house capture.

Fig.11 shows the foreground-only in-house capture of the main paper (Sec. 4.4; five Orbbec Femto Bolt sensors), whose cameras run independent auto exposure and auto white balance, so camera boundaries may differ in color cast as well as in brightness. We run both variants with a wider gain bound and weaker smoothing than the Panoptic default (|g|≤0.4, i.e. gains in [0.67,1.49], and λₛₘ=5); the 24×16 grid, the solver, and all other seam-correction parameters are as in Tab.4. The foreground-only reconstruction uses 0.01m voxels in a 2m cube, a 0.10m depth tolerance, a four-voxel truncation band, a 100-face component threshold, and at most 20 inpainting iterations. The view is a turntable render of one frame seen from behind; no held-out camera exists for this capture, so the comparison is qualitative. The sequence was recorded by the authors; the person shown took part voluntarily and gave informed consent to being recorded and to the use of the recordings in this paper and its supplementary video.

Two cameras texture most of the back (red and yellow in the source-camera mosaic), and their boundary crosses the T-shirt and the plaid shirt at the waist. Without correction, the T-shirt region textured by the yellow camera is darker and slightly greenish next to the bright white of the red camera, and the plaid shirt steps in brightness across the boundary; accordingly, both fields brighten the yellow camera by up to about 1.5× toward the center of its view. The luminance field removes the brightness steps as well as the RGB field does: on the T-shirt fabric on both sides of the boundary, the difference of the mean CIELAB lightness of the two sides drops from about 8 to 3 units with either variant, while the distance between their mean (a^*,b^*) stays at 2–3 units with and without correction, close to the visibility threshold. (The fabric pixels are those in the T-shirt zoom box with L^*>55 in the uncorrected render that lie within 25 pixels of both cameras’ regions of the source-camera mosaic, in the 1440×1440 renders.) Consistently, the three channels of the RGB field agree with their mean to within 1% on average (Fig.11(c)): even with independent white balance, the exposure difference dominates on this capture, and the luminance default suffices here too (the figure applies 0.5\exp(gₖ) to sRGB rather than linear values, exaggerating the tint). As on Panoptic, the fields are smooth and low-frequency; they shift each camera’s colors as a whole rather than re-texturing the surface. The green fringes at the silhouette stem from background pixels mixed into depth-edge faces of the input images and are present in all variants.

Appendix D Offline Texturing on Our Geometry

The Offline baseline of Sec.4 pairs SPSR geometry with mvs-texturing [45], so it differs from our method in both geometry and texturing. To isolate the texturing step, we instead apply mvs-texturing to our own per-frame meshes and evaluate from held-out cameras (Tab.7). This auxiliary comparison uses a separate mesh set (frames 400–429 of each sequence) and a two-method coverage intersection; its scores support comparisons within this experiment, rather than direct comparisons with Tab.2.

We verified the consistency of the offline texturing pipeline: re-texturing the same SPSR meshes matches the reference renders to 34–41 dB PSNR. mvs-texturing is run with hole filling enabled; we also tried both settings of its keep-unseen-faces option.

In this auxiliary comparison, offline texturing on our geometry performs worse than our texturing in all three metrics. Some faces unseen by the input views remain untextured (rendered blank), while our inpainting supplies colors for these faces. This result is specific to the dense, noisy per-frame Marching-Cubes meshes tested here.

Appendix E Voxel Size: Quality versus Runtime and Memory

Section 4 uses 0.02m voxels, the setting at which the full pipeline stays well within the 33ms real-time budget. Finer voxels recover geometric detail that 0.02m loses (thin structures, small objects, sharper silhouettes) but the dense TSDF grid grows cubically. To quantify this tradeoff we run the identical pipeline on office2 at 0.02m, 0.01m, and 0.005m (the cmu-room volume of 5.8×2.7×5.8 m, i.e. 290×135×290, 580×270×580, and 1160×540×1160 voxels) and report held-out re-rendering quality, per-stage runtime, and GPU memory (Tab.8). All three settings use the same pipeline and the same shared valid-pixel mask (the intersection of the three runs’ coverage), so the rows are directly comparable to each other. The comparison in Sec.4 includes other reconstruction methods and uses a different frame subset and coverage intersection (AppendixB); its absolute scores therefore should not be compared directly with this ablation.

Quality.

Halving the voxel size to 0.01m changes PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS by -0.12 dB, -0.027, and +0.038, respectively. Fig.12 shows the sharper chair and table rim and the additional holes on the wall and floor. At 0.005m, the changes relative to 0.02m are -1.25 dB, -0.170, and +0.175. The truncation band is four voxels, i.e. 2cm, at this fine setting. On band2, halving the voxel size changes the same metrics by -0.37 dB, -0.050, and +0.061. 0.02m remains the setting with a clear margin under the real-time budget; 0.01m slightly exceeds it (see below).

Runtime and memory.

Halving the voxel size multiplies the cell count by eight and the frame time by 2.6–4.0×: 13.1ms at 0.02m, 34.6ms at 0.01m, and 138.9ms at 0.005m over the same 2000 frames (band2: 12.8 and 35.3ms at 0.02 and 0.01m). The stages scale differently. TSDF fusion and Marching Cubes grow with the cell count (0.4→2.3→15.6 and 0.5→1.9→10.8 ms); noise removal, texture mapping, inpainting, and seam correction grow with the output face count (about 0.6M, 2.9M, and 12.4M faces per frame), and the GPU→CPU download of the finished mesh becomes the largest single stage at fine voxels (2.9→11.3→45.6 ms) because the output itself is about 0.85GB per frame at 0.005m. The dense grid, edge table, and mesh buffers take 0.4, 2.3, and 16.6GB of static device memory at the three sizes (peak 2.7, 5.7, and 24.1GB including per-frame allocations and the input buffers), so 0.005m needs a 24 GiB-class GPU and, at about 7.2fps, is an offline setting on this hardware, while 0.01m fits an 8GB GPU at about 28.9fps, just short of the real-time budget (32.4ms without the input upload and preprocessing). Marching-cubes edge indices exceed 2³¹ at 0.005m on this volume, so that build uses 64-bit edge keys (a compile-time option; the default build is unchanged).

Appendix F Occlusion-Aware View Selection

The per-face view selection (Sec.3.4) tests all three vertices of a face against the chosen camera’s depth image and rejects the camera when the depth of a vertex differs from the observed depth at its projection by more than a threshold τ_occ, in either direction. We use τ_occ=$10cm$ and compare it with a loose 1.1m tolerance. The loose test admits large depth discrepancies, allowing foreground texture to be projected onto occluded background surfaces. The fixed 10cm tolerance corresponds to five voxels at 0.02m. Rejected assignments leave faces without a camera, which the inpainting stage fills with flat color. On the common held-out mask, the default changes PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS by +0.67 dB, +0.028, and -0.022 on office2, and +0.41 dB, +0.028, and -0.021 on band2 (Tab.9). Fig.13 shows the effect and Tab.9 reports the held-out metrics of both settings on the same build and mask.

Appendix G Application to SfM+MVS

Our method can also texture surfaces reconstructed from image-based depth and camera estimates rather than RGB-D sensors. Fig.14 shows an example using the door sequence of ETH3D [43]: we take the point-cloud output of VGGT [46] and apply our textured-meshing pipeline to the derived geometry and camera views. This example is qualitative, but it illustrates that the texturing stage is not tied to Kinect-style RGB-D input.

Appendix H Use of Large Language Models

In line with the WACV 2027 policy on large language models (LLMs), we disclose that an LLM-based coding assistant was used in two ways. It helped polish the English of this paper, and it facilitated the experiments: it assisted in writing and running the scripts that drive the reconstruction and evaluation campaigns, compute the metrics, generate the plots and the supplementary video, and check the reported numbers against the measured data, as well as in refactoring the code for release. The method, its CUDA implementation, the experimental design, and all claims are the author’s; every statement and number was verified by the author, who takes full responsibility for the content.

item.title: 镜头和物体要一起动：UniCaMo 把 3D 相机轨迹与稀疏物体轨迹编码进初始噪声 ｜ UniCaMo: Unified Camera and Motion Control for Video Diffusion Models
item.description:
一句话：不做后处理、不加控制分支：直接构造「运动一致的噪声」，让相机与物体运动各自可控。

要点：

  • 输入是四件套：参考图、文本提示、稀疏 3D 物体轨迹、3D 相机轨迹；目标是让两者分别可控且相互不打架
  • 关键手法是「3D-grounded 噪声构造」：把参考图噪声传播与新出现区域的高斯球面噪声表示结合起来，直接构造出编码了目标运动的初始噪声
  • 相比加控制分支或事后修补，这种做法把运动一致性放到生成起点，因而更简单也更稳定

为什么值得看：做虚拟制片或预告片时，最常被要求的就是「镜头这么走、人物那样动」，而现有视频模型往往只能控一个。把运动写进初始噪声是条便宜的路，值得试。

中文摘要：UniCaMo 面向「图像 + 文本生成视频」的扩散模型，解决相机与物体运动需要同时可控的问题。它的输入包括参考图、文本提示、稀疏的 3D 物体轨迹与 3D 相机轨迹；核心做法是直接构造「运动一致」的初始噪声：把参考图噪声传播与新暴露区域的高斯球面噪声表示结合起来，让噪声本身就编码了期望的运动，而不是靠额外的控制分支或事后修补。作者称这种方式简单且有效，能在同一框架内分别控制相机与物体的运动。对虚拟制片、预告片与游戏过场这类需要精确镜头的场景，这种把控制前置到噪声层的思路比堆控制网络更轻。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·核心检索（English）

原文发布：2026-11-02

本期推送：2026-11-04

UniCaMo: Unified Camera and Motion Control for Video Diffusion Models

Abstract

We present UniCaMo, an unified framework for joint control of camera and object motion in image-and-text-to-video diffusion models. Given a reference image, text prompt, sparse 3D object trajectories, and a 3D camera trajectory, UniCaMo constructs motion-consistent input noise that directly encodes the desired motion. Our 3D-grounded noise construction combines reference-derived noise propagation with a spherical Gaussian noise representation for newly revealed regions, providing a simple and effective motion prior without requiring reconstruction of unseen scene geometry. UniCaMo requires no architectural modifications or dedicated control modules and can be adapted using lightweight LoRA fine-tuning with low training data volume. Experiments on standard controllable video generation benchmarks demonstrate state-of-the-art motion controllability and high visual quality with minimal inference overhead. Qualitative videos are available on our project page: https://phongnhhn.info/Unicamo/.

1 Introduction

Controllable video generation is important for applications ranging from visual content creation to robotics and embodied AI [(Wang et al., 2026a; Jang et al., 2025)], and has received increasing attention from the research community. Existing approaches generally start from a pretrained image-and-text-to-video diffusion model and finetune it to introduce controllability, broadly following two directions. One line of work adds adaptation or control modules that inject motion guidance into the generation process [(Chu et al., 2025; He et al., 2024; Bai et al., 2025a; Li et al., 2025a)]. Motion constraints are typically injected late in the generation pipeline, when visual content has already begun to emerge, leaving limited flexibility to resolve motion ambiguity in a geometrically coherent manner while maintaining realism and temporal consistency. These methods also augment already large video diffusion models with additional architectural components, increasing model complexity and inference cost. An appealing alternative is to impose motion at the very beginning of generation by exploiting the input noise. Video diffusion models generate videos by progressively denoising an initial sequence of Gaussian noise maps; rather than modifying the model architecture, the desired motion can therefore be encoded directly into these input noise maps [(Burgert et al., 2025; Chang et al., 2025)].

Existing input-noise-based methods, however, typically rely on 2D optical flow guidance and address object and camera motion separately. These limitations are closely related: the apparent motion of an object in a video is jointly determined by its 3D motion and the changing camera viewpoint, making it inherently ambiguous 111 The HTML page provides a visualization of motion-noise between existing 2D and our 3D-aware approaches. to specify and control the two independently in 2D image space. Moreover, complex motions—such as one person moving around another (Fig. 1)—are difficult to express without explicit depth and viewpoint information. These observations motivate the central question of this work: can we jointly control camera and object motions in 3D by manipulating only the input noise, without modifying the architecture of the underlying video diffusion model?

To answer this question, we propose UniCaMo, a unified framework for joint camera and object motion control through view-and-motion-consistent input noise. UniCaMo lifts the reference image into 3D, where users specify the desired camera motion together with sparse 3D object trajectories. We construct the input noise according to these motions, using reference-derived noise where geometric correspondences are available and a spherical Gaussian noise representation to provide persistent noise for regions newly revealed by camera or object motion. Importantly, this construction need not recover the true geometry of unseen regions; it provides a plausible and geometrically consistent motion prior, while the pretrained video diffusion model supplies the visual and motion priors needed to synthesize realistic content. The resulting sequence of 2D noise maps directly initializes the video diffusion model, enabling joint 3D motion control without additional control modules or architectural modifications. Because the desired 3D motion is already explicitly encoded in the input noise, the model does not need to learn the motion-control mapping entirely from data, allowing effective adaptation with lightweight LoRA fine-tuning and a relatively small amount of computation for training.

Overall, UniCaMo offers three key advantages over existing controllable video generation approaches: (1)unified 3D control with lightweight adaptation: UniCaMo jointly controls object and camera motion directly in 3D, avoiding the ambiguity of 2D motion specification and separate treatment of the two motions, requiring only lightweight LoRA adaptation; (2)simple and effective motion representation: its 3D-grounded noise construction provides a plausible and geometrically consistent motion prior without requiring explicit reconstruction of unseen scene geometry; and (3)state-of-the-art performance: UniCaMo achieves superior controllability and video quality over the evaluated baselines.

2 Related Work

Video diffusion models have made remarkable progress since their early development based on 3D U-Net architectures [(Bar-Tal et al., 2024; Blattmann et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2023; Guo et al., 2023)]. Recent large-scale latent diffusion and transformer-based models [(Hong et al., 2022; Kong et al., 2024; Wan et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2024)] achieve substantially improved visual fidelity, temporal coherence, and adherence to conditioning signals. As these models become increasingly capable, a natural next step is to provide finer control over the generated motion, particularly the motions of objects and the camera.

Existing motion-controlled video generation methods differ primarily in the motion representation and how it is incorporated into the diffusion model. For object motion, masks, boxes, and keypoints provide coarse spatial guidance, whereas optical flow and point trajectories enable finer-grained control [(Wang et al., 2024a; Li et al., 2025a; Geng et al., 2025; Yin et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2025b)]. Camera motion is commonly represented by 6DoF poses or trajectories and incorporated through dedicated conditioning mechanisms [(He et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024b; Bahmani et al., 2025)]. More recent methods pursue joint object and camera control using trajectory-based conditioning, geometry-aware representations, or richer 3D information [(Li et al., 2025a; Geng et al., 2025; Chu et al., 2025; Zheng et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026)]. These approaches generally introduce motion control through additional conditioning signals or modifications within the denoising process.

UniCaMo instead encodes object and camera motion directly into the input noise, connecting our work to structured noise initialization for controllable video generation. Noise-warping methods construct temporally correlated Gaussian noise by propagating noise according to motion fields. [Chang et al. (2025)] highlight the importance of maintaining appropriate Gaussian noise statistics, while Go-with-the-Flow [(Burgert et al., 2025)] demonstrates efficient object motion control by warping input noise without an inference-time control module. Related work further shows that training with warped noise can induce useful equivariances and facilitate efficient sampling [(Liu and Vahdat, 2025)]. These approaches, however, primarily operate with 2D motion fields or correspondences. UniCaMo extends this paradigm to joint 3D object and camera control by constructing view-and-motion-consistent noise: noise follows specified object trajectories while remaining consistent across changing viewpoints. A spherical noise representation provides persistent noise for newly revealed regions without explicitly reconstructing unseen scene geometry.

3 UniCaMo – Joint Camera and Object Motion Control

This section describes UniCaMo, our unified framework for joint camera and object motion control in video diffusion through view-and-motion-consistent input noise. UniCaMo requires no architectural modifications to the underlying video diffusion model, enabling lightweight fine-tuning with modest training data while introducing minimal additional overhead at inference time. We first provide an overview of the framework, followed by the details of noise construction and model training.

3.1 Major components and overview

Our overall pipeline is shown in Fig.2, UniCaMo takes as input a reference image and a text prompt describing the desired scene and action, and outputs a generated video. In between, the framework comprises two stages: (1) an interactive interface through which users specify the desired object and camera motions in 3D, and (2) a motion-guided generation model that constructs motion-and-view-consistent noise from the reference image and specified motions to initialize an image-to-video diffusion model.

The interactive interface first lifts the reference 2D image into a 3D point cloud, allowing the scene to be viewed and interacted with directly in 3D. Users specify object motion using sparse 3D point tracks on objects of interest, together with a desired 3D camera trajectory. This is an important distinction from prior approaches that specify motion using 2D point tracks in the 2D image plane, which are inherently ambiguous with respect to depth and viewpoint and can be insufficient for expressing complex motions, particularly when multiple objects cross or move around one another. By operating directly in 3D, UniCaMo provides a more expressive and geometrically explicit representation for jointly specifying object and camera motion.

The motion-guided generation model builds upon a pretrained image-to-video diffusion model [(Wan et al., 2025)] that takes a sequence of Gaussian noise maps and progressively denoises them into video frames, conditioned on the reference image and text prompt. The input noise and output video therefore have a direct spatiotemporal correspondence: each noise map corresponds to an output frame, and spatial locations in the noise map influence corresponding regions of that frame. Prior work has shown that imposing coherent motion across the input noise maps can induce corresponding motion in the generated video [Burgert et al. (2025); Liu and Vahdat (2025)]. UniCaMo exploits this property by constructing motion-consistent noise maps whose cross-frame correspondences reflect the user-specified 3D object and camera motions. Starting from a pretrained video diffusion model, we subsequently fine-tune it to better exploit these motion-consistent noise maps for controllable generation.

The key challenge is to construct consistent noise correspondences across frames given only the reference image and the user’s sparse 3D object trajectories and camera poses. Prior methods [(Burgert et al., 2025; Liu and Vahdat, 2025)] commonly rely on ground-truth video to compute dense optical flow, which creates a systematic training–inference mismatch when such video is unavailable; our approach seeks to eliminate this discrepancy entirely. While noise associated with the reference image can be propagated according to the specified object and camera motions, these motions may reveal regions that are not visible in the reference frame and therefore have no corresponding noise values. UniCaMo addresses this problem by surrounding the reference point cloud with a 3D spherical noise representation, which provides persistent noise anchors for such unseen regions. Combining the reference-derived and spherical noise allows UniCaMo to construct a complete sequence of 2D noise maps consistent with the desired object and camera motions.

Importantly, the resulting noise sequence represents only one plausible realization consistent with the desire motion. Recovering the true 3D geometry of occluded and out-of-view regions from a single reference image is fundamentally ill-posed and, more importantly, unnecessary for our purpose. Instead, the 3D sphere provides a simple and effective construction for assigning persistent noise values to otherwise undefined regions and maintaining their consistency across viewpoints. The sphere therefore does not represent the true scene geometry, nor does it constrain the generated scene to have spherical structure; it merely provides a geometrically consistent motion prior. The final video is determined jointly by this prior, the reference image, the text prompt, and the rich visual and motion statistics learned by the diffusion model from large-scale video data. Thus, rather than explicitly reconstructing unseen scene content, UniCaMo leverages the generative power of the pretrained model to synthesize plausible geometry and appearance while using the structured noise to guide the desired object and camera motions.

3.2 Motion-Consistent Noise Construction

Given a reference image and the desired object and camera motions specified relative to it, our goal is to construct a sequence of 2D Gaussian noise maps whose cross-frame correspondences follow these motions. The motion specification consists of (i) a sparse set of target 3D point tracks T={xᵢᵗ∈ℝ³ |i=1,N̄,t=1,T̄} and (ii) a sequence of target camera poses ℙ={Pᵗ|t=1,T̄}, where N is the number of point tracks and T is the number of video frames. We first lift the reference image into a 3D point cloud using off-the-shelf 3D reconstruction methods [Huang et al. (2025); Li et al. (2025c); Wang et al. (2026b)] and associate its points with Gaussian noise sampled for the reference frame. Foreground noise is then propagated according to the specified object trajectories T and camera poses ℙ, while background noise is propagated according to ℙ alone. This determines consistent noise values for regions represented by the reference point cloud, but leaves regions that are occluded or outside the reference field of view undefined. To complete these regions, we surround the reference point cloud with a 3D spherical noise representation that provides persistent noise values across viewpoints. Together, these steps produce a complete sequence of motion-consistent noise maps used to initialize the video diffusion model.

Foreground noise propagation. We obtain a foreground mask of the reference image [(Carion et al., 2025)] and retain the 3D point tracks in T associated with the foreground objects of interest. For each frame t, we project each 3D point xᵢᵗ onto the image plane using the corresponding camera pose Pᵗ and rescale the projected coordinates to the latent resolution. Specifically, given an image resolution of W×H and a latent resolution of Wₗₐₜ×Hₗₐₜ, we scale the projected coordinates by Wₗₐₜ/W and Hₗₐₜ/H. Let uᵢᵗ∈ℝ² denote the resulting latent-space location of xᵢᵗ. Starting from i.i.d. Gaussian noise sampled for the reference frame, we propagate noise along each trajectory by copying a (2R-1)×(2R-1) patch centered at uᵢ¹ in the first frame to its corresponding location uᵢᵗ in each subsequent frame. We use R=2 by default, corresponding to a 3×3 patch. In this way, foreground noise follows both the specified 3D object motion and the changing camera viewpoint.

Background noise propagation. For the background, we use the 3D point cloud obtained by unprojecting the reference image with its estimated depth and associate each point with an i.i.d. Gaussian noise value in place of its RGB color. The background point cloud remains fixed in world coordinates and is rasterized into each target frame according to the corresponding camera pose Pᵗ. Its projected noise therefore moves solely according to the camera trajectory. Thus, foreground noise follows both object and camera motion, whereas background noise follows camera motion alone.

Spherical noise representation. The foreground and background propagation described above, however, cannot assign noise to regions newly revealed by object or camera motion, as these regions have no corresponding points in the reference point cloud. To provide temporally consistent noise for such regions, we surround the reference point cloud with a 3D sphere centered at the camera center of the reference frame. Let Cᵗ∈ℝ³ denote the camera center at frame t, and let d_\max⁰ denote the maximum estimated depth of the reference image. We set the sphere radius to r=\max (τ·\maxₜ∥Cᵗ-C¹∥₂, d⁰_\max), where τ=1.2 provides a margin around the camera trajectory. We parameterize the sphere using latitude and longitude and assign its surface a fixed Gaussian noise texture E∈ℝ^C×Hₑₙᵥ×Wₑₙᵥ, where Hₑₙᵥ and Wₑₙᵥ are proportional to the video resolution scaled by a factor k=4, and C is the latent channel count of the video diffusion model.

For each frame, we cast a ray from the camera center through each latent location and compute its intersection with the sphere. The intersection point is converted to latitude–longitude coordinates, which are used to sample the corresponding value from the fixed Gaussian noise texture E. Because all frames sample from the same spherical noise texture, rays intersecting the same spherical location receive the same noise value across viewpoints. The sphere therefore provides persistent and view-consistent noise for regions that cannot be associated with the reference point cloud. Details of the ray–sphere intersection are provided in the appendix.

Depth-aware Noise Composition. We finally combine the foreground, background, and spherical noise contributions into a complete noise map for each frame. Multiple foreground and background points may project to the same latent location, particularly under object motion, occlusion, and viewpoint changes. Rather than resolving such collisions through arbitrary ordering [(Chu et al., 2025)] or averaging [(Burgert et al., 2025)], we exploit their explicit 3D geometry. For each latent location receiving multiple contributions from the foreground trajectories or background point cloud, we apply a z-buffer rule and retain the contribution with the smallest camera-space depth, i.e., the point closest to the camera. This enforces a geometrically meaningful visibility ordering and prevents noise associated with occluded surfaces from overwriting visible ones. Wherever this propagation provides a valid noise value, we retain it; locations that remain undefined are filled with the corresponding noise sampled from the sphere. This preserves the explicit geometric correspondences available from the reference image while using the spherical representation only where such correspondences are unavailable. The result is a complete sequence of motion noise maps consistent with both the specified 3D object trajectories and camera poses, providing the motion-aware initialization for subsequent video generation.

4 Experiments

We evaluate UniCaMo in three settings: object motion control, camera motion control, and joint object and camera motion control. For object motion control, we use MoveBench [(Chu et al., 2025)], a recent benchmark comprising approximately 1,000 diverse, high-quality videos. For camera motion control, we randomly sample unseen 300 clips from RealEstate10K (RE10K) [(Zhou et al., 2018)]. Finally, to evaluate joint control, for which no suitable benchmark currently exists, we curate unseen 300 real-world videos from publicly available sources [(JovianZM, 2024)] spanning diverse object motions and camera trajectories, following the setup in previous work [(Chu et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026)].

Using existing protocol [(Chu et al., 2025; Ren et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2024b)], we evaluate three complementary aspects of the generated videos: (i) visual quality, measured by FID [(Heusel et al., 2017)], FVD [(Unterthiner et al., 2019)], PSNR, and SSIM [(Wang et al., 2004)]; (ii) object-motion fidelity, measured by the endpoint error (EPE) of the generated trajectories [(Chu et al., 2025)]; and (iii) camera-motion fidelity, measured by rotation error (RotErr), translation error (TransErr), and camera motion consistency (CamMC), which quantify the deviation between the generated and reference camera trajectories.

4.1 Comparisons with State-of-the-Art Methods

We compare UniCaMo against a broad range of prior motion-controllable video generation methods, covering object motion control, camera motion control, and joint control. Among these, methods such as Wan-Move [(Chu et al., 2025)] and SymphoMotion [(Zhang et al., 2026)] support both object and camera motion control, while methods such as Go-with-the-Flow [(Burgert et al., 2025)] and ImageConductor [(Li et al., 2025b)] focus on object motion control, and CamI2V [(Zheng et al., 2024)] and CameraCtrl [(He et al., 2024)] focus on camera motion control. We generally evaluate these methods using their publicly released models. To enable more controlled comparisons, however, we additionally construct variants of relevant baselines that match UniCaMo in either the motion specification or the underlying video diffusion model. In particular, Wan-Move + TAPIP3D tracks projects the same 3D object tracks used by UniCaMo onto the image plane and provides the resulting 2D tracks to Wan-Move, thereby matching the quality of the input trajectories. Go-with-the-Flow (Wan2.1-I2V-14B) uses the same Wan2.1-I2V-14B backbone as UniCaMo and is retrained on the same data with the same training recipe, including the LoRA rank and training schedule, leaving the noise-construction strategy as the primary difference. These variants help disentangle the benefits of UniCaMo’s 3D motion specification from those of its motion-and-view-consistent noise construction.

Object motion control. Table 1 reports quantitative results on MoveBench, with results reported separately for single-object and multi-object motion. UniCaMo outperforms prior motion-control methods across all metrics, achieving lower FID and FVD, higher PSNR and SSIM, and lower trajectory error (EPE). The advantage is particularly pronounced on the 192 multi-object cases, where UniCaMo achieves the lowest FVD and EPE, demonstrating stronger adherence to the specified motions in more complex multi-object scenarios. Qualitative comparisons are shown in Fig. 3.

Camera control. Table 2 summarizes the camera-control results. UniCaMo achieves the lowest TransErr (1.89) and CamMC (1.98), while matching the best RotErr (0.26) and achieving FID 5.99 and FVD 39.93. These results support our design of motion-and-view-consistent noise: the spherical noise representation provides persistent noise correspondences across changing viewpoints, including newly revealed regions, enabling the generated video to better follow the specified camera trajectory. Qualitative comparisons are shown in Fig. 4.

Joint camera and object motion control. We evaluate joint control on our 300 curated clips, each containing simultaneous object and camera motion, and report both object- and camera-control metrics in Table 3. We use this curated dataset because MoveBench and RealEstate10K evaluate object and camera motion control separately and therefore do not capture the joint setting for which UniCaMo is designed. UniCaMo achieves the best performance across all eight metrics, with particularly strong gains in this more challenging setting, where the specified object trajectories and camera motion must be satisfied simultaneously. Qualitative comparisons are shown in Fig. 5.

Supplementary videos. Please check our provided HTML page and appendices to see more videos and comparisons.

4.2 Ablation Studies

To assess the contribution of each component, we begin from purely random Gaussian noise (Setting A) and introduce our components one at a time, measuring the gain each provides over the preceding setting. Results are reported in Table4.

Effect of foreground noise. Propagating noise along the foreground 3D tracks (B) show significant improvements over fully independent Gaussian noise (A). It more than halves the trajectory error and substantially reduces every camera metric, while also lowering FID and FVD. Motion written into the initialisation is therefore inherited by the generated video. The top-left of Fig. 6 shows the corresponding qualitative result: random noise still produces a coherent video rather than collapsing outright, but it no longer follows the trajectories specified by the user.

Effect of background noise. Extending propagation from the foreground alone (B) to the background point cloud (C) benefits camera control. This is expected, since the background carries information about scene geometry and layout, and therefore a camera signal that foreground tracks alone cannot supply. The top-right of Fig. 6 illustrates this: Setting B still reproduces the correct object motion, but the camera fails to follow the user’s intention.

Effect of spherical noise. Adding the spherical representation for regions absent from the reference point cloud (E) yields a further camera-control gain over C, while FID and FVD remain essentially unchanged, indicating that the gain is specific to camera fidelity rather than to appearance. The bottom-left of Fig. 6 shows where this matters most: when the camera translates over a long distance or rotates through a large angle, extensive novel-view regions are revealed, and the spherical noise supplies most of their content.

Effect of depth-aware noise composition. Resolving collisions with the depth-aware z-buffer rather than compositing in 2D (D) improves performance across the board: EPE drops from 3.35 to 2.95, RotErr from 1.74 to 1.23, TransErr from 18.85 to 16.27 and CamMC from 19.56 to 16.74, with FID and FVD also improving. Ordering contributions by camera depth therefore matters throughout the sequence, not only in explicitly occluded regions. The bottom-right of Fig. 6 shows the failure mode: without depth-aware composition, the motion noise of the grinder is overwritten and washed out by the background, leaving the object static in Setting D.

5 Conclusions

We presented UniCaMo, a unified framework for joint 3D camera and object motion control in image-to-video diffusion models. UniCaMo encodes the desired motion directly into the diffusion initialization by combining noise propagation along 3D object trajectories with a spherical noise representation that maintains persistent noise correspondences across changing viewpoints and newly revealed regions. This view-and-motion-consistent noise enables precise control without additional adaptation modules or architectural modifications to the underlying video diffusion model, requiring only lightweight fine-tuning. Experiments across object motion, camera motion, and joint control demonstrate that UniCaMo achieves strong controllability and visual quality, establishing structured noise initialization as a simple and effective approach to unified 3D motion control in video generation.

AI use statement

In this study, generative AI tools were used exclusively to correct grammatical and spelling errors. All AI-assisted edits were reviewed, and every modification proposed by these tools was independently verified by two authors. The authors accept full responsibility for the final content of the manuscript, including any text, claims, or artifacts produced with the assistance of generative AI.

Reproducibility statement

We have provided key algorithms in the main text and the appendices. Full codebase, model checkpoints and datasets will be publicly available upon acceptance.

（参考文献见原文。）

Technical appendices and supplementary material

Appendix A User Interface

To support unified control of both object and camera motion at inference time, we implement an interactive graphical user interface (GUI) that enables users to define 3D object trajectories and 3D camera trajectories through an intuitive two-phase workflow. Fig. 7 shows a visualization of our GUI and results.

Data Processing.

Given a single input image, we first run ViPE [(Huang et al., 2025)] to estimate monocular depth and camera intrinsics. Using the estimated depth map and camera parameters, we reconstruct a dense 3D point cloud of the scene. This point cloud serves as the spatial context for all subsequent editing operations.

2D Object Selection.

In the first phase, the GUI displays the input image as a 2D canvas. The user selects the object(s) of interest by drawing polygon masks directly on the image. Multiple objects can be selected as separate groups, each receiving its own mask. From each object mask, we proportionally sample 3D point tracks: for an object whose mask covers n pixels out of the total H×W image, we allocate \max(1,⌊n/(H×W)×N⌋) of the N=1024 total point tracks. The remaining tracks are sampled uniformly from regions outside all masks to represent background motion. Each sampled pixel is mapped to its corresponding 3D world-space coordinate via the reconstructed point cloud.

3D Object Motion Editing.

In the second phase, the GUI transitions to a 3D view showing the reconstructed point cloud alongside the sampled point tracks. The user defines target object trajectories by placing keyframes along a desired 3D path using interactive translation and rotation gizmos (6-DoF transform controls). Intermediate frames are obtained via linear interpolation between keyframes, producing continuous target motion trajectories for all points within each object group.

Camera Trajectory Editing.

Camera motion is edited through a separate set of 6-DoF gizmos that control the virtual camera’s position and orientation at user-specified keyframes. The camera trajectory is visualized as a sequence of frustums connected by a spline curve, allowing the user to intuitively design complex camera paths including panning, tilting, dollying, and orbiting. As with object motion, intermediate camera poses are linearly interpolated between keyframes.

Export and Video Generation.

Once the user finalizes both object and camera trajectories, the GUI exports a single .npz file containing: (i) 3D point track coordinates of shape (T,N,3), (ii) per-frame visibility flags of shape (T,N), (iii) camera intrinsics of shape (T,3,3), and (iv) camera extrinsics (world-to-camera) of shape (T,4,4). These exported signals are directly fed into our Guidance-based Noise Warping module (Section3.2) to construct the 3D-grounded motion-consistent noise, which then initializes the video diffusion model for generation.

Appendix B Implementation Details

B.1 Training and inference details

Given a ground-truth training video, we first preprocess it using off-the-shelf models to obtain the signals needed for motion-consistent noise construction. Specifically, we estimate camera intrinsics, extrinsics, and depth using ViPE [(Huang et al., 2025)], foreground masks using SAM3 [(Carion et al., 2025)], and sparse 3D point tracks using TAPIP3D [(Zhang et al., 2025a)]. These quantities capture the object and camera motions of the target video and allow us to apply the procedure in Sec. 3.2 to construct a sequence of 2D Gaussian noise maps whose cross-frame correspondences are consistent with those motions. This naturally defines a supervised training pair: the motion-consistent noise sequence serves as the input initialization to the video diffusion model, while the original video serves as the target output. Importantly, the extracted geometric and motion signals are used only to construct the noise initializer and are not provided to the model as additional conditioning inputs.

We curate 400K training clips from DynPose100K++, WSDG-1M, and 4DNeX [(Huang et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025)], and precompute and cache all signals required for noise construction. To standardize captions across data sources, we re-caption all clips using Qwen2.5-VL [(Bai et al., 2025b)], following the Wan-Move prompt-extension protocol [(Chu et al., 2025)]. We fine-tune a pretrained Wan2.1-I2V-14B model [(Wan et al., 2025)] using flow matching, with the motion-consistent noise sequence as initialization and the reference frame and text prompt as conditioning. We apply LoRA only to the DiT denoiser, while freezing the VAE and all encoders. We use a LoRA rank of 64 with α=1 and train for 10K steps in bfloat16 with gradient checkpointing on 32 NVIDIA H100 GPUs, using a batch size of 1 per GPU, for approximately three days. To improve robustness to different guidance densities, we randomly sample 512–1024 points from the extracted 3D tracks during training. At inference time, we use classifier-free guidance with γ=5.0. UniCaMo introduces no additional model parameters at inference time and incurs only approximately 0.2,s of noise-construction overhead per sample, preserving the runtime efficiency of the base model.

B.2 Implementation Details of Foreground Noise Propagation

Patch copy–paste along trajectories.

We initialize the first-frame latent noise as i.i.d. Gaussian,

Z_T¹∼ℕ(0,I).(1)

For each tracked point i and frame t, let (uᵢᵗ,vᵢᵗ) be its (integer) latent coordinates. To propagate an identifiable noise footprint along the trajectory, we copy a small square patch around the track location in frame 1 to the corresponding location in frame t. Using a patch radius r, we define a patch of (2r-1)×(2r-1) pixels where the copy follows:

Z_Tᵗ [uᵢᵗ+Δu, vᵢᵗ+Δv]:=Z_T¹ [uᵢ¹+Δu, vᵢ¹+Δv].(2)

where Δu and Δv are the pixel offsets. For r=2, the patch size is 3×3, and the offset is in {-1,0,1}. By transporting the same local noise pattern across time, motion becomes visible to the latents so that visual features in the diffusion process are encouraged to follow the specified trajectory. When multiple trajectories project to the same latent location at time t, naive composition yields ambiguous assignments and can introduce inconsistent motion cues. We then apply the Depth-aware Noise Composition rule described in Section3.2 to resolve the overlap.

B.3 Implementation Details of Spherical Noise Sampling

Ray construction (pixel → world ray).

For each pixel (pₓ,p_y) (we use pixel centers), we form a unit ray direction in camera coordinates using intrinsics (fₓ,f_y,cₓ,c_y):

d_c(pₓ,p_y)=(1)/(∥(pₓ-cₓ/fₓ, (p_y-c_y)/(f_y), 1)∥₂)\beginbmatrixpₓ-cₓ/fₓ [2.0pt] (p_y-c_y)/(f_y) [2.0pt] 1\endbmatrix,(3)

and then apply a camera-to-world transformation to determine the ray direction in the world space:

d_w(pₓ,p_y)=Rᵗ d_c(pₓ,p_y),(4)

where Rᵗ is the rotation from T_c→wᵗ. The origin of the ray is at the camera location.

Ray-sphere intersection and spherical UV.

Let S be the sphere center with radius r. Let oᵗ be the ray origin and d_w be the ray direction in the world space. We define the direction from the sphere center S to the ray origin as Oᵗ=oᵗ-S. We perform ray-sphere intersection by solving a quadratic equation. With b=⟨d_w,Oᵗ⟩ and c=∥Oᵗ∥₂²-r², the (non-negative) discriminant is

Δ=b²-c,

(5)

and we take the exiting intersection (consistent with the camera being inside or near the sphere):

τ=-b+√Δ.

(6)

The hit point and outward normal are

P=oᵗ+τd_w, and n=P-S/r.

(7)

We convert the normal to spherical coordinates using longitude–latitude mapping:

u=fract ((atan2(nₓ,n_z))/(2π)+1/2),(8)
v=(\arccos(clip(n_y,-1,1)))/(π),(9)

where fract(·) wraps u into [0,1).

Sampling sphere noise and downsampling to latent.

We sample the Gaussian noise map at the computed spherical coordinates using nearest-neighbor lookup, yielding a per-frame noise image. This yields a 3D-consistent noise field while preserving the spatial Gaussianity per frame.

Appendix C Additional Ablation Studies

C.1 Effect of various hyperparameters.

Degradation rate. Our motion-consistent noise is spatially Gaussian but introduces cross-frame correlations that differ from the independent Gaussian prior used to train the backbone. We therefore blend it with independent Gaussian noise using a randomly sampled degradation rate θ∈[0,0.5]. At θ=0, the initialization preserves the motion signal most strongly, yielding the best control fidelity (EPE 1.88, PSNR 18.35), but also deviates most from the original noise prior, resulting in lower video quality (FID 26.93, FVD 235.3). Increasing θ reduces this mismatch and monotonically improves FID and FVD, at the cost of motion-control fidelity. We adopt θ=0.2 as a good trade-off between video quality and control fidelity (Table5 (a) and Fig. 12).

Point tracks. We extract 1024 tracks per video using TAPIP3D [(Zhang et al., 2025a)] and vary the number used during training to assess robustness to the track budget (Table5(b) and Fig. 13). Visual quality is relatively insensitive to this choice, with FID and FVD varying by at most 0.4 and 9.4, respectively. Control fidelity is more sensitive: PSNR decreases from 18.15 with 1024 tracks to 16.44 with 512 and 16.12 with 256, while EPE increases from 1.92 to 2.38. We therefore use 1024 tracks by default, although performance degrades gracefully as the number of tracks decreases.

Patch size. We vary the patch dimension (2R-1) used to propagate noise along the 3D point tracks; results are reported in Table5(c) and Fig. 14. R=2 performs best across all five metrics. Both a smaller patch (R=1) and a larger one (R=3) degrade performance, suggesting that the patch should be large enough to provide a sufficiently strong motion signal while remaining sufficiently localized to avoid interference between neighboring trajectories. We therefore use R=2 by default.

C.2 Robustness to Errors in 3D Estimation

UniCaMo depends on off-the-shelf modules for depth, camera pose and 3D point tracking, both when constructing training data and when preparing inference guidance, and errors in those estimates propagate into the constructed noise. To make the model tolerant of them, we add a small perturbation to the clean motion-visible noise during both training and inference. We assess that tolerance in two ways on the multi-object split of MoveBench (Table6).

Perturbed depth. We perturb the per-pixel depth estimated by ViPE [(Huang et al., 2025)] by a controlled percentage. At 5% and 10% the effect is small — 0.04 FID and 0.02 EPE, and 1.06 FID and 0.18 EPE respectively — which spans the error regime of modern depth estimators. Only at 30% does quality degrade appreciably (5.12 FID, 0.65 EPE). This is expected: a perturbation of that magnitude changes the depth ordering of the scene, and therefore which surfaces occlude which, so generation is guided by a geometrically different scene.

Alternative 3D foundation models. We also replace the estimated camera poses and depth with those of other state-of-the-art 3D foundation models. UniCaMo works with every estimator tested, and its accuracy tracks that of the estimator: FID and EPE both improve monotonically from MegaSaM [(Li et al., 2025c)] through ViPE [(Huang et al., 2025)] to VGGT-Ω[(Wang et al., 2026b)], which gives our best overall result (25.93 FID, 1.88 EPE). UniCaMo can therefore inherit future advances in 3D estimation without retraining.

Appendix D Additional Qualitative Visualizations

In this section, we provide more qualitative results for camera control (see Fig. 8), motion control (see Fig. 9), joint camera and motion control (see Fig. 10). Finally, we show our superior results compared with other baseline on some complex trajectory samples in the Fig. 11. Overall, UniCaMo display precise controllable video generation capabilities even in extreme out-of-domain cases.

Appendix E Discussion, Limitations, and Future Work

While our 3D-grounded, motion-consistent noise enables flexible control of object and camera motion, the method has limitations. First, the Foreground Noise Propagation stage depends heavily on accurate 3D point tracks and camera poses, so tracking or calibration errors can degrade controllability. Second, the Spherical Noise Sampling stage uses a coarse 3D sphere proxy, which may fail to capture dynamic background geometry. Future improvements in 3D tracking, depth estimation, and noise representations would further enhance our approach.

一句话：不做后处理、不加控制分支：直接构造「运动一致的噪声」，让相机与物体运动各自可控。

要点：

  • 输入是四件套：参考图、文本提示、稀疏 3D 物体轨迹、3D 相机轨迹；目标是让两者分别可控且相互不打架
  • 关键手法是「3D-grounded 噪声构造」：把参考图噪声传播与新出现区域的高斯球面噪声表示结合起来，直接构造出编码了目标运动的初始噪声
  • 相比加控制分支或事后修补，这种做法把运动一致性放到生成起点，因而更简单也更稳定

为什么值得看：做虚拟制片或预告片时，最常被要求的就是「镜头这么走、人物那样动」，而现有视频模型往往只能控一个。把运动写进初始噪声是条便宜的路，值得试。

中文摘要：UniCaMo 面向「图像 + 文本生成视频」的扩散模型，解决相机与物体运动需要同时可控的问题。它的输入包括参考图、文本提示、稀疏的 3D 物体轨迹与 3D 相机轨迹；核心做法是直接构造「运动一致」的初始噪声：把参考图噪声传播与新暴露区域的高斯球面噪声表示结合起来，让噪声本身就编码了期望的运动，而不是靠额外的控制分支或事后修补。作者称这种方式简单且有效，能在同一框架内分别控制相机与物体的运动。对虚拟制片、预告片与游戏过场这类需要精确镜头的场景，这种把控制前置到噪声层的思路比堆控制网络更轻。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·核心检索（English）

原文发布：2026-11-02

本期推送：2026-11-04

UniCaMo: Unified Camera and Motion Control for Video Diffusion Models

Abstract

We present UniCaMo, an unified framework for joint control of camera and object motion in image-and-text-to-video diffusion models. Given a reference image, text prompt, sparse 3D object trajectories, and a 3D camera trajectory, UniCaMo constructs motion-consistent input noise that directly encodes the desired motion. Our 3D-grounded noise construction combines reference-derived noise propagation with a spherical Gaussian noise representation for newly revealed regions, providing a simple and effective motion prior without requiring reconstruction of unseen scene geometry. UniCaMo requires no architectural modifications or dedicated control modules and can be adapted using lightweight LoRA fine-tuning with low training data volume. Experiments on standard controllable video generation benchmarks demonstrate state-of-the-art motion controllability and high visual quality with minimal inference overhead. Qualitative videos are available on our project page: https://phongnhhn.info/Unicamo/.

1 Introduction

Controllable video generation is important for applications ranging from visual content creation to robotics and embodied AI [(Wang et al., 2026a; Jang et al., 2025)], and has received increasing attention from the research community. Existing approaches generally start from a pretrained image-and-text-to-video diffusion model and finetune it to introduce controllability, broadly following two directions. One line of work adds adaptation or control modules that inject motion guidance into the generation process [(Chu et al., 2025; He et al., 2024; Bai et al., 2025a; Li et al., 2025a)]. Motion constraints are typically injected late in the generation pipeline, when visual content has already begun to emerge, leaving limited flexibility to resolve motion ambiguity in a geometrically coherent manner while maintaining realism and temporal consistency. These methods also augment already large video diffusion models with additional architectural components, increasing model complexity and inference cost. An appealing alternative is to impose motion at the very beginning of generation by exploiting the input noise. Video diffusion models generate videos by progressively denoising an initial sequence of Gaussian noise maps; rather than modifying the model architecture, the desired motion can therefore be encoded directly into these input noise maps [(Burgert et al., 2025; Chang et al., 2025)].

Existing input-noise-based methods, however, typically rely on 2D optical flow guidance and address object and camera motion separately. These limitations are closely related: the apparent motion of an object in a video is jointly determined by its 3D motion and the changing camera viewpoint, making it inherently ambiguous 111 The HTML page provides a visualization of motion-noise between existing 2D and our 3D-aware approaches. to specify and control the two independently in 2D image space. Moreover, complex motions—such as one person moving around another (Fig. 1)—are difficult to express without explicit depth and viewpoint information. These observations motivate the central question of this work: can we jointly control camera and object motions in 3D by manipulating only the input noise, without modifying the architecture of the underlying video diffusion model?

To answer this question, we propose UniCaMo, a unified framework for joint camera and object motion control through view-and-motion-consistent input noise. UniCaMo lifts the reference image into 3D, where users specify the desired camera motion together with sparse 3D object trajectories. We construct the input noise according to these motions, using reference-derived noise where geometric correspondences are available and a spherical Gaussian noise representation to provide persistent noise for regions newly revealed by camera or object motion. Importantly, this construction need not recover the true geometry of unseen regions; it provides a plausible and geometrically consistent motion prior, while the pretrained video diffusion model supplies the visual and motion priors needed to synthesize realistic content. The resulting sequence of 2D noise maps directly initializes the video diffusion model, enabling joint 3D motion control without additional control modules or architectural modifications. Because the desired 3D motion is already explicitly encoded in the input noise, the model does not need to learn the motion-control mapping entirely from data, allowing effective adaptation with lightweight LoRA fine-tuning and a relatively small amount of computation for training.

Overall, UniCaMo offers three key advantages over existing controllable video generation approaches: (1)unified 3D control with lightweight adaptation: UniCaMo jointly controls object and camera motion directly in 3D, avoiding the ambiguity of 2D motion specification and separate treatment of the two motions, requiring only lightweight LoRA adaptation; (2)simple and effective motion representation: its 3D-grounded noise construction provides a plausible and geometrically consistent motion prior without requiring explicit reconstruction of unseen scene geometry; and (3)state-of-the-art performance: UniCaMo achieves superior controllability and video quality over the evaluated baselines.

2 Related Work

Video diffusion models have made remarkable progress since their early development based on 3D U-Net architectures [(Bar-Tal et al., 2024; Blattmann et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2023; Guo et al., 2023)]. Recent large-scale latent diffusion and transformer-based models [(Hong et al., 2022; Kong et al., 2024; Wan et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2024)] achieve substantially improved visual fidelity, temporal coherence, and adherence to conditioning signals. As these models become increasingly capable, a natural next step is to provide finer control over the generated motion, particularly the motions of objects and the camera.

Existing motion-controlled video generation methods differ primarily in the motion representation and how it is incorporated into the diffusion model. For object motion, masks, boxes, and keypoints provide coarse spatial guidance, whereas optical flow and point trajectories enable finer-grained control [(Wang et al., 2024a; Li et al., 2025a; Geng et al., 2025; Yin et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2025b)]. Camera motion is commonly represented by 6DoF poses or trajectories and incorporated through dedicated conditioning mechanisms [(He et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024b; Bahmani et al., 2025)]. More recent methods pursue joint object and camera control using trajectory-based conditioning, geometry-aware representations, or richer 3D information [(Li et al., 2025a; Geng et al., 2025; Chu et al., 2025; Zheng et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026)]. These approaches generally introduce motion control through additional conditioning signals or modifications within the denoising process.

UniCaMo instead encodes object and camera motion directly into the input noise, connecting our work to structured noise initialization for controllable video generation. Noise-warping methods construct temporally correlated Gaussian noise by propagating noise according to motion fields. [Chang et al. (2025)] highlight the importance of maintaining appropriate Gaussian noise statistics, while Go-with-the-Flow [(Burgert et al., 2025)] demonstrates efficient object motion control by warping input noise without an inference-time control module. Related work further shows that training with warped noise can induce useful equivariances and facilitate efficient sampling [(Liu and Vahdat, 2025)]. These approaches, however, primarily operate with 2D motion fields or correspondences. UniCaMo extends this paradigm to joint 3D object and camera control by constructing view-and-motion-consistent noise: noise follows specified object trajectories while remaining consistent across changing viewpoints. A spherical noise representation provides persistent noise for newly revealed regions without explicitly reconstructing unseen scene geometry.

3 UniCaMo – Joint Camera and Object Motion Control

This section describes UniCaMo, our unified framework for joint camera and object motion control in video diffusion through view-and-motion-consistent input noise. UniCaMo requires no architectural modifications to the underlying video diffusion model, enabling lightweight fine-tuning with modest training data while introducing minimal additional overhead at inference time. We first provide an overview of the framework, followed by the details of noise construction and model training.

3.1 Major components and overview

Our overall pipeline is shown in Fig.2, UniCaMo takes as input a reference image and a text prompt describing the desired scene and action, and outputs a generated video. In between, the framework comprises two stages: (1) an interactive interface through which users specify the desired object and camera motions in 3D, and (2) a motion-guided generation model that constructs motion-and-view-consistent noise from the reference image and specified motions to initialize an image-to-video diffusion model.

The interactive interface first lifts the reference 2D image into a 3D point cloud, allowing the scene to be viewed and interacted with directly in 3D. Users specify object motion using sparse 3D point tracks on objects of interest, together with a desired 3D camera trajectory. This is an important distinction from prior approaches that specify motion using 2D point tracks in the 2D image plane, which are inherently ambiguous with respect to depth and viewpoint and can be insufficient for expressing complex motions, particularly when multiple objects cross or move around one another. By operating directly in 3D, UniCaMo provides a more expressive and geometrically explicit representation for jointly specifying object and camera motion.
