    Face landmark detection achieves high recall on human faces (92%) but fails almost entirely on animals (12–18%), as it is trained exclusively on human face data. Standard Sapiens degrades on non-human faces (35–42%) due to its human-centric training, despite being a strong foundation model. SAM 3 offers the broadest single-model coverage (72% overall) due to its class-agnostic design, but provides coarser segmentation boundaries than landmark-based methods. Fine-tuned Sapiens substantially improves animal face detection (85–89%) while retaining strong human performance (90%), validating the effectiveness of our fine-tuning strategy. The four-model ensemble with adaptive per-region selection achieves nearly 100% overall recall by combining the accuracy of face landmark detection on humans, fine-tuned Sapiens’ robustness on animals, and SAM 3’s fallback coverage for edge cases.

    Nose Landmark Ablation. We evaluate the impact of our nose-landmark-free template design on animal face rigging quality. When nose anchor keypoints are included (as in prior template designs), the pipeline produces severely distorted nose-mouth regions on 78% of animal assets and crashes on 10%, driven by the two failure modes discussed in Section4.5: incorrect nose segmentation, and—even when the nose mask is plausible—unstable keypoints from uniform boundary sampling on small, irregular nose contours. Removing nose anchors and allowing the optimization to position the nose region from the surrounding border, eye, and mouth anchors eliminates these distortion artifacts and removes crashes attributable to nose-anchor instability in this ablation. Figure11 provides visual evidence for both failure modes across a range of character topologies.

    Riggability Checker. The hybrid VLM+CV approach outperforms either component alone (Table3): the VLM provides strong archetype identification and accessory detection, while CV filtering catches geometric edge cases (no-face assets, degenerate meshes).

    5.6 Latency Breakdown

    The face pipeline executes on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU. End-to-end latency is approximately 20–30 s per asset, including data I/O. Stage 1 (riggability assessment, face parsing, keypoint extraction, and template fitting) takes 8–10 s, while Stage 2 (mesh fusion, inner-mouth fitting, UV/texture processing, and blendshape transfer) takes 10–15 s. Compared to manual sculpting workflows that typically take hours to days, this represents a reduction of 2–3 orders of magnitude.

    6 Limitations and Future Work

    OmniFaceRig is limited to visible-faced characters covered by our human, long-muzzle, and short-muzzle template families. Unusual anatomies—including sharp beaks, wide-mouthed fish-like faces, compound eyes, or strongly elongated snouts (Figure12)—may be rejected or fitted unreliably. Extending coverage requires additional templates, segmentation labels, and riggability criteria. Even a valid completed rig can retain localized fitting or penetration artifacts under extreme mouth motion or unusual muzzle geometry; Figure10 compares one such near-failure with its artist-authored reference. The 0.45% animal penetration rate and 97.5% success rate quantify these remaining cases rather than implying perfectly intersection-free output. The 20–30 s pipeline targets offline or batch processing rather than real-time editing. Future work will broaden topology coverage and further integrate perception with geometry. Additional riggability-checker failure modes (annotation borderline cases and VLM-only semantic errors) are discussed in Appendix A.5.

    7 Conclusion

    We presented OmniFaceRig, a fully automatic inner-mouth-aware face rigging pipeline for 3D characters. Given a static surface-only 3D mesh with no pre-modeled oral cavity, OmniFaceRig produces a production-ready rig with up to 155 FACS blendshapes and procedurally generated inner-mouth geometry (teeth, gums, and tongue), with no manual intervention at any stage. Our segmentation ensemble, topology-specific templates, and collision treatment support human and animal topologies; independent artist references show high success with low error and penetration. We also release Omni-Bench, to our knowledge the first open benchmark of more than 1,000 rigged biped characters with FACS facial blendshapes and inner-mouth geometry, to catalyze future research in automatic facial rigging.

    （参考文献见原文。）

    Appendix

    Appendix A Supplementary Riggability Assessment Details

    This section expands the design of the hybrid riggability checker introduced in the main paper. We give the per-question signal assignment, the geometric criteria used to validate segmentation masks, the landmark-based mouth-quality gate, the mouth-signal fusion logic, and a brief discussion of the remaining failure modes that bound the accuracy of the gate.

    A.1 VLM+CV Signal Architecture

    The checker fuses one semantic signal and two CV-derived signals computed from a single rendered view of the input asset:

  • •

    VLM semantic signal. Gemini 2.5 Flash Image is the primary vision-language model, with a Llama 4 multimodal model as fallback when the primary response is unavailable or invalid. It answers a fixed set of high-level questions about the rendered character (face type, number of faces, eye orbits, accessories, mouth state, and teeth visibility). These questions capture failure modes that are inherently semantic and hard to phrase as geometric thresholds.

  • •

    Segmentation-mask signal. The face/eye/mouth masks produced by the segmentation ensemble are evaluated against geometric plausibility criteria: presence of each region, inclusion inside the face boundary, plausible eye-to-head ratio, and acceptable lip-seal curvature.

  • •

    Landmark-quality signal. For human-like faces, the regularity of mouth landmarks is summarized by a lip-evenness statistic and used as a quality gate before mouth evidence enters the fusion step.

    • The three signals are not treated as redundant: each question in the underlying checker template is assigned to the signal that is empirically most reliable for it, as summarized in Table A.1.

    A.2 Geometric Criteria from Segmentation Masks

    The segmentation-based checks (Q5, Q9, Q10, plus mask inclusion tests) are summarized in Table A.2. Their binary decision rules are calibrated once on a development split and held fixed across all evaluations; they are deliberately conservative so that the checker mostly rejects inputs that would otherwise crash or distort the downstream registration stage.

    A.3 Landmark-Assisted Mouth Validation

    For human-like inputs, we use mouth landmarks as a quality gate before they are fused with the VLM and segmentation signals. Let κₗᵢₚ denote the coefficient of variation (standard deviation divided by mean) of the spacing between consecutive lip-contour landmarks. We mark the mouth landmarks as unreliable when κₗᵢₚ exceeds a calibrated threshold; the underlying intuition is that on assets with a poorly modeled or absent mouth, the landmark detector still emits points, but those points become irregularly spaced. Failing the gate sets the landmark mouth evidence to “unavailable” for the subsequent fusion step.

    For non-human assets, where human-trained mouth-landmark detectors are not reliable, the landmark signal is ignored and the mouth decision is determined by the VLM and the segmentation mask alone.

    A.4 Mouth-Signal Fusion Logic

    The final eligibility decision is the conjunction of all per-question results in Table A.1. Q1–Q3 and Q6–Q8 are decided directly by the VLM; Q5, Q9, Q10 are decided by the segmentation-mask checks in Table A.2; and Q4 (mouth presence) uses explicit fusion because mouth localization is one of the most common downstream failure sources.

    Concretely, for a human-like asset, the mouth decision is:

  • 1.

    If κₗᵢₚ exceeds the landmark-quality threshold, treat the landmark evidence as unreliable and rely on the VLM and segmentation signals.

  • 2.

    Otherwise, take a majority vote over (i) the VLM mouth prediction, (ii) the segmentation-based mouth-detected flag, and (iii) the landmark-based mouth-detected flag.

    • For non-human assets, the same step degenerates to a conjunction of the VLM and segmentation-mask signals. The majority-vote design recovers the cases that a strict “VLM and segmentation” rule would miss when exactly one of the three signals is wrong but the other two agree.

    A.5 Discussion of Remaining Failure Modes

    Empirically, the hybrid VLM+CV checker on the mixed riggability validation set exhibits two dominant failure categories. The first is annotation borderline cases, where the ground-truth label itself is ambiguous (e.g., partially occluded faces or stylized characters that are arguably riggable). The second is VLM-only semantic errors: misclassification of eyewear, mouth state, or teeth visibility—attributes that segmentation masks and landmarks only partially corroborate. These are the natural targets for future improvement of the checker, since the geometric and landmark signals have already absorbed most of the failures they are capable of catching.

    Appendix B Supplementary Stage-2 Rig Construction Details

    This section expands the four implementation components underlying the three Stage-2 steps in the main paper: face-region fusion; inner-mouth construction; texture/UV transfer; and blendshape transfer with post-processing. The shared difficulty across these components is that the input asset is surface-only: there is no pre-modeled oral cavity, no animation-grade facial topology, and no separation between expressive and structural regions.

    B.1 Face-Region Fusion

    The fitted face mesh produced by Stage 1 defines the region of the input asset that will be replaced. A high-quality animated topology—designed with radial edge loops around the eyes and mouth—is first aligned to the fitted template through their shared UV correspondence, then reprojected onto the input surface so that it inherits the asset’s own facial geometry. The original face region of the input is removed via a Boolean operation against a convex hull of the fitted region, the new animated topology is inserted in its place, and the boundary between the new face and the rest of the asset is stitched by closest-point welding followed by small-edge collapse to clean up degenerate polygons. This operation is intentionally local: it preserves the asset’s identity, hairstyle, and non-face geometry while introducing the radial edge flow that downstream expression deformation relies on.

    B.2 Inner-Mouth Construction

    Because the input contains no oral cavity, the inner-mouth geometry (teeth, gums, and tongue) cannot be recovered from the asset itself. We instead maintain a small library of inner-mouth template archetypes, summarized in Table B.1; the appropriate archetype is selected by the VLM during Stage 1 and fitted to the character as described below.

    Each face template defines an inner-mouth region, and every teeth archetype is spatially registered to that region at rest. After the character-specific face template is fitted to the target surface, its inner-mouth region is deformed as-rigid-as-possible (ARAP) to the new shape. We then estimate, by SVD, the rigid transformation between the canonical and deformed inner-mouth regions and apply it to the selected teeth, gum, and tongue archetype. A convex hull of the aligned teeth provides the collision proxy. At rest, a point-to-SDF penalty moves intersecting outer-face points outside this hull; the same penalty is applied again during per-expression deformation transfer. This treatment is particularly important for long-muzzled animals, where initial collisions may otherwise occur.

    B.3 Texture and UV Transfer

    After the new face and inner-mouth surfaces are inserted, the global UV layout is rebuilt. The face region is allocated a larger fraction of the texture domain than non-face regions so that high-frequency facial detail is preserved at any rendering resolution, and the inner-mouth surfaces are placed on a separate texture channel to keep their material parameters independent. The asset’s original appearance is then transferred onto the rebuilt UV layout by sampling the original texture through the geometric correspondence between the original and merged surfaces; this preserves the character’s identity and material details while letting the newly synthesized geometry inherit a coherent appearance.

    B.4 Blendshape Transfer and Post-Processing

    FACS expression shapes are produced by transferring local deformation gradients from a canonical rigged template to the merged character mesh using sparse deformation transfer. Adapting the deformation gradients to the target character’s own proportions is what keeps the transferred expressions character-specific rather than collapsing the rig toward an “average human face,” and is what allows the same set of FACS shapes to be applied to humans, humanoids, long-muzzled animals, and short-muzzled animals without per-character authoring.

    The transferred deformations are then blended outward from the facial template region into the adjacent head surface so that expression motion fades smoothly into the rest of the asset. Sparse deformation transfer alone cannot enforce certain physical and geometric constraints—eyelids must close without self-intersection, eye-gaze shapes require a known rotation center, jaw motion must move the lower teeth, and extreme mouth poses can re-introduce teeth–face intersections. A small set of expression-specific post-processing rules, summarized in Table B.2, handles these cases.

    B.5 Design Tradeoffs and Outlook

    The four implementation components of Stage 2 are coupled but decomposable: face-region fusion fixes the surface topology, inner-mouth construction synthesizes the missing oral cavity, UV/texture transfer preserves the character’s original appearance, and blendshape transfer turns the static rig into an animatable one. A common thread is that each component substitutes a procedural geometric operation for what is traditionally a manual authoring step, which is also what makes the full pipeline fully automatic.

    The two design choices that most directly enable cross-topology generalization are the use of multiple inner-mouth archetypes (Table B.1) and the SDF-based collision refinement at both the rest pose and the per-expression level. Without the archetype split, a single human-shaped teeth template either intersects long muzzles or sits incorrectly in animals with non-human teeth structure (e.g., cats, bears, gorillas); without the SDF refinement, expression shapes such as a wide jaw open or a strong smile can re-introduce intersections that the rest-pose placement avoids. Together with the topology-specific face templates of Stage 1, these choices let the same Stage 2 procedure produce rigs for humans, humanoids, long-muzzled animals, and short-muzzled animals without per-asset manual authoring.

    Together, these components turn a static, surface-only 3D character mesh—without any pre-modeled oral cavity, without any animation-grade facial topology, and without any per-character authored expressions—into a full inner-mouth-aware FACS facial rig.

    Appendix C Additional Qualitative Results

    This section provides additional qualitative result grids beyond Figure14 in the main paper. Each grid follows the same controlled layout as the main qualitative figure: the leftmost column shows the original static surface-only asset, and the remaining six columns show generated expressions with inner-mouth geometry from the OmniFaceRig output. These additional results demonstrate robustness across more identities, styles, and topology families without overloading the main paper.

一句话：内口腔（牙、龈、舌）一直靠手工摆；这条把地标、模板与 blendshape 全自动化。

要点：

  • 现状是明显的瓶颈：面部绑定要同时做 FACS blendshape 与内口腔几何（牙齿、牙龈、舌头），而内口腔部件通常手工摆放，地标标注与逐角色模板调整也是常规工序
  • OmniFaceRig 是全自动端到端流程：输入一个只有表面、没有预先修改的静态 3D 角色网格，直接产出可用的面部绑定
  • 覆盖「多样 3D 角色」，说明它不依赖某一种拓扑或某一家美术规范

为什么值得看：对话类玩法、虚拟主播、数字人都在同一个坑里：内口腔是手工活，且换角色就得重来。把这一步自动化，等于把「角色能不能做表情特写」从美术资源问题变成管线问题。

中文摘要：面部绑定是 3D 角色制作里的主要瓶颈之一：既要生成符合 FACS 的 blendshape，又要补上内口腔几何（牙齿、牙龈、舌头）。现有管线依然高度依赖设计师：内口腔部件常靠手工摆放，地标标注和按角色调整模板也是例行工作。OmniFaceRig 提出一个全自动的端到端流程：输入一个只有表面几何、未经任何预处理的静态 3D 角色网格，即可自动完成面部绑定，并且面向多样化的角色（不绑定单一拓扑或美术规范）。对需要大量角色做表情特写的项目（对话玩法、虚拟主播、数字人），这一步自动化直接决定了产能上限。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·核心检索（English）

原文发布：2026-11-02

本期推送：2026-11-04

OmniFaceRig: Fully Automatic Inner-Mouth-Aware Face Rigging Across Diverse 3D Character Topologies

Abstract

Facial rigging—creating Facial Action Coding System (FACS) blendshapes together with inner-mouth geometry (teeth, gums, and tongue)—remains a major bottleneck in 3D character production. Existing pipelines still depend on substantial designer effort: inner-mouth components are commonly placed by hand, and landmark annotation and per-character template adjustments are routine. We present OmniFaceRig, a fully automatic end-to-end pipeline that converts a static surface-only 3D character mesh, with no pre-modeled oral cavity, into an inner-mouth-aware FACS rig with up to 155 blendshapes, procedurally fitted teeth, gums, and tongue, and re-packed UV/texture. OmniFaceRig supports diverse topologies, including humans, humanoids, long-muzzled animals (elongated snouts; e.g., dogs, wolves, foxes), and short-muzzled animals (compact or nearly absent snouts; e.g., cats, bears, rabbits, tigers), with no manual landmarks, no user-provided templates, and no per-asset template setup. OmniFaceRig combines a hybrid vision-language model (VLM) and computer vision (CV) riggability checker, a four-model face detection and segmentation ensemble (face landmark detection, Sapiens, SAM 3, and fine-tuned Sapiens), dense keypoint-driven template registration, procedural inner-mouth construction, and collision-aware blendshape transfer. To handle non-human characters, it automatically selects from a small library of topology-specific templates with a nose-landmark-free design and uses as-rigid-as-possible (ARAP) deformation with signed-distance-field (SDF) constraints for inner-mouth fitting to reduce teeth–face intersections. We also introduce Omni-Bench, an open-source benchmark of more than 1,000 biped 3D characters rigged with FACS facial blendshapes and inner-mouth geometry, spanning realistic humans, humanoids, cats, dogs, and other animals. Experiments show high final rigging success on screened Omni-Bench candidate inputs, nearly complete face detection recall from the segmentation ensemble, reliable inner-mouth placement with low penetration, and 20–30 s end-to-end latency on a single A100 GPU including data I/O. Together, OmniFaceRig provides an automatic path from static generated characters to animation-ready facial rigs across both human and non-human topologies. Additional results and resources are available on our project page.

††date: June 9, 2026 (v1); revised October 29, 2026 (v2)††Project Page: https://omnifacerig.github.io/††Dataset: https://github.com/facebookresearch/omnifacerig††Published in: ACM Transactions on Graphics 45(6), Article 231 (SIGGRAPH Asia 2026), doi:10.1145/3842582††Keywords: auto-rigging, facial blendshapes, FACS, benchmark dataset, deformation transfer

1 Introduction

Facial rigging—creating Facial Action Coding System (FACS) blendshapes and inner-mouth geometry (teeth, gums, and tongue) for 3D character animation—remains one of the most labor-intensive steps in the character production pipeline. A skilled technical artist may spend hours to days sculpting blendshapes for a single character, involving careful topology design, facial landmark placement, expression sculpting, and teeth fitting.

At the same time, 3D asset creation itself has become dramatically more accessible. Recent text-to-3D and image-to-3D methods can generate textured objects or characters directly from prompts or reference images [(Poole et al., 2023; Lin et al., 2023; Jun and Nichol, 2023; Liu et al., 2023; Tang et al., 2024; Ren et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2026)], and similar capabilities are increasingly available in commercial 3D-generation tools. However, these systems primarily produce static surface meshes and textures. For characters, the generated assets are often plausible as visual meshes but are not animation-ready facial rigs: they typically lack FACS controls, robust facial topology for deformation, and the oral-cavity geometry required for inner-mouth-aware expressions. This makes generated characters natural inputs to an automatic rigging pipeline, but not substitutes for such a pipeline.

Existing rigging solutions address parts of this problem but remain incomplete and, in practice, only semi-automatic. Deformation transfer [(Sumner and Popović, 2004)] and parametric face models [(Cao et al., 2014; Li et al., 2017)] enable facial rig creation but assume compatible mesh topologies, require manual landmark annotation, and are designed exclusively for human faces. Inner-mouth geometry (teeth, gums, and tongue) is particularly costly to author because the input mesh normally contains no corresponding interior surfaces: in production pipelines, teeth, gums, and tongue are almost universally placed and tuned by hand, and manually tuned or human-specific teeth templates routinely fail on stylized or non-human faces. To our knowledge, no existing system delivers a fully automatic, end-to-end pipeline that produces FACS blendshapes with newly generated inner-mouth geometry from a static surface-only mesh—let alone across both human and non-human topologies.

We present OmniFaceRig, an end-to-end pipeline for face auto-rigging across diverse 3D character topologies—including humans, humanoids, long-muzzled animals (e.g., dogs, wolves, foxes), and short-muzzled animals (e.g., cats, bears, rabbits, tigers). These animal labels describe coarse facial topology for template selection rather than biological taxonomy: long-muzzled characters have elongated, forward-protruding snouts, while short-muzzled characters have compact or nearly absent snouts. Given a static surface-only 3D mesh with no pre-modeled oral cavity, OmniFaceRig produces a production-ready facial rig with up to 155 FACS blendshapes, procedurally generated inner-mouth geometry (teeth, gums, and tongue), and re-packed UV/texture—all fully automatic with no manual intervention at any stage. In particular, OmniFaceRig eliminates the manual inner-mouth placement, landmark annotation, user-provided templates, and per-asset template setup that bottleneck prior pipelines, allowing the entire facial rig to be generated directly from the input mesh (Figure1). Our key contributions are:

  • 1.

    To our knowledge, the first fully automatic, end-to-end face auto-rigging pipeline that starts from a static surface-only input mesh and requires no manual inner-mouth placement, landmark annotation, user-provided templates, or per-asset template setup.

  • 2.

    Inner-mouth-aware rig construction: OmniFaceRig procedurally generates teeth, gums, tongue, and oral-cavity support geometry that are absent from the input mesh, then integrates them with FACS blendshape transfer using as-rigid-as-possible (ARAP) deformation, signed-distance-field (SDF) constraints, and collision-aware deformation.

  • 3.

    Omni-Bench: to our knowledge, the first open-source benchmark of more than 1,000 biped 3D characters with FACS facial blendshapes and inner-mouth geometry (teeth, gums, and tongue), spanning realistic humans, humanoids, domestic cats and dogs, and wild animals—all in T-pose and all rigged by OmniFaceRig.

  • 4.

    Generalization across diverse non-human topologies: our method rigs long-muzzled animals (dogs, wolves, foxes, etc.) and short-muzzled animals (cats, bears, rabbits, tigers, etc.) via a small library of topology-specific templates with a nose-landmark-free design and ARAP+SDF teeth placement, demonstrating that the same pipeline transfers from humans to animals without architectural changes.

    • 2 Related Work

    2.1 3D Asset and Character Generation

    Text-to-3D and image-to-3D generation have rapidly lowered the barrier to creating 3D assets. Methods such as DreamFusion [(Poole et al., 2023)], Magic3D [(Lin et al., 2023)], Shap-E [(Jun and Nichol, 2023)], and Zero-1-to-3 [(Liu et al., 2023)] generate textured objects from language or image inputs, while character-focused systems such as Make-It-Vivid [(Tang et al., 2024)] and Make-A-Character [(Ren et al., 2023)] target animatable or stylized 3D characters. Similar capabilities are also increasingly available in commercial 3D-generation services, making static character asset creation accessible to non-expert users. However, these systems primarily target visible geometry and appearance. Their outputs are generally static surface assets, often without production facial topology, FACS controls, or interior oral-cavity geometry. Our work is complementary: OmniFaceRig takes such generated surface meshes as input and converts them into animation-ready, inner-mouth-aware facial rigs.

    2.2 Parametric Face Models vs. Blendshape Rigging

    Parametric face models provide statistical representations of human facial geometry. The 3D Morphable Model (3DMM) [(Blanz and Vetter, 1999)], FaceWarehouse [(Cao et al., 2014)], and FLAME [(Li et al., 2017)] established linear shape spaces for face reconstruction. Extensions include multilinear models [(Brunton et al., 2014; Vlasic et al., 2005)] that factor identity and expression, and disentangled representations [(Fernandez Abrevaya et al., 2019; Jiang et al., 2019)] that separate shape components for more flexible control. Methods like CoMA [(Ranjan et al., 2018)] and DECA [(Feng et al., 2021)] leverage these models to reconstruct animatable faces from images. However, parametric models are bound to a fixed topology and blendshape set, and cannot be applied to novel characters with arbitrary topologies, stylized proportions, or non-human features.

    In contrast, production pipelines rely on FACS [(Ekman and Friesen, 1978)] and blendshape rigging [(Lewis et al., 2014; Lewis and Anjyo, 2010)], which offer animators intuitive, localized control while preserving character-specific geometry [(Seol et al., 2011; Kavan et al., 2024)]. [Orvalho et al. (2012)] provide a comprehensive survey of facial rigging techniques, covering the evolution from manual sculpting to semi-automatic methods. On the representation side, spectral methods have also been explored for compact animation representations [(Wang et al., 2015)]. Our method follows this production paradigm, generating FACS blendshapes for arbitrary target meshes.

    In conventional digital-content-creation workflows using tools such as Maya or MotionBuilder, technical artists typically prepare animation-friendly facial topology, align landmarks or templates, place and adjust teeth, gums, and tongue, sculpt or transfer expression shapes, and manually correct collisions. OmniFaceRig targets these repeated geometric preparation and cleanup steps while retaining the standard FACS blendshape representation used by downstream animation tools.

    2.3 Traditional and Learning-Based Facial Auto-Rigging

    Traditional methods.[Noh and Neumann (2001)] introduced expression cloning via vertex displacement transfer. [Sumner and Popović (2004)] proposed deformation transfer using triangle affine transformations—the foundational technique our system builds upon. [Orvalho et al. (2008)] extended this to transfer rigs across different face models. [Li et al. (2010)] further developed example-based facial rigging. [Seol et al. (2012)] introduced spacetime expression cloning for blendshapes. [Liu et al. (2011)] proposed a framework for locally retargeting and rendering facial performance. [Blanco i Ribera et al. (2017)] addressed retargeting with automatic range of motion alignment. These methods achieve high quality but require manual correspondence establishment, which does not scale.

    Learning-based methods.[Li et al. (2020a)] used CNNs to predict blendshape offsets via geometry images. [Chandran et al. (2020)] introduced semantic deep face models, later used transformers for topology-independent shape modeling [(Chandran et al., 2022b)], and proposed anatomically-constrained facial performance retargeting [(Chandran et al., 2022a)]. Blendshape editing has also been explored through sketching interfaces [(Cetinaslan and Orvalho, 2020a)] and localized Jacobian transpose descent [(Cetinaslan and Orvalho, 2020b)]. [Wang et al. (2023b)] proposed a method for fully automatic blendshape generation for stylized characters, and [Ming et al. (2024)] introduced high-quality mesh blendshape generation from face videos via neural inverse rendering. On the representation side, MeshCNN [(Hanocka et al., 2019)] and DiffusionNet [(Sharp et al., 2022)] provide mesh-native learned features that benefit downstream tasks. Neural Face Rigging (NFR) [(Qin et al., 2023)] pioneered neural deformation for in-the-wild facial meshes but is limited to human faces and cannot handle disconnected components. Fabrig [(Zhu and Joslin, 2024)] proposes a cloth-simulated transferable 3D face parameterization. Neural Facial Deformation Transfer (NFDT) [(Chandran et al., 2025)] uses a decoder-only transformer for high-fidelity transfer. Neural Face Skinning (NFS) [(Cha et al., 2025)] proposes mesh-agnostic skinning. RigAnyFace [(Ma et al., 2025)] represents the current state of the art, using 2D supervision to scale training with unlabeled data. Most recently, CANRig [(Mohammadi et al., 2026)] introduces cross-attention mechanisms for neural face rigging with variable local control, and ControlFace [(Jang et al., 2025)] harnesses 3DMM-conditioned rendering for flexible face rigging. Zero-shot approaches [(Wang et al., 2023a)] and image-space portrait and talking-face animation methods [(Yang et al., 2024; Xie et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025)] have also been explored for stylized characters, and dyadic audiovisual models generate speech-aligned gestures and expressions [(Agrawal et al., 2025)]. DreamFace [(Zhang et al., 2023)] generates animatable 3D faces under text guidance. As summarized in Table1, our method addresses critical gaps: inner-mouth modeling (teeth, gums, and tongue) and non-humanoid character rigging.

    2.4 Rigging for Non-Humanoid Characters

    Prior work has explored automatic generation and stylization of facial rigs [(Danieau et al., 2019)]. Extending facial rigging to animals requires handling substantially different anatomy. On the 3D shape modeling side, SMAL [(Zuffi et al., 2017)] and BARC [(Rüegg et al., 2022)] model quadruped animal shape and pose using category-specific priors. However, these parametric animal models do not address facial rig construction or blendshape generation. For facial landmark detection on non-photorealistic characters, [Cheng et al. (2024)] proposed methods for stylized character facial landmark detection, addressing the domain gap between real human faces and artistic character designs. Recent learning-based rigging methods [(Qin et al., 2023; Ma et al., 2025)] are trained on human datasets with human-centric priors and do not generalize to animal faces. Critically, nearly all existing methods focus on the outer facial surface, ignoring the oral cavity (teeth, gums, tongue). Our approach introduces a robust multi-model segmentation ensemble that identifies facial regions across species, decoupling geometric processing from human-specific priors. OmniFaceRig generates FACS blendshapes that explicitly include inner-mouth geometry (teeth, gums, and tongue) for both humans and animals.

    3 Omni-Bench: Benchmark Dataset

    To facilitate future research in automatic facial rigging, we release Omni-Bench, to our knowledge the first open-source benchmark of biped 3D characters with FACS facial blendshapes and inner-mouth geometry (teeth, gums, and tongue). The source characters are static surface meshes generated with AssetGen [(Wang et al., 2026)]. All released assets are selected from inputs that pass the initial VLM+CV riggability screen, are processed by OmniFaceRig, and are provided in biped T-pose with generated rig outputs.

    Existing facial datasets leave complementary gaps. BFM [(Paysan et al., 2009)] is a parametric model, while FaceScape [(Zhu et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2020)], Multiface [(Wuu et al., 2022)], and VOCASET [(Cudeiro et al., 2019)] focus on human outer-face geometry or captured motion rather than complete FACS rigs. ICT FaceKit [(Li et al., 2020b)] includes oral components but is a single parametric model. Large character collections such as RaBit [(Luo et al., 2023)] and Anymate [(Deng et al., 2025)] lack both FACS facial blendshapes and inner-mouth structures.

    Omni-Bench contains more than 1,000 rigged biped 3D characters; the public v1 release provides 1,345 assets, comprising 809 realistic or stylized humans/humanoids and 536 animals. They span human professions, fantasy races, science fiction, nature and elemental humanoids, domestic cats and dogs, and wild felines and canines (281 short- and 255 long-muzzled faces). Figure13 summarizes this diversity. The rig-quality experiments use smaller subsets with independent artist-authored references (Section5.3).

    The riggability screen should be interpreted as an input eligibility filter rather than a guarantee of final rigging success. It removes obvious invalid assets—for example, missing faces, severe eye or mouth occlusions, non-standard viewpoints, or unsupported facial topologies—before full processing. A screened asset can still fail during later stages because of segmentation errors, unstable template fitting, or implausible mouth localization. We therefore report final Success Rate separately in the experiments (Section5.3) as the percentage of screened Omni-Bench candidate inputs for which the full OmniFaceRig pipeline completes and passes final geometric quality checks. Success Rate is measured before unsuccessful outputs are excluded, rather than on the released assets alone.

    As shown in Table2, Omni-Bench uniquely combines human and animal full-character assets with up to 155 auto-generated FACS shapes with teeth, gums, and tongue. All assets are in biped T-pose, processed by the same pipeline, and released with source meshes, segmentation and keypoint images, solved templates, and FBX/glTF/USDZ rigs.

    4 Method

    4.1 Pipeline Overview

    OmniFaceRig takes a static surface-only 3D mesh with no pre-modeled oral cavity and produces a production-ready FACS rig with teeth, gums, and tongue (Figure2). Stage 1: Face Template Fitting (Sections4.2 to 4.5) combines face localization, multi-model segmentation, hybrid VLM+CV riggability assessment, keypoint extraction, and rigid/non-rigid registration to align a topology-specific template to the input. Stage 2: Blendshape Rig Construction (Section4.6) fuses the fitted face with the asset, generates and registers inner-mouth geometry, rebuilds its UV texture, and transfers the canonical FACS blendshapes.

    4.2 Riggability Assessment

    Before processing an asset through the rigging pipeline, OmniFaceRig performs an automatic eligibility check. This is critical in production settings where input assets are generated automatically (e.g., from text-to-3D models) and may include characters with no visible face, heavily occluded facial features, non-standard orientations, or facial topologies outside the current template library.

    Our riggability assessment is a VLM+CV hybrid system combining two complementary approaches:

    VLM Understanding. We use Gemini 2.5 Flash Image as the primary vision-language model (VLM), with a Llama 4 multimodal model as a fallback when the primary response is unavailable or invalid. We render the input 3D mesh from a frontal viewpoint and query the VLM to identify: (1) the character archetype (human, humanoid, feline, canine, or other); (2) face covering status (glasses, goggles, masks, eye patches); and (3) teeth state (open mouth, closed mouth, emotional expression). The VLM’s flexibility allows easy adaptation to new assessment criteria without retraining. The VLM has two roles. First, it filters out assets that are unlikely to be riggable by the current system, including no-face assets, faces with severe eye or mouth occlusion, and unsupported facial topologies such as highly exaggerated beaked birds or other shapes outside our human, long-muzzle, and short-muzzle template families. Second, for assets that pass this eligibility check, it selects downstream configuration choices: (i) the face template variant—one of human, long-muzzle, or short-muzzle—based on the character’s facial topology (see Section4.5); and (ii) the teeth archetype (human, canine, or monster), which Stage 2 (Section4.6) uses for inner-mouth fitting.

    CV Segmentation Filtering. After face localization, we compute face segmentation masks using the multi-model ensemble described in Section4.4. Assets where no valid face region is detected, or where the face area falls below a minimum threshold, are filtered out. This CV-based check catches cases where the VLM may be overconfident—for example, detecting a “face” on a purely mechanical character with no actual facial geometry.

    Hybrid Decision. The final eligibility decision combines VLM predictions with CV filtering results. We evaluate the hybrid approach on a mixed riggability validation set of approximately 500 assets, including Omni-Bench candidates, a subset of a separate benchmark collection, and additional generated or collected examples. This validation set intentionally includes both riggable and non-riggable inputs; metrics compare the automatic checker decision against human ground-truth riggability labels (Table3).

    The hybrid approach leverages the VLM’s strong image understanding for high-level decisions while using CV signals for geometric validation, consistently outperforming either component alone. Additional details on the per-question signal assignment, segmentation-mask checks, and mouth-signal fusion are provided in Appendix A.

    4.3 Sapiens-Based Segmentation Models

    4.3.1 Pretraining

    Our learned parsers use Sapiens-1B [(Khirodkar et al., 2024)], a high-resolution ViT encoder trained by masked reconstruction on a large human-centric corpus. Its patch-level representation preserves the local boundary cues needed for hairlines, eyelids, lips, teeth, and inner-mouth regions. We adapt this shared encoder to stylized characters before supervised parser training; the full pretraining and adaptation schedule is reported in Section5.2.

    4.3.2 Segmentation Fine-Tuning

    We attach a lightweight three-stage deconvolutional decoder and fine-tune it while freezing the ViT backbone. Two checkpoints share this architecture but use different label spaces: a 41-class stylized parser for human-like characters and a 38-class humanoid parser for animals and strongly non-human characters. The former retains fine facial and accessory labels, whereas the latter trades some granularity for stability on cats, dogs, and heavily stylized faces. At inference, their labels are collapsed into the geometric cues required downstream: face boundary, eyes, nose or muzzle extent, mouth opening, inner-mouth support, and occlusion regions. Training details are given in Section5.2.

    4.4 Face Detection and Segmentation

    Robust face detection and segmentation are critical prerequisites for template fitting. Render and Face Detection. For each input asset, we render the 3D mesh from a frontal viewpoint and use an in-house face detector and sparse landmark estimator, with MediaPipe [(Lugaresi et al., 2019)] as a fallback, to obtain a face bounding box and sparse 2D landmarks. The box is expanded using predefined asymmetric margins to include additional forehead, jaw, and lateral-face context; the enlarged region is then cropped and resized so that the face is approximately centered. Downstream stages consume only the resulting bounding box and landmark coordinates and are therefore not tied to a proprietary landmark representation. The cropped face image is the input to all subsequent face-parsing modules. Multi-Model Segmentation. While face parsing methods such as BiSeNet [(Yu et al., 2018)] and the RoI Tanh-polar Transformer [(Lin et al., 2021)] have achieved strong results on photographic human faces and support downstream tasks such as age estimation [(Lin et al., 2025)], AI-generated characters exhibit highly stylized proportions and diverse topologies that challenge any single detector or parser. To maximize coverage, we combine the Sapiens-based parsers from Section4.3 with two complementary models—the in-house face landmark detector described above and the off-the-shelf SAM 3—and adaptively select the best result for each facial region:

  • 1.

    Face Landmark Detection: The in-house detector and sparse landmark estimator described above, with MediaPipe as a fallback. It provides high-precision eye, mouth, and face-boundary cues on human and near-human faces.

  • 2.

    Sapiens[(Khirodkar et al., 2024)]: The base human parser described in Section4.3. It provides strong human nose, lip, and facial-skin estimates, but degrades on strongly non-human faces because of its human-centric training distribution.

  • 3.

    SAM 3 (Segment Anything Model 3) [(Carion et al., 2026)]: Building on the Segment Anything foundation [(Kirillov et al., 2023)] and its video extension SAM 2 [(Ravi et al., 2025)], SAM 3 is a class-agnostic segmentation foundation model that provides zero-shot segmentation masks from point or box prompts. SAM 3 generalizes well to stylized and non-human faces but produces coarser boundaries compared to landmark-based methods. We use SAM 3 for face region segmentation on characters where face landmark detection and Sapiens fail.

  • 4.

    Fine-Tuned Sapiens: Our stylized and humanoid Sapiens checkpoints from Section4.3. The riggability stage selects the 41-class stylized variant for human-like characters and the 38-class humanoid variant for cats, dogs, and heavily stylized assets; these models serve as the primary dense parsers whenever face landmark detection or the base Sapiens model becomes unreliable.

    • All four models run in parallel, and the system selects the best result independently for each facial region:

  • •

    Humans primarily use landmark cues for eyes/mouth and Sapiens for nose/skin.

  • •

    Stylized humanoids primarily use the 41-class fine-tuned parser.

  • •

    Animals primarily use the 38-class parser, with SAM 3 as fallback.

  • •

    If a preferred model fails, only that region switches to the next-best output.

    • The combined multi-model ensemble achieves a face detection recall of nearly 100% across our test sets, compared to 88% for the best single model in isolation. This improvement is especially pronounced on challenging cases: animal characters with fur-covered face boundaries, humanoid characters with exaggerated feature proportions, and characters wearing partial face accessories. Figure5 illustrates single-model and per-region ensemble results.

    Landmark Extraction (2D & 3D). After segmentation, we extract 2D and 3D keypoints from the final segmentation masks. The nose or muzzle mask remains available as a semantic and geometric cue, but it is excluded from the fitting-anchor set described in Section4.5. The registration correspondences are instead sampled from the face boundary, eyes, and mouth using mask contours and face-landmark predictions. We then back-project each 2D anchor onto the input 3D mesh by ray-casting from the rendered camera through the pixel and intersecting the asset surface, yielding the paired 3D position. The resulting 2D + 3D anchor correspondences are the input to template registration (Section4.5).

    4.5 Template Registration

    4.5.1 Template Design

    The core of OmniFaceRig’s face fitting stage is a small library of quad-mesh templates with anchor keypoints, designed for robust fitting across diverse character topologies. The anchor keypoints correspond to facial landmarks (eyes, mouth, face boundary) whose 3D positions are computed from the segmentation ensemble output (Section4.4). To accommodate the wide variation in facial shape across topologies, we provide three face template variants, and the VLM (Section4.2) automatically selects the appropriate one for each input asset:

  • •

    Human template — targets human and humanoid characters with conventional facial proportions (flat-fronted face, defined chin, eyes and mouth on roughly the same plane).

  • •

    Long-muzzle template — targets long-muzzled animals with elongated, forward-protruding snouts, such as dogs, wolves, foxes, and horses.

  • •

    Short-muzzle template — targets short-muzzled animals with compact or nearly absent snouts, such as cats, bears, rabbits, and tigers.

    • The three variants differ only in their canonical vertex positions: the human template provides a conventional facial initialization, while the two animal templates initialize the optimization closer to elongated or compact muzzle proportions. Their shared connectivity keeps the downstream fitting and animation pipeline unchanged across categories (Figure6).

    All three templates share three common design principles that make fitting robust across diverse character types:

  • •

    Nose-landmark-free design. Anchor target positions are computed by uniformly sampling along the corresponding segmentation-mask boundary, and nose anchors are particularly fragile under this scheme for two compounding reasons. First, nose segmentation accuracy itself is consistently low on animal faces (feline noses are small and short; canine noses merge into the muzzle) and on many stylized humanoids, so the underlying mask is unreliable. Second, even when the nose mask is plausible, the nose contour tends to be small, irregular, or weakly defined, so uniform boundary sampling yields unstable keypoints that do not correspond across assets. We therefore exclude the nose region from the anchor keypoints entirely; the nose vertices are positioned by the optimization itself, guided by the surrounding border, eye, and mouth anchors. This makes fitting independent of nose segmentation quality, and the resulting nose region naturally adapts to actual face proportions—compact for cats, elongated for dogs, standard for humans.

  • •

    Decoupled fitting and animated topology. The fitting template (optimized for keypoint correspondence) and the animated topology (designed with radial edge loops around eyes and mouth for muscle-direction deformation) are maintained as separate meshes linked by UV correspondence. This decoupling allows independent optimization: the fitting template can be modified for better landmark matching without affecting the animation-quality edge flow, and vice versa.

  • •

    Minimum region fitting. The template adheres to the convex hull of facial features rather than extending to the neck and chin. This “minimum region” design produces tighter fits, reduces artifacts at the face-asset merge boundary, and improves robustness on characters with unusual neck or chin geometry (e.g., characters with armor, scarves, or elongated chins).

    • 4.5.2 Keypoint Computation and Fallback Mechanisms

    Template fitting is driven by 68 facial anchor correspondences distributed around the face boundary, eyes, and mouth. These sparse anchors constrain the correspondence objective, while all remaining template vertices are optimized through the regularized non-rigid deformation. The target positions are computed from the segmentation ensemble: eye corners and contours from face landmark detection or fine-tuned Sapiens, mouth corners from landmark detection, and face boundary from segmentation mask edges.

    To avoid invalid keypoint errors in the evaluated assets, we implement three fallback mechanisms:

  • 1.

    Mesh-surface fallback for border keypoints. After correcting invalid border keypoints to the nearest face mask boundary, some corrected positions still fail 3D projection because the face mask and the actual mesh surface do not perfectly overlap. When a border keypoint has no valid 3D position after mask-boundary correction, we search for the nearest pixel on the actual mesh surface and compute the 3D position directly from the mesh geometry at that pixel.

  • 2.

    3D anchor-based fallback. When a keypoint’s 2D-to-3D projection fails (e.g., the 2D position lands in an area with no mesh geometry), we fall back to computing its 3D position from the already-resolved 3D positions of neighboring anchor keypoints, maintaining a running map of resolved positions so that later keypoints can reference those resolved earlier.

  • 3.

    Adaptive eye mask selection. Both segmentation-based and landmark-based eye masks can contribute to the face boundary computation, but including both can produce an overly large convex hull. We use only one eye mask source, selected adaptively: human assets use landmark-based eyes (higher precision), non-human assets use segmentation-based eyes (more robust), with auto-fallback if the preferred source is unavailable.

    • After these correspondence fallbacks, we apply standard global similarity and regularized non-rigid registration.

    4.5.3 Template Fitting Optimization

    Given the template mesh and computed keypoint correspondences, the fitting stage deforms the template to match the input asset via a two-stage optimization.

    Stage 1: Global Similarity Alignment. We find the best similarity transformation (rotation R, uniform scale s, translation t) aligning template keypoints vᵢ to asset keypoints pᵢ by minimizing:

    Eₛᵢₘ=∑_i∈K∥sRvᵢ+t-pᵢ∥²

    		(1)

    where K is the set of corresponding keypoints.

    Stage 2: Per-Vertex Non-Rigid Deformation. We optimize per-vertex displacements dᵢ for all vertices to minimize a composite energy function:

    E(D)=λ₁E_corr+λ₂Eₛₘₒₒₜₕ+λ₃E_edge+λ₄Eₜᵣᵢ+λ₅E_flip+λ₆E_reg

    		(2)

    where each energy term controls a different aspect of data fitting or geometric regularization to make this fitting pipeline robust to various input cases. We set λ₁=20.0 for the correspondence term and λ₂,…,λ₆=1.0 for the geometric regularizers. The larger correspondence weight drives the sparse anchors toward their targets, while the smoothness, edge-length, triangle-shape, flip-prevention, and displacement terms preserve local structure in an elastic/ARAP-style manner. The terms are defined as follows:

    Correspondence energy (E_corr) is the main data term that pulls the template keypoints toward their corresponding asset keypoints:

    E_corr=∑_i∈KH(∥v^′ᵢ-pᵢ∥)

    		(3)

    where v^′ᵢ=vᵢ+dᵢ represents the deformed template vertex positions, pᵢ represents target landmark points, and H is a robust penalty function such as a Huber loss to ignore outliers.

    Smoothness energy (Eₛₘₒₒₜₕ) enforces smooth deformations by encouraging neighboring vertices connected by a mesh edge 𝔼 to move in a similar way:

    Eₛₘₒₒₜₕ=∑_(i,j)∈𝔼∥dᵢ-dⱼ∥²

    		(4)

    Edge-length preservation energy (E_edge) encourages the deformation to remain locally rigid by preserving original edge lengths up to global scale:

    E_edge=∑_(i,j)∈𝔼(∥v^′ᵢ-v^′ⱼ∥-∥vᵢ-vⱼ∥)²

    		(5)

    Triangle shape preservation energy (Eₜᵣᵢ) preserves local triangle shapes more strongly than edge-length preservation alone and prevents skinny or sheared triangles:

    Eₜᵣᵢ=∑_t∈T∥Gₜ-G^′ₜ∥_F²

    		(6)

    where Gₜ and G^′ₜ denote triangle shape matrices encoding the edge lengths and angles before and after deformation, respectively.

    Triangle flip penalty (E_flip) penalizes orientation reversal and reduces triangle flips and foldovers to prevent self-intersections:

    E_flip=∑_t∈T\max(0,-nₜ·n^′ₜ)³

    		(7)

    where nₜ and n^′ₜ denote triangle normals before and after deformation, respectively.

    Offset regularization energy (E_reg) discourages unnecessarily large deformations and improves numerical stability:

    E_reg=∑ᵢ∥dᵢ∥²

    		(8)

    For normalized meshes, this optimization achieves near-zero alignment error (<10⁻⁵). The nose-landmark-free template design and triangle flip penalty improve fitting robustness across diverse face proportions (compact for cats and elongated for dogs) without category-specific optimization rules; end-to-end failures are reported separately through Success Rate.

    4.6 Blendshape Rig Construction

    Given the fitted face mesh produced by Stage 1 (Section4.5), Stage 2 constructs a production-ready FACS blendshape rig in three steps. The original asset is assumed to provide only the visible surface and source textures, with no pre-existing teeth, gums, tongue, or oral-cavity geometry. Stage 2 therefore consumes three additional inputs: the original static asset mesh (for surrounding geometry and source textures), the teeth template selected by the VLM in Stage 1 (Section4.2), and a canonical FACS blendshape template.

    (1) Face Mesh Fusion. The fitted template positions are first transferred to a high-quality animated topology mesh via UV correspondence, then reprojected onto the input character geometry. Eye regions are inset using virtual eyeball centers (computed via Procrustes alignment of eyelid vertices) to allow eyelid closure without self-intersection. The prepared template then replaces the face region on the original mesh: a 3D convex hull is computed for a subtractive Boolean (cut out the old face), the template border vertices are stitched to the remaining mesh boundary via closest-point welding, and small-edge collapse removes degenerate polygons (merge in the new face). This ensures proper radial topology flow around eyes and mouth for high-quality facial deformation.

    (2) Teeth Registration and Texture Baking.Teeth registration. Because generated characters contain no oral-cavity geometry, the canonical face template specifies an inner-mouth region to which each teeth archetype is spatially registered at rest. After the character-specific face template is fitted to the target surface, we deform this inner-mouth region to the target shape using as-rigid-as-possible (ARAP) deformation [(Sorkine and Alexa, 2007)]. We then estimate the best-fitting rigid transformation between the canonical and deformed inner-mouth regions using singular value decomposition (SVD) and apply it to the selected teeth archetype. A convex hull constructed from the aligned teeth serves as a collision proxy. At rest, an SDF-based refinement resolves initial collisions, which are particularly common for elongated dog snouts, by moving intersecting outer-face points out of the teeth volume. The selected archetype supplies the teeth, gums, and tongue as a consistent inner-mouth assembly (Figure7). Texture baking. After mesh merging, UV islands are re-packed using an automated UV layout solver to maximize packing area with no overlap between shells, with sufficient padding to prevent visible seams during mipmap rendering. The face region is scaled up to allocate approximately 10× more texel density than non-face regions, ensuring high-quality facial texture across levels of detail (LOD). The original texture is resampled onto the new UV layout using a vectorized approach: for each pixel in the output texture, we find the barycentric coordinate and primitive ID on the merged mesh’s UV layout, convert to world-space position, find the closest point on the original mesh, and sample the source texture at the corresponding UV. Teeth geometry uses a separate texture channel.

    (3) FACS Blendshape Transfer. Facial expressions are created by transferring blendshapes from the canonical FACS blendshape template to the merged character mesh using sparse deformation transfer[(Sumner and Popović, 2004)]. For each reference shape, triangle-level affine deformations are computed and transferred to the target mesh’s triangle structure, preserving character-specific geometry while reproducing the expression. The transferred shapes are applied to the merged mesh using Point Deform with Delta Mush smoothing to blend into adjacent non-template regions. Post-processing includes: (a) contact-aware eyelid closure[(Lewis et al., 2014)]—upper eyelid vertices are snapped to lower lids and edge-relaxed for closed-eye shapes; (b) eye gaze shapes—rotation around the virtual eyeball center; and (c) collision-aware deformation transfer. Standard deformation transfer can move the outer face surface through the inner-mouth geometry, particularly for expressions with strong lip motion such as FACS Action Unit 12 (AU12, the lip-corner puller). We therefore reuse the convex hull of the aligned teeth as a collision surface during gradient-based shape transfer. The collision term is formulated as a point-to-SDF penalty: outer-face points are penalized when they enter the SDF of the teeth hull. This constraint is applied for every transferred expression, substantially reducing visible lip–inner-mouth intersections (Figure8). Teeth geometry follows jaw-related shapes via radial basis function (RBF) warping converted to rigid transforms. The system supports three configurable shape-set tiers selected per application: Core (13 shapes) for basic dialog and emotion on mobile characters, Additional (46 shapes) for finer muscle control suitable for mid-fidelity game characters, and Full (155 shapes) for production VR applications where expression fidelity is paramount.

    The output of Stage 2 is the final FACS blendshape rig, ready to be driven by arbitrary expression weights at run-time. Additional implementation details for face-region fusion, inner-mouth construction, UV/texture transfer, and expression post-processing are provided in Appendix B.

    5 Experiments

    5.1 Setup

    Rig-quality comparisons use screened Omni-Bench candidate subsets with independent artist-authored reference rigs (Section5.3); the riggability and segmentation evaluations use the sets described with Tables3 and 5. All inference-time experiments use a single NVIDIA A100 GPU; segmentation fine-tuning is an offline step on the multi-GPU setup below.

    5.2 Implementation Details

    Sapiens Pre-Training. We use Sapiens-1B [(Khirodkar et al., 2024)] as the base segmentation backbone for all Sapiens-based parsers in OmniFaceRig. Following Section4.3, the encoder is initialized with masked-reconstruction pretraining: we first train at 512×512 resolution for efficiency, then briefly switch to 1024×1024 resolution for high-resolution facial boundary cues. The pretraining corpus contains approximately 4B curated realistic human images. We then perform a mid-stage unsupervised adaptation on 20M in-domain stylized character images. In our downstream parsing experiments, these two stages improve segmentation accuracy by 2–3%, and the in-domain adaptation makes the subsequent supervised parser training more annotation-efficient.

    Fine-Tuned Sapiens Training. To extend Sapiens’ face parsing capability to stylized and non-human characters, we construct a custom training dataset of approximately 10,000 annotated 2D images covering humans, humanoids, and animal species such as felines, canines, ursines, and other stylized creatures, all rendered in frontal T-pose. We use an 80/10/10 train/validation/test split. The dataset contains approximately 60% animal, 20% stylized-humanoid, and 20% human examples; this animal-heavy distribution targets the largest domain gap of the human-centric pretrained backbone. Starting from the pretrained encoder, we attach a lightweight three-stage deconvolutional decoder and train two compatible parser heads: a 41-class stylized parser for human-like characters and a 38-class humanoid parser for cartoon animals and strongly non-human characters. Both heads use the same curated image pool with task-specific label vocabularies. For evaluation and geometric fitting, these fine-grained labels are collapsed into the face-relevant cues consumed by the rigging pipeline: face boundary, eyes, nose or muzzle extent, mouth opening, teeth or inner-mouth support, and accessory-aware occlusion regions.

    During fine-tuning, we freeze the Sapiens-1B ViT encoder to preserve its open-world visual features and train only the segmentation decoder heads. Training uses AdamW with a learning rate of 1×10⁻⁴, cosine decay with 500 warmup steps, batch size 16, and class-balanced cross-entropy loss for imbalanced facial regions. Training runs for 50 epochs on 8× NVIDIA A100 GPUs, taking approximately 24 hours. We apply standard data augmentation: random horizontal flip, color jitter, random rotation (±15∘), and random scale (0.8–1.2×). The fine-tuning images cannot be publicly released because the internally collected and manually annotated data are subject to licensing restrictions; we instead report the label configuration, model architecture, training protocol, and evaluation definitions.

    The fine-tuned parsers achieve a mean Intersection-over-Union (mIoU) of 87.3% on our held-out test set after collapsing predictions to the rigging-relevant facial cues, compared to 62.1% for the original Sapiens parser. The improvement is most pronounced on animal faces: cat face mIoU improves from 31.2% to 84.5%, and dog face mIoU from 28.7% to 81.9%, while human face mIoU remains stable (89.1% → 91.2%).

    5.3 Evaluation Metrics and Baselines

    Drawing upon the evaluation protocols established by recent state-of-the-art methods [(Ma et al., 2025; Qin et al., 2023; Cha et al., 2025)], we employ a comprehensive set of metrics. Before evaluation, each full-body T-pose mesh is isotropically normalized to fit a unit sphere in meter-scale coordinates, where one coordinate unit corresponds to one meter. We use Mean Absolute Error (MAE) and 95th-Percentile Vertex Error (Q95) to measure the mean and worst-case per-vertex Euclidean distance between the predicted expression mesh and ground truth, and report these distances in millimeters. Penetration Rate is the percentage of outer-face vertices lying inside the signed-distance field (SDF) of the aligned-teeth convex hull, aggregated over all expression–vertex tests of valid outputs. To quantify pipeline robustness, we introduce Success Rate, tracking the percentage of successfully rigged assets among screened candidate inputs that have passed the VLM+CV riggability checker. Finally, Processing Latency measures the end-to-end execution time in seconds.

    All rig-quality evaluations (Table4 and the animal results in the following subsection) use subsets of the screened Omni-Bench candidate inputs for which independently artist-authored reference rigs are available. We compare against Neural Face Rigging (NFR) [(Qin et al., 2023)] and Deformation Transfer (DT) [(Sumner and Popović, 2004)] on the overlapping human/humanoid setting. We do not directly re-evaluate RigAnyFace [(Ma et al., 2025)], because neither its implementation nor the evaluation data required to reproduce its published numbers are publicly available.

    5.4 Quantitative Results

    Table4 uses independent artist-authored ground truth, not corrected OmniFaceRig outputs. For the same 300 surface-only inputs, artists authored the target inner-mouth geometry and FACS blendshapes. The 200-human portion includes realistic/photorealistic faces; the remaining 100 are stylized humanoids. For a fair comparison, MAE and Q95 are computed only over corresponding outer-face vertices for all methods; the disconnected teeth, gums, and tongue components are excluded from both OmniFaceRig outputs and artist-authored references. Errors use each method’s valid outputs, whereas Success Rate covers all 300 inputs: DT succeeds on 246, NFR on 256, and OmniFaceRig on 297. Baselines are restricted to this setting because DT and NFR do not produce equivalent animal rigs with generated inner mouths.

    NFR’s prescribed preparation requires manually isolating the head, removing garments, internal sockets, and eyeballs, cutting the eye and mouth openings, and normalizing the target. OmniFaceRig uses the original surface-only full-character mesh without per-asset preprocessing, better preserving the pursed lips (Figure9, third column) and handling the non-human face.

    On 200 animals with topology-compatible artist-authored references, OmniFaceRig produces 195 valid rigs (97.5% success). Valid outputs obtain 2.60 mm MAE, 6.77 mm Q95, and 0.45% penetration. Figure14 shows surface-only inputs alongside generated expressions and inner-mouth geometry across human, humanoid, and animal characters.

    5.5 Ablation Studies

    Segmentation Model Ablation. We evaluate the contribution of each model in our four-model ensemble (Table5) by comparing face detection recall on the Omni-Bench evaluation inputs for individual models and the full ensemble.

    Face landmark detection achieves high recall on human faces (92%) but fails almost entirely on animals (12–18%), as it is trained exclusively on human face data. Standard Sapiens degrades on non-human faces (35–42%) due to its human-centric training, despite being a strong foundation model. SAM 3 offers the broadest single-model coverage (72% overall) due to its class-agnostic design, but provides coarser segmentation boundaries than landmark-based methods. Fine-tuned Sapiens substantially improves animal face detection (85–89%) while retaining strong human performance (90%), validating the effectiveness of our fine-tuning strategy. The four-model ensemble with adaptive per-region selection achieves nearly 100% overall recall by combining the accuracy of face landmark detection on humans, fine-tuned Sapiens’ robustness on animals, and SAM 3’s fallback coverage for edge cases.

    Nose Landmark Ablation. We evaluate the impact of our nose-landmark-free template design on animal face rigging quality. When nose anchor keypoints are included (as in prior template designs), the pipeline produces severely distorted nose-mouth regions on 78% of animal assets and crashes on 10%, driven by the two failure modes discussed in Section4.5: incorrect nose segmentation, and—even when the nose mask is plausible—unstable keypoints from uniform boundary sampling on small, irregular nose contours. Removing nose anchors and allowing the optimization to position the nose region from the surrounding border, eye, and mouth anchors eliminates these distortion artifacts and removes crashes attributable to nose-anchor instability in this ablation. Figure11 provides visual evidence for both failure modes across a range of character topologies.

    Riggability Checker. The hybrid VLM+CV approach outperforms either component alone (Table3): the VLM provides strong archetype identification and accessory detection, while CV filtering catches geometric edge cases (no-face assets, degenerate meshes).

    5.6 Latency Breakdown

    The face pipeline executes on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU. End-to-end latency is approximately 20–30 s per asset, including data I/O. Stage 1 (riggability assessment, face parsing, keypoint extraction, and template fitting) takes 8–10 s, while Stage 2 (mesh fusion, inner-mouth fitting, UV/texture processing, and blendshape transfer) takes 10–15 s. Compared to manual sculpting workflows that typically take hours to days, this represents a reduction of 2–3 orders of magnitude.

    6 Limitations and Future Work

    OmniFaceRig is limited to visible-faced characters covered by our human, long-muzzle, and short-muzzle template families. Unusual anatomies—including sharp beaks, wide-mouthed fish-like faces, compound eyes, or strongly elongated snouts (Figure12)—may be rejected or fitted unreliably. Extending coverage requires additional templates, segmentation labels, and riggability criteria. Even a valid completed rig can retain localized fitting or penetration artifacts under extreme mouth motion or unusual muzzle geometry; Figure10 compares one such near-failure with its artist-authored reference. The 0.45% animal penetration rate and 97.5% success rate quantify these remaining cases rather than implying perfectly intersection-free output. The 20–30 s pipeline targets offline or batch processing rather than real-time editing. Future work will broaden topology coverage and further integrate perception with geometry. Additional riggability-checker failure modes (annotation borderline cases and VLM-only semantic errors) are discussed in Appendix A.5.

    7 Conclusion

    We presented OmniFaceRig, a fully automatic inner-mouth-aware face rigging pipeline for 3D characters. Given a static surface-only 3D mesh with no pre-modeled oral cavity, OmniFaceRig produces a production-ready rig with up to 155 FACS blendshapes and procedurally generated inner-mouth geometry (teeth, gums, and tongue), with no manual intervention at any stage. Our segmentation ensemble, topology-specific templates, and collision treatment support human and animal topologies; independent artist references show high success with low error and penetration. We also release Omni-Bench, to our knowledge the first open benchmark of more than 1,000 rigged biped characters with FACS facial blendshapes and inner-mouth geometry, to catalyze future research in automatic facial rigging.

    （参考文献见原文。）

    Appendix

    Appendix A Supplementary Riggability Assessment Details

    This section expands the design of the hybrid riggability checker introduced in the main paper. We give the per-question signal assignment, the geometric criteria used to validate segmentation masks, the landmark-based mouth-quality gate, the mouth-signal fusion logic, and a brief discussion of the remaining failure modes that bound the accuracy of the gate.

    A.1 VLM+CV Signal Architecture

    The checker fuses one semantic signal and two CV-derived signals computed from a single rendered view of the input asset:

  • •

    VLM semantic signal. Gemini 2.5 Flash Image is the primary vision-language model, with a Llama 4 multimodal model as fallback when the primary response is unavailable or invalid. It answers a fixed set of high-level questions about the rendered character (face type, number of faces, eye orbits, accessories, mouth state, and teeth visibility). These questions capture failure modes that are inherently semantic and hard to phrase as geometric thresholds.

  • •

    Segmentation-mask signal. The face/eye/mouth masks produced by the segmentation ensemble are evaluated against geometric plausibility criteria: presence of each region, inclusion inside the face boundary, plausible eye-to-head ratio, and acceptable lip-seal curvature.

  • •

    Landmark-quality signal. For human-like faces, the regularity of mouth landmarks is summarized by a lip-evenness statistic and used as a quality gate before mouth evidence enters the fusion step.

    • The three signals are not treated as redundant: each question in the underlying checker template is assigned to the signal that is empirically most reliable for it, as summarized in Table A.1.

    A.2 Geometric Criteria from Segmentation Masks

    The segmentation-based checks (Q5, Q9, Q10, plus mask inclusion tests) are summarized in Table A.2. Their binary decision rules are calibrated once on a development split and held fixed across all evaluations; they are deliberately conservative so that the checker mostly rejects inputs that would otherwise crash or distort the downstream registration stage.

    A.3 Landmark-Assisted Mouth Validation

    For human-like inputs, we use mouth landmarks as a quality gate before they are fused with the VLM and segmentation signals. Let κₗᵢₚ denote the coefficient of variation (standard deviation divided by mean) of the spacing between consecutive lip-contour landmarks. We mark the mouth landmarks as unreliable when κₗᵢₚ exceeds a calibrated threshold; the underlying intuition is that on assets with a poorly modeled or absent mouth, the landmark detector still emits points, but those points become irregularly spaced. Failing the gate sets the landmark mouth evidence to “unavailable” for the subsequent fusion step.

    For non-human assets, where human-trained mouth-landmark detectors are not reliable, the landmark signal is ignored and the mouth decision is determined by the VLM and the segmentation mask alone.

    A.4 Mouth-Signal Fusion Logic

    The final eligibility decision is the conjunction of all per-question results in Table A.1. Q1–Q3 and Q6–Q8 are decided directly by the VLM; Q5, Q9, Q10 are decided by the segmentation-mask checks in Table A.2; and Q4 (mouth presence) uses explicit fusion because mouth localization is one of the most common downstream failure sources.

    Concretely, for a human-like asset, the mouth decision is:

  • 1.

    If κₗᵢₚ exceeds the landmark-quality threshold, treat the landmark evidence as unreliable and rely on the VLM and segmentation signals.

  • 2.

    Otherwise, take a majority vote over (i) the VLM mouth prediction, (ii) the segmentation-based mouth-detected flag, and (iii) the landmark-based mouth-detected flag.

    • For non-human assets, the same step degenerates to a conjunction of the VLM and segmentation-mask signals. The majority-vote design recovers the cases that a strict “VLM and segmentation” rule would miss when exactly one of the three signals is wrong but the other two agree.

    A.5 Discussion of Remaining Failure Modes

    Empirically, the hybrid VLM+CV checker on the mixed riggability validation set exhibits two dominant failure categories. The first is annotation borderline cases, where the ground-truth label itself is ambiguous (e.g., partially occluded faces or stylized characters that are arguably riggable). The second is VLM-only semantic errors: misclassification of eyewear, mouth state, or teeth visibility—attributes that segmentation masks and landmarks only partially corroborate. These are the natural targets for future improvement of the checker, since the geometric and landmark signals have already absorbed most of the failures they are capable of catching.

    Appendix B Supplementary Stage-2 Rig Construction Details

    This section expands the four implementation components underlying the three Stage-2 steps in the main paper: face-region fusion; inner-mouth construction; texture/UV transfer; and blendshape transfer with post-processing. The shared difficulty across these components is that the input asset is surface-only: there is no pre-modeled oral cavity, no animation-grade facial topology, and no separation between expressive and structural regions.

    B.1 Face-Region Fusion

    The fitted face mesh produced by Stage 1 defines the region of the input asset that will be replaced. A high-quality animated topology—designed with radial edge loops around the eyes and mouth—is first aligned to the fitted template through their shared UV correspondence, then reprojected onto the input surface so that it inherits the asset’s own facial geometry. The original face region of the input is removed via a Boolean operation against a convex hull of the fitted region, the new animated topology is inserted in its place, and the boundary between the new face and the rest of the asset is stitched by closest-point welding followed by small-edge collapse to clean up degenerate polygons. This operation is intentionally local: it preserves the asset’s identity, hairstyle, and non-face geometry while introducing the radial edge flow that downstream expression deformation relies on.

    B.2 Inner-Mouth Construction

    Because the input contains no oral cavity, the inner-mouth geometry (teeth, gums, and tongue) cannot be recovered from the asset itself. We instead maintain a small library of inner-mouth template archetypes, summarized in Table B.1; the appropriate archetype is selected by the VLM during Stage 1 and fitted to the character as described below.

    Each face template defines an inner-mouth region, and every teeth archetype is spatially registered to that region at rest. After the character-specific face template is fitted to the target surface, its inner-mouth region is deformed as-rigid-as-possible (ARAP) to the new shape. We then estimate, by SVD, the rigid transformation between the canonical and deformed inner-mouth regions and apply it to the selected teeth, gum, and tongue archetype. A convex hull of the aligned teeth provides the collision proxy. At rest, a point-to-SDF penalty moves intersecting outer-face points outside this hull; the same penalty is applied again during per-expression deformation transfer. This treatment is particularly important for long-muzzled animals, where initial collisions may otherwise occur.

    B.3 Texture and UV Transfer

    After the new face and inner-mouth surfaces are inserted, the global UV layout is rebuilt. The face region is allocated a larger fraction of the texture domain than non-face regions so that high-frequency facial detail is preserved at any rendering resolution, and the inner-mouth surfaces are placed on a separate texture channel to keep their material parameters independent. The asset’s original appearance is then transferred onto the rebuilt UV layout by sampling the original texture through the geometric correspondence between the original and merged surfaces; this preserves the character’s identity and material details while letting the newly synthesized geometry inherit a coherent appearance.

    B.4 Blendshape Transfer and Post-Processing

    FACS expression shapes are produced by transferring local deformation gradients from a canonical rigged template to the merged character mesh using sparse deformation transfer. Adapting the deformation gradients to the target character’s own proportions is what keeps the transferred expressions character-specific rather than collapsing the rig toward an “average human face,” and is what allows the same set of FACS shapes to be applied to humans, humanoids, long-muzzled animals, and short-muzzled animals without per-character authoring.

    The transferred deformations are then blended outward from the facial template region into the adjacent head surface so that expression motion fades smoothly into the rest of the asset. Sparse deformation transfer alone cannot enforce certain physical and geometric constraints—eyelids must close without self-intersection, eye-gaze shapes require a known rotation center, jaw motion must move the lower teeth, and extreme mouth poses can re-introduce teeth–face intersections. A small set of expression-specific post-processing rules, summarized in Table B.2, handles these cases.

    B.5 Design Tradeoffs and Outlook

    The four implementation components of Stage 2 are coupled but decomposable: face-region fusion fixes the surface topology, inner-mouth construction synthesizes the missing oral cavity, UV/texture transfer preserves the character’s original appearance, and blendshape transfer turns the static rig into an animatable one. A common thread is that each component substitutes a procedural geometric operation for what is traditionally a manual authoring step, which is also what makes the full pipeline fully automatic.

    The two design choices that most directly enable cross-topology generalization are the use of multiple inner-mouth archetypes (Table B.1) and the SDF-based collision refinement at both the rest pose and the per-expression level.
