Its surface positions are linear in these DoFs, allowing piecewise-linear collision trajectories and a pose-independent mass matrix at fixed rest geometry. This offers a compact representation for stiff parts, while full-space FEM retains local deformation where it is needed. DiffGIPC carries both representations into the same backward system, retaining contact, friction, and joint coupling between bodies.

    Compact rigid-body states have supported differentiable learning and control [(Belbute-Peres et al., 2018; Degrave et al., 2019)], including articulated dynamics in Nimble [(Werling et al., 2021)]. Shape optimization requires an additional distinction between the motion representation and the geometry being designed. Contact-based assemblies and shock-protecting microstructures [(Tozoni et al., 2021; Huang et al., 2024b)] use geometric changes to alter load transfer and contact-dependent mechanical response. Pneumatic actuator design and garment reconstruction [(Gjoka et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025)] likewise optimize rest geometry through its effect on deformation. These applications motivate retaining a rich design space even when the motion state can be compact.

    SDRS uses convex polyhedra and auxiliary separating planes to maintain differentiability under large shape changes [(Ye et al., 2025)]. Our focus is mesh-based design and control of affine bodies interacting with deformable objects under IPC. Affine rest-shape changes affect both the mass matrix and the maps from affine DoFs to surface points. Differentiating these dependencies allows a body’s shape to be optimized for its frictional interactions with other objects. Derivatives of joint targets and forces likewise account for the coupled response of articulated and deformable bodies. For a fixed motion representation, additional design parameters do not enlarge the per-frame backward system. Each affine body therefore contributes only twelve motion DoFs, even when its rest shape is described by many design parameters. Contact processing still depends on surface resolution, while parameter-gradient evaluation requires additional work as the number of design parameters grows.

    GPU computation for trajectory adjoints

    Compact coordinates reduce adjoint system size, while efficient linear solvers further reduce the cost of trajectory differentiation. PD-based local-global methods exploit a fixed global matrix to reuse precomputed factors. [Zeng et al. (2025)] use a sparse representation of its inverse to accelerate GPU forward simulation. DiffPhD adopts this strategy for differentiable simulation, reusing an inverse factor across forward, backward, and frictional-contact computations [(Lai et al., 2026)]. In IPC, however, the frame Hessian varies with deformation and contact, so a fixed factorization cannot be reused across all adjoint systems along a trajectory. Preconditioned iterative solvers provide an alternative, with effective preconditioning reducing the number of iterations [(Chen et al., 2021; Wu et al., 2022)]. GIPC parallelizes IPC computation [(Huang et al., 2024a)], while StiffGIPC provides efficient FEM-ABD coupling and GPU solvers across a wide range of stiffnesses [(Huang et al., 2025a)], and AGIPC further reduces GPU linear-solve costs through adaptive in-solve algebraic coarsening [(Wang et al., 2026)]. These methods advance GPU IPC efficiency, with StiffGIPC supplying the forward simulation foundation for our work.

    DiffGIPC combines coupled frame-wise adjoint solves with parallel gradient accumulation on the GPU. Compact affine coordinates reduce PCG’s numerical workload, making repeated CPU kernel launches and convergence synchronization more prominent. Conditional CUDA Graphs reduce this overhead by keeping iteration control and convergence checks on the GPU, with compatible graphs reused across frames as the Hessian changes. After each solve, local derivative products are accumulated in parallel to compute physical-parameter gradients and update earlier-frame adjoint right-hand sides.

    3. A Unified Differentiable IPC Framework

    The framework separates the coordinates needed to describe contact geometry from those needed to solve motion. Collision and friction derivatives are evaluated at world-space surface points and mapped into a coupled system of FEM vertex positions and affine body coordinates. This preserves cross-object derivatives while assigning twelve motion DoFs to each affine body.

    The forward formulation builds on StiffGIPC [(Huang et al., 2025a)]. Simulation DoFs describe solved motion, whereas physical parameters are inputs changed by the optimizer. One frame is an accepted time step of length h, and mesh connectivity is fixed within each differentiated trajectory. The state and incremental potential below define the single-step adjoint. Section 4 extends it through time, Section 5 supplies affine design and control derivatives, and Section 6 develops their GPU computation and task interface.

    3.1. Simulation degrees of freedom and contact points

    A free FEM vertex i is represented by its world-space position x_t,i∈ℝ³ at frame t. An affine body b is represented by its translation p_t,b∈ℝ³ and affine transformation A_t,b∈ℝ^3×3. Let α_t,b,1ᵀ, α_t,b,2ᵀ, and α_t,b,3ᵀ be the rows of A_t,b. Stacking these vectors with the translation defines the body’s twelve DoFs:

    (1)A_t,b=\beginbmatrixα_t,b,1ᵀ α_t,b,2ᵀ α_t,b,3ᵀ\endbmatrix,
    q_t,b=[p_t,bᵀ,α_t,b,1ᵀ,α_t,b,2ᵀ,α_t,b,3ᵀ]ᵀ∈ℝ¹².

    For a surface vertex with rest position x̄ᵢ, the world-space position is

    (2)

    x_t,i=p_t,b+A_t,bx̄ᵢ.

    Let I₃ denote the 3×3 identity matrix and e₁, e₂, and e₃ the Cartesian unit vectors. With rest position fixed, the Jacobian of this position with respect to q_t,b is the 3×12 matrix

    (3)Jᵢ=J(x̄ᵢ)=[I₃ e₁x̄ᵢᵀ e₂x̄ᵢᵀ e₃x̄ᵢᵀ],
    x_t,i=Jᵢq_t,b.

    All surface vertices on body b share the same q_t,b, but each has its own rest-dependent map Jᵢ.

    For N_A free affine bodies and N_F free FEM vertices, we collect the simulation DoFs in

    (4)

    yₜ=[q_t,1ᵀ,…,q_t,N_Aᵀ,x_t,1ᵀ,…,x_t,N_Fᵀ]ᵀ.

    The total number of simulation DoFs is n=12N_A+3N_F. The set and ordering of free DoFs do not change throughout each trajectory. Adding surface vertices to an affine body can increase contact work, but does not enlarge its block in the linear system. Rest coordinates are design parameters, not additional simulation DoFs.

    For contact c, we collect the world-space positions of its n_c surface points into xₜᶜ. Let yₜ∈ℝⁿ contain the free simulation DoFs. The Jacobian K_t,c describes how changes in these DoFs affect the contact-point positions:

    (5)xₜᶜ=[x_t,i₁ᵀ,…,x_t,i_n_cᵀ]ᵀ,
    K_t,c=(∂xₜᶜ)/(∂yₜ)∈ℝ^3n_c×n.

    The three-row map for vertex i is denoted by Kₜⁱ=∂x_t,i/∂yₜ∈ℝ^3×n. The contact map K_t,c stacks the maps of its participating vertices. For a free FEM vertex, its three positional DoFs appear directly in yₜ, so these rows contain an identity block I₃ in the corresponding columns. For a point on a free affine body, its position depends on the body’s twelve affine DoFs through Jᵢ, so these rows contain Jᵢ in that body’s columns. For each free point, columns outside its associated vertex or body block are zero. A fixed point contributes three zero rows. For fixed rest geometry and DoF ordering, Kₜⁱ is unchanged across frames. When differentiating with respect to the free motion DoFs, we hold the rest geometry and prescribed motion fixed. When differentiating with respect to the rest shape, we also differentiate the dependence of the affine point maps Jᵢ, and hence K_t,c, on the rest positions (Section 5.2).

    3.2. Incremental potential and its energy gradient

    Let θ∈ℝ^n_θ collect the physical parameters selected for optimization, such as material and friction coefficients, rest coordinates, initial states, and joint controls. Here n_θ is the number of selected scalar parameters. These parameters are held fixed during one forward simulation. A joint-control schedule can still contain different prescribed values for different frames. For a given θ, each time step of length h computes the simulation DoFs yₜ by minimizing the incremental potential

    (6)Φₜ(yₜ)=\tfrac12∥yₜ-ŷₜ∥_M²
    +∑_e∈𝔼wₑ(h,θ)Ψ_t,e(yₜ,yₜ₋₁;θ).

    The first term accounts for inertia, with ∥v∥_M²=vᵀMv. The mass matrix M is expressed in the simulation coordinates: it contains vertex-mass blocks for FEM and a 12×12 block for each affine body. Section 5 gives the affine mass matrix and its rest-shape derivatives. The predictor ŷₜ is computed from earlier states and prescribed accelerations aₜ. For dynamic bodies, backward Euler (BDF1) gives

    (7)

    ŷₜ=2yₜ₋₁-yₜ₋₂+h²aₜ, t≥2.

    At the first step, the predictor is ŷ₁=y₀+hẏ₀+h²a₁, where y₀ specifies the initial configuration and ẏ₀ contains the initial FEM vertex velocities and the initial velocities of the affine coordinates.

    The second term in Equation (6) sums the contributions from FEM elastic energy, affine shape energy, collision, friction, and joints. Each contribution is indexed by e∈𝔼 and written as wₑ(h,θ)Ψ_t,e, with energy function Ψ_t,e and scalar weight wₑ(h,θ). The collision energy is the non-penetration barrier, distinct from the friction energy for tangential resistance. IPC’s friction energy depends on the relative tangential displacement of the two configurations, determined by yₜ and yₜ₋₁. Its tangent bases and normal forces are held fixed from the previous-frame positions when solving for yₜ, and their dependence on those positions is included in the derivative with respect to yₜ₋₁.

    At a minimum of the incremental potential, its gradient gₜ with respect to the free simulation DoFs satisfies the stationarity equation

    (8)gₜ(yₜ,yₜ₋₁,yₜ₋₂;θ):=∇_yₜΦₜ
    =M(yₜ-ŷₜ)
    +∑_e∈𝔼wₑ(h,θ)∇_yₜΨ_t,e
    =0.

    The energy gradient gₜ is also the nonlinear residual of this equation. For each parameter choice, the forward solver finds DoFs that satisfy this stationarity condition. Differentiating the condition determines how a parameter change affects the solved DoFs and the loss evaluated on them.

    3.3. Parameter gradients from the step equation

    Consider first a single time step from a prescribed initial state, omitting the frame index. The solved DoFs satisfy g(y,θ)=0. A parameter change affects this equation both directly and through the resulting change in y. Differentiating the stationarity equation gives

    (9)

    \underbrace(∂g)/(∂y)_Hdy/dθ+\underbrace(∂g)/(∂θ)_G=0.

    Here, G is the partial derivative of the energy gradient with respect to the physical parameters. The derivative H with respect to the DoFs is the Hessian of the incremental potential:

    (10)

    H=(∂g)/(∂y)=∇_y²Φ.

    Both matrices are evaluated at the converged DoFs satisfying g(y,θ)=0. Rather than forming dy/dθ explicitly, we use the adjoint below. Restoring the frame index, we denote these matrices by Hₜ∈ℝ^n×n and Gₜ∈ℝ^n×n_θ.

    For a scalar loss L(y,θ), let ℓ_y=∇_yL and ℓ_θ=∇_θL denote its partial gradients with respect to the DoFs and physical parameters, respectively. The chain rule gives

    (11)

    ∇_θL=ℓ_θ+(dy/dθ)ᵀℓ_y.

    Explicitly computing dy/dθ becomes costly as the number of optimized parameters grows. We avoid forming this matrix and compute the loss gradient by solving the adjoint system:

    (12)

    Hᵀλ=ℓ_y.

    The solution λ is the adjoint vector. Combining this solve with Equation (9) gives the parameter gradient

    (13)

    ∇_θL=ℓ_θ-Gᵀλ.

    For a single time step, all parameter gradients share the same coupled FEM-affine adjoint. Section 4 extends this formulation through time.

    3.4. Collision and friction derivatives across representations

    Collision and friction energies are evaluated at world-space surface points, whereas the adjoint in Equation (12) acts on simulation DoFs. The map K_t,c from Equation (5) converts the point-space derivatives into FEM and affine coordinates. The collision energy uses GIPC’s squared-log barrier on squared distance [(Huang et al., 2024a)]

    (14)

    b_bar(d)=\begincasesκ(d-d̂)²\log²(d/d̂),&0

    where d is the squared distance, d̂ is its activation threshold, and κ is the barrier coefficient. This squared-log form is the GIPC barrier, rather than the original IPC single-log form. At each Newton iteration, we truncate the step along the search direction using continuous collision detection to prevent intersections, followed by line search to ensure a decrease in the incremental potential. Backward differentiation uses the converged frame state and its associated collision and friction data.

    For a contact c at frame t, let g_t,cˣ and H_t,cˣ denote the gradient and Hessian of the collision energy with respect to the stacked world-space point positions xₜᶜ. The superscript x denotes point coordinates, whereas y denotes simulation DoFs. With rest geometry fixed, the point map K_t,c from Equation (5) is constant with respect to yₜ. The chain rule therefore gives the contributions to the frame energy gradient and Hessian:

    (15)

    g_t,cʸ=K_t,cᵀg_t,cˣ, H_t,cʸ=K_t,cᵀH_t,cˣK_t,c.

    The same transformation applies to friction derivatives with respect to the current-frame DoFs. Friction derivatives with respect to earlier states are included in the trajectory calculation in Section 4.

    Each point contributes through the map associated with its object. For point i on affine body b and point j on affine body b^′, let Hᵢⱼˣ be their 3×3 point-space Hessian block. Mapping this block gives a 12×12 contribution to H_bb^′^AA. If the second point is instead a FEM vertex j, its identity map gives a 12×3 contribution to H_bj^AF. For the point pair (i,j), the block contributions are

    (16)ΔH_bb^′^AA,(i,j)=JᵢᵀHᵢⱼˣJⱼ,
    ΔH_bj^AF,(i,j)=JᵢᵀHᵢⱼˣ.

    All surface vertices of an affine body share its twelve DoFs. The contributions of all relevant point pairs are summed into the corresponding body blocks, without introducing independent vertex DoFs. For distinct points on the same body, both ordered point-block contributions must be included when they map to the same diagonal body block.

    After assembly, grouping affine (A) and finite-element (F) DoFs gives the frame Hessian

    (17)

    Hₜ=\beginbmatrixH_AA&H_AF H_FA&H_FF\endbmatrix, H_FA=H_AFᵀ.

    The diagonal blocks H_AA and H_FF collect derivatives within the affine and FEM coordinates. Collision and friction contribute H_AF and H_FA, while joints couple affine bodies within H_AA. These cross blocks let a loss on one object influence parameters of another. Compact affine coordinates reduce system size while the cross terms preserve the interacting response.

    The same point maps form the loss-gradient vector ℓ_y on the right-hand side of Equation (12). For a loss evaluated on world-space surface points, its gradient with respect to the affine coordinates of body b, whose surface-vertex index set is V_b, is

    (18)

    ∇_q_bL=∑_i∈V_bJᵢᵀ∇_xᵢL.

    For a FEM vertex, the loss gradient with respect to its DoFs equals that with respect to its world-space position. These mappings hold with rest geometry fixed. Section 5.2 includes the additional dependence of the point maps and surface positions on rest shape. Section 4 extends this coupled adjoint to trajectories, where earlier states affect both later motion and the loss.

    4. Frame-Wise Adjoint

    The single-step adjoint captures interactions at one frame. A trajectory also depends on how earlier motion changes later inertia and friction. We account for these dependencies by backward substitution through the causal sequence of frame equations. Each reverse frame solves one coupled FEM-affine system, then contributes to the parameters and earlier states that influenced it. Algorithm 1 summarizes this recurrence. We derive its temporal structure and then specify the inertia and friction terms, using the converged states and recorded data that define the forward equations.

    4.1. Equations for the whole trajectory

    Let yₜ∈ℝⁿ contain the free simulation DoFs in the order defined in Section 3.1. The equation at frame t depends on its current state, a subset of earlier solved states, and the physical parameters:

    (19)

    gₜ(yₜ,{yₛ:s∈D(t)},θ)=0.

    The set D(t)⊆{1,…,t-1} identifies those earlier frames. The initial state is an input rather than a solved frame: its optimized components contribute to Gₜ, while unselected components remain fixed. Prescribed joint commands likewise enter Gₜ through the applied controls. The matrices Hₜ and Gₜ retain their state and parameter definitions from Section 3.3. Temporal dependence introduces the additional derivative

    (20)

    C_t,s=(∂gₜ)/(∂yₛ)∈ℝ^n×n, s∈D(t).

    Thus Hₜ describes the coupled response within frame t, whereas C_t,s describes its dependence on an earlier state and vanishes for s∉D(t). Both current and earlier solved states vary with θ. Differentiating Equation (19) includes these changes together with the direct parameter derivative:

    (21)

    Hₜdyₜ/dθ+∑_s∈D(t)C_t,sdyₛ/dθ+Gₜ=0.

    With Sₜ=dyₜ/dθ∈ℝ^n×n_θ, the equations for all frames form the block system

    (22)

    \beginbmatrixH₁&0&⋯&0 C_2,1&H₂&⋱&⋮ ⋮&⋱&⋱&0 C_T,1&⋯&C_T,T-1&H_T\endbmatrix_J\beginbmatrixS₁ S₂ ⋮ S_T\endbmatrix_S=-\beginbmatrixG₁ G₂ ⋮ G_T\endbmatrix_G.

    Causality makes J block lower triangular, with the frame Hessians Hₜ on the diagonal and nonzero off-diagonal blocks only for dependencies in D(t).

    The predictor in Equation (7) depends on yₜ₋₁ and yₜ₋₂. Friction adds to the first of these dependencies, through C_t,t-1. For the first three solved frames, the system is

    (23)

    \beginbmatrixH₁&0&0 C_2,1&H₂&0 C_3,1&C_3,2&H₃\endbmatrix\beginbmatrixS₁ S₂ S₃\endbmatrix=-\beginbmatrixG₁ G₂ G₃\endbmatrix.

    This three-frame system illustrates the reverse calculation below. The sensitivities Sₜ and the assembled trajectory matrix are used for the derivation, but are not formed by the backward algorithm.

    4.2. Reverse-time adjoint equations

    We extend the single-step adjoint in Equation (12) to the trajectory loss L(y₁,…,y_T;θ). Let ℓₜ=∇_yₜL denote its partial gradient with respect to the simulation DoFs at frame t, and let ℓ_θ denote its partial parameter gradient with all simulated states fixed. For a loss evaluated only on the final state, ℓₜ=0 for t4.1, the chain rule extends Equation (11) to

    (24)∇_θL=ℓ_θ+∑ₜ₌₁ᵀ(dyₜ/dθ)ᵀℓₜ
    =ℓ_θ+∑ₜ₌₁ᵀSₜᵀℓₜ
    =ℓ_θ+Sᵀℓₐₗₗ,

    where ℓₐₗₗ stacks the per-frame loss gradients in the same order as the blocks of S. The first term accounts for the explicit parameter dependence of the loss. The second accounts for changes in the simulated trajectory.

    To evaluate the trajectory contribution without computing S, we introduce an adjoint vector λₜ for each frame and solve

    (25)

    Jᵀ\beginbmatrixλ₁ ⋮ λ_T\endbmatrix (Λ)=\beginbmatrixℓ₁ ⋮ ℓ_T\endbmatrix_ℓₐₗₗ.

    Combining this equation with JS=-G from Equation (22) gives

    (26)

    Sᵀℓₐₗₗ=SᵀJᵀΛ=-GᵀΛ.

    The transpose reverses the causal order: Jᵀ is block upper triangular, so the trajectory adjoint is solved from the last frame backward. For the three-frame example,

    (27)

    \beginbmatrixH₁ᵀ&C_2,1ᵀ&C_3,1ᵀ 0&H₂ᵀ&C_3,2ᵀ 0&0&H₃ᵀ\endbmatrix\beginbmatrixλ₁ λ₂ λ₃\endbmatrix=\beginbmatrixℓ₁ ℓ₂ ℓ₃\endbmatrix.

    Backward substitution first determines λ₃, then includes its effect when solving for the earlier adjoints:

    H₃ᵀλ₃=ℓ₃,
    H₂ᵀλ₂=ℓ₂-C_3,2ᵀλ₃,
    (28)H₁ᵀλ₁=ℓ₁-C_2,1ᵀλ₂-C_3,1ᵀλ₃.

    Applying the same backward substitution to all T frames gives

    (29)

    Hₜᵀλₜ=ℓₜ-∑_\beginsubarraycτ>t t∈D(τ)\endsubarrayC_τ,tᵀλ_τ, t=T,…,1.

    Only later equations that depend on yₜ contribute to its right-hand side. The resulting adjoints account for these temporal effects in the parameter gradient:

    (30)∇_θL=ℓ_θ-GᵀΛ
    =ℓ_θ-∑ₜ₌₁ᵀGₜᵀλₜ.

    4.3. Computing one coupled system per frame

    For each frame t, bₜ denotes the right-hand side of its adjoint equation. The vector θ̄ accumulates contributions to the loss gradient with respect to the physical parameters θ. The reverse pass starts from the direct loss derivatives, bₜ=ℓₜ for t=1,…,T and θ̄=ℓ_θ. Before frame t is solved, bₜ combines the direct loss gradient with respect to its motion DoFs yₜ with all contributions propagated from later frames that depend on yₜ. The backward pass processes frames in reverse order. For each frame, Hₜ is first assembled from that frame’s saved converged state. The adjoint is then obtained by solving

    (31)

    Hₜᵀλₜ=bₜ.

    Let Δbₛ⁽ᵗ⁾ and Δθ̄⁽ᵗ⁾ denote frame t’s contributions to an earlier-frame right-hand side and the parameter gradient, respectively. They are given by

    (32)Δbₛ⁽ᵗ⁾=-C_t,sᵀλₜ,s∈D(t),
    (33)Δθ̄⁽ᵗ⁾=-Gₜᵀλₜ.

    The history contributions are summed into the corresponding bₛ, giving the right-hand side in Equation (29). The parameter contributions are summed into θ̄. After all frames have been processed, θ̄=∇_θL, as given by Equation (30).

    Each history contribution reaches frame s3). The products in Equations (32) and (33) are evaluated locally without assembling full C_t,s or Gₜ. Only the current frame’s Hessian is retained during this reverse traversal, together with the saved trajectory and accumulated right-hand sides.

    Each retained Hₜ preserves cross-object coupling, while backward substitution carries that response through time. The trajectory length determines the number of frame solves. Additional parameters contribute local derivative products and share these solves, making the same recurrence suitable for low-dimensional controls and detailed shape design.

    4.4. Inertia and initial-state dependencies

    The history contribution in Equation (32) requires the derivative of gₜ with respect to each earlier state. For inertia, gₜⁱⁿ=M(yₜ-ŷₜ). Substituting the BDF1 predictor from Equation (7) and differentiating with respect to yₜ₋₁ and yₜ₋₂ gives

    (34)

    C_t,t-1ⁱⁿ=-2M, C_t,t-2ⁱⁿ=M.

    Substituting these blocks into Equation (32) gives the inertial parts of Δbₛ⁽ᵗ⁾, denoted by the superscript in:

    (35)Δbₜ₋₁^(t),in=2Mλₜ,t≥2,
    Δbₜ₋₂^(t),in=-Mλₜ,t≥3.

    The same mass products apply to both representations: M contains the FEM vertex-mass blocks and the 12×12 mass block of each affine body.

    The initial configuration and velocity are inputs to the simulation, not additional solved frames. Their contributions therefore enter the parameter-gradient contribution in Equation (33), rather than a right-hand-side vector b₀. The first-step predictor is ŷ₁=y₀+hẏ₀+h²a₁, so the inertial derivatives with respect to y₀ and ẏ₀ are -M and -hM, respectively. For each frame t, the partial derivatives of gₜ with respect to the optimized initial configuration and velocity form the corresponding Gₜ. We evaluate these derivatives at the converged state of frame t and accumulate their contributions to the initial-state gradients using Equation (33).

    For the velocity-reset approximation of quasi-static behavior, we set the predictor velocity to zero at every step, giving ŷₜ=yₜ₋₁+h²aₜ. The mass-weighted quadratic term in Equation (6) remains, so each update still depends on the previous configuration. Differentiating its energy gradient with respect to yₜ₋₁ contributes -M to C_t,t-1. Substituting this contribution into Equation (32) gives the inertial contribution

    (36)

    Δbₜ₋₁^(t),in=Mλₜ, t≥2.

    4.5. Friction between frames

    Friction adds a second source of temporal dependence: its energy uses both the current displacement and contact quantities computed from the previous configuration. DiffIPC differentiates this dependence for finite elements [(Huang et al., 2024c)]. Here the point maps carry these history derivatives into the coupled FEM-affine recurrence, including contacts whose points use different motion representations. For contact c, let g_t,c^fr,x be the friction energy gradient with respect to the current world-space point positions xₜᶜ. The maps K_t,c and K_t-1,c relate the same contact points to the simulation DoFs at the two frames. With rest geometry fixed, these maps do not depend on the solved DoFs. Differentiating g_t,c^fr,y=K_t,cᵀg_t,c^fr,x with respect to yₜ₋₁ therefore gives

    (37)

    (∂g_t,c^fr,y)/(∂yₜ₋₁)=K_t,cᵀ(∂g_t,c^fr,x)/(∂xₜ₋₁ᶜ)K_t-1,c.

    This is the contact’s contribution to C_t,t-1. For t≥2, contact c contributes Δbₜ₋₁^(t,c),fr to the earlier-frame right-hand side. Equation (32) gives

    (38)

    Δbₜ₋₁^(t,c),fr=-K_t-1,cᵀ((∂g_t,c^fr,x)/(∂xₜ₋₁ᶜ))ᵀK_t,cλₜ.

    Summing these per-contact vectors gives the friction part of Δbₜ₋₁⁽ᵗ⁾. Each contact point retains its FEM or affine map, so the same expression covers contact between the two representations.

    The relative tangential displacement is computed from the corresponding vertex displacements using closest-point interpolation weights and a tangent basis. These weights, the tangent basis, and the normal force are computed from the converged configuration of the previous frame. They remain fixed throughout the current frame’s solve. When differentiating with respect to the previous-frame positions, we also include the derivatives of these quantities. Appendix A.1 gives the friction law and its derivatives.

    5. Affine-Body Derivatives for Shape, Initial States, and Control

    The coupled adjoint describes how a loss responds to motion. To optimize an affine body’s shape or controls, we must also differentiate how those parameters enter the frame equations. In particular, an affine body can expose many rest-shape coordinates for design, while adding only twelve motion DoFs per solve. A rest-shape change affects mass and inertia, world-space contact geometry, and the maps from point-space forces to affine coordinates. Friction adds the dependence on that geometry at the previous frame.

    We derive these parameter derivatives, followed by initial-state and joint-control derivatives. For a scalar parameter θₖ, the partial derivative ∂gₜ/∂θₖ forms column k of Gₜ, evaluated at fixed solved DoFs. The adjoint accounts for the resulting motion response, and Equation (30) combines -Gₜᵀλₜ with the explicit loss derivative ℓ_θ. The following derivatives preserve this separation, allowing surface design, placement, and control to share the twelve-DoF affine representation.

    5.1. Rest-dependent mass and inertia

    For affine body b, let Ω_b be its rest domain and ρ_b its constant density. For a material point with rest position x̄, the map J(x̄) in Equation (3) gives its world-space position as xₜ=J(x̄)q_t,b. With rest geometry fixed, its velocity is ẋₜ=J(x̄)q̇_t,b. The corresponding mass block is

    (39)

    M_b=∫_Ω_bρ_bJ(x̄)ᵀJ(x̄) dV.
item.content:encoded:
一句话：罚函数会穿透、速度级约束会漂移；IPC 不穿透但又太慢——这条要三样都要。

要点：

  • 可微接触问题的两难：罚函数与速度级约束能给出快速梯度，但会允许穿透或位置漂移；IPC（Incremental Potential Contact）用几何障碍与连续碰撞检测保证不穿透，代价是前向与反向反复评估很贵
  • DiffGIPC 把 IPC 式的接触放到 GPU 上，并用「混合坐标」表述降低求解成本
  • 目标是让接触密集的可微仿真既保持非穿透，又能在合理时间内拿到梯度

为什么值得看：机器人、可变形物与角色接触的仿真里，「可微」和「不穿透」长期只能二选一。这条把两者放在一起做，且走 GPU——对做物理驱动动画与可微渲染的团队是底层能力。

中文摘要：接触密集的可微逆问题既需要高效梯度，又需要可靠的非穿透约束。现有可微方法能提供快速仿真与刚柔耦合，但基于罚函数或速度级约束的接触处理会允许穿透或位置漂移；Incremental Potential Contact（IPC）用几何障碍与连续碰撞检测严格维持非穿透，代价是前向与反向评估反复进行、成本很高。DiffGIPC 因此提出在 GPU 上实现的「混合坐标」可微接触力学，把 IPC 式非穿透与可负担的梯度计算结合起来，目标是让接触密集的可微仿真在保持非穿透的同时，把求解时间压到可用范围。

主题：图形学

来源：arXiv·核心检索（English）

原文发布：2026-11-03

本期推送：2026-11-04

DiffGIPC: Differentiable Mixed-Coordinate Contact Mechanics on GPU

© none

Abstract.

Contact-rich inverse problems require efficient gradients and reliable enforcement of non-penetration. Existing differentiable methods provide fast simulation and rigid-deformable coupling, but contact treatments based on penalties or velocity-level constraints can permit penetration or positional drift. Incremental Potential Contact (IPC) maintains non-penetration through geometric barriers and continuous collision detection (CCD). However, repeated forward and backward evaluations remain costly in full-space finite-element (FEM) implementations, particularly when nearly rigid components retain many vertex degrees of freedom (DoFs). We present DiffGIPC, a GPU-accelerated differentiable IPC framework for optimizing interacting deformable and nearly rigid bodies. Our affine-body derivatives enable rest-shape design, initial-state optimization, and articulated control while retaining only twelve motion DoFs per affine body. These gradients account for how changes in geometry, placement, and actuation affect other objects through collision and friction. We preserve these interactions in one coupled FEM-affine adjoint system per frame, reducing the backward-system size without discarding the dependencies that drive the inverse problem. GPU-optimized backward computation further reduces the cost of repeated gradient evaluations. A reusable PyTorch interface connects supported physical parameters to user-defined parameter maps and losses across design, identification, motion, placement, and articulated control. Experiments demonstrate peak speedups over DiffIPC of approximately 150.0× with full-space FEM and 4133.3× with affine bodies for combined forward simulation and backward differentiation.

Keywords:

differentiable simulation, contact, affine body dynamics, finite elements, GPU simulation, articulated control, inverse design

1. Introduction

Gradient-based design, system identification, and control often optimize one object’s parameters for their effect on another object. A hanger’s shape determines whether a garment remains supported. An initial velocity determines where another body moves after collision, and a robot command changes the motion of a grasped deformable object. In each case, the gradient must follow forces transmitted through contact and the subsequent motion. Computing these derivatives efficiently is particularly challenging when a scene combines deformable objects with detailed, nearly rigid components: the representation must resolve the interactions without making every stiff component expensive to differentiate.

Existing methods address different parts of this problem. Differentiable projective-dynamics methods, including DiffPD and DiffCloth [(Du et al., 2021; Li et al., 2022)], accelerate repeated solves through local-global iterations and matrix prefactorization. Representing nearly rigid components as stiff deformable meshes nevertheless retains vertex-level motion DoFs, increasing simulation and differentiation costs even when only near-rigid motion is required [(Lai et al., 2026)]. ADD [(Geilinger et al., 2020)] provides fully implicit, two-way coupled rigid and deformable dynamics with analytic adjoints, but uses penalty-based normal contact, which does not strictly prevent interpenetration. DiffIPC [(Huang et al., 2024c)] differentiates fully implicit FEM dynamics with friction, using IPC barriers and continuous collision detection to maintain non-penetration. Its full-space representation, however, carries the motion DoFs of every stiff component into the backward solve, making repeated evaluations costly in its CPU implementation. The resulting opportunity is to combine contact-coupled differentiation with compact motion coordinates and efficient GPU execution.

We present DiffGIPC, a GPU-accelerated framework for differentiating coupled FEM-affine IPC simulations (Figure 2). Building on the forward formulation of StiffGIPC [(Huang et al., 2025a)], we derive frame-wise adjoints directly in the mixed motion coordinates. Full-space FEM retains the freedom needed for local deformation, while each affine body contributes only twelve motion DoFs regardless of its surface resolution. Contact and joint derivatives couple interacting bodies within each frame. Inertia and friction make the time integration equations depend on earlier states. The backward systems therefore remain compact while preserving cross-object coupling and the temporal dependencies required for coupled inverse problems.

Compact motion coordinates alone do not provide shape or control gradients. Changing an affine rest surface changes its mass, the positions at which contact is evaluated, and the maps that convert point-space forces to affine coordinates. Under friction, the same rest change also moves the previous-frame points used to define sliding and the lagged contact quantities. We differentiate these dependencies explicitly, together with initial states and revolute or prismatic joint controls, and accumulate them in parallel without enlarging the adjoint system. To retain the advantage of compact systems, conditional CUDA Graphs are employed to keep preconditioned conjugate gradient (PCG) iterations and convergence checks on the GPU, thereby reducing the overhead of repeated kernel launches and CPU–GPU synchronization. A PyTorch interface connects these physical gradients to user-defined parameter maps and losses.

In summary, our contributions are:

  • •

    Coupled FEM-affine adjoints for differentiable IPC. We derive trajectory adjoints in mixed FEM and affine coordinates, preserving contact, friction, and joint coupling while using only twelve motion DoFs per affine body.

  • •

    Affine-body derivatives for shape design and articulated control. We derive gradients for affine rest shapes, initial states, and joint controls, including shape-dependent inertia and frictional contact.

  • •

    A reusable GPU optimization pipeline. We develop a GPU-parallel adjoint and gradient-accumulation pipeline with conditional CUDA Graphs and a PyTorch interface for design, system identification, and control.

  • •

    Fully GPU-parallel differentiable IPC. We present the first fully GPU-parallel differentiable IPC framework for coupled nearly rigid and deformable bodies, with substantial speedups demonstrated across contact-rich inverse problems.

    • Our evaluation examines the benefits of GPU execution and compact motion representations across contact-rich inverse problems. For comparison with DiffIPC, we retain full-space FEM in both systems and use relatively low-resolution benchmarks to keep evaluation times manageable for the CPU-based baseline. Even at these resolutions, DiffGIPC achieves 12.3–34.1× speedups in complete backward evaluation and 10.6–60.9× speedups in combined forward and backward evaluation, covering initial motion, rest shape, material, and friction optimization. A separate resolution study examines how performance scales with geometric detail and the additional benefit of affine coordinates. Further experiments demonstrate cloth design, affine shape optimization, stable placement, and articulated control. The source code of our framework will be released.

    2. Related Work

    Efficient differentiable simulation and contact

    Inverse problems such as parameter identification from measured motion [(Hahn et al., 2019; Jatavallabhula et al., 2021)] require repeated simulation and gradient evaluations, making the efficiency of both computations important. DiffTaichi automates the differentiation of parallel simulation programs through source-code transformations [(Hu et al., 2020)]. Brax integrates differentiable rigid-body simulation and learning on accelerators, reducing data transfer between simulation and optimization [(Freeman et al., 2021)]. ChainQueen [(Hu et al., 2019)] uses explicit MLS-MPM with parallel local updates, but stiff materials require small time steps. Implicit deformable simulation methods [(Rojas et al., 2021; Liang et al., 2019; Li et al., 2026)] offer greater time-step stability, at the cost of solving linear systems during both simulation and differentiation. Projective dynamics (PD) reduces this cost through local projections and a global system whose matrix can be prefactorized for fixed discretization and coefficients [(Bouaziz et al., 2014)]. DiffPD reuses this factorization in its backward iterations [(Du et al., 2021)]. Quasi-Newton methods support more general hyperelastic energies through efficient approximate systems [(Liu et al., 2017)], and DiffQN further reduces differentiation costs by reusing factorizations from the forward simulation [(Cai et al., 2025)]. More recently, DiffPhD combines GPU factor reuse with techniques for heterogeneous and hyperelastic materials [(Lai et al., 2026)].

    For contact-rich inverse problems, these computational benefits must also be considered alongside the contact response being differentiated. DiffPD’s penalty formulation supports frictional sliding but permits interpenetration, whereas its complementarity formulation enforces non-penetration under a sticky-contact assumption [(Du et al., 2021)]. DiffCloth differentiates the dry-friction PD formulation of [Ly et al. (2020)], supporting sliding cloth contact [(Li et al., 2022)]. However, its self-collision treatment considers only vertex-vertex pairs and does not handle vertex-face or edge-edge self-collisions. DiffPhD supports Signorini-Coulomb contact on the GPU, but its velocity-level enforcement can produce position drift under quasi-static support [(Lai et al., 2026)]. These limitations are particularly relevant when the optimized behavior depends on sustained support, sliding, or contact between thin surfaces. They motivate efficient differentiation of contact models that preserve geometric non-penetration throughout the simulated motion.

    Differentiable contact and coupled dynamics

    [Qiao et al. (2020)] enable differentiable two-way coupling between rigid bodies and cloth, using local impact zones to reduce the cost of collision handling and differentiation. ADD provides fully implicit rigid-deformable coupling with analytic adjoints [(Geilinger et al., 2020)]. Its normal penalty makes contact differentiable while allowing finite overlap. Increasing the penalty stiffness reduces overlap at the cost of poorer conditioning. IPC instead combines a geometric barrier with continuous collision detection to maintain intersection-free motion from feasible initial configurations [(Li et al., 2020)]. DiffIPC brings this contact model to differentiable FEM simulation and supports shape, material, friction, and initial-state optimization [(Huang et al., 2024c)]. It therefore provides a strong basis for inverse problems in which penetration would change the intended interaction. However, representing nearly rigid components with highly stiff, full-space FEM retains vertex-level motion DoFs even when their local deformation is negligible. In its CPU-based implementation, repeated simulation and differentiation of these large systems remain costly. DiffGIPC addresses this cost with coupled FEM-ABD adjoints and GPU backward computation while retaining IPC’s geometric contact safeguards.

    Compact coordinates for coupled design and control

    Reducing motion DoFs addresses a cost that faster linear algebra alone does not remove. Modal and adaptive subspaces reduce deformable motion to a smaller set of directions [(Barbič and James, 2005; Trusty et al., 2024)]. Their accuracy depends on whether those directions capture the deformation induced by loads and contact. Hyper-reduced PD also approximates local constraint projections [(Brandt et al., 2018)], while subspace mixed FEM combines reduced positions with stretch variables to handle heterogeneous materials [(Trusty et al., 2023)]. These approaches retain selected deformation modes and reduce their evaluation cost. For components whose internal deformation is negligible, rigid-body coordinates avoid resolving these modes altogether. Rigid IPC preserves non-penetration in this representation by accounting for curved rotational trajectories in collision detection [(Ferguson et al., 2021)]. ABD relaxes exact rigidity through a stiff orthogonality energy and uses twelve affine DoFs per body [(Lan et al., 2022)]. Its surface positions are linear in these DoFs, allowing piecewise-linear collision trajectories and a pose-independent mass matrix at fixed rest geometry. This offers a compact representation for stiff parts, while full-space FEM retains local deformation where it is needed. DiffGIPC carries both representations into the same backward system, retaining contact, friction, and joint coupling between bodies.

    Compact rigid-body states have supported differentiable learning and control [(Belbute-Peres et al., 2018; Degrave et al., 2019)], including articulated dynamics in Nimble [(Werling et al., 2021)]. Shape optimization requires an additional distinction between the motion representation and the geometry being designed. Contact-based assemblies and shock-protecting microstructures [(Tozoni et al., 2021; Huang et al., 2024b)] use geometric changes to alter load transfer and contact-dependent mechanical response. Pneumatic actuator design and garment reconstruction [(Gjoka et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025)] likewise optimize rest geometry through its effect on deformation. These applications motivate retaining a rich design space even when the motion state can be compact.

    SDRS uses convex polyhedra and auxiliary separating planes to maintain differentiability under large shape changes [(Ye et al., 2025)]. Our focus is mesh-based design and control of affine bodies interacting with deformable objects under IPC. Affine rest-shape changes affect both the mass matrix and the maps from affine DoFs to surface points. Differentiating these dependencies allows a body’s shape to be optimized for its frictional interactions with other objects. Derivatives of joint targets and forces likewise account for the coupled response of articulated and deformable bodies. For a fixed motion representation, additional design parameters do not enlarge the per-frame backward system. Each affine body therefore contributes only twelve motion DoFs, even when its rest shape is described by many design parameters. Contact processing still depends on surface resolution, while parameter-gradient evaluation requires additional work as the number of design parameters grows.

    GPU computation for trajectory adjoints

    Compact coordinates reduce adjoint system size, while efficient linear solvers further reduce the cost of trajectory differentiation. PD-based local-global methods exploit a fixed global matrix to reuse precomputed factors. [Zeng et al. (2025)] use a sparse representation of its inverse to accelerate GPU forward simulation. DiffPhD adopts this strategy for differentiable simulation, reusing an inverse factor across forward, backward, and frictional-contact computations [(Lai et al., 2026)]. In IPC, however, the frame Hessian varies with deformation and contact, so a fixed factorization cannot be reused across all adjoint systems along a trajectory. Preconditioned iterative solvers provide an alternative, with effective preconditioning reducing the number of iterations [(Chen et al., 2021; Wu et al., 2022)]. GIPC parallelizes IPC computation [(Huang et al., 2024a)], while StiffGIPC provides efficient FEM-ABD coupling and GPU solvers across a wide range of stiffnesses [(Huang et al., 2025a)], and AGIPC further reduces GPU linear-solve costs through adaptive in-solve algebraic coarsening [(Wang et al., 2026)]. These methods advance GPU IPC efficiency, with StiffGIPC supplying the forward simulation foundation for our work.

    DiffGIPC combines coupled frame-wise adjoint solves with parallel gradient accumulation on the GPU. Compact affine coordinates reduce PCG’s numerical workload, making repeated CPU kernel launches and convergence synchronization more prominent. Conditional CUDA Graphs reduce this overhead by keeping iteration control and convergence checks on the GPU, with compatible graphs reused across frames as the Hessian changes. After each solve, local derivative products are accumulated in parallel to compute physical-parameter gradients and update earlier-frame adjoint right-hand sides.

    3. A Unified Differentiable IPC Framework

    The framework separates the coordinates needed to describe contact geometry from those needed to solve motion. Collision and friction derivatives are evaluated at world-space surface points and mapped into a coupled system of FEM vertex positions and affine body coordinates. This preserves cross-object derivatives while assigning twelve motion DoFs to each affine body.

    The forward formulation builds on StiffGIPC [(Huang et al., 2025a)]. Simulation DoFs describe solved motion, whereas physical parameters are inputs changed by the optimizer. One frame is an accepted time step of length h, and mesh connectivity is fixed within each differentiated trajectory. The state and incremental potential below define the single-step adjoint. Section 4 extends it through time, Section 5 supplies affine design and control derivatives, and Section 6 develops their GPU computation and task interface.

    3.1. Simulation degrees of freedom and contact points

    A free FEM vertex i is represented by its world-space position x_t,i∈ℝ³ at frame t. An affine body b is represented by its translation p_t,b∈ℝ³ and affine transformation A_t,b∈ℝ^3×3. Let α_t,b,1ᵀ, α_t,b,2ᵀ, and α_t,b,3ᵀ be the rows of A_t,b. Stacking these vectors with the translation defines the body’s twelve DoFs:

    (1)A_t,b=\beginbmatrixα_t,b,1ᵀ α_t,b,2ᵀ α_t,b,3ᵀ\endbmatrix,
    q_t,b=[p_t,bᵀ,α_t,b,1ᵀ,α_t,b,2ᵀ,α_t,b,3ᵀ]ᵀ∈ℝ¹².

    For a surface vertex with rest position x̄ᵢ, the world-space position is

    (2)

    x_t,i=p_t,b+A_t,bx̄ᵢ.

    Let I₃ denote the 3×3 identity matrix and e₁, e₂, and e₃ the Cartesian unit vectors. With rest position fixed, the Jacobian of this position with respect to q_t,b is the 3×12 matrix

    (3)Jᵢ=J(x̄ᵢ)=[I₃ e₁x̄ᵢᵀ e₂x̄ᵢᵀ e₃x̄ᵢᵀ],
    x_t,i=Jᵢq_t,b.

    All surface vertices on body b share the same q_t,b, but each has its own rest-dependent map Jᵢ.

    For N_A free affine bodies and N_F free FEM vertices, we collect the simulation DoFs in

    (4)

    yₜ=[q_t,1ᵀ,…,q_t,N_Aᵀ,x_t,1ᵀ,…,x_t,N_Fᵀ]ᵀ.

    The total number of simulation DoFs is n=12N_A+3N_F. The set and ordering of free DoFs do not change throughout each trajectory. Adding surface vertices to an affine body can increase contact work, but does not enlarge its block in the linear system. Rest coordinates are design parameters, not additional simulation DoFs.

    For contact c, we collect the world-space positions of its n_c surface points into xₜᶜ. Let yₜ∈ℝⁿ contain the free simulation DoFs. The Jacobian K_t,c describes how changes in these DoFs affect the contact-point positions:

    (5)xₜᶜ=[x_t,i₁ᵀ,…,x_t,i_n_cᵀ]ᵀ,
    K_t,c=(∂xₜᶜ)/(∂yₜ)∈ℝ^3n_c×n.

    The three-row map for vertex i is denoted by Kₜⁱ=∂x_t,i/∂yₜ∈ℝ^3×n. The contact map K_t,c stacks the maps of its participating vertices. For a free FEM vertex, its three positional DoFs appear directly in yₜ, so these rows contain an identity block I₃ in the corresponding columns. For a point on a free affine body, its position depends on the body’s twelve affine DoFs through Jᵢ, so these rows contain Jᵢ in that body’s columns. For each free point, columns outside its associated vertex or body block are zero. A fixed point contributes three zero rows. For fixed rest geometry and DoF ordering, Kₜⁱ is unchanged across frames. When differentiating with respect to the free motion DoFs, we hold the rest geometry and prescribed motion fixed. When differentiating with respect to the rest shape, we also differentiate the dependence of the affine point maps Jᵢ, and hence K_t,c, on the rest positions (Section 5.2).

    3.2. Incremental potential and its energy gradient

    Let θ∈ℝ^n_θ collect the physical parameters selected for optimization, such as material and friction coefficients, rest coordinates, initial states, and joint controls. Here n_θ is the number of selected scalar parameters. These parameters are held fixed during one forward simulation. A joint-control schedule can still contain different prescribed values for different frames. For a given θ, each time step of length h computes the simulation DoFs yₜ by minimizing the incremental potential

    (6)Φₜ(yₜ)=\tfrac12∥yₜ-ŷₜ∥_M²
    +∑_e∈𝔼wₑ(h,θ)Ψ_t,e(yₜ,yₜ₋₁;θ).

    The first term accounts for inertia, with ∥v∥_M²=vᵀMv. The mass matrix M is expressed in the simulation coordinates: it contains vertex-mass blocks for FEM and a 12×12 block for each affine body. Section 5 gives the affine mass matrix and its rest-shape derivatives. The predictor ŷₜ is computed from earlier states and prescribed accelerations aₜ. For dynamic bodies, backward Euler (BDF1) gives

    (7)

    ŷₜ=2yₜ₋₁-yₜ₋₂+h²aₜ, t≥2.

    At the first step, the predictor is ŷ₁=y₀+hẏ₀+h²a₁, where y₀ specifies the initial configuration and ẏ₀ contains the initial FEM vertex velocities and the initial velocities of the affine coordinates.

    The second term in Equation (6) sums the contributions from FEM elastic energy, affine shape energy, collision, friction, and joints. Each contribution is indexed by e∈𝔼 and written as wₑ(h,θ)Ψ_t,e, with energy function Ψ_t,e and scalar weight wₑ(h,θ). The collision energy is the non-penetration barrier, distinct from the friction energy for tangential resistance. IPC’s friction energy depends on the relative tangential displacement of the two configurations, determined by yₜ and yₜ₋₁. Its tangent bases and normal forces are held fixed from the previous-frame positions when solving for yₜ, and their dependence on those positions is included in the derivative with respect to yₜ₋₁.

    At a minimum of the incremental potential, its gradient gₜ with respect to the free simulation DoFs satisfies the stationarity equation

    (8)gₜ(yₜ,yₜ₋₁,yₜ₋₂;θ):=∇_yₜΦₜ
    =M(yₜ-ŷₜ)
    +∑_e∈𝔼wₑ(h,θ)∇_yₜΨ_t,e
    =0.

    The energy gradient gₜ is also the nonlinear residual of this equation. For each parameter choice, the forward solver finds DoFs that satisfy this stationarity condition. Differentiating the condition determines how a parameter change affects the solved DoFs and the loss evaluated on them.

    3.3. Parameter gradients from the step equation

    Consider first a single time step from a prescribed initial state, omitting the frame index. The solved DoFs satisfy g(y,θ)=0. A parameter change affects this equation both directly and through the resulting change in y. Differentiating the stationarity equation gives

    (9)

    \underbrace(∂g)/(∂y)_Hdy/dθ+\underbrace(∂g)/(∂θ)_G=0.

    Here, G is the partial derivative of the energy gradient with respect to the physical parameters. The derivative H with respect to the DoFs is the Hessian of the incremental potential:

    (10)

    H=(∂g)/(∂y)=∇_y²Φ.

    Both matrices are evaluated at the converged DoFs satisfying g(y,θ)=0. Rather than forming dy/dθ explicitly, we use the adjoint below. Restoring the frame index, we denote these matrices by Hₜ∈ℝ^n×n and Gₜ∈ℝ^n×n_θ.

    For a scalar loss L(y,θ), let ℓ_y=∇_yL and ℓ_θ=∇_θL denote its partial gradients with respect to the DoFs and physical parameters, respectively. The chain rule gives

    (11)

    ∇_θL=ℓ_θ+(dy/dθ)ᵀℓ_y.

    Explicitly computing dy/dθ becomes costly as the number of optimized parameters grows. We avoid forming this matrix and compute the loss gradient by solving the adjoint system:

    (12)

    Hᵀλ=ℓ_y.

    The solution λ is the adjoint vector. Combining this solve with Equation (9) gives the parameter gradient

    (13)

    ∇_θL=ℓ_θ-Gᵀλ.

    For a single time step, all parameter gradients share the same coupled FEM-affine adjoint. Section 4 extends this formulation through time.

    3.4. Collision and friction derivatives across representations

    Collision and friction energies are evaluated at world-space surface points, whereas the adjoint in Equation (12) acts on simulation DoFs. The map K_t,c from Equation (5) converts the point-space derivatives into FEM and affine coordinates. The collision energy uses GIPC’s squared-log barrier on squared distance [(Huang et al., 2024a)]

    (14)

    b_bar(d)=\begincasesκ(d-d̂)²\log²(d/d̂),&0

    where d is the squared distance, d̂ is its activation threshold, and κ is the barrier coefficient. This squared-log form is the GIPC barrier, rather than the original IPC single-log form. At each Newton iteration, we truncate the step along the search direction using continuous collision detection to prevent intersections, followed by line search to ensure a decrease in the incremental potential. Backward differentiation uses the converged frame state and its associated collision and friction data.

    For a contact c at frame t, let g_t,cˣ and H_t,cˣ denote the gradient and Hessian of the collision energy with respect to the stacked world-space point positions xₜᶜ. The superscript x denotes point coordinates, whereas y denotes simulation DoFs. With rest geometry fixed, the point map K_t,c from Equation (5) is constant with respect to yₜ. The chain rule therefore gives the contributions to the frame energy gradient and Hessian:

    (15)

    g_t,cʸ=K_t,cᵀg_t,cˣ, H_t,cʸ=K_t,cᵀH_t,cˣK_t,c.

    The same transformation applies to friction derivatives with respect to the current-frame DoFs. Friction derivatives with respect to earlier states are included in the trajectory calculation in Section 4.

    Each point contributes through the map associated with its object. For point i on affine body b and point j on affine body b^′, let Hᵢⱼˣ be their 3×3 point-space Hessian block. Mapping this block gives a 12×12 contribution to H_bb^′^AA. If the second point is instead a FEM vertex j, its identity map gives a 12×3 contribution to H_bj^AF. For the point pair (i,j), the block contributions are

    (16)ΔH_bb^′^AA,(i,j)=JᵢᵀHᵢⱼˣJⱼ,
    ΔH_bj^AF,(i,j)=JᵢᵀHᵢⱼˣ.

    All surface vertices of an affine body share its twelve DoFs. The contributions of all relevant point pairs are summed into the corresponding body blocks, without introducing independent vertex DoFs. For distinct points on the same body, both ordered point-block contributions must be included when they map to the same diagonal body block.

    After assembly, grouping affine (A) and finite-element (F) DoFs gives the frame Hessian

    (17)

    Hₜ=\beginbmatrixH_AA&H_AF H_FA&H_FF\endbmatrix, H_FA=H_AFᵀ.

    The diagonal blocks H_AA and H_FF collect derivatives within the affine and FEM coordinates. Collision and friction contribute H_AF and H_FA, while joints couple affine bodies within H_AA. These cross blocks let a loss on one object influence parameters of another. Compact affine coordinates reduce system size while the cross terms preserve the interacting response.

    The same point maps form the loss-gradient vector ℓ_y on the right-hand side of Equation (12). For a loss evaluated on world-space surface points, its gradient with respect to the affine coordinates of body b, whose surface-vertex index set is V_b, is

    (18)

    ∇_q_bL=∑_i∈V_bJᵢᵀ∇_xᵢL.

    For a FEM vertex, the loss gradient with respect to its DoFs equals that with respect to its world-space position. These mappings hold with rest geometry fixed. Section 5.2 includes the additional dependence of the point maps and surface positions on rest shape. Section 4 extends this coupled adjoint to trajectories, where earlier states affect both later motion and the loss.

    4. Frame-Wise Adjoint

    The single-step adjoint captures interactions at one frame. A trajectory also depends on how earlier motion changes later inertia and friction. We account for these dependencies by backward substitution through the causal sequence of frame equations. Each reverse frame solves one coupled FEM-affine system, then contributes to the parameters and earlier states that influenced it. Algorithm 1 summarizes this recurrence. We derive its temporal structure and then specify the inertia and friction terms, using the converged states and recorded data that define the forward equations.

    4.1. Equations for the whole trajectory

    Let yₜ∈ℝⁿ contain the free simulation DoFs in the order defined in Section 3.1. The equation at frame t depends on its current state, a subset of earlier solved states, and the physical parameters:

    (19)

    gₜ(yₜ,{yₛ:s∈D(t)},θ)=0.

    The set D(t)⊆{1,…,t-1} identifies those earlier frames. The initial state is an input rather than a solved frame: its optimized components contribute to Gₜ, while unselected components remain fixed. Prescribed joint commands likewise enter Gₜ through the applied controls. The matrices Hₜ and Gₜ retain their state and parameter definitions from Section 3.3. Temporal dependence introduces the additional derivative

    (20)

    C_t,s=(∂gₜ)/(∂yₛ)∈ℝ^n×n, s∈D(t).

    Thus Hₜ describes the coupled response within frame t, whereas C_t,s describes its dependence on an earlier state and vanishes for s∉D(t). Both current and earlier solved states vary with θ. Differentiating Equation (19) includes these changes together with the direct parameter derivative:

    (21)

    Hₜdyₜ/dθ+∑_s∈D(t)C_t,sdyₛ/dθ+Gₜ=0.

    With Sₜ=dyₜ/dθ∈ℝ^n×n_θ, the equations for all frames form the block system

    (22)

    \beginbmatrixH₁&0&⋯&0 C_2,1&H₂&⋱&⋮ ⋮&⋱&⋱&0 C_T,1&⋯&C_T,T-1&H_T\endbmatrix_J\beginbmatrixS₁ S₂ ⋮ S_T\endbmatrix_S=-\beginbmatrixG₁ G₂ ⋮ G_T\endbmatrix_G.

    Causality makes J block lower triangular, with the frame Hessians Hₜ on the diagonal and nonzero off-diagonal blocks only for dependencies in D(t).

    The predictor in Equation (7) depends on yₜ₋₁ and yₜ₋₂. Friction adds to the first of these dependencies, through C_t,t-1. For the first three solved frames, the system is

    (23)

    \beginbmatrixH₁&0&0 C_2,1&H₂&0 C_3,1&C_3,2&H₃\endbmatrix\beginbmatrixS₁ S₂ S₃\endbmatrix=-\beginbmatrixG₁ G₂ G₃\endbmatrix.

    This three-frame system illustrates the reverse calculation below. The sensitivities Sₜ and the assembled trajectory matrix are used for the derivation, but are not formed by the backward algorithm.

    4.2. Reverse-time adjoint equations

    We extend the single-step adjoint in Equation (12) to the trajectory loss L(y₁,…,y_T;θ). Let ℓₜ=∇_yₜL denote its partial gradient with respect to the simulation DoFs at frame t, and let ℓ_θ denote its partial parameter gradient with all simulated states fixed. For a loss evaluated only on the final state, ℓₜ=0 for t4.1, the chain rule extends Equation (11) to

    (24)∇_θL=ℓ_θ+∑ₜ₌₁ᵀ(dyₜ/dθ)ᵀℓₜ
    =ℓ_θ+∑ₜ₌₁ᵀSₜᵀℓₜ
    =ℓ_θ+Sᵀℓₐₗₗ,

    where ℓₐₗₗ stacks the per-frame loss gradients in the same order as the blocks of S. The first term accounts for the explicit parameter dependence of the loss. The second accounts for changes in the simulated trajectory.

    To evaluate the trajectory contribution without computing S, we introduce an adjoint vector λₜ for each frame and solve

    (25)

    Jᵀ\beginbmatrixλ₁ ⋮ λ_T\endbmatrix (Λ)=\beginbmatrixℓ₁ ⋮ ℓ_T\endbmatrix_ℓₐₗₗ.

    Combining this equation with JS=-G from Equation (22) gives

    (26)

    Sᵀℓₐₗₗ=SᵀJᵀΛ=-GᵀΛ.

    The transpose reverses the causal order: Jᵀ is block upper triangular, so the trajectory adjoint is solved from the last frame backward. For the three-frame example,

    (27)

    \beginbmatrixH₁ᵀ&C_2,1ᵀ&C_3,1ᵀ 0&H₂ᵀ&C_3,2ᵀ 0&0&H₃ᵀ\endbmatrix\beginbmatrixλ₁ λ₂ λ₃\endbmatrix=\beginbmatrixℓ₁ ℓ₂ ℓ₃\endbmatrix.

    Backward substitution first determines λ₃, then includes its effect when solving for the earlier adjoints:

    H₃ᵀλ₃=ℓ₃,
    H₂ᵀλ₂=ℓ₂-C_3,2ᵀλ₃,
    (28)H₁ᵀλ₁=ℓ₁-C_2,1ᵀλ₂-C_3,1ᵀλ₃.

    Applying the same backward substitution to all T frames gives

    (29)

    Hₜᵀλₜ=ℓₜ-∑_\beginsubarraycτ>t t∈D(τ)\endsubarrayC_τ,tᵀλ_τ, t=T,…,1.

    Only later equations that depend on yₜ contribute to its right-hand side. The resulting adjoints account for these temporal effects in the parameter gradient:

    (30)∇_θL=ℓ_θ-GᵀΛ
    =ℓ_θ-∑ₜ₌₁ᵀGₜᵀλₜ.

    4.3. Computing one coupled system per frame

    For each frame t, bₜ denotes the right-hand side of its adjoint equation. The vector θ̄ accumulates contributions to the loss gradient with respect to the physical parameters θ. The reverse pass starts from the direct loss derivatives, bₜ=ℓₜ for t=1,…,T and θ̄=ℓ_θ. Before frame t is solved, bₜ combines the direct loss gradient with respect to its motion DoFs yₜ with all contributions propagated from later frames that depend on yₜ. The backward pass processes frames in reverse order. For each frame, Hₜ is first assembled from that frame’s saved converged state. The adjoint is then obtained by solving

    (31)

    Hₜᵀλₜ=bₜ.

    Let Δbₛ⁽ᵗ⁾ and Δθ̄⁽ᵗ⁾ denote frame t’s contributions to an earlier-frame right-hand side and the parameter gradient, respectively. They are given by

    (32)Δbₛ⁽ᵗ⁾=-C_t,sᵀλₜ,s∈D(t),
    (33)Δθ̄⁽ᵗ⁾=-Gₜᵀλₜ.

    The history contributions are summed into the corresponding bₛ, giving the right-hand side in Equation (29). The parameter contributions are summed into θ̄. After all frames have been processed, θ̄=∇_θL, as given by Equation (30).

    Each history contribution reaches frame s3). The products in Equations (32) and (33) are evaluated locally without assembling full C_t,s or Gₜ. Only the current frame’s Hessian is retained during this reverse traversal, together with the saved trajectory and accumulated right-hand sides.

    Each retained Hₜ preserves cross-object coupling, while backward substitution carries that response through time. The trajectory length determines the number of frame solves. Additional parameters contribute local derivative products and share these solves, making the same recurrence suitable for low-dimensional controls and detailed shape design.

    4.4. Inertia and initial-state dependencies

    The history contribution in Equation (32) requires the derivative of gₜ with respect to each earlier state. For inertia, gₜⁱⁿ=M(yₜ-ŷₜ). Substituting the BDF1 predictor from Equation (7) and differentiating with respect to yₜ₋₁ and yₜ₋₂ gives

    (34)

    C_t,t-1ⁱⁿ=-2M, C_t,t-2ⁱⁿ=M.

    Substituting these blocks into Equation (32) gives the inertial parts of Δbₛ⁽ᵗ⁾, denoted by the superscript in:

    (35)Δbₜ₋₁^(t),in=2Mλₜ,t≥2,
    Δbₜ₋₂^(t),in=-Mλₜ,t≥3.

    The same mass products apply to both representations: M contains the FEM vertex-mass blocks and the 12×12 mass block of each affine body.

    The initial configuration and velocity are inputs to the simulation, not additional solved frames. Their contributions therefore enter the parameter-gradient contribution in Equation (33), rather than a right-hand-side vector b₀. The first-step predictor is ŷ₁=y₀+hẏ₀+h²a₁, so the inertial derivatives with respect to y₀ and ẏ₀ are -M and -hM, respectively. For each frame t, the partial derivatives of gₜ with respect to the optimized initial configuration and velocity form the corresponding Gₜ. We evaluate these derivatives at the converged state of frame t and accumulate their contributions to the initial-state gradients using Equation (33).

    For the velocity-reset approximation of quasi-static behavior, we set the predictor velocity to zero at every step, giving ŷₜ=yₜ₋₁+h²aₜ. The mass-weighted quadratic term in Equation (6) remains, so each update still depends on the previous configuration. Differentiating its energy gradient with respect to yₜ₋₁ contributes -M to C_t,t-1. Substituting this contribution into Equation (32) gives the inertial contribution

    (36)

    Δbₜ₋₁^(t),in=Mλₜ, t≥2.

    4.5. Friction between frames

    Friction adds a second source of temporal dependence: its energy uses both the current displacement and contact quantities computed from the previous configuration. DiffIPC differentiates this dependence for finite elements [(Huang et al., 2024c)]. Here the point maps carry these history derivatives into the coupled FEM-affine recurrence, including contacts whose points use different motion representations. For contact c, let g_t,c^fr,x be the friction energy gradient with respect to the current world-space point positions xₜᶜ. The maps K_t,c and K_t-1,c relate the same contact points to the simulation DoFs at the two frames. With rest geometry fixed, these maps do not depend on the solved DoFs. Differentiating g_t,c^fr,y=K_t,cᵀg_t,c^fr,x with respect to yₜ₋₁ therefore gives

    (37)

    (∂g_t,c^fr,y)/(∂yₜ₋₁)=K_t,cᵀ(∂g_t,c^fr,x)/(∂xₜ₋₁ᶜ)K_t-1,c.

    This is the contact’s contribution to C_t,t-1. For t≥2, contact c contributes Δbₜ₋₁^(t,c),fr to the earlier-frame right-hand side. Equation (32) gives

    (38)

    Δbₜ₋₁^(t,c),fr=-K_t-1,cᵀ((∂g_t,c^fr,x)/(∂xₜ₋₁ᶜ))ᵀK_t,cλₜ.

    Summing these per-contact vectors gives the friction part of Δbₜ₋₁⁽ᵗ⁾. Each contact point retains its FEM or affine map, so the same expression covers contact between the two representations.

    The relative tangential displacement is computed from the corresponding vertex displacements using closest-point interpolation weights and a tangent basis. These weights, the tangent basis, and the normal force are computed from the converged configuration of the previous frame. They remain fixed throughout the current frame’s solve. When differentiating with respect to the previous-frame positions, we also include the derivatives of these quantities. Appendix A.1 gives the friction law and its derivatives.

    5. Affine-Body Derivatives for Shape, Initial States, and Control

    The coupled adjoint describes how a loss responds to motion. To optimize an affine body’s shape or controls, we must also differentiate how those parameters enter the frame equations. In particular, an affine body can expose many rest-shape coordinates for design, while adding only twelve motion DoFs per solve. A rest-shape change affects mass and inertia, world-space contact geometry, and the maps from point-space forces to affine coordinates. Friction adds the dependence on that geometry at the previous frame.

    We derive these parameter derivatives, followed by initial-state and joint-control derivatives. For a scalar parameter θₖ, the partial derivative ∂gₜ/∂θₖ forms column k of Gₜ, evaluated at fixed solved DoFs. The adjoint accounts for the resulting motion response, and Equation (30) combines -Gₜᵀλₜ with the explicit loss derivative ℓ_θ. The following derivatives preserve this separation, allowing surface design, placement, and control to share the twelve-DoF affine representation.

    5.1. Rest-dependent mass and inertia

    For affine body b, let Ω_b be its rest domain and ρ_b its constant density. For a material point with rest position x̄, the map J(x̄) in Equation (3) gives its world-space position as xₜ=J(x̄)q_t,b. With rest geometry fixed, its velocity is ẋₜ=J(x̄)q̇_t,b. The corresponding mass block is

    (39)

    M_b=∫_Ω_bρ_bJ(x̄)ᵀJ(x̄) dV.

item.title: 球面参数化别再「先投影再算」：闭曲面的精确敏感度与可证明条件，直接在 3D 上做 ｜ Representation-Aware Closed-Surface Parameterization: Exact Sensitivity Analysis and Provable Conditions
item.description:
一句话：大量方法为了省事先把封闭曲面投到平面再算，但投影前与演化中的扰动会引入偏差。

要点：

  • 常规做法：把亏格 0 的封闭曲面参数化到标准域（如单位球），为了简单先用平面投影、在平面上计算，而不是直接在 3D 曲面上做
  • 代价是投影之前与几何演化过程中引入的扰动会带来偏差，而这类偏差很少被显式分析
  • 这篇给出「表示感知」的闭曲面参数化：精确的敏感度分析与可证明的条件，让误差可被界定而不是被忽略

为什么值得看：参数化精度会一路传导到贴图、法线与形变。把「投影近似」的误差写成可证明的条件，等于给几何处理管线一个可验收的标准——尤其对需要高质量 UV 的资产管线。

中文摘要：曲面参数化是几何处理与形状分析的基础任务。对拓扑封闭的曲面，常见做法是把它参数化到 ℝ³ 中的标准域（例如亏格 0 曲面映射到单位球）。为简化实现，许多方法会先用平面投影、在平面上完成计算，而不是直接在 3D 曲面上运算；但投影之前以及几何演化过程中引入的扰动会带来偏差，而这类偏差通常没有被显式分析。这篇论文提出「表示感知」的闭曲面参数化框架，给出精确的敏感度分析与可证明的条件，使投影近似的误差可以被界定，而不是被默默忽略。对依赖参数化质量的贴图与形变管线，这意味着多了一道可验收的依据。

主题：图形学

来源：arXiv·核心检索（English）

原文发布：2026-11-03

本期推送：2026-11-04

Representation-Aware Closed-Surface Parameterization: Exact Sensitivity Analysis and Pole-Aware Planar Preconditioning

Abstract

Surface parameterization is a fundamental task in geometry processing and shape analysis. In particular, for topologically closed surfaces, it is common to parameterize them onto a standardized closed domain in ℝ³, with a prime example being a unit sphere for genus-0 closed surfaces. For simplicity, many parameterization methods use planar projections and perform computations on the plane rather than directly on the 3D surface. However, perturbations introduced before projection or geometric evolution propagate through the computation and may affect map quality, convergence, stopping behavior, and geometric validity. To address this issue, in this work we formulate representation sensitivity as a branchwise input–output problem, separating smooth propagation through active Jacobians from changes in anchors, stopping rules, and fallback events. Under consistent piecewise-linear assembly, the unmodified south-pole Beltrami correction in the FLASH method for spherical conformal parameterization reduces exactly to source-mesh harmonic extension. On a fixed-anchor branch, the corrected map factors into chart transition, harmonic propagation, and inverse stereographic projection, yielding an explicit sensitivity Jacobian and a finite-triangle conditioning bound. Separately, we introduce a bounded five-parameter affine preconditioner over planar scale, translation, and anisotropy and evaluate candidates on the corrected spherical map. Across 30 genus-0 surfaces, it reduces median polar upper-tail log-condition and chord-angle distortion by 10.17% and 10.97%, respectively, with both measures improving on every mesh. The harmonic realization agrees with the original FLASH correction to numerical precision and gives a median correction-stage speedup of 1.63×. We apply the same framework to other spherical mapping methods, including the conformalized mean-curvature flow (cMCF) and spherical density-equalizing maps (SDEM), to quantify transient amplification, terminal attenuation, and changes in stopping behavior and geometric validity, and the experimental results show fewer residual flips and increasingly consistent improvements in fixed-template remeshing. Altogether, our work highlights the importance of representation selection as a structural and practical component of spherical parameterization and downstream computation.

1 Introduction

Parameterization of closed surfaces provides a common computational domain for surface registration, shape comparison, remeshing, and related imaging and geometry-processing tasks [33]. In particular, for genus-0 closed surfaces, it is common to consider spherical parameterizations. Existing approaches include spherical conformal parameterizations [15, 14, 11, 13, 20, 7, 23], spherical area-preserving parameterizations [19, 27, 24], and methods that balance angle and area distortion [29]. Other constructions promote local rigidity or use hierarchical optimization [37, 18], control quasi-conformal distortion or enforce injectivity [6, 32], or support remeshing and surface sampling [31, 5].

It is noteworthy that directly solving for the optimal parameterizations on the spherical domain is usually computationally challenging. For instance, the harmonic energy minimization approach [13] involves solving a nonlinear optimization problem on the sphere via an iterative scheme. Also, the conformalized mean-curvature flow (cMCF) method [20] evolves the surface through geometry-dependent implicit updates, and the spherical density-equalizing map (SDEM) method [27] deforms a spherical map iteratively based on the physical principle of density diffusion with certain projection steps involved. To simplify the computation, many prior methods have considered the use of planar charts or intermediate embeddings to represent the closed target surface. For instance, Haker et al. [15] developed a linearized method for computing spherical conformal parameterizations via solving the Laplace equation on a planar domain followed by the stereographic projection onto the sphere. The FLASH method [7] further combined planar computations with quasi-conformal pole correction based on the linear Beltrami solver (LBS) [25] to improve conformality near the pole.

While surface parameterization methods are typically evaluated through map-level quantities such as angle and area distortion and local injectivity, numerical accuracy in parameterization-based computations also depends on how geometry is represented in the parameter domain. Aflalo et al. [1] showed that controlling the conformal factor is important for accurate geodesic computation on a flattened domain. In stereographic constructions, pole-related distortion has also motivated the use of curved parameter elements [3]. These observations suggest treating representation changes as an input–output sensitivity problem, in the sense of classical conditioning analysis [16]. In FLASH’s stereographic pipeline [7], chart perturbations change the finite target geometry and enter the subsequent pole correction. In iterative methods, initial-state perturbations enter geometry-dependent updates and can affect the trajectory, stopping index, and geometric validity. On a fixed execution path consisting of differentiable operations, the chain rule propagates local sensitivities through the active computations [12]. A representation-aware analysis must therefore account for both smooth propagation within a fixed branch and changes in discrete choices such as anchors, stopping rules, and fallback events.

In this work, we formulate representation sensitivity in spherical parameterization as a branchwise input–output problem. For the projection-based FLASH method for spherical conformal parameterization, we derive an exact reduction of the unmodified south-pole Beltrami correction to harmonic extension with the intrinsic source-mesh Dirichlet operator (see Figure 1 for an illustration). On a fixed-anchor branch, this reduction gives a closed-form factorization of the corrected map and an explicit Jacobian that separates chart transition, harmonic propagation, and inverse stereographic projection. We also derive a finite-triangle conditioning bound that relates the effect of inverse stereographic projection to planar element shape and radial variation. This factorization identifies how planar representation changes reach the final spherical map and provides the basis for a bounded five-parameter affine preconditioner over planar scale, translation, and anisotropy. Candidate planar representations are generated through a multistart search subject to north–south size-balance constraints. Their quality is assessed on the fully corrected FLASH maps, so the optimization targets the representation ultimately passed to downstream computation while preserving distortion and geometric-validity constraints. We further apply the representation-sensitivity framework to other representative spherical parameterization methods, including cMCF and SDEM, as mechanism-level studies of initial-state perturbation propagation. Products of state-dependent step Jacobians reveal transient amplification, terminal attenuation, and changes in stopping behavior and geometric validity. These experiments quantify how representation perturbations are transmitted through iterative parameterization algorithms and identify trajectory-level quantities that can guide future sensitivity-aware initialization. For FLASH, the proposed preconditioning reduces the median polar upper-tail log-condition and chord-angle distortions by 10.17% and 10.97%, respectively, across a cohort of 30 genus-0 closed surfaces, with both measures improving on every mesh. Downstream experiments further show that preconditioned FLASH initializations reduce residual flips in SDEM and improve local conditioning and element quality in fixed-template remeshing. The main contributions of this work are as follows:

  • •

    We formulate representation sensitivity as a branchwise input–output problem for closed-surface parameterization, with applications to genus-0 spherical parameterization algorithms.

  • •

    For the FLASH method for spherical conformal parameterization, we prove that, under consistent piecewise-linear assembly and the unmodified Beltrami correction, the LBS stiffness matrix coincides with the intrinsic Dirichlet stiffness matrix of the source mesh. This identity yields an exact source-mesh harmonic extension, a fixed-anchor closed-form representation of the corrected map, and a factorized sensitivity Jacobian. Numerical tests validate the Jacobian and verify the equivalence of the original and harmonic correction realizations.

  • •

    We apply the framework to cMCF and SDEM to quantify how initial-state perturbations propagate through state-dependent iterations, including transient amplification, terminal attenuation, stopping-index changes, and loss of geometric validity.

  • •

    We derive a finite-triangle conditioning bound and combine it with the exact FLASH sensitivity structure to design a bounded five-parameter affine preconditioner. Experiments evaluate its effect on the corrected spherical map and its downstream benefits for SDEM and fixed-template remeshing.

    • The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 introduces the proposed representation-perturbation framework and the fixed-branch stability condition. Section 3 develops the exact chart dependence of the FLASH correction, including the harmonic reduction, the fixed-anchor factorization, and the pole-aware Jacobian. Section 4 applies the perturbation framework to cMCF and SDEM. Section 5 presents the bounded affine preconditioner and the constrained search procedure. Section 6 reports the numerical validation and downstream experiments. We discuss the principal findings and limitations in Section 7 and conclude our work in Section 8.

    2 Discrete setting and representation perturbations

    For the method-specific analysis and numerical experiments below, let M=(V,F) be a connected, closed, oriented, nondegenerate genus-0 triangular mesh with n vertices. A spherical realization S∈(S²)ⁿ assigns a unit vector to each vertex and retains the source connectivity. Following standard elementwise analysis of triangulated surface parameterizations [10], we measure distortion on the affine map from each source face to its target chord triangle, the flat triangle joining the three spherical vertices. Spherical areas are used separately for area diagnostics and validity checks. This distinction prevents smooth conformality, chord-triangle distortion, and spherical area distortion from being conflated.

    A representation perturbation changes the numerical input while the algorithmic settings remain fixed. For the FLASH method for spherical conformal parameterization [7], it acts on the planar coordinates after north–south balancing and on the initial state in the iterative experiments. The resulting trajectories are compared under the same mesh, solver, and stopping rules.

    2.1 Propagation on a fixed computational branch

    Let X₀ be a baseline state and write X⁽⁰⁾_θ=G_θ(X₀), X⁽ᵏ⁺¹⁾_θ=T_k,σₖ(X⁽ᵏ⁾_θ), and S_θ=Ψ(X^(K)_θ), where G₀ is the identity. The discrete variable σₖ records choices such as anchors, retries, and fallback rules. We call a neighborhood a fixed branch when these choices and the stopping index K remain constant. For differentiable active maps, the chain rule gives

    D_θS_θ=ℙ_θ D_θG_θ(X₀),(1)
    ℙ_θ=DΨ(X^(K)_θ)DT_K-1,σ_K-1(X^(K-1)_θ)⋯DT_0,σ₀(X⁽⁰⁾_θ).(2)

    The rightmost factor selects the perturbation directions; ℙ_θ propagates them through the solver. Analytic active maps yield an analytic composition on the same branch. These are standard composition properties, used here to organize method-specific calculations.

    Figure 2 summarizes the common structure used in the three numerical settings. A perturbation may act on the planar chart in FLASH [7], on the initial state of cMCF [20], or on the coupled initial state of SDEM [27]. Each method then propagates that perturbation through its own active map, and the resulting output is evaluated through geometric distortion, density, or downstream behavior.
